title: The Spy Next Door review – a wild story … once the endless string of men have stopped talking  | Television | The Guardian
description: The gripping case of Russian spy Anna Chapman somehow becomes quite dull in parts of this very male documentary. Thank goodness for the only woman to speak in it – who livens things up ahead of a thrilling ending
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: The gripping case of Russian spy Anna Chapman somehow becomes quite dull in parts of this very male documentary. Thank goodness for the only woman to speak in it – who livens things up ahead of a thrilling ending
Content: No new revelations … and Anna Chapman, pictured here, doesn’t appear in person in the Channel 4 documentary.Photograph: Shutterstock/Channel 4 / ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNo new revelations … and Anna Chapman, pictured here, doesn’t appear in person in the Channel 4 documentary.Photograph: Shutterstock/Channel 4 / ShutterstockTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Spy Next Door review – a wild story … once the endless string of men have stopped talkingThe gripping case of Russian spy Anna Chapman somehow becomes quite dull in parts of this very male documentary. Thank goodness for the only woman to speak in it  – who livens things up ahead of a thrilling endingHannah J DaviesWed 12 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn June 2010,Anna Chapmanwas arrested in New York City as part of a major FBI operation targeting Russian spies. Members of the “illegals programme” had, for decades, ingratiated themselves into American workplaces and communities, all while working for Russia’s foreign intelligence service (SVR). While Chapman was ostensibly in the US to sell real estate to wealthy Russians, she was something of an outlier among the group. The 28-year-old had been in Manhattan for only a year, having spent much of the previous decade in London. There, she had married (and later separated from) a British citizen, Alex Chapman. It was also where she may or may not have been initially recruited as a Russian state asset. Her connections to Britain would, for a while, make Anna Chapman a tabloid mainstay; here we see her ex, Marcus Read, reading an old interview he did with the Mirror, headlined “My crazy six weeks of passion with Russian spy girl Anna Chapman”.The working title of this two-part documentary was Red Hot Spy: The Anna Chapman Story. Indeed, much is made of how irresistibly alluring and apparently manipulative Chapman was, and the pull of her flame-coloured locks (tabloid infamy also coincided with a dye job). Read met Chapman in Zimbabwe, and she ended up joining him in Brighton for a time, before ditching him at a techno night to embark on a relationship with Alex Chapman. “Here I am, 20-odd years later ,still talking about it,” says Read, perhaps wistful, clearly still incredulous. It is, maybe, the first clue that The Spy Next Door doesn’t contain any big new revelations about Chapman (who has returned to Russia and didn’t want to be involved with the programme), but rather is a slick reworking of old news.View image in fullscreen‘Here I am, 20-odd years later still talking about it’ … Marcus Read on his relationship with Chapman.Photograph: Curious FilmsStill, it is rather slick. Former US intelligence staff paint a picture of a slippery young spy who managed to blend in with a crowd of freelancers on laptops at her local Starbucks, all while sending sensitive data dumps to her handlers. We also hear from esteemed figures such as Sir Roderic Lyne, British ambassador to Russia between 2000 and 2004, who outlines the wider political context that made the Chapman case – and the broader FBI operation – so charged. From the early 00s, Tony Blair and George Bush – and later Barack Obama – were adopting a canny keep-your-friends-close-and-Putin’s-inner-circle-closer approach to foreign policy. Lyne says: “[the west] said, we no longer consider ourselves as adversaries.” Cue archive footage of Obama and the then-Russian president Dmitry Medvedev gorging on cheeseburgers and Coca-Cola. How times have changed.Back to Chapman, then, and this woman with “an air of mystique”, as Read puts it. He knew little about her, except that her father had been in the KGB. Ed Foley, an FBI agent, says that Anna “knew exactly what she was doing” when she was in New York. She didn’t seem to have undergone sophisticated training, but she had a talent for social engineering and, he says, “seduction”.The Bechdel testwas the least of Chapman’s problems, but it is a little tiresome to hear an endless string of men (and it is all men, apart from one) talk about her. Foley says that Chapman was “quite literally in bed with some of the top Wall Street financial people, people who had influence in political circles”, adding “you sleep around with anybody … she could’ve been the first lady of New York City”. But where does sex end and spy craft begin?There is an interesting documentary somewhere in here, but – ironically – it’s not the parts about Chapman that are the most engrossing. The only woman interviewed here is Marina Litvinenko, widow of Alexander, killed in London in 2006. Russia has never admitted killing Litvinenko with a cup of polonium-laced tea but, in 2021, the European court of human rights ruled that it was responsible. What we hear from Litvinenko is brief but impactful, not least when it comes to her view on how Russia would later use Chapman in its propaganda efforts. And, from Litvinenko to Boris Berezovsky – found dead at his home in Ascot in 2013 – via a string of other suspicious deaths on UK soil, there is another, more intriguing set of threads that is mentioned only briefly here (for more, maybe tryPatrick Radden Keefe’s nonfiction book London Falling).The final sting on Chapman is told in tense, exciting fashion, with asides for all the surreal details of course (her ex-husband being advised by the infamous spin doctor Max Clifford, for one). But ultimately this programme is little more than a salacious look at a footnote in spy history. “Red hot” indeed.The Spy Next Door: The Anna Chapman Story is on Channel 4Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDocumentaryFactual TVAnna ChapmanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: How the Other Half Loves review – Alan Ayckbourn’s ingenious farce brings the houses down | Stage | The Guardian
description: The suburban romp of envy and infidelity in two different homes comes bouncing back to life with a fizzing cast led by Roger Allam
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: The suburban romp of envy and infidelity in two different homes comes bouncing back to life with a fizzing cast led by Roger Allam
Content: Crossed lines … Roger Allam  in How the Other Half Loves at the Old Vic, London.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreenCrossed lines … Roger Allam  in How the Other Half Loves at the Old Vic, London.Photograph: Manuel HarlanStageReviewHow the Other Half Loves review – Alan Ayckbourn’s ingenious farce brings the houses downThe Old Vic, LondonThe suburban romp of envy and infidelity in two different homes comes bouncing back to life with a fizzing cast led by Roger AllamMark LawsonWed 12 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarly in a career that reaches 92 plays withThe Trial of Romeo Oscarat his Scarborough home base next month, Alan Ayckbourn often spins titles from expressions: Absurd Person Singular, Relatively Speaking, Joking Apart and How the Other Half Loves, his ninth play.In How the Other Half Loves (1969), the pun is doubled. Two couples – the Phillipses and Featherstones – envy how the well-to-do Fosters, boss Frank and wife Fiona, live. But structurally, the Phillipses and Fosters occupy half the set each, actors blanking out characters in the other house even while making phone calls to each other side by side. In the second scene, when the Featherstones – unwittingly used as adultery alibis by Mr Phillips and Mrs Foster – simultaneously attend dinner parties on consecutive nights with the other couples, the two actors in both scenes swivel their heads at tables laid across each other.View image in fullscreenUpdating attitudes … Ayesha Antoine in How the Other Half Loves.Photograph: Manuel HarlanTying with the middle act of Michael Frayn’sNoises Offas the most ingeniously crafted and reliably hilarious half hour in English farce, it started Ayckbourn’s experiments in theatrical time and space, leading to audiences seeing a cross-section of three apartments in The Things We Do for Love (1997), and House & Garden (1999) occupying two theatres simultaneously.While the geometric cleverness in How the Other Half Loves remains fresh, other aspects date: men can’t make their own breakfast, have their clothes laid out for them by (further wordplay) “the other half” and offices were completely male. The domestic honorific “dear” has been cut. However, Ayckbourn’s policy of allowing every actor a big moment gives the wives more agency than much 1970s comedy. Even Mrs Featherstone, nicknamed “Mouse”, finally roars.Director Philip Breen sensibly treats it as a period drama, with 1969 hits including The Boxer and Where Do You Go to My Lovely? covering scene changes. Rob Howell’s sets and costumes delight in an era where transistor radios, Trimphones and egg nog were exotic novelties, as time again has made them.The cast of six, though, is more than half the joy, their verbal and physical humour stopping the show as surely as big numbers in musicals.Roger Allam’s Frank, managerial pomposity concealing kindness, has a magnificent scene as a hapless marital Poirot, wildly mis-summarising who was in which room with whom when. Laura Elsworthy’s Mary wins a big laugh via a feat of backstage athleticism. Ayesha Antoine’s Teresa shows how spirited acting can update an older play’s social attitudes. Ayckbourn followed this with (so far) 83 more plays but his early work can still deliver two great halves and, this London summer, a tempting sex farce double bill with Florian Zeller’sThe Truth.At theOld Vic, London, until 19 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreAlan AyckbournOld Vic TheatreRoger AllamreviewsShareReuse this content

title: From a Gavin and Stacey star to Dani Dyer’s return: every Strictly Come Dancing 2026 contestant rated | Strictly Come Dancing | The Guardian
description: The wait is over. From soap stars to athletes and Kim Kardashian’s hairdresser, we’ve rated this year’s celebrity hoofers in terms of likely glitterball success
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: The wait is over. From soap stars to athletes and Kim Kardashian’s hairdresser, we’ve rated this year’s celebrity hoofers in terms of likely glitterball success
Content: Strictly’s new presenters … Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe.Photograph: BBC/Ray BurmistonView image in fullscreenStrictly’s new presenters … Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe.Photograph: BBC/Ray BurmistonStrictly Come DancingFrom a Gavin and Stacey star to Dani Dyer’s return: every Strictly Come Dancing 2026 contestant ratedThe wait is over. From soap stars to athletes and Kim Kardashian’s hairdresser, we’ve rated this year’s celebrity hoofers in terms of likely glitterball successMichael HoganWed 12 Aug 2026 12.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 12.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo Tessbot. No Clauditorium. Three new presenters, five new professionals and a new-look “vodcast” It Takes Two sister show. Yes, the fast-approaching 24th series represents Strictly Come Dancing’s biggest ever shake-up. This has become a make-or-break year for the BBC’s ballroom behemoth.Lineup announcements have been strung out over two months, like a boring byelection, but the Strictly class of 2026 is finally complete. There are the usual grumbles about a lack of household names, with theories that the casting department prioritised social media followings over mainstream fame. My personal feeling is they have smashed it with the women, who comfortably overshadow the far weaker lineup of men. This raises the pleasing possibility of the first back-to-back female champions since Abbey Clancy and Caroline Flack more than a decade ago.So who will be getting double-dipped in orange emulsion and rolled in glitter on autumnal Saturday nights? Whose mantelpiece could be graced by the glitterball trophy? And who’ll be sent home before we’ve even bothered to learn their name? We’ve rated this year’s celebrity hoofers from worst to best in terms of likely sparkly success. Staaaaaart ranking …15. John NellisHe’s a “football influencer”, apparently. A job I didn’t know existed until I started typing this. It says here that the YouTuber is “one of Britain’s biggest sports content creators” with a whopping 20 million followers across social media. The Northern Irishman has never danced before, so should be choreographic cannon fodder. Shame it wasn’t John Nettles. He could’ve foxtrotted to the Bergerac and Midsomer Murders theme tunes.14. Graeme HallView image in fullscreenThe ‘Dogfather’ Graeme Hall.Photograph: BBC Studios/PAWill he perform a pekingese waltz, a King Charleston spaniel or a chihuahua cha-cha? Will he be terrier-ble or could he make it to Blackpoodle? Going from house training to dance training is canine cult hero Graeme “the Dogfather” Hall, presenter of Channel 5’s Dog’s Behaving (Very) Badly. Not the most glamorous piece of casting, perhaps, but at least it allows all manner of hound-based hilarity. Let him off the leash and go for rumba walkies. Good boy.13. Shaun Wright-PhillipsView image in fullscreenOn the ball … Shaun Wright-Phillips.Photograph: BBC/PAWhat’s the betting they tried his dad, Ian Wright, first? Strictly got its first ever footballing winner last year in Karen Carney, but former England winger Wright-Phillips will do well to make the away fixture at Blackpool. He’s a pint-sized 5ft 5in, so expect short king Shauny to be paired with one of the pocket rocket female pros, such as Jowita Przystał. Shame Tess is no longer around to say “look at their little faces”.12. Chris AppletonView image in fullscreenTressed to kill … Chris Appleton.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios“Kim Kardashian’s hairdresser” is stretching the definition of “celebrity” to snapping point. Who next? Jane McDonald’s chiropodist? Olly Murs’ dental hygienist? The bloke who does Christopher Biggins’ gutters? The Leicester-born coiffure-wrangler’s other clients include Ariana Grande, Katy Perry and J-Lo. A factor in his casting is surely the hope of seeing a Kardashian in the studio audience. We imagine he’ll be pretty good. And possibly give his pro partner a glow-up. Going anywhere nice on your holidays, hun?11. Melanie WaltersView image in fullscreenFresh from Barry Island … Melanie Walters.Photograph: BBC Studios/PAWhat’s occurrin’? Stopping off at Elstree en route to Billericay will be the actor best known as Gwen from Gavin & Stacey. The Barry-based matriarch is constantly making omelettes in the Anglo-Welsh romcom. That extra protein could come in handy on long training days. At 64, she’s the oldest contestant in the field, but Walters teaches pilates, so is fit and flexible. Stacey’s mum has got it going on. Just ask Dave Coaches. Hey, maybe we’ll finally find out what happened between Uncle Bryn and his nephew Jason on that fateful fishing trip. Lush and tidy indeed.10. Will BestHis Big Brother co-host AJ Odudu reached the final five years ago. Can Will Best follow in her twinkle-toed footsteps? He recently won Celebrity Mastermind with the specialist subject of Danny Dyer, so will be embarrassingly excited to dance alongside Dyer’s daughter. He’s fit, funny and annoyingly multitalented, so could prove a surprise package. He also hosted a flop ITV talent show called Dance Dance Dance, which feels like an omen of … something?9. Sarah StoreyShe swims! She cycles! But can she samba? Dame Sarah Storey began her sporting career in the pool, before switching to the velodrome. Her 30 medals, including 19 golds, make her Team GB’s most decorated Paralympian of all time. Having hung up her Lycra onesie this summer, she becomes the first Dame to hit the ballroom floor and the sixth Paralympian. None reached the final but the ever-competitive Storey will have the podium in her sights. What’s the Storey? Glitterball glory?8. Tabby StoeckerView image in fullscreenHitting the dancefloor running … Tabby Stoecker.Photograph: BBC Studios/PAThe field’s other decorated athlete is Team GB skeleton racer Stoecker, who won gold at the recent Winter Olympics in Milano Cortina. She’s clearly a teacher’s pet at theBBCbecause she’ll also join the next series of Gladiators as “Goldstar”. A former gymnast and circus performer, Stoecker should hit the dancefloor running. Prepare for lifts, tricks and a sled-themed VT with her terrified pro partner.7. Delta GoodremView image in fullscreenAussie, Aussie, Aussie … Delta GoodremPhotograph: BBC/PAThe 41-year-old Australian diva went down a storm at this year’s Eurovision, finishing fourth (she wuz robbed) with power ballad Eclipse. Goodrem played Nina Tucker in Neighbours before joining the long line of Ramsay Street residents who changed lanes to pop. Erinsborough alumni have mixed fortunes on Strictly. Jason Donovan reached the final, but Stefan Dennis, the flamin’ galah, got an early Qantas flight home last year (other long-haul airlines are available). Non-Brits never win, but Delta could dance into December.6. Lawrence RobbView image in fullscreenStage-school trained … Lawrence Robb.Photograph: BBC Studios/PAEmmer-males have tasted Strictly success in recent years. Kelvin Fletcher lifted the glitterball trophy in 2019 and Lewis Cope was a quarter-finalist last year. Waltzing out of the Woolpack in their welly-booted footsteps is Glaswegian actor Robb, AKA Mackenzie “Mack” Boyd, part of the Dales soap’s Dingle dynasty. He’s stage school-trained with West End experience, so there could be ringer rumblings. All the Dingle ladies, put your hands up.5. Bethany AntoniaSwapping Westeros for Borehamwood is Lady Baela Targaryen from GoT prequel House of the Dragon. Expect sword props, castle themes and gags about the judges being dragons. Antoniahas been acting professionally since age 14, went to stage school and is starring in West End musical Hadestown, so we suspect she’ll be a helluva hoofer. Winter is coming and she’ll go far. If not, she’ll probably have Anton’s head on a spike and Craig shot on the toilet with a crossbow.4. Cach MercerView image in fullscreenLet’s hear it for the boy … Cach Mercer.Photograph: BBC/BBC StudiosHe got a text! From the BBC casting department! Some ballroom purists have bemoaned the inclusion of the 2025 Love Island champion as a sign of the show salsa-ing downmarket. There might also be ringer rumblings when this bombshell enters the Strictly villa. Mercer used to be a pro dancer – albeit specialising in hip-hop and Afrobeats, rather than ballroom and Latin. Could go a long way but won’t win. It is what it is, babe. You’re just not a glitterball type on paper.3. Dani DyerView image in fullscreenChip off the old block … Dani Dyer.Photograph: BBC/BBC StudiosSurprising precisely nobody, last year’s pre-series injury dropout is back for another go. The daughter and near-namesake of adored cockney thesp Danny Dyer won Love Island and Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins, so she has form in such contests. Dyer Jr married West Ham captain Jarrod Bowen last year, so expect footbantz™ from new host Josh Widdicombe. Like last year, we predict a waltz to Hammers anthem I’m Forever Blowing Bubbles, while her soppy dad gets weepy in the front row. Jog on, you melt.2. Jaime WinstoneGet outta my pub! Get into my ballroom! Actor Jamie, daughter of Ray Winstone, is probably best known for her acclaimed portrayal of blond-beehived whirlwind Barbara Windsor in BBC biopic Babs. She later stepped into Windsor’s high heels to play the young Peggy Mitchell in EastEnders flashbacks. Winstone loves to dance, relishes a challenge and “can’t wait to enter my showgirl era”, which sounds promising. Pray for a front-row clash of the geezer dads between Ray and Danny Dyer. It’ll be like a glittery Guy Ritchie film.1. Lacey TurnerView image in fullscreenIn with a shout … Lacey Turner.Photograph: BBC/BBC StudiosSwapping doof-doofs for cha-chas is this year’s obligatory EastEnders actor. Turner moved into Albert Square aged 16 as gobby-but-lovable Stacey Slater and stayed on and off for 20 years. She also starred in BBC army drama Our Girl. Having turned Strictly down for the last decade, Turner says it was “about time”. Three former castmates – Jill Halfpenny, Kara Tointon and Rose Ayling-Ellis – have taken the glitterball trophy back to the Queen Vic. Stace is surely in with a shout of making it four. Dot, Dr Legg and Ethel’s little Willy would be proud.Explore more on these topicsStrictly Come DancingBBCTelevisionEntertainment TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Farage has turned Clacton into a human zoo. Here’s the truth about what’s happening here | Sarah Elizabeth Cox | The Guardian
description: When I moved to the town in 2022 I loved the beach walks, cheap drinks and panoramic coastal views. Now it feels like a never-ending circus, says historian Sarah Elizabeth Cox
Author: Sarah Elizabeth Cox
Headline: When I moved to the town in 2022 I loved the beach walks, cheap drinks and panoramic coastal views. Now it feels like a never-ending circus, says historian Sarah Elizabeth Cox
Content: Clacton pier, 6 August 2026.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenClacton pier, 6 August 2026.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersOpinionClacton byelection August 2026Farage has turned Clacton into a human zoo. Here’s the truth about what’s happening hereSarah Elizabeth CoxWhen I moved to the town in 2022 I loved the beach walks, cheap drinks and panoramic coastal views. Now it feels like a never-ending circusWed 12 Aug 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTShareClacton town centre is bustling, the beaches are packed and the pier’s raking in cash. We can credit the weather, but no doubt press coverage and Count Binface’s promotional videos have got us on radars too. The tourists look like they’re having a lovely time.I moved to Clacton in 2022 and the first year was brilliant. It started with beach walks, cheap drinks and decorating a flat with panoramic sea views, and ended fat and happy from chips and ice-cream, a newborn baby in tow. Privileged with my health and stable income, albeit strained by aTruss-era mortgage, it was a place I loved, and was proud of.ThenNigel Faragetargeted us, and shit hit the fan.With the general election in 2024, the world’s press descended, and then came thousands of social media comments that left me embarrassed, sad and fuming. You’re all thick, racist, gullible, hateful, toothless, jobless old fools, we were told. You deserve him. The worst of the snobbery was, sadly, on my lefty social media platform of choice, Bluesky.Farage was elected with 46% of a 58% turnout. Fine,somepeople actually are gullible fools. But the other parties rolled over and failed to bother, treating us with contempt. I didn’t support, but I understood, why 46% voted as they did. I still loved Clacton, but it got harder to defend. Then things died down and we were forgotten again by everyone, including our new MP.The gag about Farage not knowing where we are isn’t exactly true – he pops by for photo opportunities like a ceremonial mayor – but he seemsless keen on surgeries, or representing Clacton in the Commons. Snaps for the local newspaper’s Facebook make fans think he’s doing great things for businesses and charities. It’s smoke and mirrors. Check Hansard for “Clacton” and see how many times he’s raised a Clacton issue in parliament (six times). Then do “Colchester” for Pam Cox and “Ipswich” for Jack Abbott. Compare and contrast.We wanted him to actually be an MP. To notice the homeless people, freezing all winter in closed bank doorways, and now lining the coastal paths in tents. To notice how we’ve been priced off the railways – the commuter trains are empty. The worsening health, declining life expectancy. The low employment rates and lack of affordable homes. We don’t have an A&E. We don’t have maternity care after 5pm. It would have been nice too, if he’d spent more time doing what he said he would, and what Binface has achieved instead – promoting our towns and villages’ positives. There are many, I promise.Nobody wanted a byelection. For the many people struggling here, there is little energy for another awful circus. Clacton didn’t need yet more focus on Farage, Farage, Farage, while the area’s entrenched and complex problems continue to be ignored by him and by the government.This summer, the media presence has been even bigger than in 2024. Content creators and reporters continually vox pop outside Wetherspoons, cherrypicking quotes about how great Nigel is, how persecuted Nigel is. Well, we’re being swarmed with migrants, aren’t we? Getting put up in hotels while we struggle. It’s not like it used to be round here. The Turks, they’re taking over with the barber shops. Or, I don’t really do politics. They’re all the same as each other. A welcome few, it has been pleasing to see, have started to notice the slipperiness, the back of fag packet policies and his absence.The “Migrants Out” leaflets were pushed into our homes, a turquoise Reform bus did the rounds and sad men with silly hats and placards yelled things in the town square. I’ve seen anti-racism campaigners told to F off, and can’t leave my flat without the smug face of a British Democratic party candidate leering down at me from giant poster boards. It has all felt surreal, hostile, dividing. Generally bad vibes.The nasty, stereotyping, hurtful comments about us continue. With some exceptions – like Tim Burrows’thoughtful portrait of Clacton– we’re a human zoo, and the butt of a joke. Farage used us as a pawn, and the media treats us as clickbait.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYet in shops, the gym, pubs, on the beach, in the street, at the park, at nursery drop off, I’ve not overheard a single conversation about any of it, unless it was between a reporter and a local. Not one. The leaflets started getting left in the hallway, unread. Few of my family or neighbours plan to vote. We’re angry at him, but we are also bored, and exhausted.My prediction: It’ll be a low turnout, Farage way ahead, with Binface second but the only real winner. I’ll read about how we wasted the chance for a hilarious outcome, you idiots. You gullible, racist fools. You deserve him. And so on. Then it’ll die down again, briefly, and we can get back to what’s left of the summer, the lives Farage has no clue about or interest in and keep talking about the things that really matter in Clacton: litter, landlords, potholes, parking and whether there’ll be a second series ofSecret Lives of Gypsy Wives.Sarah Elizabeth Cox is a historian, and communications manager for a science charityExplore more on these topicsClacton byelection August 2026OpinionNigel FarageReform UKImmigration and asylumVoter apathycommentShareReuse this content

title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 6: Chelsea | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: After a period of underachievement and upheaval for the Blues, the arrival of Xabi Alonso could signal a change in fortunes
Author: Billy Munday
Headline: After a period of underachievement and upheaval for the Blues, the arrival of Xabi Alonso could signal a change in fortunes
Content: New manager Xabi Alonso during a pre-season training session in Indonesia.  Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesAfter a period of underachievement and upheaval for the Blues, the arrival of Xabi Alonso could signal a change in fortunesByBilly MundayWed 12 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:3rd (NB: this is not necessarily Billy Munday’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:10thProspectsAfter a season of struggle and regression, with two head coaches and two spells under a caretaker, there is cautious optimism that this campaign will bring something like stability. Much of that optimism centres around the appointment of Xabi Alonso, an elite manager with something to prove. There is also an expectation that the young players brought in as part of BlueCo’s £1.8bn splurge in recent years are beginning to come into their best years. There is no European football to complicate the schedule and a return to the Champions League by finishing in the top four or five would suffice for now. More importance will be placed on the domestic cups after a season without trophies.Alonso’s squad is more rounded than what Enzo Maresca or Liam Rosenior had at their disposal. Maxence Lacroix and Morgan Rogers bring quality to positions whereChelseawere lacking it – at centre-back and out wide. Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson – the “uncs” as Tosin Adarabioyo has called them – will contribute as much off the pitch as on it. The signing of Marco Palestra, a specialist wing-back, suggests Alonso wants to be tactically flexible. He has used a back four and a back three in pre-season.What about Cole Palmer? For so much of his time at Stamford Bridge, Chelsea’s form has been tied to his. When he has struggled to be 100% fit, the team have suffered too. After being omitted from England’s World Cup squad, Palmer had a seven-week break and sought advice from a specialist on the groin injury that hampered him last season. “I got bored after six weeks,” Palmer said after returning for pre-season. “I was sat in Marbella thinking: ‘I want to go back in.’” With the prospect of linking up with Rogers and João Pedro, who has also had a good rest, Palmer has plenty of reasons to be excited.Past five seasonsOff-field pictureJuly ended with Chelsea being fined £10m and receiving a suspended transfer ban over multiple violations of transfer rules under the ownership of Roman Abramovich. An appeal from the club saved them from a six-point deduction. Chelsea were deemed compliant with the Premier League’s profitability and sustainability rules for the three-year period ending in 2025 despite posting an English record £262.4m pre-tax loss for the 2024-25 season. They have not been cowed by failure to qualify for Europe and have spent over £300m on new signings. For the fourth year in a row, Chelsea look likely to start the season without a front-of-shirt sponsor.Owner-fan relationshipSupporter protests against the ownership of Todd Boehly’s BlueCo have been a frequent sight on matchdays, including before May’s FA Cup finaldefeat by Manchester City. There have been reservations about the club’s youth-oriented transfer policy from the start and last season’s failings prompted the co-owner Behdad Eghbali to admit the need “to add more ready-made players” to the squad. Whether fans were expecting the arrivals of Welbeck and Henderson is another question. The introduction of a ticket ballot system for home games has also been unpopular with regular match-going supporters.The managerIt was a bit of a coup for Chelsea to secure Alonso’s services this summer, especially given the Liverpool job was available. The Spaniard has a reputation to rebuild after his dream job at Real Madrid ended in the sack after six months. “I got a scar, now it is healed,” he said. Alonso’s record of developing young players, such as Florian Wirtz, at Bayer Leverkusen while simultaneously delivering silverware is a match made in heaven for the Chelsea hierarchy. One detail to note: Alonso has been appointed as manager, rather than head coach like his predecessors. He has also brought in Austin MacPhee, Aston Villa’s set-piece guru.Star signingView image in fullscreenChelsea broke the British transfer record to pry Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesChelsea went one better than Manchester City’s £116m signing of Elliot Anderson by bringing in Rogers, who had been linked with Arsenal, for a new British record fee of £117m. Although he started England’s World Cup semi-finaldefeat by Argentinaon the right wing, Rogers has thrived for Aston Villa playing largely off the left and should slot in there nicely at Chelsea. The 24-year-old has proved himself in the Premier League and his best-buddy relationship with his former Manchester City youth teammate Palmer is a major plus. “I can see them linking really well,” Alonso said.Stat attackHas anyone checked Chelsea haven’t built a squad of Benjamin Buttons? The average age of their starting XI has decreased over the past three seasons when they were already the youngest team in Premier League history. You can see why they signed Henderson and Welbeck.YoungestSet for a breakthroughRobert Sánchez is still Chelsea’s No 1 but he may face serious competition this season from the 21-year-old Mike Penders. The goalkeeper, who was third-choice for Belgium at the World Cup, was signed from Genk in 2024 and spent last season on loan at Strasbourg in Ligue 1. The comparisons with Thibaut Courtois, who Chelsea signed from Genk at a similar age, are obvious. Like Courtois, Penders is 6ft 7in and therefore has a massive reach, but he also earns plaudits for his passing. Chances will come in cup competitions, but the clamour for Penders to be first choice might become hard to ignore.World Cup impactEnzo Fernández had a rollercoaster of a World Cup. Chelsea’s vice-captain popped up with crucial late goals for Argentina in the knockout stages, including a winning header against Egypt and the equaliser against England. But the abiding memory was his part in Argentina’s unsavoury approach in the final against Spain, where he received one yellow card for dissent and another for sending Pau Cubarsí flying. Real Madrid said in July they had “no intention” of pursuing a move that Fernández seemed to covet earlier this year when he said he would “love” to live in Madrid – comments that earned him a two-game ban under Rosenior. How about living in Manchester? City have been linked.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27ChelseaPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s been a revelation’: how heat pumps can cool your home as temperatures soar | Heat pumps | The Guardian
description: It might seem an unlikely way to stop overheating, but many owners have found the tech a lifeline in hot weather
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: It might seem an unlikely way to stop overheating, but many owners have found the tech a lifeline in hot weather
Content: A recent study found that using a heat pump for cooling can ‘significantly reduce overheating’ in modern homes.Photograph: NAPA74/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenA recent study found that using a heat pump for cooling can ‘significantly reduce overheating’ in modern homes.Photograph: NAPA74/Getty Images/iStockphotoHeat pumps‘It’s been a revelation’: how heat pumps can cool your home as temperatures soarIt might seem an unlikely way to stop overheating, but many owners have found the tech a lifeline in hot weatherZoe WoodWed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“If it is 35C outdoors, I can get the temperature down to 21C,” says Andrew Ingram of the sanctuary that his living room has provided this summer.“On the nights I’ve slept in there, you have to put your thick pyjamas on,” jokes Ingram, who lives in Maidenhead, Berkshire, with his wife, Sue.“When I post on Facebook about it, people say: ‘That’s air conditioning’ and I say: ‘No, it’s the heat pump.’ It’s just working the other way around.”Rather than generating heat from burning fuel, a heat pump transfers heat energy from one place to another. However, despite the name, heat pumps can be used for cooling, too.The energy is released through an “emitter” such as a radiator or underfloor heating. The Ingrams have an air source heat pump. It extracts heat from the air outside and uses it to warm the radiators of their three-bedroom house (this is called an air-to-water system).In 2023, when the Ingrams ripped out their gas boiler, the firm suggested they consider whether they wanted to cool any rooms.View image in fullscreenAndrew and Sue Ingram with the GivEnergy home battery storage and inverter system they use with their heat pump.“We thought about it because the sitting room gets really hot, and that’s the room we spend time in,” Ingram says.“It’s been a revelation. We bought it on the basis that there might be a heatwave, and it’s been an absolute lifeline this year.“You know those times when you are really feeling exhausted and want to sit somewhere cool. We turn it right down and then let the temperature drift back up again.”The couple have radiators throughout but the living room also has another “emitter” – called a fan coil unit. This is an appliance that blows air over hot or cold pipes. The whole new home energy system cost roughly £18,600, with the cooling aspect accounting for £1,700 of that.“If you’re pumping cool water around a property, it’s a bit like putting cool beer in a glass on a warm day,” says Ingram of what is potentially one of the pitfalls of cooling this way.double quotation markIf you’re pumping cool water around a property, it’s a bit like putting cool beer in a glass on a warm dayAndrew Ingram“You get loads of condensation, so you either have to wrap pipes in quite sophisticated trunking or do what we did, which is have them outside.“We used the cooling a bit in 2024, and, guess what, in 2025 even more – and in 2026 we’ve been a rather popular place for people to visit.”The government’s boiler upgrade scheme offers grants of £7,500 to assist homeowners in England and Wales with the cost of installing an air-to-water or ground-to-water system (a heat pump that extracts heat from the ground through buried pipes).Households not connected to the gas grid qualify for an additional £1,500 in support, increasing the grant to £9,000.If you live in Scotland, you may be able to get aninterest-free loan or a grantto make your home more energy efficient.To qualify for funding, the heat pump must be certified through theMicrogeneration Certification Scheme, which certifies installers.Previously heat pumps that also cooled required planning permission, as the permitted development rights rules (legal permissions that allow certain home improvements without a planning application) stated they had to be solely for heating. The PDRhas now been updatedto allow cooling.To date, Britons have mostly installed air-to-water systems, and of the UK’s 358,000 heat pumps, approximately 323,000 are this type, according to MCS data.This could be about to change because the government is to offer£2,500 grantsfor air conditioning units that can heat and cool. The air-to-air heat pumps move heat using wall-mounted fans and cost about £4,500 to fit in a flat or small house. (Air-to-water heat pumps typically cost in the region of £12,000.)The run ofheatwaveshas thrown the spotlight on “heat-trap homes”.A recent report by the Climate Change Committeesaid that hotter heatwaves could lead to 92% of existing homes overheating by 2050 and they mayrequire air conditioning, as passive measures such as drawing curtains and opening windows are unlikely to be enough.A recent study conducted in theEnergy House 2.0– a £16m climate-controlled chamber at the University of Salford – found that using a heat pump for cooling can “significantly reduce overheating” in modern homes.View image in fullscreenA heat pump transfers heat energy from one place to another.Photograph: David McGill/AlamyTwo new modern houses have been built inside the weather simulation facility so that scientists can test how “real” homes perform under extreme conditions.The Salford scientists paired a heat pump with fan coils in one of the houses. When the lab weather was 32C, the rooms stayed comfortable – between 19C and 24.9C. With the heat pump running around the clock, the cost was £2.50-£3 a day.Prof Lubo Jankovic, the scientist leading the research, says the results “demonstrate that reversible heat pumps can play an important role in protecting future homes against overheating”.But Jankovic says the challenge of designing systems with both heating and cooling in mind “needs to be addressed before cooling this way becomes mainstream”.With the October price cap predicted to exceed£1,700 a yearfor a typical dual fuel bill, the big question for many is: will a heat pump save me money?double quotation markThe charity Nesta runs the ‘visit a heat pump’ scheme, which offers tours of more than 1,200 homesA recent poll by the consumer group Which? revealed growing consumer interest in heat pumps, but also that they were a “high-stakes gamble” owing to their unfamiliarity, high upfront costs and uncertain impact on bills.One way to get a better understanding is to look round a home with one and quiz the owner. The charity Nestaruns the “visit a heat pump”scheme, which offers tours of more than 1,200 homes, including the Ingrams’.When it comes to bills, the Energy Saving Trust says the biggest saving comes in homes that switch to a dedicated heat pump energy tariff and add other green technologies such as solar panels.The tariff is vital because heat pumps run on electricity, which is generally more expensive per unit than gas. On a standard tariff, this can lead to substantial energy bills, negating some of the efficiency benefits.Heat pump users moving on to a time-of-use tariff can saveabout £330 a yearcompared with sitting on a flat-rate tariff, the trust says. This rises to about £800 with extras such as solar, although these add to the upfront costs.The Ingrams have solar panels and a home battery to help keep their bills down. “There’s lots of juice in the batteries from the solar,” Ingram says. “The batteries charge up overnight if they’re not full, but they have been recently. So if you want to run the pump, it is running on free or very cheap electricity.”Explore more on these topicsHeat pumpsHome improvementsExtreme heatExtreme weatherEnergy industryEnergy billsEnergy efficiencyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nurses fainting in ‘inhumane’ conditions due to extreme heat, union warns | Nursing | The Guardian
description: RCN calls for more air conditioners as Burnham faces pressure to recognise urgency of adaptation to climate crisis
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: RCN calls for more air conditioners as Burnham faces pressure to recognise urgency of adaptation to climate crisis
Content: The Royal College of Nursing said that members were left dizzy, nauseous or at risk of fainting while dripping with sweat ‘from head to toe’.Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Royal College of Nursing said that members were left dizzy, nauseous or at risk of fainting while dripping with sweat ‘from head to toe’.Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesNursingNurses fainting in ‘inhumane’ conditions due to extreme heat, union warnsRCN calls for more air conditioners as Burnham faces pressure to recognise urgency of adaptation to climate crisisPeter Walker,Tobi ThomasandAletha AduWed 12 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNurses are collapsing during shifts amid “inhumane and impossible” conditions caused by extreme heat, their union has warned, asAndy Burnhampromised to grapple with “the bigger questions” of climate adaptation.Amid growing pressure from Labour backbenches to fully acknowledge the urgency of adaptation measures as the climate crisis bites, Burnham said he was for now focusing on the immediate crises caused by an ongoing summer of extreme heat.Speaking after a meeting of the government’s Cobra emergency committee, Burnham refused to say if the summer had made the case against renewed drilling in the North Sea, which his government is considering.“It is really important that we deal today with the situation that we are in right now and we focus on making sure that we have the serious incidents under control across the country, and those incidents are under control,” he said.“The bigger questions obviously will come at the right moment in time,” he added.An amber warning for heat across large parts of England will come into force again on Thursday morning, with temperatures forecast to reach 36C or potentially higher.Train passengers on some networks are being warned by rail operators to only travel if the journey is vital, saying services are likely to be disrupted because of the weather.Three-quarters of England is now officially in drought. Firefighters are continuing totackle a blaze in the New Forest in Hampshire, with warnings across parts of eastern and southern Scotland about a very high risk of wildfires.With the number of days of 30C-plus heat in the UK already at a new record of 35, the Royal College ofNursingbecame the latest union to warn of unsafe working conditions for many members in hospital wards and care homes.The RCN, which runs an advice hotline, said some staff had collapsed. Others were left dizzy, nauseous or at risk of fainting while dripping with sweat “from head to toe”. They also faced pressure to keep elderly and vulnerable patients safe alongside keeping medications cool.Working within a critical care unit in an NHS hospital in the south-west of England, a 37-year-old nurse told the Guardian her ward had reached temperatures of more than 30C and staff were struggling in the conditions.“Our ward doesn’t have air conditioning, and so we’re all really struggling. We’ve had hot summers before, but I can’t remember ever working in conditions like these back to back,” she said.Another nurse, working in a community health centre in England, said: “It gets to the point you dread going to work, especially when wearing PPE and providing patient care. We drip with sweat from head to toe.”Prof Nicola Ranger, the general secretary and chief executive of the RCN, said that these testimonies were a “wake-up call”, calling for an urgent programme to install air conditioning, improve ventilation and ensure heat-appropriate uniforms were available.On Monday, the Fire Brigades Unionwarned thatfirefighters needed new equipment and resources to face the growing threats from a climate changing at speed.Accordingto a freedom of informationrequest submitted by the Guardian, just 20 staff are working on climate adaptation within the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.The government has been warnedby the climate change adaptation committeethat it is lagging far behind in terms of adapting to a new climate.Speaking on Wednesday morning, Burnham raised the idea of a possible ban on disposable barbecues, which are a known fire risk. Later in the day, he said retailers should withdraw them from sale, adding: “Longer term we will look at whether a temporary ban in the summer months is justified.”One Labour MP, Chris Hinchliff, who had previously warned Burnham about the need to prepare the country for a fast-changing climate, called for more immediate action, saying the summer “has to be a real wake-up call for Westminster”.Some Labour MPs are also privately concerned that he has as yet not shown he understands the urgency of the issue.“Adaptation has always been the poor relation in government,” one Labour MP said. “Look how much better we are at getting energy projects off the ground than reservoirs.”Some MPs argued Burnham took too long to hold a Cobra meeting, with one saying: “He barely talks about the climate crisis. He should be doing as many social media video clips on this as he does on the cost of living crisis.”Hinchliff, the MP for North East Hertfordshire, said the events of the summer should be enough to spark action.He said: “It’s a well-recognised fact that our country was built for a climate that no longer exists. It’s putting enormous pressure on our infrastructure, our railways, our schools, our hospitals, and it threatens a real impact on people’s living standards. This has to be one of the top priorities for government.“It is indisputable that up to now we haven’t treated these issues with the importance that they deserve, and the proof is what we are experiencing.”Another MP said Burnham should use the subject to his advantage and “lean into climate adaptability”.“Let Nigel Farage be on the side of the wildfires – he can be the pro-wildfire politician, and Andy can be the anti-wildfire prime minister. This is an opportunity for him to seize,” they added.Health and social care secretary Yvette Cooper said: “The extreme heat is hitting public health and our NHS. Across the NHS and social care, staff are doing a remarkable job to respond to rising A&E attendances and ambulance call-outs, heat problems among the elderly and difficult working conditions. I want to thank them for all their work.“But I have also been clear that the NHS now needs to plan for summer pressures in the way we currently plan for winter pressures. That includes making sure buildings are more resilient in these new extreme heat conditions as well as responding to additional patient needs.”Explore more on these topicsNursingUK weatherClimate crisisAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Always cracking jokes’: questions raised over Jason Arday’s claim he was non-verbal as a child | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Fellow pupils at his primary school have challenged Cambridge academic’s story, though others support it
Author: Lanre Bakare
Headline: Fellow pupils at his primary school have challenged Cambridge academic’s story, though others support it
Content: Jason Arday wrote that he had been ‘unable to speak until I was 11 years old’.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday wrote that he had been ‘unable to speak until I was 11 years old’.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianJason Arday‘Always cracking jokes’: questions raised over Jason Arday’s claim he was non-verbal as a childFellow pupils at his primary school have challenged Cambridge academic’s story, though others support itLanre Bakare,Aamna MohdinandSammy GecsoylerWed 12 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe story of Jason Arday’s extraordinary rise to becoming the youngest black professor in the history of theUniversity of Cambridgeis all the more remarkable for one claim: that he did not learn to speak until just shy of his 12th birthday.This claim was mentioned in a letter announcinghis resignation last week, which came amidmounting questionsabout his academic work and statements he had made about his past.Arday wrote that becoming a professor at Cambridge was something he “could scarcely have imagined” as an autistic child who was “unable to speak until I was 11 years old”.His memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, was published by Simon & Schuster in the US on Tuesday and is due to be published in the UK on 27 August. It tells the story of how he joined Cambridge aged 37 despite having been non-verbal throughout his childhood and only learning to read and write aged 18.But interviews with former schoolmates have produced conflicting accounts of his childhood. Two remember him speaking at primary school, describing a chatty child who loved making jokes, while two others say they did not hear him speak until he reached secondary school.Jonathan Stewart, 40, told the Guardian he remembered Arday from when they were children growing up in south London. He described him as a good mimic who entertained other pupils by putting on accents and singing songs.View image in fullscreenJonathan Stewart, a YouTuber, said Arday ‘was always cracking jokes’ and ‘would even put on voices’ at school.Photograph: TikTok.com/strictlyvibeswithgaStewart, a YouTuber who says he was in the year below Arday at Heathbrook primary school in Nine Elms, south-west London, said the academic was known as the class clown. “He was always cracking jokes. He was the comedian guy, he would even put on voices,” claimed Stewart, who said he regularly attended church with Arday.Stewart said that in the Sunday school minibus that would pick them up, Arday would entertain his peers by singing the jingle from the 90s advert forBaby All Gonedolls. He said Arday, a talented goalkeeper, would bring in his own pair of gloves and dive to save shots, even on the school’s concrete playground.Another man, 40, who was also in the year below Arday at Heathbrook and asked not to be named, said: “I don’t remember too much about him but I certainly recollect him being able to speak.” Both this man and Stewart said they were in touch with people who had been in Arday’s class.Arday writes in his memoir that as he approached the age of 12 the local council was on the verge of pulling his speech therapy support because he had made so little progress.“But miraculously, just a few days shy of my 12th birthday, I spoke. It was at the start of one of my sessions, and Katrina [his speech therapist] had just said: ‘Hello, Jason.’ At that moment, I was fiddling with my hearing aid, which was bothering me, and then I took it out of my ear and said hello back to her.”Arday said his mother was present to witness the moment, and that beforehand he had “said bits of words and made various noises out of context” but never replied with the correct phrase or at the right time.Arday denied the accounts provided by Stewart and the second man and organised for the Guardian to be sent statements by two school friends, Nick Clark and Mike Freeman, who said the account in his memoir accurately reflected the boy they remembered at school.Clark said: “As a boy, I remember Jason not speaking and being regularly removed from class for additional support throughout his time at Heathbrook. I was not in his secondary school, but we joined the same football team at 13, when we became great friends, playing football together ever since.”Clark’s mother, Caroline Russell-Clark, also sent a statement saying she helped out at Heathbrook for a couple of years when Arday was very young.“When my son, Nick Clark, was in nursery at Heathbrook, I was asked to help three-year-old Jason, who had serious learning difficulties … I helped him listen to stories and read to him on many occasions,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“He moved up to reception [class] and the deputy headteacher … asked me in to help support him, and another child. She gave me reading tasks to do with him and also asked me to explain various activities. Jason never spoke to me but he was well behaved and an engaging child.”Plagiarism and a pig’s head: the rise and fall of Jason Arday – podcastRead moreRussell-Clark said Arday remained in the same class as her son throughout primary school. “I do not remember him speaking until he was playing in the same football team as my son aged 14/15.”Freeman said: “I remember him not speaking during our time at Heathbrook primary school. He was regularly taken out of class for his educational needs. His severe special needs didn’t stop him playing football and games with me and others as he was still friendly and could communicate through play and actions.”Ardayresigned from Cambridge last weekafter being accused of plagiarism in his academic work. Questions were also raised about a long line of claims about his backstory, from endurance running, football exploits and charity fundraising to academic positions, qualifications and authorship. Arday said the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.Stewart said: “It took someone so long to get in the position that he got into and it’s tarnished. It’s gone and [the black community is] going to be scrutinised more than ever now. I can’t tell my sons: ‘Go look at him as somebody to look up to.’”Arday claimed to have completed 30 marathons in 35 days, run 600 miles in six days and raised £5m for charity over several years. After facing questions, he revised some of those claims and instead said he was part of a fundraising group that he was unable to name for legal reasons.He alsotold the Guardianhe had been the target of threats after his Cambridge appointment, including having a severed pig’s head delivered to his parents’ home. Subsequent investigations found no evidence to support this claim.Simon & Schuster, which bought Arday’s memoir for a seven-figure sum,according to the academic, is pressing on with its publication and launch in the UK. The publisher did not respond to requests for comment.Additional reporting: Kevin RawlinsonExplore more on these topicsJason ArdayUniversity of CambridgeAcademicsHigher educationRaceAutismfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Double murderer and rapist Simon Levy sentenced to whole-life tariff | Crime | The Guardian
description: Errors by police and prosecutors after first murder had left serial sex offender free to kill again
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Errors by police and prosecutors after first murder had left serial sex offender free to kill again
Content: Simon Levy, 40, was found guilty at the Old Bailey of murdering two women and raping a third.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PASimon Levy, 40, was found guilty at the Old Bailey of murdering two women and raping a third.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PACrimeDouble murderer and rapist Simon Levy sentenced to whole-life tariffErrors by police and prosecutors after first murder had left serial sex offender free to kill againVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentWed 12 Aug 2026 15.46 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 07.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSimon Levy, the prolific sexual predator left free by police and prosecution errors to murder two women, will never leave prison after being sentenced to a rare whole-life tariff.Judge Lucraft KC said Levy, 40, “ruthlessly” exploited women for his sexual pleasure, and had a proven history of sexual offending dating back to 2018.Levy will be one of a group of just 76 people currently confined to jail for the rest of their lives.Police have admitted that it is likely his second murder victim could have been saved were it not for errors by officers and the prosecution service.The sentencing was watched by the families of his murder victims, Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, killed in south-eastLondonin March 2025 and Sheryl Wilkins, murdered five months later in Tottenham, north London. Wilkins was murdered just a day short of her 40th birthday and had 83 marks on her body.Levy was also convicted of attacking and raping another woman, aged 35, in Tottenham in January 2025, known as “ED” to protect her anonymity. She survived and gave damning testimony of how she was beaten, suffocated and raped.Levy, from Tottenham in north London, was on bail as a suspect for the first murder when he committed the second, after police said they lacked sufficient evidence to charge him.Before the killings he already had an extensive history of sexual offending and was on the sex offender register, having been jailed in 2021 for two sexual assaults.Sentencing Levy at the Old Bailey on Wednesday, the judge told him he was “someone who appears to have a morbid fascination with sex, rape and crime”. Lucraft added: “You will be in prison for life.”View image in fullscreenSheryl Wilkins (left) was murdered by Simon Levy five months after he killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo (right).Photograph: Metropolitan policeMonths before the first killing, British Transport Police arrested Levy for sexual assaulting women on trains but made errors that delayed charging him, leaving him free.In total he carried out 10 attacks on trains in London, many while on bail for the first set of train attacks. He was convicted of those crimes earlier this year.The prosecutor, Tom Little KC, said Levy’s offending was so severe it deserved a whole-life tariff, and an aggravating feature was that sexual violence was “inextricably interwoven with the killing” of both victims.The sentencing heard harrowing testimony from the victims’ loved ones that the women were vulnerable because they were sex workers and used drugs, but that they were much loved and central to the lives of their families.Wilkins’s mother, Mary, said her daughter was a sacrifice to keep others safe: “You have done this before and wouldn’t have stopped. Our Sheryl has ended your chances of hurting anyone else.“She lost her life to do this, but we truly believe Sheryl has saved countless women from being subjected to your disgusting and horrendous acts. I hope you never walk the streets again as you are a threat to all women.”Wilkins’s sister, Lindsey Hicks, said: “You, Simon Levy, have destroyed our lives. Sheryl was a beautiful soul … the pain you have put her through is unbearable. I hope you rot in prison for the rest of your life.”The woman Levy attacked in January 2025 told the court she was a “mum and a classical pianist” from eastern Europe and had been trafficked into the UK and used drugs to deal with the pain.She said Levy was a “monster” but said she was stronger now, and had vowed to overcome the “humiliation” he had inflicted on her. He had tried to steal her “soul and dignity” as he set on her, she said, and had left her for dead after raping and strangling her. She vowed: “‘I will play music again and smile.”The woman said that when she first told officers of the attack they “spoke to me like a child”. This was in January 2025, before the other two murders.View image in fullscreenScreengrab from a video of Judge Mark Lucraft KC at the Old Bailey, central London, sentencing Levy.Photograph: PA Video/PAThe judge and DCI Neil John, of the Met police, said the woman’s bravery was crucial to ensuring Levy was jailed for life. After all the Met’s failings, its murder team had arrested Levy for Wilkins’s murder, then found Levy’s first victim and got a full statement, and also linked him to the first murder, of Valencia-Trujillo.John said: “I must also commend the victim-survivor who showed considerable bravery and presented vital evidence in court. Her testimony was crucial.”The judge said: “It takes considerable courage to come to court and to give evidence … she should be commended for doing so.”Victims groups have described the litany of failings in the Levy case as staggering. Government sources say they have no plans for an independent inquiry into the errors – but they come after other scandals highlighting catastrophic errors by police that led to women being seriously hurt or murdered.Police errors were a factor in allowing the black cab rapistJohn Worboys to drug and rape scores of women.And the murderer and kidnapper of Sarah Everard,Wayne Couzens, had earlier exposed himself repeatedly,but police had taken no action and left him as a serving police officer.Another Met officer,David Carrick, was able to use his status to intimidate and sexually assault women, while complaint after complaint against him was ignored.Harriet Wistrich, of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said: “The catalogue of combined failures in this case provides terrifying evidence that our criminal justice system is in a state of collapse.“Given the series of catastrophic failures by the Met police on top of an appalling history of police failures … we must conclude that the Met police are not fit for purpose.”0:52Bodycam footage shows arrest of Simon Levy – videoNext year the official Angiolini inquiry, set up after the Couzens scandal, will report and is considering a finding that police are institutionally misogynist.Met commissioner Sir Mark Rowley, who said in 2023 his officers would take the “terrorism approach to male predatory violence”, said his force had apologised and blamed errors in the wider criminal justice system, and not just by police: “He was repeatedly by the police put before the courts seeking remanding in custody. The police were saying this guy is too dangerous to be on the streets, and between CPS and the courts, they kept bailing him.”He added: “We need a justice system that helps us rather than keeps putting dangerous people back on the streets when that’s obviously the wrong answer …”Two Met officers are under investigation by the police watchdog in relation to the case. Levy’s risk assessment was downgraded by the Met in August 2024 from high to medium, in part because he was blind in one eye, believed by detectives to be a reprisal for the rape of another woman.British Transport Police moved one officer, blamed for the delay in charging Levy for the train attacks, out of investigations, and verbally told off his supervisor, but have not referred themselves to the police watchdog.Prosecutors admitted bungling efforts to have Levy remanded in custody after the first murder and after he was charged with the train attacks. They failed to provide three court hearings with key information demonstrating the full extent of the danger he posed to women.A Crown Prosecution Service source said people have and will continue to be disciplined, but refused to give details.When first arrested for murder, Levy, who lived with his mother and sister, was wearing children’s pyjamas. He needed an appropriate adult present when detectives interviewed him and had dyslexia, autism and learning difficulties. He is believed to have been long-term unemployed.Explore more on these topicsCrimePoliceViolence against women and girlsMetropolitan policeLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Politicians among mourners at funeral service for Ann Widdecombe | Ann Widdecombe | The Guardian
description: Family, friends and colleagues attend service at Buckfast Abbey, which former MP described as her ‘safe haven’
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Family, friends and colleagues attend service at Buckfast Abbey, which former MP described as her ‘safe haven’
Content: The funeral procession at Buckfast Abbey in Buckfastleigh. Before the service, police officers and sniffer dogs searched the grounds.Photograph: Mike Davies on behalf of Buckfast Abbey/PAView image in fullscreenThe funeral procession at Buckfast Abbey in Buckfastleigh. Before the service, police officers and sniffer dogs searched the grounds.Photograph: Mike Davies on behalf of Buckfast Abbey/PAAnn WiddecombePoliticians among mourners at funeral service for Ann WiddecombeFamily, friends and colleagues attend service at Buckfast Abbey, which former MP described as her ‘safe haven’Rachel HallWed 12 Aug 2026 13.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout 100 family, friends and colleagues of Ann Widdecombe have attended a funeral service for the former Conservative minister, who was killed in her home in Devon last month.Politicians and broadcasters were among the mourners at Buckfast Abbey in Buckfastleigh, a Catholic abbey in Devon where Widdecombe regularly worshipped and which she described as her “safe haven”.A 90-minute requiem mass – where prayers are offered for the soul of the dead – was held for the former MP and Reform UK spokesperson.Before the service, police officers and sniffer dogs could be seen searching the grounds.Widdecombe died on 8 July, aged 78, after she was hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor. Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham, South Yorkshire, was charged with her murder on 20 July.It is understood that Reform leader, Nigel Farage, did not attend the funeral because he did not wish to be a distraction. He is expected to attend a public memorial planned for later this year.View image in fullscreenBuckfast Abbey paid tribute to Ann Widdecombe, recalling her ‘sharp intellect’ and dedication to public service.Photograph: Mike Davies on behalf of Buckfast Abbey/PAThose slated to attend included the shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, the former Conservative justice minister Crispin Blunt and the broadcaster Iain Dale.The private mass featured a homily from the Rt Rev David Charlesworth, the abbot of Buckfast. He said: “In the midst of the shock, clamour and sometimes unwarranted comment surrounding her death, our response is to pray for the repose of her soul, to give thanks for her fortitude, and offer Holy Mass in this abbey church, which Ann called her safe haven.”An earlier statement from the abbey said: “Ann was a woman of profound faith, a faith which found expression in the public forum of politics. Ann was unafraid to express her unwavering convictions, formed through her Roman Catholic faith. She had a sharp intellect and was a dedicated public servant.”View image in fullscreenMourners arriving for the funeral.Photograph: Matt Keeble/PAThe order of service showed tributes would be paid by the Rev Roger Widdecombe, Widdecombe’s nephew, and Christian Sweeting, a close friend.Donations made in her memory will be divided between the Leprosy Mission and Abound, supporting the projects of the Christian Endeavour Hostel in India.Widdecombe was first elected as a Conservative MP for Maidstone in 1987 and became a prisons minister in the 1990s. She later became a member of the European parliament for the Brexit party. At the time of her death she was a spokesperson on immigration and justice for Reform UK. She had also appeared on Strictly Come Dancing and Celebrity Big Brother.Explore more on these topicsAnn WiddecombenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cruise ships, quiet towns and an all-day festival: millions flock to eclipse viewing spots across Europe | Solar eclipses | The Guardian
description: Beginning in Russia’s remote Arctic north, the eclipse traced an arc over much of western Europe – with the best views in Spain, Iceland and Greenland
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Beginning in Russia’s remote Arctic north, the eclipse traced an arc over much of western Europe – with the best views in Spain, Iceland and Greenland
Content: Prague Castle is silhouetted against a partial solar eclipsePhotograph: Martin Divíšek/EPAView image in fullscreenPrague Castle is silhouetted against a partial solar eclipsePhotograph: Martin Divíšek/EPASolar eclipsesCruise ships, quiet towns and an all-day festival: millions flock to eclipse viewing spots across EuropeBeginning in Russia’s remote Arctic north, the eclipse traced an arc over much of western Europe – with the best views in Spain, Iceland and GreenlandAshifa Kassamin Madrid,Miranda BryantandChris Michaelin LondonWed 12 Aug 2026 15.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt was a moment of awe shared by millions across Europe: an eclipse that blocked out the sun, plunging parts of the continent into a daytime darkness in which temperatures dropped and birds suddenly went quiet.Wednesday’s eclipse began in Russia’s remote Arctic north, going on to trace an arc over much of western Europe. From the UK to northern Italy, tens of millions of people turned to the sky as the light of the setting sun was almost completely blocked out.The most sought-after experiences were in Greenland,Icelandand Spain along with a small strip of Portugal. It was in parts of these countries that totality – referring to when the moon completely covers the sun’s light – was on offer, drawing millions of local people and thousands of tourists from across the globe into the path of the eclipse.“It was one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever seen in my life,” Sara García Alonso, a reserve astronaut for the EuropeanSpaceAgency, told broadcaster RTVE. “It gave me goosebumps.”Standing next to her, the astronaut Pablo Álvarez Fernández nodded in agreement: “It had been described to me so many times, but it was much more beautiful than what I had expected.”In Iceland, people flocked by air, land and sea to take in the country’s first total solar eclipse in 72 years. Amid concerns that clouds would block the view, a record 31 cruise ships plied the waters off the western part of the country, hoping to secure a top view for about 53,000 passengers and crew.View image in fullscreenThe sun during a partial solar eclipse and partially obscured by clouds, the International Space Station silhouetted as it transits at roughly five miles per second.Photograph: Nasa Handout/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople gather to observe the total solar eclipse, as clouds cover the sky, in ReykjavikPhotograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenPassengers on board the Ambassador cruise ship Ambition watching the start of the total solar eclipse off the coast of GreenlandPhotograph: Owen Humphreys/PAThe eclipse-themed activities included a day-long music festival hosted by the Icelandic artist Björk in Víðistaðatún park, offering a DJ-curated backdrop as people took in the eclipse. The 10-hour set list included two minutes set aside for totality, the artist said on social media, while the festival website noted that every ticket included a pair of approved solar eclipse glasses.Those watching from Iceland included the US space agency, Nasa, which followed the moon’s shadow using a high-altitude WB-57 aircraft while Nasa-funded teams launched balloons to study the atmospheric impact of the sudden darkness and cooling.View image in fullscreenA WB-57 Canberra aircraft is pictured during a media visit ahead of a Nasa-supported missionPhotograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenCary Klemm, sensor equipment operator, and pilot John Gustine of Nasa’s Johnson Space Centre pose in front of a WB-57 Canberra aircraftPhotograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenA WB-57 Canberra aircraftPhotograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenA gyroscopic sensor system aboard a WB-57 Canberra aircraftPhotograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersIn Spain, wheresome of the best viewsof the total eclipse were expected, the hours leading up to the celestial alignment were filled with frenzied debate about weather forecasts and where best to watch the phenomenon.More than 450,000 tourists had arrived in the country from as far as Canada and Australia, crisscrossingSpainby train, bus and caravan to stake out the perfect viewing spot.View image in fullscreenThe sun’s corona glows as the moon completely blocks the sun during the totality phase of the total solar eclipse as seen from San Asensio, La Rioja region, SpainPhotograph: Ander Gillenea/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople wait for a solar eclipse at the beach in A Coruña, SpainPhotograph: Lavandeira/EPAView image in fullscreenA beachgoer wearing special eclipse glasses looks up during the beginning phase of a solar eclipse at Puerto de Sagunto beach near Valencia, SpainPhotograph: Alberto Saiz/APView image in fullscreenThe sun’s corona glows as the moon completely blocks the sun during the totality phase of the total solar eclipse as seen from Arenal beach in Llucmajor, on the Balearic island of MallorcaPhotograph: Jaime Reina/AFP/Getty Images“Our car was cancelled,” one woman, who had travelled from Brazil with her sister to take in the eclipse, said on social media. After her appeals to hitch a ride to their chosen site were met with no response, they took matters into their own hands. “So we took a three-hour bus, a 20-minute taxi and two-hour hike. Arrived at the location!”About 10,000 metres above sea level, the Spanish airline Iberia livestreamed the moment when the sun, moon and Earth aligned from a special charter flight. “Some flights take us to new destinations. Others allow us to see the world from a different perspective,” the airline said as it announced the charter flight.Spanish officials estimated that as many as 6 million people were expected to flock to the path of the eclipse, which stretched about 124 miles (200km) from A Coruña in Spain’s north-west to the Mediterranean island of Mallorca. On Wednesday, just hours before the eclipse, officials reported traffic jams on the major thoroughfares out of Madrid and Barcelona.Others took their chances in the cities. In Madrid’s Parque del Oeste, hundreds gathered in hopes of catching a good view of the eclipse, cheering as they watched the moon cover the sun – plunging the park into darkness – and gasping as the outer corona left a glowing halo around the moon. Just over a minute later, when daylight returned to the park, the crowd burst into raucous cheers.It was, in the words of César González, an astronomer and science communicator at the Madrid Planetarium, “a spectacular experience”. He had left Madrid early in the morning to set himself up in a field in northern Spain to watch the eclipse. “Until one goes and experiences it, there’s no way to explain what it is to see an eclipse.”View image in fullscreenMario Garrido, a member of the Los Taraos amateur astrophotography group, waits to shoot a total solar eclipse in Berlanga de Duero, central SpainPhotograph: Bernat Armangué/APView image in fullscreenThe moon completely covers the sun during a total solar eclipse as seen from the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory in Arcos de las Salinas, near Teruel, SpainPhotograph: Christian Hartmann/ReutersView image in fullscreenArtists use self-made artefacts to observe a solar eclipse before totality near the small village of Castell de Cabres, SpainPhotograph: Eva Manez/ReutersView image in fullscreenA composite image of seven separate photographs taken with a single fixed camera shows stages of a solar eclipse before, during and after totality, as seen from Arija, SpainPhotograph: Borja Suárez/ReutersHe was able, however, to explain the impact. “In broad daylight, all of a sudden the light dims to a point where you can see the brightest stars in the sky. When totality starts, the temperature drops several degrees. If you’re in a field and surrounded by animals, their behaviour often changes. The birds stop singing because they think it’s nightfall. And all of this lasts for a few minutes – in this case around 1 minute and 45 seconds.”In Spain, most eclipse watchers were heading to rural areas, filling often quiet villages and towns clogged with skygazing tourists. The eclipse had helped putsome parts of “empty Spain”on the map; this week people linked to Nasa turn up in northern Spain’s Villalibado to set up a live broadcast for millions of people around the world, breathing new life into a municipality whoselast two residentsleft in 1998.Throughout human history, eclipses have sparked amazement, fear and reverence. In villages and cities across Europe, the eclipse forged ad hoc communities, as people came together to witness one of nature’s great wonders.In Camberwell, south London, an impromptu crowd of all ages gathered in Brunswick Park to experiment with different methods of seeing the eclipse, which reached 92% totality.
