Some held up colanders, others a spatula with holes, still others makeshift pinhole cameras made of old candy boxes.Ludmila, a Ukrainian woman in her 70s, said she had worked at an observatory in Crimea for 30 years. “What a surprise to find an actual refractor,” she said, pointing to a telescope with a solar filter taped on the end brought out by a resident. “It’s like a wonderful gift.”Later, as the eclipse passed its zenith and the sun began to set for real, dozens of neighbours who had never previously spoken to each other stayed on picnic blankets to drink beer and swap photos.

title: Israeli militants besiege two Palestinian families in their West Bank homes | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Settlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terror
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Settlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terror
Content: Refqa Hassan watches as Israeli settlers besiege her family home for the fourth consecutive day in the town of Qusra.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAView image in fullscreenRefqa Hassan watches as Israeli settlers besiege her family home for the fourth consecutive day in the town of Qusra.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAWest BankIsraeli militants besiege two Palestinian families in their West Bank homesSettlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terrorEmma Graham-Harrisonin QusraWed 12 Aug 2026 17.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 18.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli militants have besieged two Palestinian families in their homes since the weekend, aiming to take over their properties in theWest Bankvillage of Qusra through a campaign of terror.A group of settlers and soldiers set up a tent outside the home of Yousef Hassan on Sunday afternoon, trapping him inside with his wife and two young daughters.The Israeli men gathered just metres away from the spot where 28-year-old Amir Moatasem Odeh waskilledby a settler in March. Another attacker stabbed his father. No one has been arrested over the murder and assault.“Every night, the settlers throw stones, use obscene language and shout during the night. We are living in a state of terror,” Hassan said. His mother, brother and sister, and three neighbours have also been blockaded inside, and their power and water have been cut off.View image in fullscreenIsraeli soldiers stand guard next to settlers in front of Palestinian homes that they have blockaded in the village of Qusra.Photograph: Nidal Eshtayeh/APSettlers used thesame tacticsto steal another Palestinian home in neighbouring Jalud village, driving the al Tubasi family out in July after a months-long siege.They cut off water and electricity to the homes, although a solar panel allows Hassan to keep some devices charged in Qusra. They have also blocked medical care.When his younger daughter, a two-year-old, fell ill with vomiting and a high fever on Monday, settlers blocked an ambulance from reaching the house. The girls and their mother were eventually evacuated on Tuesday.They are short on food and are drinking water and juice delivered by the ambulance that came to collect his daughter. “The situation is extremely dire,” Hassan said.On Wednesday morning, the commander of Israeli forces in the region, Gen Avi Bluth, visited the families and promised to lift the siege, an Israeli military spokesperson said. Hassan confirmed the visit.“Today, the area commander came and spoke with us and assured us that he would evacuate the settlers. For the first time, I feel that there is some seriousness on the part of the army in dealing with the settlers,” Hassan said, but added that it had not yet produced tangible results.Soldiers took the tent but not bedding and other possessions and, after brief clashes with the settlers, withdrew. “The settlers are still there in front of the house, and we are still unable to leave.”View image in fullscreenYousef Hassan said Israeli settlers throw stones, use obscene language and shout during the night.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAAn Israeli military spokesperson said commanders were “gravely concerned” about the settlers’ actions and that soldiers who supported them would face disciplinary action, but declined to give a timeline for lifting the siege.On Wednesday evening, chief of the general staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Eyal Zamir, met other senior commanders to discuss the situation in Qusra. He ordered a battalion of infantry reservists back from leave to reinforce troops in the West Bank.“The battalion, which is currently undergoing a period of refreshment and training, will be deployed to the sector in order to strengthen operational control. Furthermore, additional soldiers will remain on standby for deployment as necessary,” a military spokesperson said.The military is working with the police to bring “those responsible for the disturbances to justice”, the spokesperson added.Israeli militants target Palestinians with neartotal impunityin the occupied West Bank. Since 2020, Israeli civilians and soldiers have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians there, and there has been only oneindictmentover those deaths.Violence isdeployedas part of a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing. Israel has forcibly displaced 64 Palestinian communities over the past three years, rights group B’Tselem said. Fifteen other communities have lost residents, with more than 4,800 people driven from their homes.View image in fullscreenAn Israeli settler leads his sheep as settlers besiege a Palestinian home.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA“What is happening in Qusra is not an isolated incident,” said B’Tselem’s executive director, Yuli Novak.“Settler militias, backed by the Israeli military, are expanding their attacks into Palestinian villages and towns – seizing land, attacking homes and forcing families out. Israel’s ethnic cleansing of the West Bank is accelerating and expanding in plain sight.”Dozens of Israelis from the country’s security, political and cultural elite havethreatenedlegal action against their government over its failure to tackle “Jewish terrorism” in the occupied West Bank.As the occupying power in the West Bank, Israel is responsible under international law for ensuring the safety of Palestinian civilians and meeting their basic needs.The Israeli military has declared the area a closed military zone and blocked journalists from approaching the Palestinian homes. Israeli settlers are subject to the same orders but have not been removed.Sufian Taha contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Countries in ‘armed conflict’ barred from hosting Eurovision | Eurovision | The Guardian
description: Organisers says new rule will ensure contest provides ‘safe and welcoming environment’ for participants
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Organisers says new rule will ensure contest provides ‘safe and welcoming environment’ for participants
Content: Ukraine won the Eurovision song contest in 2022 but could not then stage the 2023 event after Russia’s invasion.Photograph: Marco Bertorello/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUkraine won the Eurovision song contest in 2022 but could not then stage the 2023 event after Russia’s invasion.Photograph: Marco Bertorello/AFP/Getty ImagesEurovisionCountries in ‘armed conflict’ barred from hosting EurovisionOrganisers says new rule will ensure contest provides ‘safe and welcoming environment’ for participantsNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 12 Aug 2026 14.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBroadcasters will no longer be eligible to host theEurovisionsong contest if their state is involved in an “armed conflict” or “sensitive geopolitical situation”.Eurovision is traditionally hosted by the previous year’s winner’s broadcaster, with next year’s show due to take place in Bulgaria after the singer Dara’s victory for the country in May.The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which organises Eurovision, said it had changed the rules after feedback from participating broadcasters. It said the new rules would provide greater clarity for artists and production staff and ensure the contest provided a “safe and welcoming environment”.Eurovision has faced protests in recent years over the participation of Israel, a competitor since 1973. Five longtime participants – Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia – boycotted this year’s competition in Vienna after organisers declined to exclude Israel over its conduct in the war against Hamas in Gaza and violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.It is unclear if or when any of the boycotting countries will rejoin the contest. Israel claimed second place in this year’s competition, as it did in 2025.The Eurovision song contest director, Martin Green, said: “The Eurovision song contest is constantly evolving and our annual review of the rules is an important part of making sure the contest remains fair, transparent and consistent for all those who participate, including the millions who engage with the event globally.“Guided, as always, by feedback from our members, we have clarified and strengthened several areas for 2027. These changes are about giving everyone involved greater clarity, protecting artists and ensuring the contest continues to provide a safe and welcoming environment, while preserving the spirit and integrity that make the Eurovision song contest so special.”In potentially difficult situations outside armed conflict, the winning country will be assessed by an independent security body to help the EBU determine whether or not it could safely host.If the winning member is ruled ineligible, the EBU will identify an alternative host broadcaster to “assume all rights, obligations and liabilities associated with hosting the contest”, and it will not be required to stage the event on behalf of another member.The 2023 Eurovision song contest was held in Liverpool after Ukraine’s win the previous year. At the time, the EBU said Russia’s war made it impossible to begin the 12 months of preparation needed to organise the show.The new rule changes also increase the minimum age for artists from 16 to 18.According to organisers, the 2026 Eurovision final was watched by 130 million viewers around the world, down from 160 million in 2025.Despite the blows to Eurovision’s finances and viewership from the boycott, the contest is set for expansion, with a spin-off Eurovision song contest Asia due to take place in Bangkok in November.Last month it was announced thatCanadawould ​join the main contest, becoming the first new ⁠participant since Australia in 2015.Participation is not limited to countries in geographic Europe and instead is open to all members of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which Canada recently joined. Australia is an associate member.Explore more on these topicsEurovisionUkraineRussiaCanadaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Karoline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary, Trump says | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: US president announced departure on social media, saying Leavitt was leaving to ‘spend more time’ with family
Author: David Smith
Headline: US president announced departure on social media, saying Leavitt was leaving to ‘spend more time’ with family
Content: Karoline Leavitt on 23 July 2026 at the White House in Washington DC.Photograph: Lenin Nolly/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKaroline Leavitt on 23 July 2026 at the White House in Washington DC.Photograph: Lenin Nolly/NurPhoto/ShutterstockTrump administrationKaroline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary, Trump saysUS president announced departure on social media, saying Leavitt was leaving to ‘spend more time’ with familyUS politics – live updatesDavid Smithin WashingtonWed 12 Aug 2026 17.36 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 15.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKaroline Leavittwill step down as White House press secretary at the end of August, Donald Trump announced.The US presidentrevealed her departureon social media, saying Leavitt was leaving “so she can spend more time” with her family. The 28-year-old gave birth to a daughter, Viviana, in May, and returned from maternity leave last month.The departure of Trump’s most prominent spokesperson comes with his approval rating at a historic low as voters express discontent over rising prices and a war in Iran that has no end in sight.Trump said Leavitt, who became the youngest person to serve as White House press secretary on his return to office in January 2025, “will now be one of my top outside advisors” in a post on his Truth Social platform.Leavittwrote on X: “The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary – and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life.”Leavitt served Trump as a press aide during his first term in the White House. She ran for Congress in 2022 as the Republican nominee for New Hampshire’s first congressional district but lost the race.She joined Trump’s 2024 ​campaign ​and was transition ​spokeswoman before Trump selected ​her to ‌be White House ​press ​secretary. At 27 she was younger than Ronald Ziegler, who was 29 when he was Richard Nixon’s spokesperson.A devout Christian, Leavitt, wearing a cross necklace, and her team wouldhold a short group prayerbefore she walked into the briefing room to face reporters. The briefings rarely strayed off message or made headlines but did keep factcheckers occupied. For example, her claim that “tariffs are a tax cut for the American people,”was rated false by Politifact.In a smooth delivery with few verbal stumbles, Leavitt zealously defended the president while berating Democrats and the “fake news” media. In her first appearance on the podium, she described Trump as “the hardest-working man in politics” with “wildly popular” policies responsible for a new “golden age”.Leavitt was cordial with reporters behind the scenes but could be combative in front of the camera. In January this year, when a journalistraised the killing of Renee Goodby an ICE agent in Minneapolis, Leavitt demanded to know why Good had been killed. The reporter answered: “Because an ICE agent acted recklessly and killed her unjustifiably.” Leavitt, jabbing her finger, snapped: “You’re a leftwing hack. You’re not a reporter. You’re posing in the room as a journalist … You shouldn’t even be sitting in that seat.”Trump often praised Leavitt as an effective communicator and drawing attention to her appearance. He once told the Newsmax network: “She’s become a star. It’s that face, it’s that brain, it’s those lips – the way they move, they move like she’s a machine gun.”On Wednesday the president’s allies joined the acclaim. Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, tweeted: “Karoline Leavitt has served President Trump and the American people with courage and conviction. She’s a great colleague, a fearless voice for the President’s agenda and a true professional.”Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary,added: “Karoline Leavitt has been the most successful Press Secretary in history. Always strong, clear and right to the point … We are all Karoline Leavitt fans!”Democrats, however, took a different view. Adam Schiff, a senator for California, posted: “Karoline Leavitt is leaving the White House to spend a little more time … with the truth.”Trump did not outline plans for who might succeed her. He had four press secretaries during his first term. Sean Spicer is now a political commentator and podcaster; Sarah Huckabee Sanders is now the governor of Arkansas; Stephanie Grisham is now a fierce critic of Trump whospoke at the 2024 Democratic national convention; Kayleigh McEnany is a host on Fox News.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Potatoes ‘boil’ in the ground as record heatwave sweeps across swathes of Asia | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: South Korean farmers are suffering in record heat, as Hong Kong reports its highest ever temperature and Japan swelters through newly designated ‘cruelly hot’ days
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: South Korean farmers are suffering in record heat, as Hong Kong reports its highest ever temperature and Japan swelters through newly designated ‘cruelly hot’ days
Content: Workers picking chilli peppers under a shade parasol during a heat wave warning in Andong, South Korea. East Asia has faced a punishing summer of extreme temperatures.Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/ReutersView image in fullscreenWorkers picking chilli peppers under a shade parasol during a heat wave warning in Andong, South Korea. East Asia has faced a punishing summer of extreme temperatures.Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/ReutersExtreme weatherPotatoes ‘boil’ in the ground as record heatwave sweeps across swathes of AsiaSouth Korean farmers are suffering in record heat, as Hong Kong reports its highest ever temperature and Japan swelters through newly designated ‘cruelly hot’ daysRaphael Rashidin SeoulWed 12 Aug 2026 19.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a potato field in Yanggu county, 80 miles (130km) north-east of Seoul, Lee Sang-hyuk dug into the soil and found nothing worth saving.A week earlier the crop, located in Gangwon province, had looked fine. Now the potatoes came up soft and collapsing, “like boiled potatoes”, spoiled by heat that had turned the ground into something closer to an oven.“It’s not just one or two fields like this. How can I even put it into words? It’s so upsetting,”he toldlocal broadcaster SBS.His ruined harvest is one thread in a punishing summer across east Asia, as record heat swept throughSouth Korea, Japan and Hong Kong in recent weeks.View image in fullscreenWorkers harvest strawberries under parasols in a field in Miryang, South Korea.Photograph: YONHAP/EPAView image in fullscreenAn officer from the Korea Meteorological Administration in Seoul shows a map of the current temperatures across South Korea.Photograph: Lee Jin-man/APOn 2 August, the south-eastern city of Yangsan recorded a temperature of 42.5C, the highest registered in South Korea since modern weather observations began in 1904.The heat has since been blamed for at least 31 deaths nationwide, according to the country’s disease control agency, while more than 900,000 livestock and 1.4 million farmed fish have died.Authoritiesissued a heat warning, urging people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”.South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, told his cabinet the extreme weather was “unlike anything we have experienced before”.“We need to make efforts for a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system,” he said, “since this extreme weather is becoming the new normal.”Typhoon Dim-sum: how Hong Kong put a tasty snack on the storm mapRead moreView image in fullscreenThe dried up bed of a reservoir in Miryang on 3 August 2026, as South Korea is hit by a scorching heatwave.Photograph: Jung Yeon-Je/AFP/Getty ImagesIn neighbouring Japan, temperatures reached 40C or higher at multiple locations and the country recorded itsfirst ever “kokushobi”, or “cruelly hot day”, a new category introduced this year by the country’s weather agency for temperatures above 40C. In Tokyo,three lions diedof suspected heatstroke at a city zoo.Scientists say the extremes are part of a wider pattern. Researchers working through Japan’s Weather Attribution Centre found that the country’s intense July heat would have been “virtually impossible” without global warming.Without the warming caused by human activity, they calculated, a heatwave of this scale would occur on average once ever 10,000 years.The heat struck even as anEl Niño eventwas under way, a natural climate pattern that has in the past been associated with a lower likelihood of extreme summer heat in Japan.In Hong Kong, its observatory posted an official temperature of 36.9C, thehighest recordedthere since records began in 1884, as the outer bands of Typhoon Dolphin swept hot air over the city.View image in fullscreenA fast-food shop worker tries to cool down a person by pouring water over his head, along Nakamise Street in Tokyo.Photograph: Issei Kato/ReutersView image in fullscreenTeruo Sawatari wipes sweat from his brow, as power and water outages persist after an earthquake in Yatsushiro, Japan.Photograph: Issei Kato/ReutersThe record heat also exposed the failings of the city’s heat stress warning system for outdoor workers, which remained at its lowest tier even as temperatures reached a record high.“The threshold for the red warning is clearly set too high”, Lam Chiu Ying, a former head of theHong KongObservatory, wrote on Facebook. “If even a record-breaking temperature can’t trigger it, isn’t it just a display piece used to decorate a shop window?”Hong Kong’s Labour Department has since said it is reviewing the warning system with the observatory.View image in fullscreenResidents walk in Causeway Bay on 9 August, as Hong Kong posted its highest official temperature since records began.Photograph: China News Service/Getty ImagesIn China’s western Xinjiang region, a weather station recorded a 50C reading in July and heatwaves gripped the country’s north-east, while North Korea reported a run of tropical nights in Pyongyang, with temperatures failing to fall below 25C.June-Yi Lee, a climate scientist at Pusan National University and a coordinating lead author of the UN’s most recent climate assessment, said the regional heatwave may have been shaped by a mix of atmospheric circulation patterns and a warming climate.A strengthening ridge of high pressure over the Tibetan Plateau and western Pacific, layered on top of this year’s El Niño, may have helped create conditions for the heat, she said.View image in fullscreenLocal farmers use shade nets to protect tea trees from strong sunlight in China.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesThe World Meteorological Organization said in its latest State of the Climate in Asiareportthat the pace of Asia’s warming between 1991 and 2025 is roughly twice that of the preceding three decades.About 160 miles (257km) south of Seoul, in Gwangju, watermelon farmer Hong Kyung-hee watched fruit that would normally sell at a premium turn to mush.“The inside was good, the sweetness was good, everything was fine”, hetold KBSfrom his farm. “But after three days it changed overnight like this. In my 50 years of farming, this is the first time.”Strawberry farmer Yoon Woo-ha in Damyang county, South Jeolla province, lost seedlings that she had cultivated for three months and won’t be covered by insurance.View image in fullscreenTea farmers operate automatic sprinklers to irrigate drought-affected tea plants in Zhejiang Province, China.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesSouth Korea’s crop insurance scheme covers only designated crops, growing methods and regions, leaving farmers exposed when losses fall outside those boundaries.“When the insurance can’t cover this,” said Lee Jun-kyung, head of the Gwangju chapter of the Korean Peasants League, “it goes straight into farm household debt.”Prof Lee warned that heatwaves were expected to become more frequent and intense as the climate heated up, while compound extremes, such as consecutive heatwaves and heavy rainfall, were becoming more common.“There is an urgent need for rapid, large-scale reductions in greenhouse gas emissions to limit further global warming together with well-planned adaptation measures to address the climate change that is already occurring,” she said.Explore more on these topicsExtreme weatherAsia PacificHong KongJapanSouth KoreaClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame? | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: The climate crisis is hitting Europe hard in 2026, warming twice as fast as any other continent – and the consequences are deadly
Author: Damian Carrington
Headline: The climate crisis is hitting Europe hard in 2026, warming twice as fast as any other continent – and the consequences are deadly
Content: Firefighters battle a wildfire in the Casaboli Forest near Palermo in Italy in July 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFirefighters battle a wildfire in the Casaboli Forest near Palermo in Italy in July 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesExtreme weatherExplainerEurope is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame?The climate crisis is hitting Europe hard in 2026, warming twice as fast as any other continent – and the consequences are deadlyDamian CarringtonEnvironment editorWed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe whole world is getting hotter as carbon pollution from fossil fuel burning traps ever more heat, but Europe is heating up twice as fast as other continents. The consequences are increasingly deadly, with tens of thousands ofheatwave deathsso far this summer.Why is Europe most affected by global heating?Land requires less heat than the vast and deep oceans to warm up, so all continents are warming more quickly than the seas. But Europe is particularly vulnerable for four reasons: changed weather patterns, its closeness to the Arctic, less snow and less air pollution.graph showing warming of continentsAs a result, Europe is now 2.5C hotter than before the mass burning of fossil fuels, almost double the global average 1.4C rise. Temperatures in Europe have risen by 0.56C a decade since the mid-1990s, compared with 0.42C in North America, 0.36C in Africa and 0.27C in South America.How have Europe’s weather patterns changed?Shifts in how the atmosphere circulates over Europe have led to more frequent and more intense summer heatwaves. This includes the worst ever heatwave, in June 2026, in which a vast area of hot air was trapped under a stationary “heat dome”.Scientists are still investigating the role of global heating in causing changes in atmospheric circulation, but a link seems increasingly likely.Dr Samantha Burgess, from the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, said: “We see statistically significant changes in surface pressure patterns and other measures of circulation when we look at trends over the last 40 or more years, and on this timescale they are more likely associated with climate change than natural variability.”The association may be the result of achanging jet stream, a fast high-level wind that has a powerful influence on Europe’s weather and is itself affected by rising temperatures.Why is the Arctic important?The Arctic is the fastest warming region on the planet, despite having no land. This is because the white polar ice cap, which normally reflects the vast majority of sunlight back into space, is melting away fast. As a result, the darker ocean exposed by the melting absorbs much more heat, which then melts more ice, forming a vicious circle. With a significant proportion of Europe relatively close to the Arctic, temperatures are therefore rising faster.What about snow cover?Most of Europe had snowfall in winter in the past. Like the Arctic sea ice, this snow reflected sunlight and kept the continent cooler. But the climate crisis is shrinking snow-covered areas.In March 2025,Europe’s blanket of snow was about 1.3m km2below the 1991-2020 average, a 31% drop. That lost area is roughly the area of France, Italy, Germany, Switzerland and Austria combined. It was the third lowest snow cover since records began in 1983.Why does reduced air pollution affect temperatures?Air pollution kills millions of people globally every year and so Europe’s record of cutting toxic air levels in recent decades is unequivocally a good thing. However, cleaner air is also unmasking the impact of the rise in carbon dioxide pollution in the atmosphere.Air pollution particles can reflect the sun’s rays, directly or by seeding the formation of clouds, meaning the heat does not reach the ground. Fewer particles means less reflection and more heat that is trapped by greenhouse gases. Lower pollution might even beconnected to the increase in blocking weather patterns.How important is each of the four factors above?The short answer is that scientists don’t yet know, but they aim to have an estimate next year.Burgess said: “What we can say is that the importance of each factor must vary with season, with proximity to the Arctic important in autumn and winter, and circulation changes since the late 1970s of greater statistical significance in summer.”The drop in air pollution is most marked in winter because of declining coal heating in homes, and snow cover is a winter issue. Winter warming in Europe in recent decades has been strongest in the north, while summer warming has been strongest in the south-east.What are the consequences?The rapid heating is leading to ever more deaths and more intense wildfires and droughts. Storms, intense rainfall and floods are also being supercharged by the extra heat in the climate system. All deeply affect lives and livelihoods across the continent and will continue to worsen until emissions reach net zero. Rapid cuts in CO2pollution and the rollout of measures to protect citizens are urgently needed.The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, said in late July: “The awful costs of this climate crisis – both human and economic – are now reaching national emergency levels. What needs to be done is clear: leave coal, oil and gas behind faster, scale up renewables, and protect people.”The Guardian’s climate forum 2026: On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington and our panel of experts, including Professor Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman, for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. Book ticketshereor atguardian.liveskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis article was amended on 12 August 2026. An earlier version said the snow blanket coveringEuropein March 2025 was 1.3m km2; this should have said 1.3m km2below the 1991-2020 average.Explore more on these topicsExtreme weatherFossil fuelsPollutionClimate crisisEuropeGreenhouse gas emissionsHealthexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Nigel Farage and Count Binface: a visual guide to their electoral careers | Clacton byelection August 2026 | The Guardian
description: Farage was elected to EU parliament five times before becoming Clacton MP, while Binface has been less successful – so far
Author: Seán Clarke
Headline: Farage was elected to EU parliament five times before becoming Clacton MP, while Binface has been less successful – so far
Content: Farage (right) resigned and triggered a byelection, with Binface his main rival after the major parties pulled out.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFarage (right) resigned and triggered a byelection, with Binface his main rival after the major parties pulled out.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesClacton byelection August 2026Nigel Farage and Count Binface: a visual guide to their electoral careersFarage was elected to EU parliament five times before becoming Clacton MP, while Binface has been less successful – so farSeán ClarkeWed 12 Aug 2026 03.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 03.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage has been standing in British elections since 1994, when he narrowly beat Screaming Lord Sutch of the Monster Raving Loony party into fourth place in a Commons byelection. He was elected five times to the European parliament before achieving his goal of abolishing his seat.Finally, after 30 years of trying, he was elected to the Commons as member for Clacton in 2024. He resigned that hard-won seat in July after a parliamentary inquiry was launched into a £5m gift he accepted from a Thailand-based businessman shortly before the general election, but is standing again in the resulting byelection on Thursday. The other major parties are not putting up candidates, so the chief contenders, according to the limited polling, are Farage andCount Binface.These charts show the respective electoral histories of the two main runners.Farage historyCount Binface, or rather, his earthling avatar the comedian and writer Jon Harvey, has had a shorter and, so far, less successful electoral career, although he has stood against four prime ministers. On Thursday, he will face Farage at the ballot box for the first time, alongside his longstanding electoral adversary Laurence Fox, standing for Reclaim.Binface historyOver the years, Nigel Farage has stood against dozens of British politicians, including in 2006 a young Labour candidate by the name of Rachel Reeves.View image in fullscreenRachel Reeves at the Bromley and Chislehurst count in 2006.Photograph: Chris Young/PAIn her capacity as chancellor a few weeks ago, it fell to Reeves to accept Farage’s resignation as MP for Clacton. There was some speculation at the time that she was not obliged to do it, but she accepted the resignation on the basis that “if he [Farage] wants to spend summer arguing with a bin, I won’t stop him.”Bromley 2006 resultsThursday’s contest will, of course, not be the first time that either Farage or Binface has faced a novelty opponent. Riding high in the polls in 2015, Farage was so confident of winning Thanet South in that year’s general election that he pledged to resign as leader of Ukip if he did not take the seat.View image in fullscreenAl Murray (right) and Nigel Farage at the 2015 Thanet South count.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesThis led Al Murray, a comedian whose main persona is the Pub Landlord, a straight-talking conservative patriot, to stand against Farage. Even without the resulting split in the straight-talking conservative patriot vote, Farage would have lost the seat. Ever a man of his word, Farage resigned, and then unresigned three days later.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThanet 2015Harvey’s first electoral foray was not as Count Binface at all, but rather as the similarly behatted persona of Lord Buckethead. He was moved to adopt the Binface persona when a man got in touch claiming to hold copyright in the Buckethead character. In 2019, having failed to prorogue parliament, the then prime minister, Boris Johnson, called an early general election. A roster of novelty candidates – and Boris Johnson – ran in Uxbridge and South Ruislip, among them for the first and only time, both Count Binface and a copyright-approved Lord Buckethead.View image in fullscreenCount Binface (right) greets Lord Buckethead (left) at the Uxbridge count in 2019.Photograph: James Veysey/Rex/ShutterstockUxbridge 2019Voters in Clacton on Thursday can, of course, choose to vote for neither Binface nor Farage. In fact, there are34 candidatesin all, including three from the Monster Raving Loony party.Explore more on these topicsClacton byelection August 2026Nigel FarageCount BinfaceEnglandShareReuse this content

title: From grey water to cool spaces: 10 climate crisis policies Britain needs right now | Environment policy | The Guardian
description: Rejecting North Sea drilling licences and protecting nature are just some measures Andy Burnham must implement to ready country
Author: Matthew Taylor
Headline: Rejecting North Sea drilling licences and protecting nature are just some measures Andy Burnham must implement to ready country
Content: A burned field of wheat in Eton Wick, Windsor, in July. Experts say the UK should regenerative agriculture approaches to increase food resilience.Photograph: Maureen McLean/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA burned field of wheat in Eton Wick, Windsor, in July. Experts say the UK should regenerative agriculture approaches to increase food resilience.Photograph: Maureen McLean/REX/ShutterstockEnvironment policyFrom grey water to cool spaces: 10 climate crisis policies Britain needs right nowRejecting North Sea drilling licences and protecting nature are just some measures Andy Burnham must implement to ready countryMatthew Taylor,Sandra Laville,Damian CarringtonandPippa NeillWed 12 Aug 2026 10.34 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 09.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom record-smashing temperatures, wildfires, hosepipe bans and thousands ofpremature deaths, the climate crisis has left its mark across the summer of 2026.Tackling the root cause – the burning of fossil fuels – and ending the crisis will take years. So will fixing the UK government’scalamitousfailuretoprotect lives and livelihoodsagainst the long-predicted affects of global heating.But the climate emergency is right here, right now, and here are 10 policies that Andy Burnham’s government should consider announcing urgently.1. Reject drilling licences for the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gasfieldsThis would be a vital and confidence-boosting sign that the UK is committed to putting a rocket-booster under the clean, green andvery fast-growing economyof the 21st century, not the fossil-fuelled one of the last. It would also give diplomatic weight to the UK as it works internationally to cut emissions and end the climate crisis.The supposed benefits of approving the North Sea oil and gasfields are mostly fantasy. They will have no impact on UK energy prices – oil and gas are commodities whose price is set by international markets. As theUK Energy Research Councilsays: “Assertions that drilling the North Sea will provide energy resilience and affordability in the face of current fuel price shocks are a delusion.”As for jobs, the licences would supportvery few– again, unlike thegrowing green economy. Some also argue North Sea production is less carbon intensive than imports, but that ignores thefar cleaner recordof our main gas importer, Norway, as well as themethane emissions from LNG, and in any case the differences are small compared with CO2 savings of using renewable energy and storage instead of gas.2. Increase windfall tax on fossil fuel giants to pay for adaptation measuresWhen people say money is tight, remember theeight biggest oil companies made a staggering $93bnin the three months to the end of June – almost double their profits from the same period last year. At the same time, carbon emissions from the oil and gas these companies produce are driving the escalating climate crisis, and bills for ordinary consumers continue to rise. An increased windfall tax on these excess profits could raise huge sums for government coffers and help pay for emergency adaptation measures.View image in fullscreenGreen businesses and jobs are booming in the UK.Photograph: Peter Oliver/Alamy3. Make grey water reuse mandatory in new buildings and incentivise rainwater harvestingThe UK is predicted to face a shortfall of 5bn litres of water a day – that’s 2,000 Olympic-sized pools of water – by 2055. Grey water recycling or reuse captures water from sinks, showers, baths, washing machines and other “wash water” sources – not toilets – for use in homes. Rainwater capture is another way to make homes more water efficient and reduce the demand for drinking water. Grey water is not safe to drink but reusing it for other activities, such as toilet flushing, can reduce an individual’s water consumptionby 50%.View image in fullscreenUsing grey water to flush toilets, for example, can significantly reduce water consumption.Photograph: Claudia Gopperl/Getty Images/beyond fotomedia RFIn some water-stressed areas, developers must demonstrate no net increase in water use. But there is no mandate for grey water systems within the government’s future homes standard. The Drinking Water Inspectorate is now movingtowards removing these legislative barriers.4. Bring the water industry under national controlThe privatised water system has overseenrecord sewage pollution levelsin rivers and seas and presided over a system which critics argue prioritises shareholder dividends, big salaries and bonuses over investing in and maintaining a vital public infrastructure. More than £85bn has gone to shareholders, while the industry has failed to upgrade infrastructure to make it resilient to climate change by building reservoirs, upgrading pipes to stop leaking – a fifth of water running through pipes is lost to leakage – and making sure wastewater treatment plants have capacity for sewage treatment.View image in fullscreenWater companies have been accused of putting shareholders before investment.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesWith debts of more than £60bn, the industry in many cases is unable to provide the service it is legally bound to – treat wastewater and provide drinking water. Campaigners such as Surfers Against Sewage argue a publicly controlled water industry will remove short-term profit motives, allow access to lower-cost public borrowing for massive capital investments, and enforce a 25- to 50-year resilience strategy across regional catchments rather than the fragmented corporate boundaries that exist now.5. Invest in proper equipment for firefightersFire brigades in Britain are short of the equipmentneeded to fight large, unpredictable wildfires. While, for example, Spanish emergency services and the military extensively use specialised amphibious planes and helicopters to scoop up water and dump it on wildfires, the UK does not own any dedicated water-bombing planes. Instead, British fire services rely on ground crews, with occasional military support for heavy lifting, and privately chartered commercial helicopters equipped with suspended buckets to drop water on large wildfires.View image in fullscreenFirefighters in the UK are under increased pressure after a summer of wildfires.Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images6. Implement a maximum workplace temperatureDuring June’s heatwaves, temperatures in some workplaces became unbearable – and dangerous. Teachersreportedclassrooms reaching well over 40C with children and staff struggling to cope, while bus driversspokeabout the “horrendous” working conditions with temperatures again in excess of 40C in their cabs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Trades Union Congress (TUC) wants a maximum working temperature, a demand recently backed by the government’s advisers on the Climate Change Committee. They want rules to ensure employers take steps to reduce workplace temperatures if they get above 24C and the right for workers to stop work if they reach 30C, or 27C for those doing strenuous jobs.7. Fund cool spaces in every communityAs heatwaves intensify – and become more dangerous for younger, older and more vulnerable people – having free access to a nearby space that is cool, well-ventilated and comfortable will become increasingly important. Experts say that school halls, libraries or leisure centres are among the buildings that could be reassigned when extreme heat hits. Barcelona has been a pioneer of these climate shelters and now has more than 400 across the city. The idea has now spread across Europe and experts say this summer’s heat shows it is time the UK caught up.8. Launch a national retrofit programmeHomes in the UK are among the draughtiest and least energy-efficient in Europe. This means they are often too hot in summer and too cold in winter, leading to high bills and spiralling carbon emissions.Efforts to persuade the private sector to take on the challenge of making homes fit for the changing climate have failed. Buta report earlier this yearsuggested councils could take the lead on a retrofitting programme backed by national government. Under the plan, councils would train and employ their own retrofitting workforce and, starting with key public services such as hospitals and care homes, then work through council and social housing before moving on to privately owned homes. The report said it would not only make the country’s homes and public services more climate resilient, but it would also tackle the cost of living, create secure jobs and stimulate growth. They added it would also be a more efficient way of spending the public funds already allocated for insulation.9. Plant more trees and protect existing natureAs well as absorbing atmospheric carbon and locking it up for centuries, planting more trees creates shade that can reduce the urban heat island effect. Neighbourhoods with more than 20% urban tree canopyhave been foundto experience a net cooling effect.View image in fullscreenPlanting trees and conserving existing trees has a cooling effect.Photograph: Justin Paget/Getty ImagesMore than four in five homes and workplaces across 25 European cities have less nearby tree canopy than what is needed for meaningful cooling, according toRMIT University. While planting trees today can create cooling in the future, the researchers said a newly planted tree would not shade a building for 15 or 20 years and so conserving our existing trees was essential.“Every mature tree lost now is irreplaceable on the timeline that matters for current heatwaves,” said lead author, Dr Thami Croeser.10. Encourage regenerative agriculture approaches to increase food resilienceRegenerative farming is an approach to farming that allows the land, soil, water, nutrients and natural assets to regenerate themselves, as opposed to conventional approaches to farming that can deplete these natural resources.View image in fullscreenRegenerative farming can help crops become more resistant to drought.Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/ShutterstockThis approach can help crops become more resilient to drought and dry weather. In onestudy, regenerative management of the soil led to a 23% increase in soil moisture content, and it has been shown to increase yields.Alastair Chisholm, water, policy, regulation and governance lead at consultancy firm Arup, said current agricultural policies were not driving widespread regenerative approaches, but that changing this would be an easy win to boost food security.Explore more on these topicsEnvironment policyClimate crisisAndy BurnhamWildfiresFossil fuelsEnergyEnergy efficiencyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Top chefs find grouse in short supply as wildfires add to heat over shoots | Rural affairs | The Guardian
description: As London restaurants say wild birds are smaller and fewer this year, experts say countryside should not be ‘playground for bloodsports’
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: As London restaurants say wild birds are smaller and fewer this year, experts say countryside should not be ‘playground for bloodsports’
Content: A red grouse in heather moorland. Wildfires have been raging across the UK, burning habitats and incinerating wildlife.Photograph: Wild Dales Photography/Simon Phillpotts/AlamyView image in fullscreenA red grouse in heather moorland. Wildfires have been raging across the UK, burning habitats and incinerating wildlife.Photograph: Wild Dales Photography/Simon Phillpotts/AlamyRural affairsTop chefs find grouse in short supply as wildfires add to heat over shootsAs London restaurants say wild birds are smaller and fewer this year, experts say countryside should not be ‘playground for bloodsports’Helena HortonWed 12 Aug 2026 08.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery year on 12 August, fans of traditional British cuisine flock to plush restaurants in Mayfair to dine on grouse served with bread sauce and game chips. But those hoping to find the small wild birds, sourced from the UK’s moorlands, may be disappointed.Wildfires have been raging on moors across the UK, burning habitats and incinerating wildlife, after record-breaking heat turned the landscape into a tinderbox.The intensive management of grouse moors involves the draining of peatland and the burning of the vegetation that grows on it. Environmental experts argue that doing this creates the conditions for wildfires as dry peat acts as fuel and smoulders for extended periods, making fires almost impossible to extinguish.Because of this, the Green party in Scotland, where there are a large number of grouse shoots, has called for the Glorious Twelfth – the traditional start of the grouse shooting season, before which time the birds cannot legally be hunted – to be banned. The UK government recentlybanned the burning of vegetationon deep peat in order to preserve these habitats.The climate crisis, caused by pollution from burning fossil fuels, makes every heatwave more likely and intense. The heatwave at the end of June was themost severe ever recorded in Europeand would not have been possible without human-caused global heating.The chef Richard Corrigan, who owns Corrigan’s and Bentley’s in Mayfair, has always served grouse during his multi-decade career running kitchens. But this year they are in short supply.View image in fullscreenRichard Corrigan: ‘I am not too sure I agree with the large shoots.’Photograph: Jamie Lorriman/AlamyHe said: “I was hoping to get something on the 12th; it’s looking like it’s running a week and a half late. They will be smaller and fewer, which is fine and it is a treat. We should treat them with the respect they deserve. The hot weather hasn’t helped everything this year, that’s for sure.”Corrigan will be finding it more difficult than some chefs to get birds for the table because he has become more particular about who he buys grouse from. “We now insist [birds] come from small estates rather than the large shoots, where dozens are shot at a time. I am not too sure I agree with the large shoots. I would rather people shoot wild animals for the table rather than shoot for the sake of having a day out.”He also refuses to buy grouse from any moor that has been associated with raptor persecution – the shooting or poisoning of birds of prey to artificially boost grouse numbers. “Something that has really annoyed me is the killing of raptor birds on the estates. They are being poisoned by people on these estates. I would never buy grouse from those estates. We all know who they are,” Corrigan said.The chef, who grew up in County Meath, Ireland, said the management of the moors had led to them being more susceptible to wildfires. “I was brought up in moorland, I am very aware of the heather and the turf, they need the wetlands to be restored to keep the moors in good shape. Some estates have taken it all a bit too far and have turned it into factory grouse shooting operations.”While some will be serving their grouse with bread sauce and game chips, which are deep-fried, thin slices of potato, Corrigan is going to dish out a lighter option. “They will be on the menu barbecued with peaches and jalapeño. There is nothing better to eat than peaches from Provence and little spatchcocked grouse.”View image in fullscreenHenry Harris at Bouchon Racine.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianHenry Harris, the chef-owner ofBouchon Racinein Farringdon, London, said he was keeping his fingers crossed that he would receive grouse this week from his supplier. “I will know today whether there’s been a problem,’ he said. “If they fly, they will be shot. If it is too hot, they will not fly. If the weather really is too hot, they tend to struggle to drive them up into the air, which will mean there are less birds out there.”He added that he was concerned about the wildfires and their impact on moorland wildlife, including grouse. “People do expect us to serve it, it is very popular,” he said. “We had a queue for them last year.”Unlike Corrigan’s untraditional peach and jalapeño recipe, Harris said he would be “serving it very traditionally with a slight Gallic twist, on a lovely piece of sourdough toast with a bit of paté, armagnac sauce, bread sauce and game chips”.Ariane Burgess, the rural affairs spokesperson for the Scottish Greens, will not be joining the queue. She said the countryside should not be “managed as a playground for bloodsports”, and the moors ofScotlandwere “intensively managed so that grouse can be killed for entertainment”.She said: “Scotland’s land is one of our greatest assets. It should be supporting thriving rural communities, restoring nature and tackling the climate crisis, rather than serving as a private playground for the wealthy few.“The real glorious future for Scotland’s moors would be seeing wildlife flourish on them, peatlands restored and rural jobs created through the recovery of our natural environment.”Explore more on these topicsRural affairsHuntingBirdsWildfiresScotlandRestaurantsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Houses with long histories are magical’: David Olusoga on the home history show that’s gripped the UK | Television | The Guardian
description: At first, I worried that only historians would find A House Through Time compelling. But its appeal is so enduring that fans of the show stop me in the street to ask when they can watch more
Author: David Olusoga
Headline: At first, I worried that only historians would find A House Through Time compelling. But its appeal is so enduring that fans of the show stop me in the street to ask when they can watch more
Content: ‘The architecture of Edinburgh is special’ … David Olusoga in the Scottish capital for his new BBC Two series of A House Through Time.Photograph: BBC/Twenty Twenty Productions Ltd/Richard RankenView image in fullscreen‘The architecture of Edinburgh is special’ … David Olusoga in the Scottish capital for his new BBC Two series of A House Through Time.Photograph: BBC/Twenty Twenty Productions Ltd/Richard RankenTelevision‘Houses with long histories are magical’: David Olusoga on the home history show that’s gripped the UKAt first, I worried that only historians would find A House Through Time compelling. But its appeal is so enduring that fans of the show stop me in the street to ask when they can watch moreDavid OlusogaWed 12 Aug 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy is that some TV programmes find an audience, catch people’s imaginations and become not just watched but loved? Most of course do not. Having been making TV since my late 20s and been involved in a number of “first” series that ended up being the only series, I am painfully aware of that. If producers knew in advance which shows would be hits, there would be no flops, as the industry cliche goes.Producers and presenters are lucky if, during our careers, we get to be involved in a single show that makes that rare transition from being part of the schedule to part of people’s lives. Almost a decade ago, while we were filming the first series ofA House Through Timefor BBC Two, I was not at all convinced that this was a show that had the potential to break through.Having studied urban history for my master’s, I always loved the central premise: that we could explore the histories of Britain’s great cities through the people who had lived in a single house, from the very first resident right up to the current owners. Likewise, I was, from the start, enamoured of the astonishing array of human stories which the brilliant teams that worked on the series managed to unearth.I liked the way thehistory of the housein that first series, 62 Falkner Street in Liverpool’s Georgian Quarter, perfectly followed the broader history of Liverpool: the city’s rapid rise to wealth and power as the great port of empire, its devastation in the blitz, then a precipitous postwar decline that saw 62 Falkner Street become a warren of slum apartments seemingly doomed for demolition only to be reprieved by the gentrification of the early 21st century.However, I was concerned that audiences would struggle to understand why we had locked ourselves into the straitjacket of a single house. Why were we viewing the past through such a tiny aperture? What were we missing by being so tightly focused? At times during the scripting and the filming of that first series, I worried that perhaps I was too close to the subject and that only historians of the city would find the show compelling. I was, it turned out, doing what TV producers are infamous for doing. I was underestimating the audience.View image in fullscreen‘One of those shows that only TV could make’ … David Olusoga with Kate Lister in the garden of the Edinburgh House in A House Through Time.Photograph: BBC/Twenty Twenty Productions Ltd/Richard RankenThis month, almost 10 years after the first series was commissioned, series six of A House Through Time goes to air. We have now made 24 hour-long episodes that have explored the hidden histories of houses in Liverpool, Newcastle, Bristol, Leeds, London, Berlin and nowEdinburgh.Like everyone who presents TV shows, I am regularly stopped on the street by people who recognise me from their screen. Most often what they want to talk about is A House Through Time.Amazingly, that remains the case even after I appeared on the great TV juggernaut of our time: The Celebrity Traitors. The first question I am asked by the fans of A House Through Timeis almost always the same: when is the next series coming out? So I am left to wonder why a show about which I had doubts has been such a hit. What had I not appreciated 10 years ago?What I didn’t get back then, above all, is what old houses mean to the people who live in them. Houses with long histories are magical places. Anyone who has ever lived in such a house has, on a sleepless night or perhaps after too many glasses of wine, found themselves wondering who else had lived out their life in those same rooms. Whose hands once gripped the same banisters; who, like you, knew where the creaky floorboard was and which windows would start rattling on a windy night?A House Through Time reveals – in incredible detail – the sorts of human stories that would tumble out of our own home if only we had the time to go looking. It reminds us that houses have longer lives than we do. That no matter how many years or decades we live in them, our time there represents a single chapter in their far longer story.After making 24 hours of A House Through Time,and with the TV industry in a less healthy state than it was a decade ago, I also now appreciate, more than ever, that it is one of those shows that only TV could make.Only TV – and let’s be more specific, only public service TV – would invest the time and money needed to uncover history at this level of granularity. Only TV would believe that the stories of ordinary people – not kings or presidents or movie stars – could grip audiences of millions. And only TV is capable of assembling teams of specialist researchers, assistant producers, producer/directors, series producers and executive producers with the skills needed to track down the thousands of documents that become the jigsaw pieces that make up the bigger historical puzzle.In every series, breakthroughs have arrived at the last minute, often in the last weeks of filming, all because an assistant producer or a researcher, digging in the archives and working far beyond the call of duty, has located a missing link or noticed a tiny detail that answers a nagging question or confirms a long-held suspicion.This new series follows the same pattern but in a new nation. I have long wanted to take A House Through Time to Scotland, and series six is set in an 18th-century house up on Calton Hill in Edinburgh. The Scottish capital was hard to resist. Edinburgh is one of the handful of cities that are not just architecturally but also topographically breathtaking. Built around a castle that sits on top of an extinct volcano, with other volcanic features looming on the horizon, Edinburgh is up there with Cape Town, Hong Kong and Rio de Janeiro when it comes to the sheer drama of its setting.The architecture of Edinburgh is similarly special. Encircled by city walls, Edinburgh had a scarcity of space that meant the only direction in which to build was up. The result was a vertical city of stone tenements, some rising to 10 or more floors. Edinburgh has been described as a medieval Manhattan. When it comes to urban density and vertical living, it has more in common with Prague and Stockholm than it does with most English cities. Our house, up on Calton Hill, is one of Edinburgh’s smaller tenements – a stolid stone structure built over five floors.As with the previous series, the life stories of the people who lived in those rooms are diverse and idiosyncratic. Among the earliest tenants was a man at the centre of one of the strangest trials in Edinburgh’s history, having committed a crime so bizarre and infamous that it was depicted in engravings that were sold on the city streets. Another resident took up arms, joining a volunteer regiment during the fraught and divided years after the French revolution, when the elite and the middle classes saw the spectre of revolution in every darkened corner.One of our Victorian residents was a woman who, more than any of the figures from the past who have appeared in any of the previous series, successfully eluded the efforts of the production team to pin down her story. Why was she so elusive? Perhaps because she converted the house into what Edinburgh police records rather delicately describe as “a house of ill-fame”. Another of our 19th-century residents was a sculptor who created monuments that are still peppered across the Edinburgh cityscape, statues I have been walking past since I was brought to the city as a child in the 1970s.If there is another reason to explain why A House Through Time has caught on it is that the series plays a small part in a bigger story: the expansion of history. History has for decades been getting bigger and more inclusive. History is no longer just about “great men”. The emergence of social history, working-class history, women’s history and imperial history has uncovered the lives of people once deemed of little interest. The genealogy revolution has made millions of people into amateur historians. Today our ancestors – all of them, no matter how humble their lives – are deemed worthy of study and remembrance.A House Through Time is on BBC Two on Thursday 13 August at 9pmExplore more on these topicsTelevisionDavid OlusogaDocumentaryFactual TVSocial historyEdinburghfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Emiko Davies’ Japanese curry rice (kare raisu) – recipe | Australian food and drink | The Guardian
description: The Australian-born cook and author shares her recipe for a thick, fragrant Japanese curry – with one secret ingredient
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Australian-born cook and author shares her recipe for a thick, fragrant Japanese curry – with one secret ingredient
Content: Japanese curry needs to be thick enough so that it can be easily eaten with rice, with the help of a spoon.Photograph: Emiko DaviesView image in fullscreenJapanese curry needs to be thick enough so that it can be easily eaten with rice, with the help of a spoon.Photograph: Emiko DaviesAustralian food and drinkEmiko Davies’ Japanese curry rice (kare raisu) – recipeThe Australian-born cook and author shares her recipe for a thick, fragrant Japanese curry – with one secret ingredientEmiko DaviesWed 12 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJapanese curry – kare raisu in Japanese – is unlike any “curry” you might know from south Asian countries. That is partly because of the nature of yoshoku (western-influenced) cuisine but also because it made a roundabout route to Japan, via the British Royal Navy during the Meiji Restoration, a period when India was under British colonial rule. It arrived in the form of British “C&B” curry powder, so it was considered western food, not Indian.Currybecame a staple in the Japanese naval and army kitchens at the turn of the century and this in turn brought curry into homes and even into school lunches. Today, it is considered a national dish.View image in fullscreenToday, kaire raisu is considered a national dish in Japan.Photograph: Emiko DaviesJapanese curry needed to be thick enough so that it could be easily eaten with rice, with the help of a spoon. This can be achieved with a French-style roux base of butter, flour and liquid, or it can be thickened in a more Japanese style using a potato starchy slurry right at the end of cooking, which is my preference. Then there is the spice mix. Today, Japanese S&B curry powder is one of the best known, which contains 17 spices such as turmeric, coriander, fenugreek, cumin, cinnamon, fennel, ginger and star anise.In Japanese homes, it is most often made with a packet mix in the form of waxy cubes that you add to a stew of meat and vegetables. The cubes dissolve, turning the stew into a thick, fragrant, mild Japanese curry. Everyone has their favourite brand, or perhaps two favourite brands mixed together, that they pump up with “secret” ingredients – honey, nashi or prunes for sweetness, or coffee for colour and balance. My mother told me of a friend who liked to add dark chocolate. I know how well that works in a meaty stew – chocolate or cocoa is a popular addition to an age-old Tuscan wild boar stew that I love.Serves4300g pork loin(or beef, or other protein of choice)Vegetable oil, for greasing40g butter1 onion, sliced4cm piece of freshginger, peeled and finely grated2 tbsp mirin(or white wine)1 tbsp curry powder2 tsp garam marsala¼ tsp chilli powder,optional500ml dashi(see below), chicken stock or water, 2 cups1 tbsp soy sauce½ tsp salt1 carrot,peeled and chopped into chunky slices200g potato,peeled and chopped80g mushrooms,roughly chopped2 tsp potato starchor cornflour1 tbsp water, or as needed1 cubedark chocolate, about 10g, minimum 70% cocoa solidsRice and picklesto serve – I love beni shoga (red pickled ginger) and rakkyo pickles (pickled Chinese onion)Chop the meat into 3cm cubes. Heat a little vegetable oil in a heavy-based saucepan over a high heat and sear the meat on all sides, about four to five minutes in total. Remove the meat and set aside.Reduce the heat to medium and add the butter to the pan, followed by the onion and ginger, and stir quickly so the onion doesn’t burn, cooking with all the browned bits gathering at the bottom of the pan, for about two to three minutes. Deglaze the pan with the mirin and scrape the brown goodness off the bottom as it bubbles. Add the curry powder, garam masala and chilli powder (if using), toss to coat everything, then add the dashi, soy sauce, salt, vegetables and meat. Cover and cook for 20 minutes, turning the heat down to a gentle simmer.Meanwhile, combine the potato starch and water to make a slurry.Add the chocolate to the curry, stir though, then immediately add the slurry. Let it all bubble for one to two minutes, or until thickened. Serve immediately, ladled over warm rice, with pickles on the side.Dashi stockTo make this vegetarian, leave out the katsuobushi and double the amount of kombu. The dashi can be stored in a jar in the fridge for up to a week.Makes1 litre (4 cups)1 piece of kombu(dried kelp), about 10-15cm long or 10g10g katsuobushi(dried bonito flakes), 1 packed cupWipe the kombu with a clean cloth and place in a saucepan with one litre (four cups) of cold water. Leave to steep, if you can, for at least 30 minutes, or overnight.Set the pan over a low heat and warm until the kombu softens and the water is about to start boiling – you will see lots of tiny bubbles appear around the edges of the pan – about 10 minutes. Remove the kombu.Turn the heat up ever so slightly to medium and add the katsuobushi to the kombu-infused water. Watch carefully – just as it’s about to boil, turn off the heat, skim off any scum that rises to the top, and let it steep for five to 10 minutes.Strain the dashi through a fine-mesh sieve.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Smith Street BooksThis is an edited extract ofGohanby Emiko Davies, photography Emiko Davies, Hana Davies and Yuki Sugiura, available now through Smith Street Books (AU $49.99).Explore more on these topicsAustralian food and drinkJapanese food and drinkCurryRiceWinter food and drinkFoodrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Too many holes! Why badgers are digging up Britain’s lovingly maintained golf courses | Badgers | The Guardian
description: Thanks to the drought, these black-and-white beauties are struggling to catch worms in the rock-hard earth. But there’s still good foraging on well-watered fairways and greens
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Thanks to the drought, these black-and-white beauties are struggling to catch worms in the rock-hard earth. But there’s still good foraging on well-watered fairways and greens
Content: What’s black and white and eats greens?Photograph: Stuart P/Getty Images/500pxView image in fullscreenWhat’s black and white and eats greens?Photograph: Stuart P/Getty Images/500pxPass notesBadgersToo many holes! Why badgers are digging up Britain’s lovingly maintained golf coursesThanks to the drought, these black-and-white beauties are struggling to catch worms in the rock-hard earth. But there’s still good foraging on well-watered fairways and greensWed 12 Aug 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Badgers.Age:European badgers live for five to eight years in the wild. They have been in the UK, where this story is set, for half to three-quarters of a million years.Appearance:Black and white mustelid anarcho-syndicalists.Hardly. Badgers are quite posh, aren’t they?Well, perhaps. But everyone has their breaking point, and now I must inform you that badgers have become embroiled in an aggressive form of anti-capitalist class warfare.What turned them? The cost of living? The rise of the billionaire class?Close, but no. It was the drought.How so?This has been a historically hot summerin the UK. England and Wales endured thedriest July since records began(1836). All the grass is brown and dead. There are wildfires everywhere and 26 million people are living with a hosepipe ban.It’s awful.Yes, especially for the badgers. Most of their food lives underground, and it’s much harder to get to it when the earth has been baked dry by the sun.So what’s the solution?That’s easy: turn over a few golf courses.Are they really into clubhouse sandwiches?Not when there are nice wet lawns to tear up.Why do golf courses have wet lawns during a drought?The Water Use (Temporary Bans) Order 2010 permits exemptions for watering sports turf. That means that while you are carefully sharing your bathwater, your local golf course is hosing its lush greens.Yes, but the badgers.Oh, right. Well, if you’re a badger and you need to dig up some worms, and all the ground is hard except for golf courses, where do you think you’re going to get your worms?From golf courses?That’s right! Jim Croxton, chief executive of the British and InternationalGolfGreenkeepers Association, says: “Badgers generally dig turf to find food and August is the beginning of the period when chafer grubs are generally present.”Is it a widespreadproblem?Golf courses from Suffolk to Staffordshire to Worcestershire have reported greens being torn up by badgers,according to the Telegraph.This sounds like a victimless crime.You would think so, but the golf courses are very upset about it.How upset?A video of one ripped-up course posted to Facebook prompted the furious comment: “They’re a f*ckin pest, I’ve had countless ornamental lawns wrecked by these f*ckers.”Quite right. Will nobody think of the ornamental lawns?Exactly. It’s clear that there needs to be an urgent change to the law.To what?Well, it obviously isn’t fair that golf courses are exempt from the hosepipe ban in a time of national crisis.But then the badgers would have nowhere to eat, and theywould die.No they wouldn’t. Badgers are enterprising creatures. They’d find a way.Do say:“The badgers have absolutely massacred hole nine.”Don’t say:“Four legs good, golf clubs bad.”Explore more on these topicsBadgersPass notesGolfAnimalsWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Traitors’ Stephen Libby on fashion: need some thrifty tailoring? Try your local dry cleaner | Men's fashion | The Guardian
description: Alterations that don’t cost a fortune can transform old trousers, jackets or shirts into bespoke pieces
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Alterations that don’t cost a fortune can transform old trousers, jackets or shirts into bespoke pieces
Content: Styling: Sam Deaman.Photograph: David Newby/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStyling: Sam Deaman.Photograph: David Newby/The GuardianStephen Libby on men's fashionMen's fashionTraitors’ Stephen Libby on fashion: need some thrifty tailoring? Try your local dry cleanerAlterations that don’t cost a fortune can transform old trousers, jackets or shirts into bespoke piecesStephen LibbyWed 12 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.When I started shopping in vintage stores, I fell into the trap of thinking that if something wasn’t in my size there was nothing to be done. I’d still buy beautiful shirts that were huge, but never end up wearing them. I persevered with trousers that were three sizes too big and just scrunched in the waist with a belt, but it didn’t look good. Now I know that a belt is an accessory, not a necessity; it’s there to heighten the garment, not hold it up. And that’s because I have finally understood the power of tailoring.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Tailoring seems out of reach for most people, but more often than not a dry cleaner will be able to take in a waist or do the hem, which would set you back £30 max. And I mean, how much would you pay for a perfectly fitting pair of trousers?I started with a few items in my wardrobe that I loved but hadn’t been able to wear, and I suggest you do the same if this is your first go. You already know you love it, and you’ve already paid for it, so the incentive is there.The first thing was a pair of trousers I hadn’t worn in years. The dry cleaner took me out back, measured me and made me try the trousers on. All they needed was to take down the hem. This happens a lot to me as I have long legs and a lot of trousers sit around my ankles. In the Outer Hebrides, we say it looks like your cat died because your trousers are flying at half mast. The good thing about vintage clothing is that it often has generous hems. The dry cleaner just pinned in the waist, tightened it round my bum, and two days – and £20 – later I had a new pair of trousers.You don’t just end up with a piece of clothing in your size, you end up with something specifically for your body. Who among us is an exact high-street size anyway?double quotation markIt’s not just about adapting something to fit – you can actually create a whole new lookAlterations was more common in the 80s and 90s. People always had the sewing machine out and altering clothes was the norm. If we don’t know how to do it ourselves, I think we should make peace with the idea of outsourcing that to someone else. To that end, it’s worth checking the hems, the waistband and for extra fabric on the seam down the bum. If you take an item of clothing and look inside, it’s easy to assess if it has already been altered. I had another pair of trousers where you could see 4in of fabric had been taken in round the waist, so I took them in to be tailored again – boom, another pair of perfect trousers.I always get shirts tailored when I want something smarter to sit under a suit (they can easily take them in at the side). I also love cropped jackets. One of my favourite alterations is a suit jacket cropped into a bolero-style shape that sits just above the hip. It’s not just about adapting something to fit, you can actually create a whole new look. I once got a jumpsuit almost entirely rebuilt – they had to remove the zip, cut the torso and shorten it – and it cost £80. But it was worth it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStephen Libby on fashion: so many men have asked me for clothes advice since The TraitorsRead moreA few things I’ve learned along the way. I don’t safety pin things before I go in. I simply go and get them to measure me. Find someone you trust. They’ll get to know your style and shape. It’s intimate, but you can form a relationship. I now go once a month. I would also recommend not cropping your own clothes using wonderweb. I did this with a lovely jacket. It held together for the wedding I was going to, but when I took it to my dry cleaner they were pretty horrified that I’d tried to “web it”. They ripped it off without a word and altered it properly.Obviously I care about the planet and try to make sustainable choices, but I’m not telling people to tailor vintage clothing from up on my soapbox. The onus to do better is on larger corporations, not consumers. I’m just trying to get people to realise they have more choice in vintage shops than they think.Styling: Sam Deaman.
