title: The Plot review – exploding myths in an hour of gunpowder and treason | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Set in purgatory, Emma Howlett’s two-hander rethinks the national intrigue with 5 November
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Set in purgatory, Emma Howlett’s two-hander rethinks the national intrigue with 5 November
Content: Plenty of energy … Sophie Kean and Abby McCann in The Plot.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenPlenty of energy … Sophie Kean and Abby McCann in The Plot.Photograph: PREdinburgh festival 2026ReviewThe Plot review – exploding myths in an hour of gunpowder and treasonSummerhall, EdinburghSet in purgatory, Emma Howlett’s two-hander rethinks the national intrigue with 5 NovemberMark FisherWed 12 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 17.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNever play with matches is good advice – especially when gunpowder is involved. That the historical figures of Thomas and Robert Wintour begin this two-hander testing each other’s capacity to endure a naked flame suggests they have a high tolerance for risk. It is not clear if there are still explosives lying around, but they should know better.Not that it matters any more. These two Catholic brothers have sussed they must be in purgatory, their plot to blow up parliament having been foiled. Their accounts of what happened next are fuzzy, but they both remember being sentenced to death. They are not happy about their fate, but feel even more sympathy for the mercenary stooge known as Guy Fawkes, who has had to carry the can.Fawkes has become part of England’s self-mythology. That is one of the threads of the gunpowder plot that intrigues writer-director Emma Howlett most: beyond the simplified myth that justifies today’s 5 November fireworks, she finds a slippery pattern of power play, double dealing and political spin that implicates almost everyone except Fawkes himself.View image in fullscreenKnotty machinations … The Plot.Photograph: Giulia FerrandoThe intrigue spread through society. Alive to a good story and sensitive to the interests of James I, Shakespeare almost certainly channelled the events of 1605 into Macbeth, with its lesson about what happens to those who try to usurp a king.Ten Ways to Die Happy review – gameshow invites you to don a robe and treasure timeRead moreAll these knotty machinations feed into the TheatreGoose production, as Sophie Kean and Abby McCann put on doublet and hose to tell this very male story. They do so with much energy, but are burdened by the formality of Howlett’s vaguely period text. They declaim the dialogue where it calls for subtlety and fail to match the physical invention and lightness of touch of last year’sAether. There is an engaging drama in here somewhere – but as it is, this feels more of a history lesson.At Summerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: I was enjoying growing vegetables. Then the climate crisis raised its ugly head | Bim Adewunmi | The Guardian
description: My child and I were bonding over our hit-and-miss approach to reaping crops. But with heatwaves pushing more of Britain into drought, it’s starting to feel like a luxury we can’t afford, writes Bim Adewunmi
Author: Bim Adewunmi
Headline: My child and I were bonding over our hit-and-miss approach to reaping crops. But with heatwaves pushing more of Britain into drought, it’s starting to feel like a luxury we can’t afford, writes Bim Adewunmi
Content: ‘Fun over – time to get good at this, fast.’Photograph: Posed by model; Stefania Pelfini la Waziya/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Fun over – time to get good at this, fast.’Photograph: Posed by model; Stefania Pelfini la Waziya/Getty ImagesOpinionGardensI was enjoying growing vegetables. Then the climate crisis raised its ugly headBim AdewunmiMy child and I were bonding over our hit-and-miss approach to reaping crops. But with heatwaves pushing more of Britain into drought, it’s starting to feel like a luxury we can’t affordWed 12 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTShareFor the first time in my life, I live in a home that has real outdoor space. What a concept! There are no downsides to a garden. Back in spring, I made grand plans – I watched all the TikToks, I bought seeds and trays and pots and grow bags, I ordered soil, a trowel and a watering can. I knew what I was after: super-tiny-scale subsistence farming with a side of Zen. A little fruit, a little veg,lots of flowers to attract pollinators. And I knew I wanted my elder child to gain an understanding of how things come to be and how to cope if and when they fail.We love a tomato side salad, so that was the first thing we attempted. The seedlings flourished and then died in the first heatwave of the season. An omen, surely. The dahlias, ranunculus and freesias refused to grow, let alone bloom. My enthusiasm began to wane.But then: our first harvest! Three (three!) bright-red Tumbling Tom tomatoes. We halved them, then tossed them in olive oil with some salt and pepper. They were gone in the blink of an eye, but we were grinning as we chomped. Ah, the pleasure of growing something small you can eat. We have sown onions, carrots, lettuce and basil and eagerly await miniature crops as the days get shorter.At the back of my mind, though, isthe very real fear of food shortages. Britain is approaching its sixth climate-crisis-induced heatwave of the year. Drought no longer threatens the country –it’s here. Conflicts around the worldhave inflated food prices. Is everyone aware of this? And are they in a state of low-grade panic, too?What was supposed to feel like a fun bonding experience with my kid is morphing into something darker. Our garden has been heavy on trial and error, which feels increasingly like a luxury. Fun over – time to get good at this, fast. I know I’m doing too much, but I’ve started considering Kilner jars at TK Maxx and following homesteaders who grow their own produce. My favourite doomscroll these days is planting calendars and seed catalogues. Send tips, please. See you at the garden centre.Bim Adewunmi is a freelance journalistskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. title: Heard about the ‘luteal uglies’? Women know more about our hormones than ever – and that’s beautiful  | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: When I was younger, female biology was seen as something to be overcome. Now we can talk about the reality of living in our bodies, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: When I was younger, female biology was seen as something to be overcome. Now we can talk about the reality of living in our bodies, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: ‘Women’s hormones have become trending topics.’Photograph: d3sign/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Women’s hormones have become trending topics.’Photograph: d3sign/Getty ImagesOpinionWomen's healthHeard about the ‘luteal uglies’? Women know more about our hormones than ever – and that’s beautifulRhiannon Lucy CosslettWhen I was younger, female biology was seen as something to be overcome. Now we can talk about the reality of living in our bodiesWed 12 Aug 2026 06.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTShareHave you got the “luteal uglies”? I’m not trying to insult you, merely deploying the latest hormonal buzz phrase on social media, which refers to the phase in a woman’s cycle, two or so weeks between ovulation and menstruation, when she apparently feels at her lowest and most unattractive due to a drop in oestrogen levels.Women’s hormones have become trending topics and, as someone who only found out what a “luteal phase” is when she Googled it, mid-fertility panic, in her late 20s, I am somewhat in awe of the expertise with which younger women discuss their menstrual cycles now. They’re just so incredibly literate.Beyond being taught at school about periods and my mum explaining PMT, the impact of hormones on our emotional lives wasn’t discussed much when I was younger. In the “post-feminist” 1990s and early 2000s, female biology was seen as something to be suppressed and overcome, and the emphasis of most sex education was preventing teenage pregnancy. Being on the pill from 14 didn’t exactly put you in touch with the natural rhythms of your cycle, either, though of course it had other benefits (such as preventing the aforementioned teenage pregnancy).You can understand the rationale, which was that female biology should never hold you back. Yet sometimes that felt like pretending your reproductive system didn’t really exist, or that you should simply push through the more difficult, painful aspects. “My period always comes as a surprise to me,” a friend said recently. She’s not the only one.‘Why do I feel crappy?’: women are learning about their luteal phases - and Maha is weaponizing itRead moreThere were always girls who diligently marked the days in their diaries, but a large proportion of us barely kept track, unless of course your period arrived very late (prompting an urgent trip to the school nurse). By contrast, today’s young women have access to a plethora of period tracker apps and products, not to mention an avalanche of content pertaining to menstruation, ovulation, the luteal phase and how our hormones can impact everything from our psychological states to our body image to our sex lives. This also applies to postpartum and older women, with topics such as matrescence, perimenopause and menopause being discussed far more widely.Despite the proliferation of psychobabble and therapy-speak, there’s also some good science. I can’t help but be impressed. Knowledge is, after all, power. I’m glad I was taught that biology doesn’t have to be destiny, but it shouldn’t have meant needing to play catch-up on educating myself about my own reproductive system. Knowing what’s going on in your body and having the language to describe it can have all sorts of psychological benefits. It’s comforting that the negative body image and the tiredness, bloating and other symptoms that come with the luteal phase can be fleeting. There’s a reason you feel this way, so maybe you don’t need Botox, you just need a rest.And maybe, actually, you don’t want to have an affair, you’re just ovulating, which can increase your libido (or, to quote another friend, cause you to “go a bit feral”) andmake you appear extra attractiveto members of the opposite sex.For me, it has been important to understand that a monthly desire to explode my life is probably a mild form of premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Knowing this not only helps me warn my loved ones in a “here be dragons” sort of way, but also prompts me to try to take better care of myself instead of deciding to get divorced and move to Crete to become a ceramicist. I don’t think my symptoms are serious enough to warrant treatment, but the increase in online discussion about these issues has helped equip many with the language needed to access diagnosis. Misinformation can be an issue, though, which is why the curriculum needs to catch up.The fact is, hormones can shape our lives in profound ways. It’s something I explore in my fiction. That is not to say that we should always let them. We must, too, be vigilant. We have seen, especially in the US, how women’s cycles can be co-opted to forward patriarchal, authoritarian agendas, as in theperiod tracker data scandal, and Maga’s attempts to put women off taking birth control. I’m less worried about women’s willingness to adopt labels than I am about capitalism’s inevitable response to labels: a “fix”, whether that’s a pill that can “cure” the luteal uglies, an app that “tracks” your cycle and sells the data on, or something even more sinister.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUsually, when the mainstream media talks about this subject, it is almost always in a pro-natalist context of women needing better “fertility education” so that they don’t leave it too late to have babies, despite the fact that the biological clock is one of the few things we are very used to being lectured about. That’s why hearing reproductive education discussed in the context of aiding women’s self-understanding, wellbeing and mental health feels so radical.The information itself isn’t new – I could have looked it up in a textbook – but the way of talking about it is. It’s emancipatory, in that it encourages women to know and take control of their bodies, but it’s also realistic about the reality of living in those bodies. Women of previous generations have also navigated that balance – they weren’t all sold on the notion of “burying the body” – but never so many, all at once. It’s basically a movement, and I am here for it.Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist and the author ofFemale, NudeExplore more on these topicsWomen's healthOpinionMenstruationReproductionHealthBiologycommentShareReuse this content

title: If the markets reject OpenAI and Anthropic, the US should nationalize them | Bruce Schneier and Nathan E Sanders | The Guardian
description: From space to telecommunications, the US has a long history of fostering technology for the public good. These AI models could be aligned to democratic values, not corporate profits
Author: Bruce Schneier
Headline: From space to telecommunications, the US has a long history of fostering technology for the public good. These AI models could be aligned to democratic values, not corporate profits
Content: ‘The problem isn’t the people or the products, it’s the system.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The problem isn’t the people or the products, it’s the system.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)If the markets reject OpenAI and Anthropic, the US should nationalize themBruce SchneierandNathan E SandersFrom space to telecommunications, the US has a long history of fostering technology for the public good. These AI models could be aligned to democratic values, not corporate profitsWed 12 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTShareOpenAI, and thenAnthropic, were each formed by AI developers who feared unrestrained corporate AI development – specifically, that companies like Google and Meta would steer the technology towards deleterious, maybe even catastrophically unsafe, outcomes for society. Their founders proclaimed that their new labs, uniquely, could be trusted to develop the technology in humanity’s best interest. But each, in turn, were themselves co-opted by the same market incentives, themselves becoming corporate behemoths zealously guarding future investor value rather than the public interest.It was only a few weeks ago, in June, when OpenAI and Anthropic eachfiledfor their IPOs and were met with buzz about trillion-dollar valuations. The hype around their valuations is so extreme that many worry about their potential for concentrating wealth on a global scale. In an effort to leave something for the rest of us, some observers have proposed that the federal government seize a share of these companies’ stock to create a USsovereign wealth fund, or redistribute their revenues to produce adividendfor taxpayers.Now the headlines are about publicbacklashto AI datacenters and the AI chip giant Nvidia’sslumpingstock. The tech and AI giant SpaceX’s newly minted stock pricetankedjust weeks after its IPO. There are even questions about whether the leading AI labs will ever be sustainablyprofitable. All of a sudden, the makers of ChatGPT and Claude face strong headwinds as they seek to generate the massive equity assets that once felt all but assured.AI models have been going rogue in tests – how worried should we be?Read moreIn fact, evidence suggests the market itself could reassess that these companies offer nothing of financial value. In that case, perhaps we can return them both to their original purposes. If these AI companies should fail in the financial markets, the US should nationalize them and convert them into national labs operated under democratic control that preserve their benefit to the public interest.The economics of the big AI labs hardly guarantee a booming return on investment. Frontier AI models are both expensive to train and depreciate within months, when a newer model appears. This means that the paybackwindowto extract profit from them is very narrow. Meanwhile, enterprise clients are getting smart aboutminimizingAI token usage. Even worse, the models are basically commodities; the best ones largely perform and behave similarly, which depresses prices. Perhaps most importantly, open-source and Chinese competitors –laggingonly a few months behind the leading labs in capability – give away for free the kinds of models Anthropic and OpenAI sell.Even setting aside the model training costs, it’s not clear whether theunit economicsof AI as it’s currently conceived will ever be sustainably profitable. Many of these free and open-source models can be run locally: the large ones on private clouds and high-end servers, the smaller ones on anyone’s laptop or even cellphone, putting to question the companies’ exorbitant capital investment in datacenters.It’s not that OpenAI and Anthropic are not valuable as organizations. They have remarkably talented AI scientists and engineers that are continuously producing innovations driving a global mania for their offerings. These leading labs might not ever be profitable, but their products are doing a lot of good in the world. You may or may not be a user of or believer in their technology, but their staggering, ongoing usagegrowthsuggests that an awful lot of people would be disappointed if the companies simply disappeared.The problem isn’t the people or the products, it’s the system. As constituted,OpenAIand Anthropic may not be valuable as market equities. If the market assesses they are not capable of producing a growing financial return on investment for shareholders, the companies will collapse.Maybe private, for-profit is just not the right economic model under which to develop AI. Perhaps OpenAI should be returned to its private non-profit roots, the legacy theyfoughtso hard to changeand which Anthropic’s foundersspurned. Or possibly both could be reorganized as research centers at universities, returning to academia the scores of high-profile research faculty they havepoached.But a better outcome for society would be to establish public ownership and operation of their product-oriented capabilities. Turn OpenAI and Anthropic into US government agencies producing AI as a public good.Transitioning the big AI labs into public agencies would require some restructuring. We can separate these companies into two pieces: product innovation and compute operations. The innovation function can be publicly managed, akin to national labs. Congress could provide more rigorous oversight than the kind of unfettered venture capital these labs have recently had access to. The US has a long, successful history of these kinds of institutions, which have produced world-shaping innovations in spaceflight, telecommunications, nuclear power and more. Congress currently manages a $200bn R&Dportfolio, within which frontier AI development is, arguably, a glaring gap.‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon ValleyRead moreAI operations could be managed as a commodity resource, like public electrical or water utilities: local or regional ownership, nationwide distribution and strict regulation on how they balance fee extraction from ratepayers with raising capital for infrastructure investment. Although AI datacenters are not the same as power or water treatment plants, the US also has a long history of managing national, regional and state supercomputing centers.Other countries, includingSwitzerland,SpainandSingapore, are already operating public AI labs. They also have national supercomputing centers alreadyprovidingpublic access for running AI models for general use, as do Germany and Australia.Thebenefitsto the public are clear. Through democratic oversight, the most important AI models could become open, transparent and responsive to the demands of the public rather than private shareholders. They could be aligned to democratic values rather than corporate profits, never taking advertiser money to promote certain brands and training on only appropriately licensed data. And they could be set to focus on the realistic and pro-social goal of maximizing the usefulness of AI to society rather than the fanciful and anti-social goal of supplanting humans with artificial general intelligence.By emphasizing scientific cooperation rather than corporate competition, we could also reduce the overall resource and environmental cost associated with AI. Instead of perpetually dueling training runs of each companies’ models at ever large scales targeted to fuel investor hype, we could limit AI training resources based on cost and benefit to the public.What’s in it for the companies themselves and their employees, who sacrifice hypothetical billions in equity by ceding to public ownership? A return to their roots and to theircoremissionof developing AI safely in the public interest, if they are serious about it. Both companies are theoreticallyboundthrough their governance structures to prioritize mission over profit anyway (not that anyone really thinks that’s how they currently operate).To be clear, we’re not advocating for a golden parachute for the executives or investors, or for continuing theoutlandishpay rates of the most highly remunerated AI researchers. If the public is footing the bill, these compensation packages should be aligned to the civil service and those employees not satisfied with that can go elsewhere – if the business models of any remaining private labs still support much higher pay.While we believe that these companies are unsustainable as private firms, the timeline remains unclear. Their primary investor story is that AI is a race to “artificial general intelligence” – the kind of AI you’re used to from science fiction. The bet seems to be that the two companies can convince enough people that this outcome will turn them a profit, go public, and then make their investors and employees rich before the bubble bursts.But suppose that the bubble bursts. If the US is smart, it will catch the companies as they fall. Regardless of what the markets think, to the public, they’re too valuable to let die.Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School at Harvard University and University of Toronto’s Munk SchoolNathan E Sanders is a data scientist affiliated with the Berkman Klein Center of Harvard University and co-author, with Bruce Schneier, of the book Rewiring Democracy: How AI Will Transform Our Politics, Government, and CitizenshipExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionOpenAIAnthropicComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Ceuta showed just how easy it is to divide Europe | Paul Taylor | The Guardian
description: The migrant influx prompted recriminations and a tit-for-tat dispute between Italy and Spain. Putin, Erdoğan and others will have taken note, says the European Policy Centre’s Paul Taylor
Author: Paul Taylor
Headline: The migrant influx prompted recriminations and a tit-for-tat dispute between Italy and Spain. Putin, Erdoğan and others will have taken note, says the European Policy Centre’s Paul Taylor
Content: Spanish police check documents of travellers from Italy at Madrid Barajas airport, 8 August 2026, after a dispute between the two countries.Photograph: Spanish Police/ReutersView image in fullscreenSpanish police check documents of travellers from Italy at Madrid Barajas airport, 8 August 2026, after a dispute between the two countries.Photograph: Spanish Police/ReutersOpinionSpainCeuta showed just how easy it is to divide EuropePaul TaylorThe migrant influx prompted recriminations and a tit-for-tat dispute between Italy and Spain. Putin, Erdoğan and others will have taken noteWed 12 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 03.13 EDTShareWithin hours of the first pictures of tens of thousands of migrants swimming the short distance from Morocco to the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta hitting social media on 30 July,22 European Union leaders, the Trump administration and Israel had piled on to criticise Madrid.The outbreak of hysteria and recrimination was a case study in 21st-century politics, driven by real-time images in a media echo chamber where populists set the agenda on migration, propagating fear, prejudice and demagogic proposals. Above all, the kneejerk reactions undermined trust between European allies and dealt a setback to EU efforts to jointly manage migration, counter people-smuggling and resist the weaponisation of migrants by non-EU countries.That Donald Trump and JD Vance should seize the opportunity to accuse socialist Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez of inviting the mass influx byallowing more than 1 million irregular migrantsalready working in Spain to apply for legal status is hardly surprising, given the US administration’s own relentless drive to detain and expel illegal immigrants.On the other hand, European leaders who signed a letter to the European Commision, criticising Spain and demanding an emergency meeting of interior ministers, should ask themselves how their behaviour helps the EU implement a coherent response to migratory pressures. Many are open to charges of hypocrisy, since Germany andItalyhave, between them, regularised hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrant workers at the request of employers who need their labour as the home workforce dwindles.There was also a monstrous foreign policy double standard in the initial EU response.When Poland and Lithuania faced a sudden influx of irregular migrants from Belarus in 2021, the EU rallied behind its eastern members and imposed sanctions on Minsk’s authoritarian regime, which stood accused of weaponising displaced people from the Middle East. The previous year, the EU sent its Frontex border agency to help Greece repel a surge of migrants from Turkey at the countries’ shared border in Thrace, which had apparently been encouraged by Ankara to put pressure on the EU.View image in fullscreenCrowds gather near Fnideq on the Morocco-Spain border, 31 July 2026.Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty ImagesYet this time, EU governments quickly fell into a divisive blame game, terrified by images that recalled the loss of control over borders in south-eastern Europe in 2015, when more than 1 million mostly Syrian refugees entered the bloc. Amid the internal finger-pointing, neither the EU leaders nor the European Commission dared question the role ofMorocco, whose border guards apparently stood aside as more than 72,000 Moroccans, mostly young men, risked their lives swimming to Ceuta after seeing viral social media claims that “Spain is open”.The incident occurred on Morocco’s annual Throne Day when King Mohammed VI, who does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over the territories of Ceuta and Melilla, just happened to be visiting the nearby northern city of Tétouan, once part of the Spanish protectorate. Some commentators have called the stampede to Ceuta a “Blue March”, in reference to the massGreen Marchthat the king’s father, Hassan II, launched in 1975 in an attempt to claim the vast territory of Western Sahara, then a Spanish colony.“In Morocco, nothing happens by chance,” says Anna Terrón Cusí, a senior fellow at theMigrationPolicy Institute and a former Spanish secretary of state for immigration. Even if the stampede to Ceuta started spontaneously with social media posts, she believes “this was a multi-actor, multi-factor event. It was more a geopolitical than a migration crisis.”Intra-European party politics played a big role. It was not surprising that the Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, should lead the assault on Sánchez. She heads up the hard-right Brothers of Italy movement and faces a domestic challenge in elections next year from a new, evenfurther-right party, led by a retired general.Some Spanish and UK anti-immigration politiciansrushed to Ceutato take selfies, one from Reform UK doing a standup interview on the beach to cash in on the purported alien “invasion”.It was more bizarre that Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen, who heads a centre-left government, should co-initiate with Meloni the letter to Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, and say that the EU should consider suspendingSpainfrom the Schengen area of open-border travel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA facade of European solidarity was restored after EU interior ministers held a hastily arranged videoconference. By that time, almost all the migrants had left Ceuta and returned to Morocco after realising that they had no chance of reaching Europe. The “invasion” had deflated. In fact, irregular migrant arrivals in Spain fell sharply last year, while across the EU they’re down for the second successive year, and far below the 2015 crisis peak. But the damage was done.Italy and Spain are now engaging intit-for-tat passport and nationality controlson each other’s travellers, and Russian president Vladimir Putin, Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and King Mohammed himself will have noted how easily Europe panics and turns on its own members at the first sight of migrants on its beaches.Whether out of misinformation or malice, some EU ministers distorted the nature of the Spanish amnesty for undocumented migrants, labelling it a “pull factor” for mass migration. Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani,claimed they were being grantedSpanish and therefore European citizenship, rather than simply being given a chance to apply for temporary work visas.Europe faces what in game theory is called the “prisoners’ dilemma”, and in social sciences a “collective action problem” . EU countries have a shared interest in preserving the Schengen zone of free movement, with open internal borders vital to the smooth operation of the economy, well-managed external borders to deter irregular migrants and combat people smugglers, and legal migration routes to permit an inflow of workers needed by businesses as the European population ages and shrinks.Yet they keep undermining cooperation due to a seemingly irresistible short-term political interest in anti-migration grandstanding.Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy CentreDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Nigel Farage looks trapped and rattled – now the nationalist tide can be turned | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: There are more votes in tolerance and decency than in toxic division. It doesn’t take a great leap of political courage to fight back against Reform, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: There are more votes in tolerance and decency than in toxic division. It doesn’t take a great leap of political courage to fight back against Reform, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Nigel Farage canvassing in Clacton, Essex, on 8 August 2026.Photograph: Jacqueline Lawrie/LNPView image in fullscreenNigel Farage canvassing in Clacton, Essex, on 8 August 2026.Photograph: Jacqueline Lawrie/LNPOpinionNigel FarageNigel Farage looks trapped and rattled – now the nationalist tide can be turnedRafael BehrThere are more votes in tolerance and decency than in toxic division. It doesn’t take a great leap of political courage to fight back against ReformWed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 09.11 EDTShareNigel Farage can be confident of victory against a man posing as an ennobled space traveller with a dustbin on his head. At least, in Clacton he can.The refusal of major parties to contestthis week’s byelectionsets the bar low. But even if the competition were more serious than Count Binface, the Reform UK leader would be the favourite to win on his chosen turf. He picked the constituency as his safest shot for a parliamentary seat in the 2024 general election for a reason. Now he is betting that the stench of scandal around his personal and party finances, pungent in Westminster, won’t sicken his fans on the Essex coast.He’s probably right, which is why Labour and the Conservatives sensibly denied him the spectacle he craved – a “people versus the establishment” prize fight. The plan was to put the question of his failure to declare a£5m donationto the electoral court of Clacton. It would be settled not by adjudication of the parliamentary standards authority but with a knockout blow from the fist of Furious Farage.Unfortunately for the crypto-billionaires’ champion, the investigation hasn’t disappeared and could resume if he wins his pantomime bout witha bin.If a subsequent decision goes against him, a second byelection could follow. That twist could easily be written into Farage’s script as further proof that the system was rigged against him; that the acclamation of his innocence by his loyal Essex jury was not sufficient and they must vindicate him again, louder.The shape of the argument is textbook populism. A candidate’s virtue is measured by the volume of clamour he can summon from a crowd. Institutions of established democracy are valued only as ladders aiding his ascent. If they hold him accountable in any way, they are dismissed as tools of the elite that conspires against the will of the people.It is a sign of vulnerability that Farage’s definition of “the people” has shrunk to whatever portion of Clacton constituents turns out for him on Thursday. When his cause was Brexit, he could wield a national referendum mandate to denigrate dissent. When opinion polls and council ballots showed Reform on course to win a general election, the party leader had a putative prime ministerial swagger in his step. He has slipped.For now, Reform strategists are not too anxious about losing their headline lead to Labour. Second place, after a period of unusually hostile media coverage, while a new Downing Street regime enjoys a (probably brief) honeymoon is not a calamitous position. It could be proof of resilience as much as weakness. More worrying for Farage are histanking personal ratingsand evidence from recent Greater Manchester byelections (two for parliamentary seats; one for the mayoralty vacated by Andy Burnham) that aversion to Reform is coalescing into an effective tactical bloc vote.That sentiment is resolute. Farage has been a prominent British public figure for two decades. People who see his multiple, rebranded parties as one metastatic malignancy in the body politic are not open to persuasion that he can be something more benign. He used to curate his brand with feinted moderation. That is harder now that Reform faces competition fromRupert Lowe’s Restore Britain partyin the far-right zone where hostility to immigrants dispenses with non-racist euphemism.Lowe is more anchor of a social media channel than leader of a party. He harvests clicks in the field of digital paranoia, irrigated by extreme content on Elon Musk’s X platform, where it is axiomatic that “indigenous” Europeans face systematic replacement in their homelands by dark-skinned aliens.Restore took almost 9% of the vote in the first round of the Manchester mayoral byelection, ahead of the Tories and Liberal Democrats. Lowe, elected to parliament in 2024 as a Reform MP,has offered to form an alliancewith his old party, but with conditions attached, including the insistence that Tory defectors be barred from any future role in government.A less-rattled Farage would heap derision on his former comrade. He might even have exploited the schism to confect a new boundary between “mainstream” and “far” right. He could highlight tonal differences between his and Lowe’s politics and apply them as camouflage of respectability.That he doesn’t suggests lack of confidence in the loyalty of Reform’s hardcore vote. More disturbingly, it implies openness to the idea that, where immigration is concerned, British politics is not yet maxed-out at the furthest limits of rightward expansion.The shift is stark enough already. Parliament has passed a new act tightening border control or limiting migrants’ rights every year since 2022. Such assiduous attention to the issue has done nothing to satisfy demands for harsher measures. Nor has it refuted the absurd suggestion that mainstream politics and media, constrained by timorous liberalism, refuse to address a question that has, in reality, dominated the agenda for a generation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe legislative ratchet is also a rhetorical dial, turning public debate more shrill. The language of invasion, once the metaphorical preserve of extremists, has been normalised. Gangs ofmasked marauderswho go on racist rampages through UK towns are cast as protesters manifesting legitimate concerns. The articulation of their grievance in terms that make foreignness synonymous with parasitic consumption of benefits, criminality and sexual predation goes unchallenged.Meanwhile,net migration has fallen dramaticallyfrom its peak earlier this decade. Instead of welcoming the turning tide, the anti-immigrant right has shifted its focus from resisting new arrivals to undermining the status of legally settled communities, denying theirentitlement to public services, blocking paths to naturalisation and building a case formass deportations. This used to be the stuff of skinhead rallies and crank byelection candidates who lost their deposits. Now resistance depends on the guy with the bin on his head. Or at least, in Clacton it does.Elsewhere the picture is less bleak. Farage retreated to his coastal haven for an electoral comfort break, getting relief from scrutiny in a place where he can still enjoy unchallenged status as the man of the people. But his people are fewer than they were and never as many as he claims. If he has hit the ceiling of his national support and feels part of his base wobbling beneath him, he will try to consolidate by further radicalisation. That will then give more urgency to the anti-Reform voter coalition.He is trapped. But only if other parties refuse to follow him a single step further down the road to ethno-nationalism, where immigration policy degenerates into sinister fantasies of demographic engineering, and instead push back.It isn’t a hard choice. There are many more people in Britain who like to live happily alongside their neighbours, regardless of skin colour and country of origin, than want to burn them out of their homes. It doesn’t take a great leap of political courage to draw a line between rigorous migration control and racist demagoguery.There were good reasons for major parties to sit out this Thursday’s byelection. But from Friday onwards, the task of fighting Farage can’t be delegated to a man with a bin on his head. Not even in Clacton.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsNigel FarageOpinionClacton byelection August 2026ByelectionsLabourConservativesReform UKImmigration and asylumcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Japan’s yen: Trump wants to keep the easy-money machine running | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A cheap currency helps finance the US tech boom. Washington is intervening because allies matter only when they are useful
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A cheap currency helps finance the US tech boom. Washington is intervening because allies matter only when they are useful
Content: Donald Trump  with Sanae Takaichi, Japan's prime minister, during a meeting at the White House in March 2026.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump  with Sanae Takaichi, Japan's prime minister, during a meeting at the White House in March 2026.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionUS economyThe Guardian view on Japan’s yen: Trump wants to keep the easy-money machine runningEditorialA cheap currency helps finance the US tech boom. Washington is intervening because allies matter only when they are usefulWed 12 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTShareJapan’s yen has slid back towards 160 to the dollar, despite last month’sextraordinaryUS-Japanese intervention. Traders are betting that its role as a cheap funding pipeline for global finance will continue. Earlier this month the Trump administration stepped in to help Tokyo stabilise its currency. “Japan’s been very good to us, with the exception, of course, of Pearl Harbor,” Donald Trumpexplained. More help is likely to be on its way.But this is less a rescue of the yen than an attempt by Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, to preserve a cash spigot that benefits the US. Japan’s ultra-cheap money has become a global funding utility: bankers borrow yen, sell them for dollars and buy higher-returning US assets, notably tech shares. Rising American stock markets support collateral and investment. Japan’s “carry trade” is one of the reasons Wall Street can lever hundreds of billions into AI. ResearchsuggestsAI sucks up more than 1% of US GDP.Washington wants to keep this tap open, but not at the cost of a collapsing yen or US treasury sales. This column predicted this inApril, warning that Tokyo’s monetary choices had bound US markets to the yen trade. What Mr Bessent did was to sell at least$10bn in eurosand buy yen to arrest its slide to a 40-year low. Not telling theEuropeanssaid it all: allies matter to Washington only when they are useful.View image in fullscreenScott Bessent, the US treasury secretary.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersTraders are probing US resolve. Rising oil prices, driven by US-Irantensions, stoke Japan’s inflation and weaken the yen. Suppose it slides back to 164 yen to the dollar? Tokyo might respond with aggressive rate rises. This would be unlikely, as it would choke off theinvestment cycle that Japanis trying to create. It could also trigger achaotic market unwind: higher rates shrink the gap between investors’ returns and yen borrowing; a stronger yen also makes yen‑denominated debts costlier to repay; investors then sell US assets to buy the yen needed to close their positions. That strengthens the yen further, inflicting bigger losses and forcing more US asset sales. A currency correction could quickly become aWall Streetrout.If Mr Bessent dislikes that option, he hates the alternative: Japan selling its $1.1tn treasury pile to buy yen. Dumping US debt woulddrive yields higher– and leave Washington with a costlier interest bill. Instead, Mr Bessent has allowed Japan to borrow dollars against its treasuries and use those dollars to buy yen. He has used a Federal Reserve lending facility to help – and wants its current $60bn daily limitsubstantiallyincreased. This would give Tokyo room to stabilise the yen without having to choose between abandoning itsreflationary programmeand selling treasuries.If Mr Bessent gets his way, the Fed could turn asubstantial portionof Japan’s trillion-dollar hoard of US government securities into cash. Argentina showed Mr Bessent would put American firepower behind currencies,spending billions to prop up the peso. Japan is the bigger challenge. He is asking traders: are you sure that you want to return to 164 yen to the dollar? He has form as a currency trader. Mr Bessent made George Soros a billion dollars in 1992 by sellingpoundsand forcing sterling from the European exchange rate mechanism. In 2013, Mr Bessent helped George Soros make anotherbilliondollars betting against the Japanese currency. Margaret Thatcher famously said that “you can’t buck the market”. Mr Bessent is saying you can – as long you rewrite its rules.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on early prisoner release: don’t lose sight of systemic reform | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Empathy is a strength in a prime minister but there is a risk of letting emotional urgency obscure the strategic view in policymaking
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Empathy is a strength in a prime minister but there is a risk of letting emotional urgency obscure the strategic view in policymaking
Content: ‘Mr Burnham would be better off using his talents as a communicator to advance the argument for a reformed justice system.’ HMP Dartmoor.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures Ltd/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Mr Burnham would be better off using his talents as a communicator to advance the argument for a reformed justice system.’ HMP Dartmoor.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures Ltd/Corbis/Getty ImagesOpinionPrisons and probationThe Guardian view on early prisoner release: don’t lose sight of systemic reformEditorialEmpathy is a strength in a prime minister but there is a risk of letting emotional urgency obscure the strategic view in policymakingWed 12 Aug 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTShareThere are no votes in leniency for criminals, which is why oppositions demand harsher penalties and ministers acquiesce. It is a policy ratchet that can keep turning as long as there are enough cells to accommodate those who are jailed.But spending on new prisons, or for that matter improving conditions in thedilapidated, overcrowdedones already in use, is also not a vote-winner. Most people can think of more deserving beneficiaries of public money than prisoners.There is an argument that everyone in society benefits when incarcerated citizens are humanely treated, more likely to be rehabilitated and less likely to reoffend. It is a rare politician who asserts that view against the clamour for harshness.As a result of these dynamics, British jails are near capacity. Cutting short custodial sentences is the only way to avert chaos in the system. The last Conservative government knew this when they called the 2024 general election. That didn’t stop them lambasting Sir Keir Starmer when hebowed to the inevitableand approved a wave of early releases. Another round was due in September. That has been pushed back a month by Andy Burnham.View image in fullscreenAlex Norris, the justice secretary.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesIt is understandable that a new prime minister doesn’t want to leap into unpopular actions so soon after taking office. Mr Burnham also has a markedly different style to his predecessor, striving for empathy where Sir Keir tried to make a virtue of unsentimental analysis.In justice policy, the more empathic way means heeding the concerns of victims of crime and their families, who are naturally distressed by the thought of perpetrators getting off prematurely. In particular, Mr Burnham has signalled amenability to averting the earlier release of two men convicted of themanslaughter of Andrew Harper, a police officer. Mr Harper’s widow has campaigned on the issue, and seniorserving officershave signed an open letter lobbying to keep the killers in jail.The prime minister hastasked his justice secretary, Alex Norris, with finding a way to satisfy those requests. It isn’t straightforward without measures that change the terms of release more widely, such as a provision that none convicted of manslaughter is eligible, for example. Ministers cannot and should not customise rules ad hoc, for individual cases, but broader change starts to undermine the basic utility of a policy intended to free up prison places.Mr Burnham has already said that rapists and those convicted of some child sexual abuse offencescannot be releasedearly. That is a reasonable line to draw. But wherever the boundary falls, there will be cases that look like unmerited leniency. There will be victims of crime who feel short-changed by the justice system, which is the unavoidable outcome when the system is starved of resources.There are obvious advantages to emotional literacy in political communication. But the prime minister is at risk of becoming trapped in a cycle of concessions, driven by empathy in individual cases, that limit his room for policy manoeuvre on a more strategic level. Mr Burnham would be better off using his talents as a communicator to advance the argument for a reformed justice system that serves the whole of society. There might not be a lot of votes in it, but prime ministers who prioritise the emotional urgency of the moment over practical policy also pay an electoral penalty.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Jason Arday and the lack of oversight and quality control of academics | University of Oxford | The Guardian
description: Letter: An Oxford academic says teaching and teamwork matter just as much as a CV full of impressive research output
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: An Oxford academic says teaching and teamwork matter just as much as a CV full of impressive research output
Content: The University of Oxford. ‘Appointment panels pay too little attention to applicants’ willingness to put time and energy into teaching.’Photograph: Paul Thompson Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe University of Oxford. ‘Appointment panels pay too little attention to applicants’ willingness to put time and energy into teaching.’Photograph: Paul Thompson Images/AlamyUniversity of OxfordLettersJason Arday and the lack of oversight and quality control of academicsAn Oxford academic says teaching and teamwork matter just as much as a CV full of impressive research outputWed 12 Aug 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 12.31 EDTShareThe Jason Arday case is in danger of becoming a red herring when it comes to quality control of university appointments. An anonymous letter-writer (7 August) commented that Arday “is well known for the kindness he promotes” – a rare exception within a slew of commentary that has had nothing to say about Arday’s actual job performance. As an academic at Oxford University, I would say that underqualified appointees are significantly less common or problematic than those whose research output is excellent but who, nonetheless, devote little energy to teaching, are administratively indolent, and/or lack a collegiate sensibility.There are two main reasons for this. One is that appointment panels are excessively preoccupied by impressive publication records, and pay too little attention to applicants’ willingness to put time and energy into teaching, and to engage empathetically and constructively with both colleagues and institutional systems. Too often bad appointments occur because of, not despite, the “rigour” of our processes.Second, oversight and quality control of academics once they have been appointed is often almost nonexistent. “Dead weight” appointees get worked around, not challenged; and performance reviews at the end of probationary periods are routinely conducted without meaningful consultation with the colleagues and students that they work with. Sometimes this occurs because senior management are too far removed from the day-to-day realities of academic life, or it stems from a misguided view that research productivity is difficult, whereas the bread-and-butter of teaching and teamwork is easy.Of course, serious consequences must follow from exaggerating one’s credentials in order to gain promotion. However, although I do not knowJason Arday, it’s a good bet that, from a teaching and teamwork perspective, his (and my) university have made far worse appointments in recent years that have entirely escaped both internal scrutiny and external headlines.Name and address suppliedHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Content: A ticket inspector and passenger on a train. ‘Ozzy Osbourne came on the train intercom to make the announcements.’Photograph: UK Stock Images Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenA ticket inspector and passenger on a train. ‘Ozzy Osbourne came on the train intercom to make the announcements.’Photograph: UK Stock Images Ltd/AlamyRail transportLettersA train journey that made a lasting impressionA reader couldn’t believe his ears on a journey from Runcorn to London EustonWed 12 Aug 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTShareJimmy Cricket taking over the aeroplane’s intercom (Letters, 5 August) reminded me of a memorable train journey. title: Breakfast, lunch and natmad in Denmark – Scandinavian mealtimes explained | Denmark | The Guardian
description: Letters: Gary Calder on the differences in names for mealtimes in Scandinavia. Plus Dr Paul Brown on the class division in dinnertimes on the Titanic
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Gary Calder on the differences in names for mealtimes in Scandinavia. Plus Dr Paul Brown on the class division in dinnertimes on the Titanic
Content: A typical Swedish Christmas smörgåsbord.Photograph: knape/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA typical Swedish Christmas smörgåsbord.Photograph: knape/Getty ImagesDenmarkLettersBreakfast, lunch and natmad in Denmark – Scandinavian mealtimes explainedGary Calderon the differences in names for mealtimes in Scandinavia. PlusDr Paul Brownon the class division in dinnertimes on the TitanicWed 12 Aug 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTShareConfusion over the names of mealtimes (Letters, 2 August) also reigns in Scandinavia. Breakfast in Norway/Sweden isfrokost/frukost, butmorgenmad(morning food) in Denmark. Lunch in Norway/Sweden islunsj/lunch, butfrokostin Denmark. At least they can all agree on the main meal of the day, which ismiddag(midday/noon) but served in the early evening.If attending a wedding party or function inDenmark, don’t be surprised to be servednatmad(night food) around midnight. It is used as a friendly indication that the event has come to an end, hence its colloquial name ofskrub af mad(fuck-off food).Gary CalderChandler’s Ford, HampshireOn the Titanic, dinner for first- and second-class passengers was the meal served in the evening. For third-class passengers the meal called dinner was served in the middle of the day; later in the day they had tea and supper. Interestingly, there was no iceberg lettuce on the menus.Dr Paul BrownWest Bridgford, NottinghamshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Termtime holidays – don’t forget that teachers have families too | School holidays | The Guardian
description: Letters: A teacher asks how would parents feel if their child’s teacher took time off during the school term to get a cheaper holiday. And Nick Coupland points to the evidence that absences for family holidays do not affect academic achievement
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: A teacher asks how would parents feel if their child’s teacher took time off during the school term to get a cheaper holiday. And Nick Coupland points to the evidence that absences for family holidays do not affect academic achievement
Content: If teachers as well as pupils took time off during termtime, the classroom might end up looking like this.Photograph: James Veysey/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIf teachers as well as pupils took time off during termtime, the classroom might end up looking like this.Photograph: James Veysey/Rex/ShutterstockSchool holidaysLettersTermtime holidays – don’t forget that teachers have families tooA teacher asks how would parents feel if their child’s teacher took time off during the school term to get a cheaper holiday. AndNick Couplandpoints to the evidence that absences for family holidays do not affect academic achievementWed 12 Aug 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTShareThe broad consensus of your readers seems to be that fines for holidays in termtime are unpopular and ineffective (Letters, 5 August). So far, so true. However, one point that has not been raised is that teachers – I am one – have families too, and are likewise bound by the extortionate cost of holidays outside termtime. I wonder how readers would feel about their children’s teachers flouting the rules and taking a few days off during termtime for a cheaper holiday?Name and address suppliedI agree with Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett’s belief that “term-time holidays are clearly not the most urgent cause of poor educational outcomes” (Opinion, 2 August). Researchers at the universities of Strathclyde and Dundee found that, in contrast to overall absence, truancy, sickness and extraordinary family circumstances,absences for family holidays did not have an impact on academic achievement at the end of compulsory secondary schooling.Nick CouplandEdmonton, Alberta, CanadaHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Doué seals Super Cup glory for PSG after Madjo makes history for Aston Villa | Uefa Super Cup | The Guardian
description: After Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s opener was cancelled out by the teenage striker Brian Madjo, Désiré Doué curled in a second-half winner to give PSG a 2-1 victory against Aston Villa in Salzburg
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: After Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s opener was cancelled out by the teenage striker Brian Madjo, Désiré Doué curled in a second-half winner to give PSG a 2-1 victory against Aston Villa in Salzburg
Content: Paris Saint-Germain's Marquinhos lifts the Super Cup after victory over Villa.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersView image in fullscreenParis Saint-Germain's Marquinhos lifts the Super Cup after victory over Villa.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersUefa Super CupDoué seals Super Cup glory for PSG after Madjo makes history for Aston VillaUefa Super Cup: Paris Saint-Germain 2-1 Aston VillaKvaratskhelia 20, Doué 62; Madjo 45Ben Fisherat Red Bull ArenaWed 12 Aug 2026 18.48 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 17.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLuis Enrique says it doesn’t matter which sport he is playing – football, tennis, padel or parchis, a board game – he wants to win all of the time. InParis Saint-Germain, he has built a winning machine, the back-to-back Champions League victors maintaining a useful habit by conquering Aston Villa in an absorbing Super Cup contest in Salzburg. For PSG, after the joy of Munich and Budapest, three months ago, does a three-peat in Madrid in May beckon?Aston Villa more than played their part in an enthralling showpiece, Brian Madjo becoming the competition’s youngest scorer after the 17-year-old cancelled out Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s opener. They could have taken the game to a penalty shootout, Warren Zaïre-Emery’s extraordinary block preventing João Gomes a near-certain debut goal and Emi Buendía heading wide in stoppage time.Kvaratskhelia and Madjo show us that the beautiful game can wash away Infantino’s stain | Nick AmesRead moreVilla will take plenty of encouragement from a fearless display, Désiré Doué’s well-taken winner ultimately the difference. The goal was initially disallowed but, after a VAR review, Omar Artan – the Somali referee handed the game by Uefa after being denied entry to the US to officiate at the World Cup – awarded it after replays showed Matty Cash played Doué onside.Before kick-off, the sights and sounds were in effect an extension of Villa’s victory in Istanbul, a party atmosphere raining down from the 6,000-strong Villa following. There were huge cheers when Unai Emery’s face appeared on the big screens in opposite corners after the teams were read aloud and hearty roars for the £38m arrival Gomes and Madjo, the hulking forward who made his presence felt on his full Villa debut. Madjo’s inclusion felt particularly ominous for Tammy Abraham, the striker signed seven months ago, his £18.25m arrival yet to pay dividends.“We won’t be in our best moment,” Emery warned on the eve of the game but, after a summer of change, the future looks bright. Emery could finally unleash Madjo in a competitive game for the first time since his £10m arrival from Metz in January, Villa winning an appeal at the court of arbitration for sport (Cas) to register him after Fifa prohibited him from playing. Chelsea’s João Pedro is the only Premier League player to have outscored Madjo in pre-season and his equaliser here was on the grandest stage yet after goals against Walsall, Real Sociedad and Indonesia All Stars. Madjo occupied Willian Pacho and Marquinhos, one of the most decorated defenders in the world. The 19-year-old George Hemmings played the full game and kept Achraf Hakimi on his toes.Only five players from Villa’s memorable victory over Freiburg remained in the XI though Emi Martínez, Ezri Konsa and Ollie Watkins are still on holiday. Emery told Watkins to rest after the striker volunteered to play here. Boubacar Kamara made his first start since sustaining a serious knee injury against Tottenham in January. More new faces will join, with Villa in advanced talks to sign João Palhinha from Bayern Munich and the Atlético Madrid left-back Matteo Ruggeri expected to undergo a medical in the next 48 hours. “Overall we can feel proud of everything we’ve done,” Emery said. “Some changes will be needed but we are confident.”View image in fullscreenBrian Madjo punches the air after scoring for Aston Villa on the stroke of half-time.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersPSG seized the lead on 20 minutes through Kvaratskhelia, who had the summer off. Madjo’s clunky control allowed Vitinha to claim the ball and locate Doué. Then Kvaratskhelia took charge, jinking inside Cash and blasting his shot in at Marco Bizot’s near post. Six minutes later, it should have been 2-0 after more Kvaratskhelia brilliance, but PSG could not apply the finishing touch. Nuno Mendes galloped on to Kvaratskhelia’s flipped pass but the full-back’s cutback from the left flank evaded the £43m summer buy Maghnes Akliouche and three other blue and red shirts.Madjo had a hat-trick of chances from John McGinn’s cunning crosses before levelling. He glanced at the screens showing a replay of him misdirecting a free header. Then he overcooked a shot when looking for the far corner after Hemmings beat Hakimi. Another flunked header followed after McGinn twirled clear of Kvaratskhelia. But with the half-time whistle looming, Madjo made amends, dispatching a side-footed volley into the roof of Matvey Safonov’s net after meeting another brilliant cross from McGinn. As the ball flew towards the back post, Pacho clung to Madjo for dear life, but the teenager kept him at arm’s length to ripple the net.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOusmane Dembélé replaced Akliouche at half-time. Fabián Ruiz, the only other player missing from the XI that began against Arsenal in Budapest in May, arrived late on. Villa kept hunting, McGinn working Safonov after Madjo spread play. But PSG regained the lead just after the hour when Dembélé’s pass unlocked Villa’s defence, exposing an imperfect offside line. Dembélé zipped the ball into the right channel and, while Ian Maatsen and Pau Torres raised their hands and Doué’s goal was initially ruled out, semi-automated offside exposed Cash.Villa still had chances to level. Zaïre-Emery slid across the turf to thwart Gomes. Safonov repelled Hemmings’s strike from close range and the substitutes Alysson and Abraham almost combined to devastating effect but Abraham did not gamble in the box, much to Emery’s frustration. Perhaps Villa will, as McGinn suggested this week, prove everybody wrong – again.Explore more on these topicsUefa Super CupParis Saint-GermainAston Villamatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Hudson-Smith dazzles home fans as he surges to golden European 400m hat-trick | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: British runner Matt Hudson-Smith stormed to a historic third gold in the European Championship 400m to delight the home supporters in Birmingham
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: British runner Matt Hudson-Smith stormed to a historic third gold in the European Championship 400m to delight the home supporters in Birmingham
Content: Matt Hudson-Smith wears his crown and holds his gold medal after winning the 400m.Photograph: Morgan Harlow/APView image in fullscreenMatt Hudson-Smith wears his crown and holds his gold medal after winning the 400m.Photograph: Morgan Harlow/APEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsHudson-Smith dazzles home fans as he surges to golden European 400m hat-trickBecomes first man to win three European 400m titlesHudson-Smith: ‘Nobody is going to beat me on this track’Sean Ingleat Alexander Stadium, BirminghamWed 12 Aug 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStand … and deliver. On a balmy night in Birmingham, Matt Hudson-Smith powered past the stand ­bearing his name at the Alexander Stadium and into history by becoming the first man to win three European ­Championship 400m titles.And afterwards, as the ­adrenaline flooded his body and he posed ­wearing a crown in front of the Matthew Hudson-Smith Stand, the 31-year-old made it clear just how much it meant. “Nobody is going to beat me on this track,” he said. “This is my home. I have been here since I was nine. I know this track like the back of my hand.”European Athletics Championships: day three from Birmingham – liveRead moreBorn in Wolverhampton. Made in Birmingham. Forged in the fire of competition. But this wasn’t the ­easiest of wins given that Hudson-Smith started in lane nine, which meant he was blind to the challengers inside him.No wonder that when the starting gun went off, he went off like a man sprinting for the last bus of the night. And while he began to tie up in the final 70 metres, he easily had enough to win in 44.17sec.“I knew it would take one hell of an effort to get past me,” said ­Hudson-Smith. “Every time someone beats me, I kind of end their career. I knew that for them to beat me, they would have to have a supernatural moment.”Muhammad Abdallah Kounta, of France, took silver in 44.40, while Jonas Phijffers of the Netherlands took bronze, a hundredth of a ­second further back, in a new national record.They were happy with their spoils. But no one was more ecstatic than ­Hudson-Smith, although there was a slight edge to his celebrations, as he took a dig at the BBC afterwards for suggesting he might be carrying an injury.“You guys need to come with the facts, man,” he said. “Saying I was injured and everything. The whole point of rounds is to survive and advance. I tried to conserve in the rounds.“Me and my coach were ­laughing all the way around. I knew I was the best in the world. I knew that. On paper, I was a second faster than these guys.View image in fullscreenMatt Hudson-Smith crosses the line for a glorious gold in front his home fans.Photograph: Michael Steele/British Athletics/Getty ImagesMy coach said: ‘Once you seal the deal, make sure you do it,’” he added. “This is your home. Defend it.”The only disappointment was that the stand named after him was not packed to the rafters to celebrate his triumph. There has been a lot of talk about prices being too high. However, it is not as simple as that given that most of the £110 Category A seats in the main stand were sold out.It has been the cheaper tickets, some of which have been priced as low as £40 and £20, that have struggled to sell out.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are many reasons for that. The stadium is out of town. It is not easy to park nearby. There is a cost of living crisis and, in fairness to the organisers, the last four days of competition are said to be sell-outs. Who can blame people for waiting for the end of the week when there are more finals? EuropeanAthleticssays 80% of tickets – about 200,000 in total – have now been sold and it is expecting big crowds for the last few days. But there is perhaps another factor for that figure not being higher.The last four European championships have been staged in Rome, Munich, Berlin and Amsterdam. These are cities where it is easy to combine a city break with sport, art and culture. Birmingham just doesn’t pack that punch. As one press box wag put it, Rome has the Colosseum, Birmingham has the Bullring.“Naturally, we would love to see a full stadium for every session, because nothing compares with the energy of a packed Alexander ­Stadium and the support it gives to the athletes,” European Athletics said in a statement. “We are very pleased that demand for tickets to the second half of the championships is strong.”There was a second British success of the night as Emily Newnham came through with a late charge to take silver in the women’s 400m hurdles.The favourite, Emma Zapletalova of Slovakia won comfortably in 52.91 sec, but Newnham went from fourth over the final hurdle to second by running a personal best of 53.33. Fatoumata Binta Diallo set a national record for Portugal of 53.55 for bronze.Afterwards, Newnham dedicated her win to her mother, who has been undergoing health issues. “Mum, I love you so much,” she added. “You’re my inspiration this year. Keep fighting – you’ve got this.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Atlético Madrid agree £34.1m deal for Tottenham’s Cristian Romero | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: Centre-back Cristian Romero is closing on a move to La Liga while Hull have broken their transfer record to sign Nobel Mendy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Centre-back Cristian Romero is closing on a move to La Liga while Hull have broken their transfer record to sign Nobel Mendy
Content: Cristian Romero endured a troubled last season at Spurs.Photograph: George Wood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCristian Romero endured a troubled last season at Spurs.Photograph: George Wood/Getty ImagesTottenham HotspurAtlético Madrid agree £34.1m deal for Tottenham’s Cristian RomeroCentre-back closes on move to La Liga sideHull break their transfer record to sign Nobel MendyPA MediaWed 12 Aug 2026 18.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 19.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTottenham have reached an agreement withAtlético Madridover the sale of their captain, Cristian Romero. Romero was given the green light by the club and Roberto De Zerbi to depart Spurs this summer after a turbulent 2025-26 campaign in which he served four separate suspensions.Inter initially led the chase for the Argentina centre-back, but after talks with Spurs stalled, long-term admirers Atlético swooped in and a package of €40m (£34.1m) is set to secure Diego Simeone his target.Barcelona make improved £51m bid for Rodri as Manchester City target FernándezRead moreIt will bring a rollercoaster five-year spell in north London to an end for Romero, who joined in 2021 and enjoyed mixed success under Antonio Conte before a strong bond was formed with Ange Postecoglou.Romero wore the captain’s armband when Tottenham ended a 17-year trophy drought with victory over Manchester United in the2025 Europa League finaland produced a fine performance to ensure Postecoglou’s promise of silverware in his second season came true.However, Postecoglou’s dismissal weeks later was met with a thinly veiled social media post in the direction of Spurs’ hierarchy by Romero and more followed during a chaotic last season where only a final-day win against Everton avoided relegation.Romero, who was made captain by Thomas Frank ahead of the 2025-26 campaign, was in Argentina days before Tottenham’s 1-0 success over Everton to receive treatment on a knee injury before he got a flight back to be present in the stands. The return of Romero for the relegation decider only occurred after widespread criticism from Spurs supporters and it proved the final nail in the coffin for many fans.The World Cup winner will exit Spurs after 156 appearances and link up with his compatriot Simeone, who has repeatedly talked up the quality of the Argentinian in recent seasons and will finally get his man this summer.Tottenham have inserted a 15% sell-on clause in the deal and this imminent departure continues a summer of mass changes with De Zerbi overseeing a huge revamp of a squad which has finished 17th in consecutive seasons.Newly promotedHullhave broken their transfer record to sign the Senegal defender Nobel Mendy from Spanish side Rayo Vallecano. They also signed Australia international Lucas Herrington on Wednesday.View image in fullscreenLucas Herrington became Australia’s youngest player to make a World Cup appearance this summer.Photograph: Alex Livesey/Fifa/Getty ImagesThe Tigers have not disclosed the fee for the 21-year-old Mendy but it exceeds the reported £20m they paid for the Greece goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis last week. Mendy, who has one international cap and previously played for Paris FC and Real Betis, has signed a five-year deal, with an option for a further 12 months. He finished his only season with Rayo Vallecano with an appearance in May’sConference League final loss to Crystal Palace.“I have wanted to play in the Premier League since I was little, so it’s a great challenge to face and I am ready for it,” Mendy told Hull’s website.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHerrington, 18, became Australia’s youngest player to start a World Cup game for the Socceroos this summer, and arrived from MLS side Colorado Rapids on a five-year deal.Crystal Palacehave re-signed Aston Villa’s Evann Guessand on loan for the season with an option to buy. The Côte d’Ivoire international made 14 appearances after moving to Selhurst Park in January until the end of last season, but in July Palace opted against making the move permanent.The 25-year-old joined Villa from Ligue 1 side Nice for £30m last summer but failed to win a regular place in Unai Emery’s side.Celtichave signed the Egypt winger Haissem Hassan from Spanish club Real Oviedo, subject to international clearance. The 24-year-old, who impressed at this summer’s World Cup, joins the Scottish champions on a four-year deal, with the option of a further 12 months.“When I heard about Celtic being interested in me, I had to get here and be part of the club,” Hassan told the club’s website. Manager Martin O’Neill said Celtic had done “really well” to secure a player of Hassan’s quality amid interest from other clubs.“He is someone who I think has the ability and experience to do very well for us, performing at a high level in domestic and international football,” said O’Neill.Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurAtlético MadridTransfer windowHull CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Be adults’: Joe Root gets rid of England Test team’s midnight curfew | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Joe Root has abolished the midnight curfew for his England Test side after a string of late-night incidents
Author: Taha Hashim
Headline: Joe Root has abolished the midnight curfew for his England Test side after a string of late-night incidents
Content: Joe Root is back as the permanent England Test captain for the series against Pakistan that starts next week at Headingley.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJoe Root is back as the permanent England Test captain for the series against Pakistan that starts next week at Headingley.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEngland cricket team‘Be adults’: Joe Root gets rid of England Test team’s midnight curfew‘I don’t think they work,’ says returning Test captainRoot takes charge for three-match Pakistan seriesTaha HashimWed 12 Aug 2026 10.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe Root has abolished the midnight curfew for his England Test side, telling his players to “be adults” after a string of late-night incidents.A curfew was imposed on the ­England men’s teams after their Ashes defeat in the winter, when the on-field action was overshadowed by players’ behaviour off it. Most ­notably, there wasHarry Brook’s altercation with a nightclub bounceron the eve of a one-day international in Wellington, with the batter admitting he was fortunate to keep his position as white-ball captain.Stokes’ presence and group stage drama add to One-Day Cup’s quiet resurgenceRead moreBen Stokes and Gus Atkinson were suspended for the second Test against New Zealand in Juneafter breaking the curfew while celebrating victoryin the series opener. Stokes returned for the series closer before announcinghis retirement from international cricket, prompting the return ofRoot as Test captain.The Yorkshireman will lead next week against Pakistan, and is embarking on a new era with Stephen Fleming as red-ball head coach. The 35-year-old told the Sky SportsCricketpodcast that the ­curfew has been abolished, arguing: “I don’t think they work.” It is understood the relaxing of rules also applies to the white-ball sides.“There’s not going to be a curfew,” Root said. “I don’t think this needs to be a big deal. I don’t think they work and if you want guys to take responsibility on the field they’ve got to feel like they can be grown adults off it and make good, strong decisions.“That’s for us as a team to manage well, and self-police well, for me and [Fleming]. Ultimately, you’re grown adults. You know what it takes to play for England. You know what your responsibilities are off the field.“ We should be known for how we play our cricket and what we do on the field. We should be on the back page of papers.“Look after yourselves, look after each other, create a good, strong ­culture where you know when the right time is to celebrate and enjoy a win or to have a sensible beer, and remember you’re playing for England.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I don’t want people to feel like they can’t enjoy winning a Test match. If they want to have a beer at the right time, go and let their hair down, then that’s absolutely fine. You know what your ­responsibilities are. Be smart, be sensible and just be an adult about it.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamJoe RootCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jack Draper: ‘When you reach rock bottom like that you can come back up again’ | Jack Draper | The Guardian
description: Jack Draper tells Tumaini Carayol how he is rebuilding after the most difficult period of his career and explains his emotional reaction in Canada
Author: Tumaini Carayol
