Headline: Jack Draper tells Tumaini Carayol how he is rebuilding after the most difficult period of his career and explains his emotional reaction in Canada
Content: Jack Draper has spent the past year desperately trying to find solutions to his arm injury.Photograph: Minas Panagiotakis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJack Draper has spent the past year desperately trying to find solutions to his arm injury.Photograph: Minas Panagiotakis/Getty ImagesJack DraperInterviewJack Draper: ‘When you reach rock bottom like that you can come back up again’Tumaini Carayolin CincinnatiFormer world No 4 reflects on emotional reaction in Canada and rebuilding after the most difficult period of his careerWed 12 Aug 2026 16.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThose painful images have relentlessly spread to all corners of the internet. Deep in the final set of the first-round match at the Canadian Open against Térence Atmane just over a week ago, 15 months of pent up emotion erupted. Two games from defeat,Draper spent the entire changeover in tears.This was a devastating and alarming sight. Injuries had already defined so much of Draper’s career, but the uncertainty of trying to recover from a bone bruise injury to his left arm over the past year has been more challenging than anything he has experienced. All of his efforts since last July have been focused on trying to find a way to compete consistently at the highest level again, to no avail.Arthur Fery ready to test himself at Masters level after Wimbledon runRead moreIt was reasonable to wonder if his tears represented the realisation he may never recover, but the 24-year-old was seen on the practice court the following day in Montreal and his name did not shift from the entry list of the Cincinnati Open, where he is a wildcard recipient.Ahead of Thursday’s first-round match against Martín Landaluce, Draper speaks with admirable vulnerability and optimism about this most difficult period. “I don’t get emotional often,” he says. “There was once I got emotional in practice in May when I had really bad knee tendinitis and my arm was really sore as well. I was in so much pain. I was running and my knee [hurt] and my hitting the balls and my arm was sore.“Last week came from a place of, I think I had so much to focus on and manage, so much change going on in my tennis. I got to [No]4 in the world through doing the same things, the consistent work, the differences, and then went through this whole process of a lot of setbacks and a lot of struggle.“That’s taken a lot out of me. But then at the same time, I’m in a position where I’m having to start again. That reality is difficult sometimes.“The reason I got emotional was that through all the challenges, you can forget who you are on the court. And last week I felt like I couldn’t give any more. I was emotional because I didn’t recognise the player I was out on the court due to my injuries and due to probably the way I’ve been feeling for a long time.“When you reach rock bottom like that you can come back up again. Since then I’ve practised really well, I’ve had amazing support from the people around me and you get to a point more and more of acceptance. We’ve definitely reached that acceptance phase now.”View image in fullscreenJack Draper has reached the acceptance stage after more than a year of uncertainty due to his injury problems.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockDraper has spent the past year desperately trying to find solutions to this injury. After retreating on some of his earlier changes to his racket strings and technique,his retirement from Wimbledonon the eve of the tournament forced him to make even more extreme changes in his attempts to reduce the strain on his arm.Not only has he returned to a hybrid gut string setup, he is playing with a completely different, more flexible racket. Draper appears to be using a frame from a company other than his sponsor, Dunlop, which he declined to comment on.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“After this long period, my shift has gone away from performance,” he says. “I’m changing my string. I desperately don’t want to. I desperately know it’s hopefully not something that I’m going to have to do moving forwards, but it’s something I have to do for the nature of my injury. Same with the racket.“It’s a difficult one because I’m a winner. I’m out there, I want to perform. But I have to accept reality, which is that I have to find a way in very uncomfortable circumstances right now. But if that can get me to the end of the year where I’m feeling really good again and my body’s in a great place and my mind’s in a great place, then that’s only going to help me to move completely past this injury. But there is a way out and I’m seeing that on a day-to-day basis.”A year ago, Draper stood at a career-high ranking of No 4. Now he is ranked No 143 and the stop-and-start nature of his injury struggles mean he is not eligible for protected ranking. He is reliant solely on wildcards to compete on the ATP tour rather than in qualifying draws or on the ATP Challenger circuit.“At the very start of my injury, if I was to say to myself: ‘Right, I’m four in the world now, what’s the worst outcome?’ It would probably be where I’ve got to,” he says, smiling. “But there’s a certain peace in that and acceptance because I have to start again. And what a challenge.”Explore more on these topicsJack DraperTennisinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Lawrence and Daly lose England central contracts as Borthwick looks to World Cup  | England rugby union team | The Guardian
description: Ollie Lawrence and Elliot Daly have both lost their central contracts with Steve Borthwick omitting the pair from his 25-man squad a year before England’s World Cup campaign begins
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Ollie Lawrence and Elliot Daly have both lost their central contracts with Steve Borthwick omitting the pair from his 25-man squad a year before England’s World Cup campaign begins
Content: The Saracens back Elliot Daly is a surprise omission from England’s list of central contracts.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Saracens back Elliot Daly is a surprise omission from England’s list of central contracts.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesEngland rugby union teamLawrence and Daly lose England central contracts as Borthwick looks to World CupDuo are notable omissions from England’s 25-man listAlex Coles and Asher Opoku-Fordjour both includedGerard MeagherWed 12 Aug 2026 10.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOllie Lawrence and Elliot Daly have both lost their central contracts, with Steve Borthwick omitting the pair from his 25-man squad a year before England’s World Cup campaign begins.Neither Lawrence nor Daly – who was nursing an arm injury – featured in the three Nations Championship matches this summer but both played during the Six Nations and are the standout exclusions from Borthwick’s selections which point towards his thinking for the World Cup squad next year.Les Kiss and his Wallabies have a mountain to climb but gritty win over Japan is a big first step | Angus FontaineRead moreThe Northampton forward Alex Coles and the Sale prop Asher Opoku-Fordjour – who can play both sides of the scrum – are among the eye-catching inclusions, while Borthwick has opted against handing a contract to the South African-born centre Benhard van Rensburg, whomade his debut over the summer. Courtney Lawes, who is available again after a move to Sale from France and has made clear his desire to go to the World Cup, is also overlooked.In total, Borthwick has made five changes to the group of players who receive around £150,000 a season and over whom the head coach has greater control. Joining Coles and Opoku-Fordjour in receiving a contract having missed out a year ago are Seb Atkinson, Guy Pepper and Jack van Poortvliet. Omitted along with Lawrence and Daly are the injury-plagued Ben Curry, his Sale teammate Tom Roebuck and Tom Willis, who has rejoined Bordeaux.View image in fullscreenOllie Lawrence (left) was a regular during England’s Six Nations campaign.Photograph: JP Fletcher/Action Plus/ShutterstockAtkinson’s inclusion goes some way to explaining Lawrence’s exclusion but it is still a surprise given the Bath centre starred inEngland’s victory against the All Blackslast autumn. He and Fraser Dingwall – who also impressed against New Zealand – have fallen down the pecking order since then, however.Daly’s omission is also out of the blue given Borthwick values his versatility and just last November tipped the 33-year-old to play an important role for England at the World Cup next year. His exclusion does not rule him out of contention for the tournament in Australia, for which a larger squad of 33 will be selected, but demonstrates where he is in Borthwick’s thinking with the Nations Championship matches in November.Coles’s inclusion, meanwhile, is no surprise given he played in all 12 England Tests over the past year and started the summer matches against South Africa, Fiji and Argentina with the captain, Maro Itoje, rested. Opoku-Fordjour has only eight caps to date but his versatility sets him apart, while Atkinson has emerged as Borthwick’s first-choice inside-centre.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBorthwick made headlines when he chose to select Van Rensburg at the first possible opportunity over the summer after he qualified for England on residency grounds, but he has not been deemed worthy of a central contract. Handing Lawes a contract after a two-year sojourn in France could have sent the wrong message to players based in England but the 37-year-old will surely get his chance to stake a claim in the coming season. The same goes for Joe Marchant, who has also joined Sale.Ben Curry’s omission is unsurprising given his injury problems, while Roebuck’s standing has fallen quickly, but Borthwick has not selected a like-for-like replacement for either the Sale wing or Daly, demonstrating how fluid his back-three options are. Willis’s move to France, confirmed weeks after he was given a central contract, was embarrassing for the Rugby Football Union and Pepper is the beneficiary, while Van Poortvliet started all three summer Tests with Alex Mitchell injured.Explore more on these topicsEngland rugby union teamRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 7: Coventry | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: After 25 years away, can Coventry make their return to the top division stick under Frank Lampard?
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: After 25 years away, can Coventry make their return to the top division stick under Frank Lampard?
Content: Eyebrows were raised when Frank Lampard replaced the popular and long-serving Mark Robins, but his success at Coventry cannot be argued with. Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesAfter 25 years away, can Coventry make their return to the top division stick under Frank Lampard?ByBen FisherWed 12 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:18th (NB: this is not necessarily Ben Fisher’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:1st (Championship)Prospects“We are back”, as the banners proudly state. It is 25 years since, after relegation was confirmed, Match of the Day cameras lingered on a message held aloft by a Coventry City supporter named John Mullaney. “We’ll be back,” were the words he inked – in sky blue, of course – on a scrap of wallpaper. When Coventry celebratedreturning to the top flightandlifted the Championship trophyin front of a capacity crowd, thousands of supportersheld aloft new-look signswith a tweaked slogan to symbolise the journey coming full circle: “We are back”.It has not been without painalong the way; nine years ago they were preparing for their first season in the fourth tier for 59 years, and from 2019 to 2021 they had to share St Andrew’s with the landlords Birmingham. That was not even their first spell of homelessness; in 2013-14, they played “home” games 35 miles away in Northampton. Many supporters will recall those harder times when Frank Lampard’s side kick off the new season in the Premier League curtain-raiser at champions Arsenal a week on Friday. Many will also rememberthe work of Mark Robins, who across two spells spent more than eight years in charge, en route to this point.The biggest challenge will be adapting to the level. Lampard is aPremier Leaguegreat but only seven of his squad count experience of the division on their CVs, the returning maverick Gus Hamer boasting the most starts among them (34) from his season in the top flight with Sheffield United. “Part of that is a good thing: we’re excited, hungry and the players want to show they deserve to be here,” Lampard said. “But we also have to work to help the squad to bridge the gap.”Coventry’s recruitment has been superb under the sporting director, Dean Austin, andthe club-record £23m arrivalof Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi from the Danish side FC Nordsjælland is particularly exciting. Some of those who flourished upon joining in the second tier also look capable of stepping up, including Milan van Ewijk, Jack Rudoni and Carl Rushworth,who has signed permanentlyafter a successful loan from Brighton. Goals were no problem last season: Coventry were the highest scorers in English football’s top four tiers with 97.Aside from a playoff semi-final defeat to Sunderland last year and a bumpy start to this one, it has been largely smooth sailing since Lampard succeeded Robins in November 2024. Coventry lost seven league matches last season, only two at home, and the going will be tougher in the top tier. “We’ve won a lot of games at this club in the last year – it’s going to be much harder to do that in the Premier League,” Lampard said. “I’m not scared of that. We have to be excited by it.”Past five seasonsOff-field pictureCoventry launched a “storytelling space” at the club’s stadium to celebrate promotion and the path to this point. The first exhibition in the club’s museum is titledThe Journey Back, which tells the club’s story from homelessness to the Premier League and showcases artefacts donated by supporters, players and managers and the owner, Doug King, opened last month. Promotion means abiding by Premier League regulations and the Coventry Building Society Arena, as it is now known, has dropped in capacity by about 300 seats in order to accommodate camera gantries and other changes to ensure compliance.Owner-fan relationshipKing angered supporters when sacking Robins but his decision was ultimately vindicated. King is never too proud to get involved: see him fist pumping the crowd, belting out the Enemy’s We’ll Live and Die in These Towns, the club’s de facto pre-match anthem, from the directors’ box, or swaying to Take That, who performed a trio of gigs at the stadium he bought 12 months ago – another big tick. Such is King’s popularity, supporters chant his name and a couple last season donned fancy dress to masquerade as him, wearing lanyards, sky-blue ties and bouffant wigs. “They tried to blag themselves into the boardroom ... but I’m way more handsome than them,”Kingsaid.The managerPromotion to the Premier League, Lampard says, marked the proudest moment of his managerial career. He went to work on his coaching badges after retiring and, 12 months after taking charge of Derby, he achieved his ultimate goal in double-quick time: managing Chelsea.A lot has happened since, including a stint “babysitting” the Blues when put in interim charge in April 2023. That seven-week period was his last exposure to the top flight as a manager but the familiar voices of his assistants Joe Edwards and Chris Jones remain. After 20 months in charge, he is comfortably the longest-serving ofthe three English managers in the division(Michael Carrick, eight months; Gary O’Neil, three months). Fresh from being named the League Managers Association manager of the year, an award presented to him by Thomas Tuchel, this summer Lampard signed fresh terms until 2029.Star signingNever fall in love with a loan player? Coventry did not just score goals last season, they kept them out, too, Rushworth claiming the Championship golden glove for 17 clean sheets. An ever-present in the league, his performances earned him three end-of-season club awards. On Coventry’s open-top bus parade, Rushworth, handed a pen by the captain, Matt Grimes, signed a placard that read “Sign here Carl” in block capitals. Then, this month, he signed a real contract to join permanently from Brighton, who inserted a buyback clause. “He was this close to getting kicked out of the group chat,” the defender Jake Bidwell joked after embracing Rushworth on his return. Before his season at Coventry, he had enjoyed loans across the league pyramid with Walsall, Lincoln, Swansea and Hull, but now the highly-regarded 25-year-old will test himself at the highest level.View image in fullscreenCoventry valued Carl Rushworth so highly they spent a club-record £22.5m to sign him permanently from Brighton.Photograph: Richard Hammersley/ShutterstockStat attackArsenal were not the only champions to make good use of dead-ball situations last season. Coventry led the Championship for set-piece goals, with 29. Only Bayern Munich (0.65 goals per game) bettered their average (0.63) in the top divisions in England, France, Germany, Italy and Spain. The issue is whether they will win enough corners and free-kicks in the Premier League to exploit this ability.StatSet for a breakthroughPromotion makes the jump from the academy to the first team that little bit bigger but Kai Andrews has at least made a dent in the senior squad. The 20-year-old, who made his debut aged 17, made seven substitute appearances last season before being loaned to Hibernian. Competition has only got fiercer since but Andrews has plenty of admirers. “There’s just something more about this kid; he has a presence – and that excites me,” said Craig Bellamy, who played for Coventry at the beginning of his career and handed an 18-year-old Andrews a shock call-up to the Wales squad approaching 18 months ago.World Cup impactDid Yirenkyi have an inkling that he would soon call Brandon Thomas-Asante a clubmate after the striker set him up to score his first World Cup goal for Ghana? Thomas-Asante, one of five players to reach double figures for Coventry last season, made inroads down the left flank and then squared the ball to the six-yard box, where Yirenkyi was on hand to strikea 95th-minute winner against Panamain their opener in Toronto. Haji Wright, Coventry’s top scorer last season, made two late substitute appearances for the USA, while Aurèle Amenda was part of the Switzerland squad that reached the last 16 but did not play a minute.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27Coventry CityPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Live facial recognition cameras to be used on UK’s busiest shopping street | Metropolitan police | The Guardian
description: Sadiq Khan has indicated the technology will be deployed on London’s Oxford Street despite human rights concerns
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Sadiq Khan has indicated the technology will be deployed on London’s Oxford Street despite human rights concerns
Content: The human rights organisation Liberty said if the technology was introduced there must be ‘full transparency’ over its use.Photograph: Ian Davidson/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe human rights organisation Liberty said if the technology was introduced there must be ‘full transparency’ over its use.Photograph: Ian Davidson/SOPA Images/ShutterstockMetropolitan policeLive facial recognition cameras to be used on UK’s busiest shopping streetSadiq Khan has indicated the technology will be deployed on London’s Oxford Street despite human rights concernsRachel HallWed 12 Aug 2026 08.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheMetropolitan policeare understood to be planning to use live facial recognition (LFR) technology on Britain’s busiest shopping street.In June, the Met said it would introduce the technology in London’s West End by Christmas and into a further six areas next year.Sadiq Khan, the London mayor, has indicated that the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street will be included.This would make it among the first areas in the country to have permanent LFR infrastructure scanning the faces of people passing and comparing them with a watchlist of wanted suspects.The cameras will be fixed and could be attached to street furniture such as lamp-posts, rather than a temporary police van as has been the case in trials.Human rights groups have widely criticised LFR. One organisation described the proposed introduction on Oxford Street as an escalation in routine public surveillance. There is evidence that the algorithm used to power it candiscriminate against black people.Scotland Yard plans to use static LFR cameras in London’s West End and Soho, which have some of the highest crime rates in the city. The technology has started to be deployed at tube stations this month.During a city hall session in July, Khan said: “The Met is working really closely with the Oxford Street Development Corporation about how, when we pedestrianise that street, we use LFR in a sensible way, using the opportunity of new CCTV to use LFR.”Ruth Ehrlich, of the human rights organisation Liberty, said using live facial recognition cameras on Oxford Street would mark “a significant expansion of surveillance in public spaces” and “an escalation”.“This technology scans the faces of everyone who passes by, regardless of whether they are suspected of any wrongdoing,” she said.“If live facial recognition is to be deployed in one of the country’s busiest shopping and tourist destinations, there must be full transparency about how it will be used, what safeguards are in place and how its impact on people’s rights will be monitored.”She urged the Met not to introduce more LFR before the government produces its forthcoming legal framework for the use of facial recognition by law enforcement.Recent polling commissioned by Liberty suggested 48% of people oppose scanning the faces of those walking on high streets when there is no suspected imminent threat.Jasleen Chaggar, of the campaign group Big Brother Watch, urged the mayor to abandon the idea. “A face scan is as unique as a fingerprint,” she said. “The police cannot take your fingerprints when you are not suspected of wrongdoing. Taking a faceprint is no less intrusive just because it happens remotely.”A spokesperson for the mayor said the introduction of LFR was part of the move to make Oxford Street “a world-class, pedestrian-friendly and safe destination”.He said: “As part of delivering that, the mayor is working with the Met, West End Taskforce and Oxford Street Development Corporation on making best use of technology. Backed by record funding from city hall, the Met are leading the way in using the latest technology, including ebikes, drones and live facial recognition, to arrest dangerous criminals and tackle and prevent violence in the capital.“In Westminster, neighbourhood crime has fallen, with 14,000 fewer offences in the past year and the Met’s rollout of live facial recognition in the West End and Soho will help drive down crime rates even further.“The mayor is committed to ensuring the Met is open and transparent around where, when, why and how live facial recognition technology is used. His Office for Policing and Crime will continue to scrutinise and oversee its use to ensure there’s trust and confidence in policing, as we continue to build a safer London for everyone.”Explore more on these topicsMetropolitan policeLondonPoliceSadiq KhanSurveillanceEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Greenland forces Trump-linked US oil firm to delay drilling | Greenland | The Guardian
description: US envoy had claimed Americans could be extracting crude by as early as next year
Author: Tom Burgis
Headline: US envoy had claimed Americans could be extracting crude by as early as next year
Content: Texas-based Greenland Energy had been just weeks away from sinking its first wells into the tundra of the remote Jameson Land region of Greenland.Photograph: Biosphoto/AlamyView image in fullscreenTexas-based Greenland Energy had been just weeks away from sinking its first wells into the tundra of the remote Jameson Land region of Greenland.Photograph: Biosphoto/AlamyGreenlandGreenland forces Trump-linked US oil firm to delay drillingUS envoy had claimed Americans could be extracting crude by as early as next yearTom BurgisWed 12 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreenland authorities have forced a US oil company connected to Donald Trump to postpone drilling wells in the Arctic territory, defying claims by the US president’s envoy that Americans could be extracting crude by next year.Amid Trump’s imperialist threats, tensions have been rising on Greenland’s eastern coast after the oil companybrought drilling equipment ashorein July without permission, drawing a “strong warning” from the government.Just week before Greenland Energy intended to sink its first wells into the tundra, the government said on Thursday: “The necessary regulatory process cannot be completed, and the necessary approvals cannot therefore be obtained before the planned start of drilling.”It said that during talks Greenlandic officials had expressed concern that the timetable was too tight to assess the environmental and social impact.The authorities will have to decide whether to sanction drilling in a protected wetland that is home to rare birds and the muskoxen on which local hunters depend. At the earliest, drilling could now commence in the winter of 2027, the government and the company said.That is a long way off the prediction made as recently as May by Jeff Landry, the hard-right Louisiana governor whom Trump named as his envoy to Greenland. He said after a visit that oil supposedly lying under Greenland could ease the energy crisis caused by the US attack on Iran.Landry, whose stated goal is to “make Greenland a part of the US”, said: “We could have those barrels on production within 10 months or so.”Robert Price, the Greenland Energy chief executive, who maintains that oil worth $1tn could lie under the remote Jameson Land region, said: “Greenland Energy remains committed to advancing its oil exploration programme responsibly and in accordance with Greenland’s regulatory process, and in full compliance with Greenlandic authorities.”Price added: “We will use this time to refine our plans and deepen relationships with local communities, strategic partners and relevant authorities.”Since a rich friendput the ideaof acquiring Greenland in Trump’s head during his first term, the president has threatened to do so by buying it from Denmark, seizing it with military force or cutting a deal.Greenland issues ‘strong warning’ as Trump-linked oil firm prepares to drillRead moreShareholders in Greenland Energy had been hoping for a “Trump pump”, a presidential endorsement that could send the New York-listed stock rocketing. But on Wednesday the price fell by more than a third after the drilling delay was announced.Price had said a ship bringing 300 containers of drilling kit would set sail from Canada for Greenland in September, with a first well to be sunk the following month.He told a community meeting – falsely – that Greenland had granted permission for the company to start landing equipment.Greenland Energy’s British partner 80 Mile said in an update for investors on Wednesday that the delay was due to the need to “complete the permitting and regulatory approval process”.80 Mile holds exploration licences granted before Greenland stopped issuing them in 2021, citing the climate crisis.Greenland Energy, formed last year, has announced plans to spend $60m (£44m) raised from investors to fund drilling in exchange for a majority stake in the project.Its representatives have said its oil venture is “not related to American annexation”, yet the company has established multiple connections to the Trump administration.Phil McGraw, better known as the chatshow host Dr Phil, has a deal with Greenland Energy to “capture the mission of thesemodern-day wildcatters” for a documentary series to be broadcast on television and social media. He recently appeared in the Oval Office alongside Trump, having served on the president’s religious freedom commission.A US navy veteran who is working on Golden Dome, the missile defence plan for which Trump says controlling Greenland is “vital”, sits on Greenland Energy’s board. And Kenneth Griffin, a Wall Street billionaire who gave $1m towards Trump’s second inauguration, bought 9% of Greenland Energy’s shares in April.Rod McIllree, 80 Mile’s boss, said: “While we are disappointed that the timing of the Jameson drilling programme has been impacted, the company remains fully committed to advancing this highly prospective project.”Explore more on these topicsGreenlandOilOil and gas companiesCommoditiesEnergy industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: USS Abraham Lincoln sailors tried to jump overboard amid extended deployment – reports | US military | The Guardian
description: Aircraft carrier’s crew in ninth month at sea and has spent record 250 days consecutively without making land
Author: Ed Pilkington
Headline: Aircraft carrier’s crew in ninth month at sea and has spent record 250 days consecutively without making land
Content: The USS Abraham Lincoln sailing in the Arabian Sea on 8 May.Photograph: US Navy/Navcent Public Affairs/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe USS Abraham Lincoln sailing in the Arabian Sea on 8 May.Photograph: US Navy/Navcent Public Affairs/AFP/Getty ImagesUS militaryUSS Abraham Lincoln sailors tried to jump overboard amid extended deployment – reportsAircraft carrier’s crew in ninth month at sea and has spent record 250 days consecutively without making landEd PilkingtonWed 12 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMilitary families and Congress members are sounding the alarm about an intensifying mental health crisis onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, as its 5,000 sailors and marines endure a record-breaking deployment at sea tied to the war with Iran.Two leading specialist military papers, theNavy TimesandStars and Stripes, are reporting that there have been multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard as poor conditions and mental stresses on the Lincoln reach the breaking point. The crew is in its ninth month at sea, and has spent 250 days consecutively without making land – a record for an aircraft carrier in modern times.Worried families vented their anxieties about loved ones onboard the Lincoln at an emotional town hall meeting with navy leaders in San Diego last Thursday,Stars and Stripesreported. One spouse among the 200 or so family members said that her husband had texted her that day saying “he hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow”.Trump denies US low on key munitions in war with Iran after reports of shortagesRead moreThe families’ worries were expressed directly to navy leadership, represented at the town hall by the acting navy secretary, Hung Cao, and other top officials.A woman at the meeting told Cao that the navy had “broken trust between us and the leadership”, the paper reported.The Navy Timesgave detailsof thwarted suicide attempts onboard the aircraft carrier during the current deployment. Annabelle Loma told the outlet that her husband had tried to jump overboard after his spell at sea kept being extended.“He’s scared. He thinks he’ll get a dishonorable discharge, and just because he was burnt out his 13-year career is ruined, just like that,” she said.The paper quoted another sailor’s wife whose husband was involved in a separate incident onboard the Lincoln in which he prevented a fellow crew member from jumping, grabbing them and bringing them back on deck.Mike Levin, a Democratic member of Congress from California, has sounded the alarm over conditions onboard the warship, which is in its fifth month of combat operations against Iran. He described the lot of the crewon Xas “moldy showers, broken toilets, laundry down for weeks, long stretches with no hot water, a meal that came down to half a cup of rice and two tortillas. No soap, deodorant, or toothpaste.”Jason Crow, a Democratic Congress member from Colorado who is a former army ranger having served in Afghanistan and Iraq,has warnedthat the strain on service members and their families on the Lincoln is “building week by week”.The current crunch has been months in the making. The warship left San Diego on 21 November and was originally intended for the Pacific but was redirected to the Middle East once the US-Israel war with Iran began.Since then,MS Now revealed, the 5,000-plus crew has had only two days on land, in Guam in December and Oman in July. The deployment was scheduled to end in May but has been extended a couple of times amid the ongoing war.In April, there was a flurry of public criticism about dire conditions onboard the carrier. Photos emerged of poor-quality andrationed food, and there were reports of water shortages, moldy showers and broken laundry machines.Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary,dismissed the accountsas “more fake news”.Levin responded to Hegseth’s remark this week. He said: “These men and women signed up to serve their country. The least their country owes them is hot water, a working toilet and a real meal. Hegseth cannot even manage that, and he has the nerve to look their families in the eye and call them liars.”The Guardian contacted the US navy for its response to reports of attempts to jump overboard. After this article was published, a navy official responded, saying that they were aware that “extended deployments place a significant strain on our service members and their families, and we are grateful for the resilience and sacrifices they make”.The official said that the health and wellbeing of every Lincoln sailor was a priority: “Based on information available to the command, we have not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship.”Religious, medical and mental health professionals were available as part of a “comprehensive support network” that included “onboard deployment-resilience counselors and chaplains”. The official recognised that the war had disrupted traditional supply hubs, but added that “current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional AC and healthy meal options”.The mental health challenges faced by active-duty US navy personnel are well known. Astudy from last yearlooked at the unique stress factors faced by sailors on deployments and found the most common included loud noises, lack of rest, and inadequate mental and physical healthcare.The researchers conducted a survey of deployed sailors and found that almost half complained that they were not receiving adequate help in coping with stress at sea. The study concluded that “given the high rates of military suicide, including within the navy, efforts to improve healthcare access on ships are urgently needed”.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryUS-Israel war on IranMental healthPete HegsethTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Astronomers discover a new kind of cosmic object – a black hole ‘star’ | Black holes | The Guardian
description: The body is the size of the entire solar system and glows with a brilliant red light billions of light years from Earth
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: The body is the size of the entire solar system and glows with a brilliant red light billions of light years from Earth
Content: The black hole star, calculated to be more than 100,000 times larger than our sun.Photograph: Rohan Naidu, University of Hawai'i.View image in fullscreenThe black hole star, calculated to be more than 100,000 times larger than our sun.Photograph: Rohan Naidu, University of Hawai'i.Black holesAstronomers discover a new kind of cosmic object – a black hole ‘star’The body is the size of the entire solar system and glows with a brilliant red light billions of light years from EarthIan SampleScience editorWed 12 Aug 2026 11.46 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAstronomers claim to have discovered a new kind of cosmic object, a black hole “star”, which is the size of the entire solar system and glows with a brilliant red light.The international team made the breakthrough after focusing their attention on a mysterious red spot in images of the early solar system captured by Nasa’sJames Webb space telescope.The object was lurking in the constellation of Cetus, the Whale, billions of light years from Earth. It is thought to have formed 660m years after the big bang, astronomers’ leading theory as to how the universe began.Measurements of the exotic body found that while it resembles an immense star, it releases 100bn times more energy than any known star can produce. The energy output is far closer to that observed from black holes than stars.“We have found a new type of astrophysical object, a black hole star,” said Dr Rohan Naidu at the Kavli Institute for Astrophysics andSpaceResearch, part of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.It “shines with the energy typically associated with black holes, but at the same time bears signatures classically associated with stars”, he added.View image in fullscreenScientists made the breakthrough after focusing their attention on a mysterious red spot in images captured by Nasa’s James Webb space telescope.Photograph: Nasa, ESA, CSA, STScI, DAWN JWST ArchiveThe scientists were using the James Webb space telescope to find the most distant galaxies in the known universe. After succeeding with a galaxy named Mom-z14, which formed a mere 280m years after the big bang, they turned their attention to other cosmic objects.Writing inNature, the astronomers describe how they focused on an extremely bright red spot known as MoM-BH*-1, the reddest object in the telescope’s image archive.“The way its light is almost entirely red, and abruptly disappears below a certain wavelength, is so dramatic that there is no comparison among any known class of objects,” Naidu said.Computer simulations showed that rather than being an enormous star powered by nuclear fusion, the object is a black hole so swaddled in shrouds of dense gas that it radiates like a star.If the astronomers are correct, it suggests that scores of other mysterious Little Red Dots, or LRDs, that appear in nearly every deep space image from the James Webb space telescope are also black hole stars.Naidu suspects that black hole stars play a major role in the evolution of galaxies. They might be the seeds of present-day supermassive black holes, such as the one at the centre of the Milky Way.“For decades we have anticipated something spectacular must be afoot in the very early universe. Black hole stars may be the ‘something spectacular’. They may be the nascent, swaddled phase that marks the beginning of almost every supermassive black hole’s journey,” he said.Supermassive black holes are found at the centres of almost all galaxies such as the Milky Way and are thought to shape the fate of those galaxies.“They may govern when stars are able to form and when they cease forming, setting the course for everything that follows from star formation: the birth of planets, the rise of life, the emergence of species that may one day piece together this entire history,” Naidu said.Explore more on these topicsBlack holesAstronomyJames Webb space telescopeSpaceNasanewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Mexican governor charged in case of 43 students who vanished in 2014 | Mexico | The Guardian
description: Ángel Aguirre indicted in case that rocked Mexico and became symbol of its brutal cartel violence
Author: Oscar Lopez
Headline: Ángel Aguirre indicted in case that rocked Mexico and became symbol of its brutal cartel violence
Content: Ángel Aguirre speaking at a news conference in 2014. He is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice.Photograph: Jorge Lopez/ReutersView image in fullscreenÁngel Aguirre speaking at a news conference in 2014. He is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice.Photograph: Jorge Lopez/ReutersMexicoFormer Mexican governor charged in case of 43 students who vanished in 2014Ángel Aguirre indicted in case that rocked Mexico and became symbol of its brutal cartel violenceOscar LopezWed 12 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former governor of Guerrero state inMexicohas been formally charged over his alleged involvement in the disappearance of 43 students in 2014, a case that has become a symbol of the country’s brutal cartel violence and government impunity.Ángel Aguirre, who wasarrested last week, is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice for ordering the destruction of surveillance tapes that may have shed light on what happened to the students from the Ayotzinapa teacher training college on the night of 26 September 2014.On Wednesday, a judge ruled Mexico’s attorney general had presented enough evidence to formally charge Aguirre with forced disappearance and ordered that he remain in a maximum security prison awaiting trial.A lawyer for Aguirre denied his client’s wrongdoing. Guillermo Baradas told reporters: “We presented evidence demonstrating a high-level meeting attended by Mr Ángel Aguirre at the time the videos were allegedly handed over to him.”Aguirre’s indictment is the biggest breakthrough in the Ayotzinapa case since the 2022 arrest of Jesús Murillo Karam, who served as Mexico’s attorney general at the time of the students’ abduction.The brutality of the case rocked Mexico and continues to haunt the country more than a decade on. With the remains of only three students identified, it is not known what happened to the 40 others.On the night that they were abducted, the students from the Raúl Isidros Burgos teacher training college in the village of Ayotzinapa had commandeered several buses in the city of Iguala to get to a protest in Mexico City.But before they could leave Iguala, in Guerrero state, the students were attacked by a local criminal gang working with municipal police. A years-long international investigation determined that federal forces, both police and military, were also involved either by participating directly or failing to intervene as the students were taken away and presumably killed.The government at the time orchestrated an elaborate coverup, attempting to place blame for the attack solely on the criminal gang and local police. Suspects were tortured into giving false confessions and crime scene evidence was manipulated.Meltión Ortega, a spokesperson for the 43 students, said: “We want no more deception; we want to be told the truth and for those responsible to be punished. The victims from Guerrero deserve to have the actual perpetrators and the masterminds punished, rather than just seeing a charade, as has happened in serious cases of human rights violations.”Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has vowed to get to the bottom of what happened to the students and formedan investigative unitto dig into the case last year. “I’m going to put all my effort, all my energy, all my willpower [towards obtaining truth and justice],” she told reporters at a news conference last week.Explore more on these topicsMexicoAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump administration pulls support for annual Arctic environmental report | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Move by National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is latest government rollback of climate science activity
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Move by National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is latest government rollback of climate science activity
Content: The Arctic Sea, 1,200 nautical miles from Tromsø, Norway, on 9 July 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Arctic Sea, 1,200 nautical miles from Tromsø, Norway, on 9 July 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesTrump administrationTrump administration pulls support for annual Arctic environmental reportMove by National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is latest government rollback of climate science activityMaya YangWed 12 Aug 2026 14.17 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 16.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTrump administrationhas pulled its support for an annual report on the environmental changes across theArctic, a region that is already heating upfour times fasterthan the global average due to theclimate crisis.On Tuesday, Kim Doster, the communications director of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), said the federal agency was withdrawing its support for theArcticReport Card, which has provided environmental updates on the region to scientists and the public since 2006.Without explaining why the government stopped its support, Dostertoldthe New York Times: “Coordination of the 2026 Arctic Report Card will not be facilitated through NOAA … All data historically contributed by NOAA to the product will continue to be collected and will remain publicly available.”Doster told the outlet that other Noaa programs would continue to support research in the region that contributes to “national security, weather prediction, safety of navigation and the economic vitality of coastal communities”.Dismay as Trump officials to dismantle key ocean monitoring systemRead moreThe Guardian has approached Noaa for additional comment.Over the last 20 years, the peer-reviewed report has tracked crucial changes across the Arctic’s atmosphere, oceans, cryosphere and tundra. Theclimate crisishas made the Arctic the world’sfastest-warming region. In recent years, the region has experienced severesea ice decline,carbon sink reversalsandecosystem upheavals.In the2025 Arctic Report Card, scientists found that surface temperatures across the Arctic from October 2024 through September 2025 were the warmest recorded since 1900. It also found that in March 2025, Arctic winter sea ice reached the lowest annual maximum extent in the 47-year satellite record.Meanwhile, on land, the report noted that ongoing glacier loss contributes to steadily rising global sea levels, threatening Arctic communities’ water supplies, driving destructive floods, and increasing landslide and tsunami hazards.It also found that in more than 200 Arctic Alaska watersheds – large land areas where rain and melted snow drain northward into the Arctic Ocean – iron and other elements released by thawing permafrost haveturned rivers and streams orangein the last 10 years. The “rusting rivers” have in turn increased acidity while elevated levels of toxic metals have degraded water quality, in turn affecting aquatic habits, rural drinking water supplies and subsistence fishing.Rick Thoman, the lead editor for this year’s report, said: “We are scrambling to pull the pieces together. I am optimistic that we can find a path forward for 2027 and beyond. Given the late date, whether we can pull it together for 2026 is an open question, but we’re trying to make it happen.”Meanwhile, Twila Moon, one of the report’s editors and a scientist at the Colorado-based National Snow and Ice Data Center, said: “The US is an Arctic nation. It’s not just a distant place. It’s also our national place. So many of the changes there have impacts that reach down into our mid-latitudes, even further south.”Moon added: “Even if we’re able to move the Arctic Report Card forward in a way that brings information to people, there’s still a real loss in this not being a US federal effort. That’s a real stepping back of US leadership in the science arena, in the environmental intelligence arena, and that kind of has a whole other flavor of harm as well.”Rick Spinrad, the former Noaa administrator under Joe Biden, called the decision “really unconscionable”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It provides the baseline of what’s happening in the Arctic,” Spinrad said, referring to the report. “Then in terms of value for future planning, you can imagine anybody who’s dependent on Alaskan infrastructure – for example, like the oil pipeline, or the fishing community, or local communities that are worried about changes in weather conditions that are going to affect frost heaves on their roads,” he added, highlighting municipalities like Anchorage and Fairbanks.“Now we will not have that tool, and it will be up to them to try to ferret out where the data are, and then to find somebody who can do the analysis to tell them what the trends have been and what they can expect in the future.“It’s not clear to me why the administration made this decision. I can only infer that it’s tied to their aversion to anything associated with having a better understanding of climate change,” Spinrad added.The funding cancellation is the Trump administration’s latest move to impede government-led studies on the climate crisis and its global effects.Since retaking office last January, the Trump administration hasstripped away supportfor scientific research that mentions “climate”,dismantleda key climate research center in Colorado in a move that the governor, Jared Polis, warned would put “public safety at risk”,attempted to scrapa $368m crucial deep-sea observation system, as well asremoving key climate change reportsfrom government websites.Other federally led environmental rollbacks include Noaa’s decisionto stop trackingthe costs of climate crisis-fueled disasters, as well as thedismissal of all contributorsto the US government’s flagship report on climate crisis preparedness.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationArcticClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Humpbacks return to Rio: the whales are back from the brink of extinction – but will tourism help or hinder? | Whales | The Guardian
description: The gigantic aquatic acrobats are exciting Brazil’s tourists as numbers recover from whaling. But some marine biologists question how booming tourism and conservation can coexist
Author: Constance Malleret
Headline: The gigantic aquatic acrobats are exciting Brazil’s tourists as numbers recover from whaling. But some marine biologists question how booming tourism and conservation can coexist
Content: The humpback whale population fell below 1,000 after intense hunting but is now estimated at 35,000.Photograph: Bruna Rezende/Amigos da JubarteView image in fullscreenThe humpback whale population fell below 1,000 after intense hunting but is now estimated at 35,000.Photograph: Bruna Rezende/Amigos da JubarteSeascape: the state of our oceansWhalesHumpbacks return to Rio: the whales are back from the brink of extinction – but will tourism help or hinder?The gigantic aquatic acrobats are exciting Brazil’s tourists as numbers recover from whaling. But some marine biologists question how booming tourism and conservation can coexistSeascape: the state of our oceans is supported byAbout this contentConstance Malleretin Rio de JaneiroWed 12 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe anticipation is palpable onboard the Boaventura II as the yacht sets off fromRio de Janeiroat sunrise. Once beyond the Cagarras Islands, rocky outcrops just three miles off Ipanema beach, the group gathers at the bow and starts scanning the horizon.They do not have to wait long. “Eleven o’clock!” someone calls out, as a pod of bottlenose dolphins appears, playfully diving in and out of the water. Then, two spouts of vapour hanging in the air signal the reason for the outing: a pair of humpback whales. The majestic mammals surface to breathe with an unhurried chuff, before revealing the underside of their fluke as they dive back underwater.This is a bucket-list moment for many on the boat, heightened by the spectacular backdrop of Rio’s jungle-cloaked mountains. But such a sight has become increasingly common, as Brazil’s humpback whales return to the shores of theCidade Maravilhosa(Marvellous City) during the southern hemisphere winter after making a remarkable comeback from near-extinction.This year, one whale has even been repeatedly spotted within Rio’s Guanabara Bay. The sightings – at least 18 – are a first and have sparked speculation that humpbacks are returning to areas they once occupied centuries ago.“You can’t put a price on this show. It’s pure magic,” says the yacht’s skipper, Theo Andrade, co-founder of the tour agency ROC Sail. After working on whale-watching expeditions around breeding grounds farther north, Andrade started running his own outings in Rio this year.Luciane dos Santos, a 53-year-old passenger, is fascinated by the gentle giants and took a day out of her busy life running a drinks wholesaler in the hopes of catching a glimpse of them. “I’m amazed at how a 50-tonne animal can perform such a beautiful leap that leaves everyone spellbound,” she says.View image in fullscreenWhalewatchers onboard the Boaventura II scan the seas for a sight of whales.Photograph: Louise Raulais/ROC SailShe was not disappointed. “I feel a sense of fullness – it’s truly a gift from nature,” says Dos Santos, after a morning spent admiring six humpbacks performing their aquatic ballet.Humpbacks have always travelled along the Brazilian coast between June and November as they migrate from feeding grounds around South Georgia and the Sandwich Islands in the South Atlantic to the warmer, shallower waters of the Abrolhos Bank, off Brazil’s north-east coast, to breed.As elsewhere, indiscriminate hunting – recorded as early as about 1780 in Rio by the artist Leandro Joaquim, who painted scenes of whales being chased and harpooned in Guanabara Bay – had decimated the population by the time a global ban on commercial whaling took effect in 1986.View image in fullscreenPesca da Baleia(Whaling) by Leandro Joaquim, a 18th-century Brazilian painting depicting whale hunting in Guanabara Bay.Photograph: Alamy“At the end of the 1980s, fewer than 1,000 individuals were counted in this Brazilian group. Today, there are nearly 30,000,” says Thiago Ferrari, director of the Amigos da Jubarte (Friends of the Humpback) conservation project. Other estimates put the number closer to 35,000.Brazilian waters are home to several whale species, including the once-endangered southern right whale – believed to be the species depicted in Joaquim’s painting – and Bryde’s whale. The 15-metre-long humpback is, however, “the star of the show” due to its acrobatic performances, says Ferrari.Liliane Lodi, a marine biologist who works for the Ilhas do Rio (Islands of Rio) research project, which first registered a humpback whale in the city’s waters in 2014. The number of sightings has soared since then and, with them, observation of new and different behaviours.View image in fullscreenA humpback whale’s pectoral fin, seen against Rio de Janeiro’s mountains.Photograph: Louise Raulais/ROC Sail“Rio de Janeiro is an area of passage; it’s a migration route,” she says of humpbacks. “However, we have already registered behaviour that is typical of breeding grounds, rather than passage areas.”That includes spotting newborn calves, displays of competitive behaviour between males and recordings of haunting whale songs.This year, Lodi has been investigating the Guanabara Bay appearances. She concluded that they are of the same whale – a juvenile that has been living in the bay’s sheltered waters since mid-June, delighting early-morning canoeists. “It’s very sociable when it wants to be,” says Lodi, who enlisted the help of citizen scientists to study the animal.View image in fullscreenMariana Bueno, a researcher who accompanies ROC Sail’s whalewatching trips.Photograph: Constance MalleretSuch collaboration between science and leisure is one of the reasons advocates believe Rio’s budding whalewatching industry can be a tool for conservation, as well as a new source of tourism revenue during the winter.Mariana Bueno is an environmental sciences student employed by ROC Sail to accompany each whalewatching outing on the Boaventura II. “When you combine tourism and research,” she says, “you have infinitely better data collection than if you weren’t working together.”Having a researcher onboard, says Ferrari, is “fundamental for healthy, sustainable and orderly whale-watching tourism”. With its team of biologists, the Amigos da Jubarte non-profit environmental organisation offers free training courses in partnership with local authorities, through which they have already certified about 20 agencies for cetacean watching in Rio, including ROC Sail.Clipboard in hand, Bueno answers tourists’ questions, advises the skipper to ensure that he follows best practice – such as keeping at least 100 metres from the whales and never spending more than 30 minutes near the same individuals – and writes down details of every sighting. All of the information is passed on to Amigos da Jubarte to help research.“Surveying the number of individuals allows us to track population growth … and individual behaviour,” says Bueno. “How they’re interacting with a vessel or how curious they are about humans. These behavioural surveys then serve as the basis for formulating laws and rules.”But while Lodi recognises tourism’s contribution to research, she worries about its impact on conservation, as the trend for whale watching in Rio means more boats are clustering around the whale migration corridor just beyond the Cagarras Islands.View image in fullscreenA juvenile humpback by Ilha Fiscal in central Rio. The ‘sociable’ whale has repeatedly been sighted in Guanabara Bay.Photograph: Liliane Lodi“This population increase is a source of great happiness to us researchers. But with an increase in numbers comes an increase in [human-whale] conflicts,” she says.Sperm whales change ‘vowel’ sounds when boats are nearby, scientists discoverRead more“Fishing, tourism, large ships, chemical pollution and noise pollution, these are all challenges [and] threats,” she adds.Although Brazil has relatively robust laws protecting whales – swimming with them is prohibited, for example – the legislation needs updating and requires better monitoring to guarantee enforcement, she argues.“For a whale, it doesn’t make much difference that one operator follows best practice if the others aren’t doing so,” says Lodi. “We’re dealing with highly intelligent animals. If they’re being intensely bothered, there could be cumulative effects in the long run.”Explore more on these topicsWhalesSeascape: the state of our oceansBrazilRio de JaneiroAmericasCetaceansMarine lifeWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Just 20 of 6,600 Defra staff working on climate adaptation amid drought and wildfires | Environment policy | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: England ‘desperately unprepared’ for effects of crisis including water shortages and heatwaves
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Exclusive: England ‘desperately unprepared’ for effects of crisis including water shortages and heatwaves
Content: The UK government has been warned that it is lagging far behind in terms of adapting to a new climate as a result of global heating.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe UK government has been warned that it is lagging far behind in terms of adapting to a new climate as a result of global heating.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockEnvironment policyJust 20 of 6,600 Defra staff working on climate adaptation amid drought and wildfiresExclusive: England ‘desperately unprepared’ for effects of crisis including water shortages and heatwavesUK heatwave live – latest updatesSandra LavilleEnvironment correspondentWed 12 Aug 2026 05.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust 20 staff are working on climate adaptation within a key government department tasked with protecting the environment and maintaining food security, a freedom of information request has revealed.The officials make up 0.3% of staff within the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.The government has been warnedby the climate change adaptation committeethat it is lagging far behind in terms of adapting to a new climate as a result of global heating.The climate crisis is increasing both summer heatwaves and winter rainfall in the UK, with both drought and flooding more likely.Peak river flows could increase by up to 45%, while water supply shortfalls may surpass 5bn litres daily, the committee has warned. It said the economic cost of failing to adapt could be between 1% and 5% of UK GDP annually by 2050 – £60bn to £260bn a year.But only 20 staff out of6,613in Defra are working on climate adaptation, according to the data.“England is desperately unprepared for the impacts of the climate crisis, and these shocking figures show how few officials are working on the problem at the top of government,” said environmental writer and campaigner Guy Shrubsole, who obtained the data.Police footage shows scale of New Forest wildfireShrubsole called on the new environment secretary, Angela Eagle, to seize the moment amid heatwaves and wildfires to greatly boost staffing and funds for climate adaptation.“Andy Burnham has seen the effects of climate change in Makerfield, which flooded in past winters, and as Manchester mayor when wildfire smoke from Peak District grouse moors choked local residents,” he said. “It’s time he levelled with the country about the climate emergency and set out a radical plan to get us off fossil fuels and prepare communities for extreme weather.”The data is revealed as Burnham is being challenged by theWildife Trustsand other leading environmental NGOs in his first 100 days in office to reset the government’s approach to the environmental emergencies facing the UK. They want him to recognise that ecological restoration – such as rewetting bogs and managing natural flood defences – is essential to national security and public health.chartSince taking office Burnham has not mentioned the climate crisis, the extreme heat the UK is experiencing this summer, the wildfires that have taken hold from the south-west to the north of England,nor the drought covering almost three-quarters of the country. The UK is about to enter its fifth heatwave of the summer, as climate breakdown makes extreme heat, drought and wildfires more likely.Friends of the Earth’s head of policy, Mike Childs, said: “The UK is in the grip of a growing climate crisis. Across the UK communities are under attack from relentless heatwaves, droughts and wildfires, putting lives, homes, farmers and nature at risk.“Andy Burnham must end his silence on the climate emergency and pledge to make it a top priority by strengthening plans to protect communities from increasingly frequent and extreme weather – especially those most at risk.View image in fullscreenWheat crops on fire in the Essex countryside on 1 August.Photograph: Justin Kase z12z/Alamy“But we must also tackle the cause, not just the consequences. The government must do more to cut the pollution driving climate change by accelerating the shift to clean energy and ruling out new oil and gas developments like Rosebank and Jackdaw, and a third runway at Heathrow.”Firefighters across the country are tackling record levels of wildfires – with 966 this year, including 458 in July alone. Steve Wright, the Fire Brigades Union general secretary, is calling for 5,000 more firefighters to be recruited, saying it should be a national priority to have enough properly equipped firefighters to face the threats of climate extremes.‘Real struggle’ to tame New Forest blaze as UK set for hottest summer on recordRead moreThe UK is short of much of the key equipment to tackle wildfires that European fire fighters possess. The country does not have any dedicated fixed-wing water-bombing planes or specialist aerial firefighting aircraft.OnWednesday, No 10announced Burnham would chair an emergency Cobra meeting in response to the extreme heat.The prime minister will meet ministers, officials and agencies as high temperatures continue across the UK, with temperatures of 33C forecast on Wednesday and up to 38C on Thursday.A Defra spokesperson said: “Climate adaption underlines work throughout the whole department – from nature recovery to flooding response to sustainable farming on top of a direct and dedicated team. It is a key priority for this government.“We are already strengthening our approach to climate adaptation through our work with the National Drought Group, building nine new reservoirs across the country and investing at least £10.5 billion by March 2036 to construct new flood and coastal erosion schemes, as extreme weather becomes more frequent.”Explore more on these topicsEnvironment policyClimate crisisEconomicsWaterExtreme weatherExtreme heatnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like an alien invasion’: the neon flying squid that can fly in formation above the ocean | Marine life | The Guardian
description: Smart, sociable squid use funnel-like organ to force water to jet propel themselves along in and out of sea
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Smart, sociable squid use funnel-like organ to force water to jet propel themselves along in and out of sea
Content: Neon flying squid are about the length of a rolling pin.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNeon flying squid are about the length of a rolling pin.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianInvertebrate of the year 2026Marine life‘Like an alien invasion’: the neon flying squid that can fly in formation above the oceanSmart, sociable squid use funnel-like organ to force water to jet propel themselves along in and out of seaRevealed: the top 10 invertebrates of the yearVote for your favourite hereOliver MilmanWed 12 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a research vessel 15 years ago, a group of Japanese scientists documented something that had only previously been described by startled sailors to disbelieving listeners. They saw a formation of squid flying through the air.The shoal of about 100 squid rose unexpectedly from a patch of the Pacific Ocean around 370 miles from Tokyo and glided near the boat for about 30 metres. The astonished researchers were the first to capture photographs of such a thing, which looked like the early stages of an alien invasion.They were probably neon flying squid (Ommastrephes bartramii), the subsequent studystates, a species that is part of a 20-strong flying squid family that was known to leap from the water but, until then, was only rumoured to also be able to glide above it.The neon flying squid was able to gain such elevation by using the hyponome, a funnel-like muscular organ also present in other cephalopods, such as octopuses. The organ is able to force water out in a jet, propelling the body along both in and out of the sea. Photographs of the gliding squid show them with their arms (they have 10 limbs in all) splayed outwards.Neon flying squid are about the length of a rolling pin and tend to gather near the surface to feed upon fish and crustaceans. It’s unclear exactly why they would fly in unison in this way, with one possible explanation being that they were evading a predator, such as a shark.View image in fullscreenA neon flying squid in mid-air over the South Atlantic Ocean.Photograph: Anthony Pierce/AlamyFlying squid are found around the world and their penchant for emerging from the water sometimes results in them landing on boats. But seeing such behaviour is unusual, even for those committed to studying the species.“You have to be lucky,” said William Gilly, a Stanford University biologist who has spent several decades in squid research. “I’ve seen a small humboldt squid leap out of the water to get away from a mahi mahi fish, and the fish leaped out of the water too and caught the squid mid-air. But I’ve never seen them glide in a group.”There is little doubt about the squid’s ability to move quickly in the water, however. Gilly has tagged a humboldt, the largest of the flying squid, and tracked it swimming at 10 metres per second (36km/h) in order to escape some sea lions.Neon flying squid live across the Pacific, Atlantic and IndianOceansand are highly migratory. They have an interesting golden or silver-coloured stripe down the middle of their undersides, perhaps as a form of camouflage.In our popular imagination, the squid is often overshadowed by the octopus. But squid have their own sort of intelligence, they can change colour and they can swim more dexterously through the water than their more celebrated neighbours.They are also more friendly. “One squid alone is an unhappy creature, it’s jittery and nervous,” said Gilly. “An octopus is a loner. It will kill another octopus if you put them in a tank together. Squid are far more social.”Voting is open from 12 August to midnight on 16 August;click here to votefor your favourite invertebrate and the winner will be announced on Tuesday 18 AugustExplore more on these topicsMarine lifeInvertebrate of the year 2026OceansWildlifeInvertebratesAnimal behaviourZoologyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bridget Phillipson condemns Richard Tice’s ‘chilling attempt to silence free press’ | Richard Tice | The Guardian
description: Labour chair says Reform deputy leader is trying to harass journalists over reporting on his financial affairs
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Labour chair says Reform deputy leader is trying to harass journalists over reporting on his financial affairs
Content: Richard Tice is suing the National Crime Agency.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRichard Tice is suing the National Crime Agency.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockRichard TiceBridget Phillipson condemns Richard Tice’s ‘chilling attempt to silence free press’Labour chair says Reform deputy leader is trying to harass journalists over reporting on his financial affairsUK politics live – latest updatesRowena MasonWhitehall editorWed 12 Aug 2026 08.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRichard Tice has been accused by Labour’s Bridget Phillipson of mounting a “deeply chilling attempt to silence the free press” after he sent alegal threat to the Guardianover its reporting on his financial affairs.Lawyers for Tice, the deputy leader ofReform UK, singled out a Guardian correspondent for her journalism about a series of Tice’s financial transactions that were referred to the National Crime Agency.Tice is now suing the NCA, claiming that the information could only have come from an officer within the agency.In a separate letter to the Guardian, Tice’s lawyers made clear they would be seeking disclosure of documents that they believe could reveal the details of sources.More Reform UK transactions worth millions reported to National Crime AgencyRead moreIn response, Phillipson, the chair of the Labour party, said it was an attempt to silence journalism. She said: “Rather than answer serious allegations,Richard Ticeis now trying to harass those who have exposed them. The Reform deputy leader should drop this lawsuit [against the NCA] and come clean.“Trumped-up legal letters targeting honest journalism are very revealing. Reform have zero regard for the cornerstones of British democracy: they’re unpatriotic and pathetic.”The move was also criticised by the Liberal Democrats, anti-corruption and press freedom campaigners. The Lib Dem Cabinet Office spokesperson, Lisa Smart, said: “Weaponising the legal system to hunt down journalists’ sources is a desperate, bullying tactic. Tice has revealed what we all always knew to be true – Reform’s agenda is completely incompatible with a free and open democracy. They have proven once again that they are entirely unfit for public office.”Susan Hawley, the director of Spotlight on Corruption, said: “Using legal threats to strong-arm journalists into disclosing their sources amounts to a deeply concerning attack on press freedom.”Hawley said Tice would be better served being open about the legitimate questions being asked of him and Reform UK, rather than “trying to discredit those who have reported on them”. “Democracy depends on an independent press, and the government must get serious about introducing safeguards against abusive legal tactics.”The tangled financial web at the heart of Reform UKRead morePhil Brickell, theLabourMP and chair of the all-party group on anti-corruption, said Tice had “questions to answer as to how money donated to Reform was reportedly routed through his companies”.“What we now see is a contemptible campaign by Tice to detract from those public interest questions by threatening hard-working journalists and seeking to uncover their sources. It shows once again that the government must act to ensure that those seeking to expose wrongdoing are protected from the rich and powerful seeking to silence them.”Tice and Reform’s leader,Nigel Farage, have been under intense scrutiny in recent months because of a continuing investigation by the Guardian into their financial affairs.Separately, the Sunday Times has also published a series of stories about Reform’s funding.The Guardian revealed in a series of detailed reports that Reform UK received a secret £1m donation via a fundraising vehicle run by Tice and that Farage received asecret £5m giftshortly before he announced he would stand in the 2024 general election.The Guardian also revealed that these and other transactions were reported by bankers to the NCA over fears they could involve laundered money.View image in fullscreenBridget Phillipson said Reform UK and Richard Tice had no respect for the ‘cornerstones of democracy’.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAA “suspicious activity report” is not proof of wrongdoing, rather it is an invitation for the agency to examine the transaction to decide whether there are grounds to investigate it further. It is not the same as a crime report.Farage and Tice have denied any wrongdoing.Throughout its reports the Guardian has referred to financial industry sources.Tice has suggested in a document filed at the high court that the Guardian’s award-winning City editor, Anna Isaac, could not have had sources at multiple banks.In legal correspondence sent directly to Isaac, Tice’s lawyers suggested he was seeking to unmask sources based on his own assessment of the reporter’s work.Farage has also issued proceedings against the NCA.Jemimah Steinfeld, the chief executive of the Index on Censorship, said it had the “appearance of an attempt to force a journalist to break the golden rule: that sources must be protected”.“This has been vital public interest reporting by the Guardian. The sources of such journalism are sacred. If the facts are incorrect, then they can be challenged, but the sources should not be chased down. This appears to be a tactic designed to not only silence journalists but those who talk to them. It is a nasty tactic and we should all be concerned.”Theo Bamber, the chief executive at the News Media Association, said: “Robust protection for journalists’ sources is absolutely fundamental to ensuring that reporters can scrutinise authority and hold the powerful to account on behalf of the people impacted by their actions and decisions.“The use of legal threats by an individual or organisation trying to force journalists to disclose their confidential sources is an attack on this important principle, and one that must be resisted at every turn.”A Guardian News and Media (GNM) spokesperson said: “Richard Tice’s legal threat against the Guardian appears to be a calculated attempt to deflect attention away from legitimate questions about his financial affairs and the funding ofReform UK.“Instead of providing answers to those questions, he seems intent on intimidating journalists and seeking to expose sources. The Guardian will oppose these attacks on the freedom of the press and will not be deterred from public interest-driven investigations into politicians and the parties they represent.”Tice and his partner, Isabel Oakeshott, used social media posts on Tuesday night to criticise the Guardian. Tice said: “Lefty journos now bleating as they don’t like tables being turned on them … These lefty journos want war. They’ve got war.”Last week it emerged that the prominent Reform UK member and Brexit campaigner Arron Banks set private investigators on a Sunday Times journalist after he broke a series of stories aboutFarage.Explore more on these topicsRichard TiceReform UKParty fundingBridget PhillipsonLabourNCA (National Crime Agency)Press freedomnewsShareReuse this content

title: Eerie silence and ‘still surviving’: what happened next after steel town’s last blast furnace shut down | Wales | The Guardian
description: Exhibition in Port Talbot is part of project exploring how communities experience endings and transitions
Author: Bethan McKernan
Headline: Exhibition in Port Talbot is part of project exploring how communities experience endings and transitions
Content: Jon Pountney was one of two photographers to witness the final days inside Tata’s last blast furnace.Photograph: Jon PountneyView image in fullscreenJon Pountney was one of two photographers to witness the final days inside Tata’s last blast furnace.Photograph: Jon PountneyWalesEerie silence and ‘still surviving’: what happened next after steel town’s last blast furnace shut downExhibition in Port Talbot is part of project exploring how communities experience endings and transitionsBethan McKernanWales correspondentWed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMargaret Heggett, 95, does not remember a time when Port Talbot was ever quiet. Born and raised in the shadow of the steelworks, with a father, brother and husband who worked there, she never imagined what the town could look or sound like without its blast furnaces.“I’m not saying it was beautiful, but there were jobs. We did know the closure was coming and we have to move with the times but it’s affected the town a lot and it’s very sad,” she said.The southWalestown, one of the most deprived in the UK, is still grappling with the closure of the blast furnaces at its Tata Steel plant, which shut down in 2024 after more than 100 years, costing nearly 3,000 jobs.The transition has been difficult, with knock-on effects for supply chain workers and local businesses.
