Now, two years after the last blast furnace fell silent, an exhibition is telling the story of the closure and what has happened to the town since.View image in fullscreenThe steelworks seen from the mountains overlooking Port Talbot.Photograph: Jon PountneySteeling Ourselves, created by the Rhondda-based photographer Jon Pountney, combines photography and portraits of Port Talbot with interviews with the people living there, celebrating their “strength, creativity and determination to shape the future while preserving the memories and experiences that matter”.On display at the Plaza, a community hub, the exhibit is part of After the End, a research project by Exeter, Oxford and Liverpool John Moores universities exploring how communities experience endings and transitions.The research is intended to contribute to wider arguments about the social impact of major industrial changes, and to keep local voices in the conversation about regeneration strategies.For many interviewees, the silence after the last blast furnace shut down was eerie. “I used to camp out at night and the light was better than the northern lights,” one contributor said. “When you’re making iron, there’s 1,000-degree heat that lights the sky up and the shadow changes and it’s like a show, you know, and that’s what we were brought up on. I loved that.”View image in fullscreenA woman sunbathing on a beach with the works in the distance.Photograph: Jon PountneyPountney was one of two photographers to witness the final days inside Tata’s last blast furnace before it closed. The exhibit also captures the beats of life in Port Talbot – friends messing about near the water, camping chairs on nearby Aberavon beach, terrace streets, pushchairs, meadows and wildlife – with the huge steelworks site almost always present in the background.Heggett said: “When I was asked to take part in the project, I’d had a glass of wine, so I thought ‘why not?’. It’s been lovely to reflect on.”View image in fullscreenMargaret Heggett, 95, was photographed for the project.Photograph: Jon PountneyPeople in the town felt strongly that the blast furnace closure did not mean “writing off their community”, said Patricia Kingori, a professor of global health ethics at the University of Oxford and lead researcher on After the End.“The exhibition is really rooted in hearing the experiences of people who had this ‘ending’ imposed on them, and what we can learn from them … The pace of change is such that we haven’t really reconciled yet what work and labour will look like in the future,” she said.“Port Talbot is the canary in the coalmine. The conversations the town is having are going to be repeated in all places and walks of life at some point.”Tata Steel is transitioning to a greener electric arc furnace, although the project has been hit by delays and the plant is expected to employ a fraction of the workforce it once did.“You can live the dream from Port Talbot,” one interviewee in the project said. “We’ve insisted upon that and the fact that we’re still surviving … being creative and doing all these positive things, shows that it’s actually true.”Explore more on these topicsWalesSteel industryPhotographyExhibitionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police link Welsh valleys death to biker gang rivalry | UK news | The Guardian
description: Investigators believe Vikings and Hells Angels members involved in violence that preceded death of Brecon man
Author: Bethan McKernan
Headline: Investigators believe Vikings and Hells Angels members involved in violence that preceded death of Brecon man
Content: Tony Jones, 56, who suffered life-threatening injuries after a fight between a group of men in Wales last week.Photograph: Family handout/PAView image in fullscreenTony Jones, 56, who suffered life-threatening injuries after a fight between a group of men in Wales last week.Photograph: Family handout/PAUK newsPolice link Welsh valleys death to biker gang rivalryInvestigators believe Vikings and Hells Angels members involved in violence that preceded death of Brecon manBethan McKernanWales correspondentWed 12 Aug 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man was killed in what is believed to have been a violent brawl between rival motorcycle gangs in the south Wales valleys, police have said.Anthony “Tony” Jones, 56, of Brecon, died of his injuries in hospital after the violence in Pontnewynydd, near Pontypool, last Thursday evening, which reportedly involved knives and hammers.Firearms officers, a police helicopter and ambulances were called to the scene of the fight, in which at least a dozen men were involved. Three people were taken to hospital, at least one with critical injuries.Ten men aged between 31 and 73 were arrested, seven of whom are still in custody. On Monday, the police appealed for Anthony Paul Jones, 40, from Blaenavon, Torfaen, to come forward as part of the investigation, and said officers are also looking for a blue Ford Transit van with the registration plate MA23 FLC.Det Supt Laura Bartley, of Gwent police, the senior investigating officer, said in an update on Tuesday night that investigators believed members of two rival biker gangs, the Vikings and the Hells Angels, were involved in the incident.She said: “We remain in the early stages of this complex and fast-moving murder investigation. Our investigation is progressing at pace and multiple arrests have been made.“Detectives are working to establish the full circumstances surrounding Thursday’s incident, including the actions and movements of those involved before, during and after the disorder.“We understand this incident will cause significant concern within the community. I would like to reassure the public that officers and staff are working around the clock to progress this investigation, identify everyone involved and bring those responsible before the courts.”A police cordon remains outside the British Legion Club in Pontnewynydd, where the brawl took place, for forensic work. Torfaen council said on Tuesday that nearby Hospital Road could remain closed until into the weekend.Both the Vikings and the Hells Angels motorcycle clubs originated in the US but have chapters around the UK. While most motorcycle enthusiast groups in this country are strictly hobbyists, a small fraction self-identifying as “outlaw” or “one per cent” groups have been known to dabble in criminal activity such as drug and weapons trafficking.In March 2024, three Hells Angels bikers from Watford were jailed for attacking members of the Vikings in October 2022. Another three Hells Angels from the Greater Manchester area were handed jail time in March for firearms and drugs possession.Explore more on these topicsUK newsWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rod Stewart cancels farewell tour dates after undergoing successful heart procedure | Rod Stewart | The Guardian
description: The singer said that he was ‘already feeling better’ but forthcoming dates on his mammoth farwell tour will not now go ahead
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The singer said that he was ‘already feeling better’ but forthcoming dates on his mammoth farwell tour will not now go ahead
Content: Stewart performing in New York on 31 July.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStewart performing in New York on 31 July.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty ImagesRod StewartRod Stewart cancels farewell tour dates after undergoing successful heart procedureThe singer said that he was ‘already feeling better’ but forthcoming dates on his mammoth farwell tour will not now go aheadLaura SnapesWed 12 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRod Stewart has cancelled all coming dates on his farewell tour after undergoing a routine heart procedure.On 9 August, Stewart, 81, pulled a performance in Ohio at the last minute. After the successful insertion of a coronary stent, he announced that all dates would be cancelled.Representatives for the singer told Rolling Stone that Stewart required four weeks off to recuperate.Stewart told fans that he was “already feeling better and very much on the mend”, and extended his thanks to the medical staff who took care of him.“I’m deeply disappointed to miss these shows and sorry to let my fans down, but I look forward to getting back on stage and having a good time with you all again soon,” he wrote in an Instagram story.In June, Stewart cancelled shows on doctors’ advice. Later that month, he paused a show in Utah to use an oxygen tank after almost fainting mid-performance.Stewart had been due to perform a six-date Las Vegas residency, in addition to other dates across the US and Mexico, as part of the ongoing One Last Time farewell tour, which began in 2024.Sing when you’re winning: the 20 greatest songs about football – ranked!Read moreIn October, Ronnie Woodtold Desert Island Discsthat he and Stewart had been making music together again ahead of a potential reunion of the Faces, the rock band that formed out of the ashes of the Small Faces when singer and guitarist Steve Marriott left.Wood joined Stewart on stage at Glastonbury last year when the latterhelmed the festival’s Sunday afternoon legends slot. Prior to the performance, Stewart revealed that his fitness regime includedunderwater swimming, as recommended to him by Frank Sinatra.Stewart, a father of eight, recently welcomed his sixth grandchild.Explore more on these topicsRod StewartPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: Ex-Myanmar ambassador to UK on trial for trespassing in diplomatic residence | UK news | The Guardian
description: Kyaw Zwar Minn was ousted for declaring loyalty to Aung San Suu Kyi after 2021 coup but refused to leave his home
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Kyaw Zwar Minn was ousted for declaring loyalty to Aung San Suu Kyi after 2021 coup but refused to leave his home
Content: Kyaw Zwar Minn outside at his north London residence in 2021.Photograph: Ian West/PAView image in fullscreenKyaw Zwar Minn outside at his north London residence in 2021.Photograph: Ian West/PAUK newsEx-Myanmar ambassador to UK on trial for trespassing in diplomatic residenceKyaw Zwar Minn was ousted for declaring loyalty to Aung San Suu Kyi after 2021 coup but refused to leave his homeGeneva AbdulWed 12 Aug 2026 14.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMyanmar’s ousted ambassador to the UK has gone on trial on trespassing charges for refusing to leave a diplomatic residence after beingunceremoniously locked out of the embassyin 2021.Shortly after Myanmar’s military seized power in 2021, triggering mass protests that spiralled into a civil war, Kyaw Zwar Minn was locked out of the embassy for declaring his loyalty to the deposed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi.On Wednesday he appeared in a London court charged with trespassing at a diplomatic residence between May 2021 and November 2024. Kyaw Zwar Minn, who still lives at the ambassador’s residence in north-west London, has pleaded not guilty.The former ambassador argues that the current president, Min Aung Hlaing, the general who plunged Myanmar into conflict and economic chaos, is illegitimate and had no power to ask him to leave the property.Min Aung Hlaing’s pro-military party won a landslide victory in elections earlier this year that have been widely condemned as a sham. Min Aung Hlaing is wanted by the international criminal court for crimes against humanity against theMuslim Rohingya minority.Kyaw Zwar Minn’s lawyer, David Perry, told the court: “The military authorities could not lawfully terminate his licence at the address. Nor could they legitimately use the property.”View image in fullscreenKyaw Zwar Minnu Kyi pictured in 2021.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianProsecutors said Myanmar’s authorities instructed the former ambassador to “hand over state-owned properties” in April 2021, and that the Foreign Office also told him to leave the residence, but he did not comply.They argue that his view of the Myanmar government – which is not formally recognised by most democratic countries, including Britain – does not provide a defence.“Having been granted permission to reside at Myanmar House as the ambassador, his refusal to vacate the diplomatic premises after he was removed from that position means that he is guilty of the offence of diplomatic trespass,” the prosecutor Louise Oakley told the court.Kyaw Zwar Minnpreviously told the Guardianhe spent a night in his car outside the embassy in April 2021 after his then deputy, Chit Win, and a military attache, Soe Aung, locked him out of the building on the regime’s orders.He said at the time that he no longer felt safe at the north London residence and had contacted the police after former staff delivered a letter ordering him to move. Friends and relatives in Myanmar had been forced into hiding fearing reprisals as a result of his stance, he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe 68-year-old became a diplomat under Aung San Suu Kyi after a long career in the army and has called the “Rohingya issue” very important. Before his removal as ambassador, he had been told by a source in Myanmar’s foreign ministry that his staff were spying on him.He anticipated in 2021 that the crisis would lead to civil war. “You can see the military government is not going to step back,” he said. “More people will die and the economy is going to collapse. Then anything can happen in our country.”The court case comes as the war enters its sixth year. More than 100,000 people have been killed and more than 5 million displaced, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.Aung San Suu Kyi, now 81, has been detained on a range charges since the military took power. She was previously held under house arrest for 15 years under a past junta, and was awarded the Nobel peace prize in 1991. After her election as state counsellor in 2015, shebecame a pariahfor leading a regime that excused a genocide, jailed journalists and locked up critics.Explore more on these topicsUK newsMyanmarSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump sued over $100,000-a-month early-access offer to Truth Social posts | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Suit alleges subscription offer aims to sell privileged access to information generated in president’s official capacity
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Suit alleges subscription offer aims to sell privileged access to information generated in president’s official capacity
Content: Donald Trump has a history of using Truth Social to disclose market-sensitive news.Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump has a history of using Truth Social to disclose market-sensitive news.Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump sued over $100,000-a-month early-access offer to Truth Social postsSuit alleges subscription offer aims to sell privileged access to information generated in president’s official capacityJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonWed 12 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumphas been sued after a subscription service charging up to $100,000 a month for early access to his posts on his Truth Social platform sparked allegations of corruption.The lawsuit, filed in the US district court for the southern district ofNew York, was brought by the Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation against Trump, two of his aides and the executive office of the president.It targets “Truth API”, a paid data feed launched on 1 August by the Trump Media & Technology Group, the company behind Truth Social. The complaint calls the arrangement “extraordinary, corrupt and unconstitutional”.Trump’s media company, which also owns Truth Social, reports $238m lossRead moreThe service gives paying subscribers faster access than the general public to posts from 10 of the platform’s highest-profile accounts, including Trump’s own account, as well as those of the vice-president, JD Vance; press secretary, Karoline Leavitt; and other senior officials. Subscribers pay $100,000 a month, or $60,000 a month for a three-year commitment.The White House and Trump Media did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit.Trump has a history of using Truth Social to disclose market-sensitive news, including posts on tariffs and the war on Iran, which have triggered swings in stock and oil prices. Trump Media’s interim chief executive, Kevin McGurn,has even promoted the serviceas a way to give businesses fast access to the platform’s “most market-moving” posts. He has described it as a “high-margin” product meant to provide a “meaningful, ongoing source of revenue”.The launch followed criticism from the Democratic senators Adam Schiff and Elizabeth Warren, who had urged the Securities and Exchange Commissionto examinewhether the service amounted to market manipulation benefiting insiders at ordinary investors’ expense.According to the complaint, Trump Media disclosed on 10 August that it already had more than 10 subscribers, reportedly including financial news outlets and high-frequency trading firms, and was exploring licensing the data to prediction markets while working to block third-party tools that let outside groups scrape and archive Trump’s posts.The plaintiffs argue that the president, who remains Trump Media’s largest shareholder, with a stake worth roughly $1bn, stands to personally profit from selling privileged access to information generated in his official capacity.The suit also raises concerns about the historical record. Truth API subscribers get access to an archive of posts stretching back to 2022, including ones later deleted or altered, while McGurn has said the company intends “to create a lot of friction for those folks that aren’t coming to us directly”.The plaintiffs are asking the court to declare the arrangement unlawful and to bar the administration from relying on Truth Social as the exclusive venue for official announcements while it sells preferential access to that information.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpSocial mediaTrump administrationDigital mediaLaw (US)US politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Unexpected hearing scheduled for Luigi Mangione sparks plea deal speculation | Brian Thompson shooting | The Guardian
description: Rumors of plea deal in federal case have been circulating since June for suspect accused of killing Brian Thompson
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Rumors of plea deal in federal case have been circulating since June for suspect accused of killing Brian Thompson
Content: Luigi Mangione at a pre-trial appearance at Manhattan criminal court, in New York City, on 11 August 2026.Photograph: David Dee Delgado/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLuigi Mangione at a pre-trial appearance at Manhattan criminal court, in New York City, on 11 August 2026.Photograph: David Dee Delgado/UPI/ShutterstockBrian Thompson shootingUnexpected hearing scheduled for Luigi Mangione sparks plea deal speculationRumors of plea deal in federal case have been circulating since June for suspect accused of killing Brian ThompsonEdward HelmoreWed 12 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn unexpected hearing in the federal stalking case against Luigi Mangione has been scheduled, leading to speculation that the alleged United Healthcare CEO assassin was seeking a plea deal that would in turn end a murder prosecution due to go to trial inNew Yorkstate court next month.Prosecutors and Mangione’s lawyers filed a joint letter requesting the hearing at 11am on Friday in Manhattan federal court.Mangione has pleaded not guilty to state and federal charges in the killing of Brian Thompson on a midtown Manhattan street in December 2024.Prosecutors and Mangione’s defense team did not immediately respond to requests for comment on any plea discussion or its terms.Rumors have been circulating since late June when Mangione’s defense team met with federal prosecutors to discuss, it was widely understood, a plea deal in the federal case, set for trial early next year.Days earlier, Mangione’s attorneys indicated plans for a psychiatric defense citing “extreme emotional disturbance” in a sealed letter to New York supreme court justice Gregory Carro but abruptly reversed course and withdrew it.At that time, New York prosecutors said that they were “aware of public reporting regarding the possibility of a guilty plea in defendant’s federal case” and were prepared to lobby federal prosecutors for a stiff sentence.In a letter obtained by the Guardian, state prosecutors said “a proposed federal guilty plea would operate to defeat a just outcome in the state prosecution, the People could advise the federal district court of that consequence, and the court should consider that fact in deciding whether to accept the plea, as well as any opposition by the victim’s family to such a resolution.”The latest twist comes a a day after a hearing in state court cleared the way for Mangione’s murder trial to begin on 8 September.The trial judge ordered that jurors in the case would remain anonymous and there would be an additional overflow courtroom. Mangione’s court appearances have been mobbed by supporters, some of whom have been issued press passes, complicating the work of court officials to maintain public and press access.Explore more on these topicsBrian Thompson shootingUS politicsNew YorkUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Panama canal fees soar due to Iran war and El Niño as ship ‘pays $4m to jump queue’ | Shipping industry | The Guardian
description: Falling water levels linked to weather system are expected to limit number of slots to transit shipping lane
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Falling water levels linked to weather system are expected to limit number of slots to transit shipping lane
Content: The Panama Canal Authority runs daily auctions that allow ship owners to place bids to skip the queue.Photograph: Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Panama Canal Authority runs daily auctions that allow ship owners to place bids to skip the queue.Photograph: Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty ImagesShipping industryPanama canal fees soar due to Iran war and El Niño as ship ‘pays $4m to jump queue’Falling water levels linked to weather system are expected to limit number of slots to transit shipping laneJoanna PartridgeWed 12 Aug 2026 08.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCommercial ships travelling through the Panama canal are facing a rise in costs amid disruption triggered by the Iran war and falling water levels linked to this year’s intenseEl Niño weather system.Highlighting the fragility of global trade, a container ship reportedly paid about $4m (£3m) to jump a queue of vessels waiting to pass through the vital maritime choke point.Ships are now waiting about 10 days for their turn to pass through the trade route linking the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, the largest backlog since May, according to Argus Media. The route is favoured by shippers as it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for large retailers and energy companies that trade between Asia and the US.‘Like being in prison’: the ship crews stuck in Gulf since FebruaryRead moreWhile shipping companies usually pay a flat fee to reserve a slot to transit the canal, the Panama Canal Authority (ACP), which manages the waterway, also runs daily auctions that allow shipowners to place bids to skip the queue. Starting bids open at about $15,000 for smaller cargo vessels and $55,000 for the largest ships, but these prices can shoot up during times of heavy congestion or high demand.The buyer of the $4m transit slot was reported to be the Seaspan Benefactor, a 10,100 TEU (20-foot equivalent unit) vessel, according to Bloomberg. The payment was reportedly more than double the average bid placed during the previous seven days.Panama canal mapShipowners are willing to pay significantly higher prices at auction to avoid queues, as more vessels stay away from the Gulf and the Red Sea as fighting in the Middle East has effectively closed thestrait of Hormuzand theBab al-Mandab, the narrow waterway between the Arabian peninsula and the Horn of Africa.Prices to travel in the Panama canal’s busiest shipping lanes have hit record highs, according to the Financial Times, at a time when water levels are falling amid therapidly developing El Niño weather system.Earlier this month the ACP said it would impose limits in late August and early September on how low vessels can travel through the water, known as a ship’s draft, in an effort to keep traffic flowing.The authority had also cut the maximum authorised draft in July, in a measure forcing ships transiting its Neopanamax locks – the canal’s wider and deeper lane – to carry lighter cargoes.The decision was based on water levels and projected conditions for Gatun Lake, an artificial reservoir that feeds the canal, the ACP said, adding it was“ready to implement preventive measures”during El Niño based on lessons learned during the event in 2023-4 and as it monitors weather conditions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome shipowners are concerned the ACP could introduce restrictions on the number of vessels allowed to transit the waterway, asin 2023when a lengthy drought in the central American country led to a logjam.It comes after the ACP recorded a5% increase in the number of transitsbetween October and June, representing an average of 35 a day. A higher tonnage was carried through the canal during this period, with the increase driven by container ships and liquefied petroleum gas carriers, the ACP said.The Panama canal is not the only crucial trade route affected by low water levels, amidgrowing international concernover the economic consequences of the climate emergency.A prolonged period of dry weather across Europe has led to record low water levels on the Rhine, with traders warning that it was not possible to book some cargo shipments on the river, forcing them to pay higher costs to transport goods by road and rail instead.The Rhine is one of Europe’s main arteries for transporting grain, fuel, minerals and goods, but manufacturers have had to reduce the amount of cargo transported on ships as a result of the low water levels.Explore more on these topicsShipping industryPanama canalInternational tradeGlobal economyEconomicsUS-Israel war on IrannewsShareReuse this content

title: UK heatwaves may have cost economy £4.4bn in lost output so far this year, analysis finds | Economics | The Guardian
description: Verdant thinktank says cost could top £25bn a year by 2030 and calls for maximum temperature for working and urban redesign to cool down cities
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Verdant thinktank says cost could top £25bn a year by 2030 and calls for maximum temperature for working and urban redesign to cool down cities
Content: The thinktank said the government should also compensate workers forced to cut hours due to extreme heat.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe thinktank said the government should also compensate workers forced to cut hours due to extreme heat.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty ImagesEconomicsUK heatwaves may have cost economy £4.4bn in lost output so far this year, analysis findsVerdant thinktank says cost could top £25bn a year by 2030 and calls for maximum temperature for working and urban redesign to cool down citiesHeather StewartEconomics editorWed 12 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRepeated debilitating heatwaves this summer are likely to have cost the UK economy more than £4bn in lost economic output by the end of July, new analysis shows.Green thinktank Verdant had suggested June’s unseasonally hot weatherhad an economic cost of £2.36bn. Updating its assessment to include last month’s high temperatures, it finds a £4.4bn hit to output.Astemperatures soar once again this week, Verdant’s director, James Meadway, said: “The economic costs of climate change are already with us, and set to worsen in future years. Action by the government to protect workers and businesses from the severe effects of extreme heat is well overdue.”Direct economic costs arise because workers across many industries become less productive in heatwaves, while infrastructure and equipment overheats and has to be shut down.This week’s amber weather warning for extreme heat in England from the Met Office, comes after three previous heatwaves in the UK in May, June and July. The forecaster has said the UK ison course to record its hottest summer ever.Verdant is calling for the government to implement a maximum working temperature; and be ready to step in to compensate workers when they are forced to cut their hours because of extreme heat.chartThe report also points to the need for investment in urban redesign, to create more cooler green spaces in the UK’s towns and cities.Verdant’s estimates exclude indirect losses such as the cost of fighting wildfires, and additional electricity consumption from running fans and air conditioning. The largest effect is likely to have been felt inLondonand the south-east, where temperatures have been highest, the thinktank argues.If heatwaves continue to intensify at the same rate as in the last decade, it suggests the annual economic cost could rise to more than £25bn by 2030.Verdant relies on cross-European estimates by the insurer Allianz, that suggest for every degree above 30C that temperatures rise, workers’ output an hour declines by 3%.The estimates correspond with workby the Grantham Research Institute at London School of Economics, which suggested a £1bn-plus loss of output during June’s heatwave alone, from workers cutting back their hours or being less productive than usual, because of high temperatures.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJune heatwave in UK led to ‘mass sleep deprivation’, poll suggestsRead moreIn a survey of 2,000 people, the institute’s researchers found that 3.6% of respondents did not work at all during the week of 22 June due to searing temperatures; while 87% reported at least one health-related impact, from disrupted sleep to dizziness.Economists have increasingly warned about the mounting economic costs of extreme weather events – including the risks of higher inflation due to rising food prices, as production is hit by droughts, floods and wildfires.Almost three-quarters of England has been declared officially in drought after the repeated heatwaves, which have also affected much of Europe this summer.The London mayor, Sadiq Khan, recently pointed to the impact of this year’s extreme temperatures asevidence that Labour should take on net zero scepticsand stick to its climate targets. “The climate emergency is here – and no one can say they didn’t see it coming,” he wrote.Paul Nowak, general secretary of the TUC, said: “As climate change causes more heatwaves, workers are suffering – and productivity is taking a hit too. Many of us have experienced this directly as we’ve struggled to keep working through the heat.“Unions are calling for rules that require employers to take action to reduce temperatures when they exceed 24C, and for work to stop when temperatures reach 30C, or 27C for strenuous jobs.”Explore more on these topicsEconomicsEconomic policyExtreme heatEconomic growth (GDP)Climate crisisThinktanksUK weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: AI was supposed to destroy jobs. Where’s the carnage? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: The AI jobs apocalypse never showed up. Still, jobs are changing and economists expect more to come
Author: Varsha Bansal
Headline: The AI jobs apocalypse never showed up. Still, jobs are changing and economists expect more to come
Content: AI was supposed to massively displace workers across across industries. Economist say it’s having a very different effect.Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAI was supposed to massively displace workers across across industries. Economist say it’s having a very different effect.Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty ImagesReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)AI was supposed to destroy jobs. Where’s the carnage?The AI jobs apocalypse never showed up. Still, jobs are changing and economists expect more to comeSupported byAbout this contentVarsha BansalWed 12 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe prediction was stark:artificial intelligenceadvancements would wipe out jobs en masse. “Half” of all entry-level white collar jobs would vanish, Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, said in May 2025. A month later, OpenAI’s CEO,Sam Altman, went further, foreseeing the end of “certain job categories”. Companies began citing AI in their layoffs. Workers organized. And studentsreconsidered their future careers.But a year later, the mass carnage hasn’t shown up.Even as AI capabilities have rapidly advanced and AI companies have hurtled towards trillion-dollar stock market debuts, economic transformation hasn’t kept pace, similar to previous tech revolutions, economists say. As a result, CEOs are reframing and softening their stances, suggesting AI augments workers rather than replaces them.Despite the lack of mass job devastation, a shift is still under way: AI is changing the nature of work, with employers increasingly expecting job seekers to have AI skills. And over the long term,AI could shift more jobs to freelance and contract workas companies figure out which skills they do need, some economists predict.‘Everything about me is good in his eyes’: the women in China choosing AI boyfriends over human menRead moreData from a recentStanford Institute for Economic Policy Research analysisshows that AI hasn’t yet caused major job displacement. Since 2022, the year ChatGPT launched, the unemployment rate for the 20% of workers most exposed to AI rose by 0.77 percentage points, less than the 0.85 percentage-point increase for the least-exposed workers, the report showed. AI could be a factor in recent graduates’ rising unemployment, which hit 5.6% compared with the national average of 4.2% earlier this year. But factors including remote work and the unwinding of pandemic-era overhiring probably also played roles, the report states.“Employment trends in the occupations [where] we would expect to see the impacts first are largely stable,” said Erika McEntarfer, fellow at the Stanford Institute and co-author of the report. “It took decades for the computer revolution to fully transform labor markets in the workforce, and what we’re seeing right now looks a lot like that.”But accurately measuring AI’s impact on employment is a challenge. Government statistics are dated by nature and don’t track the impact of specific technologies, while private industry figures, though more current, are less comprehensive. So even though economists generally agree that AI will have an impact, they struggle to predict how big and when.Jobs are changing, not disappearingFor now, AI’s biggest impact is not on the number of jobs, but on the nature of them. It’s consolidating roles, discouraging new hiring for tasks that can be automated, and raising the bar for who gets in, leaving unemployment numbers largely untouched.Hiring trends show that AI is becoming more important for employers. About 74% of employers consider AI skills a strong advantage or requirement, with 13% requiring them company-wide versus just in technical roles, according toZipRecruiter’s latest employer survey. Half of the polled employers expect candidates to already be practical or advanced AI users on day one. And sometimes the requirements don’t show up directly as “AI” in job listings, but rather as rising expectations around speed, quality and self-sufficiency.“The clearest trend line is a rising bar rather than a shrinking pool,” said Nicole Bachaud, a labor economist at ZipRecruiter. “The labor market challenge for workers is increasingly about skills-matching rather than pure job scarcity.”Employers have simultaneously added and cut within the same functions – tech, customer support, and business management and operations – signaling that “employers are still figuring out the exact skill set needed for success”, Bachaud added.Nicholas Bloom, an economics professor at Stanford University, refers to this as turbulence in the job market. AI is destroying some jobs and creating others that have to implement, sell, fix and develop AI systems, he said.Robert Seamans, a professor at NYU Stern whohelped co-develop one of the standard measuresused to gauge an occupation’s exposure to AI, categorizes AI’s impact into three buckets: jobs made obsolete, jobs created and jobs changed. “The third bucket is by far the biggest,” he said. “AI is changing and will continue to change the way most of us work, much in the same way that computers and the internet have.”For instance, at the AI coding platform Bolt.new, a three-person analytics team built an agent that analyzes data across all their systems, saving them 12 to 13 hours of manual work a week, said the company’s CEO, Eric Simons. With the help of an AI agent, their output is that of a 30-to-40-person team, he added.“What it’s actually changing is how much one person can get done, and that shows up years before it ever touches a jobs number,” said Simons. “Their jobs got harder and way more interesting because they spend their time deciding which questions are worth asking instead of grinding out the answers.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWorkers may become more disposableStill, some jobs are expected to become more temporary or easily replaceable, according to Paul Osterman, professor emeritus at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and author of the newly released book Disposable Workers. More employers will probably turn to contractors and freelancers, instead of hiring more employees, as they figure out the required mix of skills needed for the AI future. This means more workers will be left without a career ladder. About 35% of the US workforce is already considered easily replaceable, according to his research. AI will only exacerbate this, he said.As a result, more workers are trying tonegotiate AI use in their collective bargaining agreements, said Tim Newman, senior vice-president of labor programs at the non-profit TechEquity. AI changes the kind of work people do as well as job quality, he said.“That’s definitely what we’re hearing from workers,” Newman said, referring to jobs changing and deteriorating in quality. “A lot of people are experiencing [that], rather than full-scale displacement.”It’ll probably take years for the full effects of AI on the economy to show up, Stanford’s Bloom said.“A lot of the things that slow adoption … are very hard to accelerate,” he said. “It’s hiring new people, changing systems, changing job titles.”The political climate surrounding datacenters and AI safety could slow adoption further, he said. “I could see politicians in the US, post-midterm, taking a strongly anti-AI turn.”But not all jobs are in the same boat, and neither are their options for adapting, said MIT’s Osterman.For high-skilled workers, the solution “is increasing your skill levels and external network, so you have some power in the labor market”, he said. “At the lower end, we’re going to need public policy to help protect people.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedUS work & careersWorkers' rightsUnemploymentUS unionsUS unemployment and employment statisticsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: EJ Swift wins the 2026 Arthur C Clarke award for science fiction | Books | The Guardian
description: The writer – who was also shortlisted in 2023 – has won the prize for her book When There Are Wolves Again, a speculative work of eco-fiction set in near-future Britain
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The writer – who was also shortlisted in 2023 – has won the prize for her book When There Are Wolves Again, a speculative work of eco-fiction set in near-future Britain
Content: ‘Powered by a passionate love of nature’ … EJ Swift.Photograph: Ella KempView image in fullscreen‘Powered by a passionate love of nature’ … EJ Swift.Photograph: Ella KempBooksEJ Swift wins the 2026 Arthur C Clarke award for science fictionThe writer – who was also shortlisted in 2023 – has won the prize for her book When There Are Wolves Again, a speculative work of eco-fiction set in near-future BritainEmma LoffhagenWed 12 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 16.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA novel about rewilding and climate activism in Britain has been named this year’s winner of theArthur C Clarke awardfor science fiction.When There Are Wolves Again by EJ Swift is an “ambitious study in the power of long-term hope in the face of climate breakdown”, said the award’s director, Tom Hunter.The award, now in its 40th year, is given each year to “the best science fiction novel” first published in the UK in the previous year. It was named after British authorArthur C Clarke, who gave a grant to establish the award in 1987. Swift receives £2,026 in prize money, in keeping with the award’s tradition of increasing it incrementally each year since 2001.When There Are Wolves Again follows two women across half a century in a near-future Britain. Lucy, whose childhood is shaped by the Covid lockdowns, becomes involved in climate activism and campaigns to revive Britain’s habitats, while Hester is a documentary-maker whose life was marked by the Chornobyl disaster. Their separate journeys eventually converge in 2070.This year, judges considered a record 132 books submitted by 52 UK publishing imprints and independent authors.View image in fullscreenInher Guardian review, Lisa Tuttle described the winning novel as “evocative and beautifully written”, praising it as a “character-driven … argument for rewilding in Britain”. Like Swift’s previous novel, The Coral Bones, she wrote, the book is “powered by a passionate love of nature and deep concern for the planet’s future”.Judging chair Dr Andrew M Butler, a critic and academic,called it “a story of environmental change and possible recovery”.Hunter added: “Science fiction at its most powerful is often not about predicting the future but showing us that no one future has to be inevitable.”Swift was chosen as the winner over five other shortlisted authors: Matt Dinniman for Dungeon Crawler Carl, Laila Lalami for The Dream Hotel, Silvia Park for Luminous, qntm for There Is No Antimemetics Division and Lorraine Wilson for The Salt Oracle.Swift’s previous novels include The Coral Bones, which was also shortlisted for theArthur C Clarke awardand the British Science Fiction Association award for best novel. She is also the author of the time-travel novel Paris Adrift and the Osiris Project trilogy, which explores the geopolitical impacts of environmental breakdown. She cites writers including Margaret Atwood, Barbara Kingsolver, Kim Stanley Robinson and Emily St John Mandel among her influences.Clarke wrote about 100 works of science fiction and nonfiction, and also co-wrote the screenplay for the 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey.Margaret Atwood won the inaugural Arthur C Clarke prize in 1987 for The Handmaid’s Tale. Subsequent winners include Colson Whitehead’s The Underground Railroad (in 2017) and Emily St John Mandel’s Station Eleven (in 2015). Last year,US author Sierra Greer won for Annie Bot,a novel told from the perspective of a robot girlfriend.Butler was joined on the judging panel by film and translation scholar Eliza Claudia Filimon, writer Antony Jones, novelist and editor Tiffani Angus, space physicist John Coxon, and games studies professor Esther MacCallum-Stewart.Explore more on these topicsBooksArthur C Clarke awardArthur C ClarkeScience fiction booksFictionAwards and prizesnewsShareReuse this content

title: The End of Oak Street review – suburban dino-survival romp is more turkey than T-rex | Movies | The Guardian
description: The director of It Follows returns after the terrible Under the Silver Lake with a sub-Spielberg pastiche of big-lizard horror and domestic unrest
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The director of It Follows returns after the terrible Under the Silver Lake with a sub-Spielberg pastiche of big-lizard horror and domestic unrest
Content: If you don’t move, it can’t see you … The End of Oak Street.Photograph: Warner Bros. Pictures/APView image in fullscreenIf you don’t move, it can’t see you … The End of Oak Street.Photograph: Warner Bros. Pictures/APMoviesReviewThe End of Oak Street review – suburban dino-survival romp is more turkey than T-rexThe director of It Follows returns after the terrible Under the Silver Lake with a sub-Spielberg pastiche of big-lizard horror and domestic unrestPeter BradshawWed 12 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Robert Mitchell is back with his first film in eight years, this time produced byJJ Abrams. It is initially amusing but oddly inert; contrived, derivative, commercially driven and weirdly inconsequential, a Spielbergian mashup about dinosaurs running amok in suburbia that doesn’t feel like homage so much as a pastiche produced by an AI Spielbergbot – except, I admit, for the moment we see two dinosaurs enjoy the full, physical flowering of romantic intimacy. That is not something Spielberg would feel comfortable showing – for dinosaurs nor, indeed, humans.I was one of the frowning naysayers unconvinced byMitchell’s madly indulgent LA fantasy-noir Under the Silver Lake, a giant disappointment compared with his breakthrough,the scary masterpiece It Follows. But at least Silver Lake had ambition and chutzpah. This feels as if Mitchell is going through the motions – someone else’s motions. We are in late-1980s small-town America; at one point, a character sits in a car listening toSteve Winwood’s Valerie. Ewan McGregor and Anne Hathaway are Greg and Denise Platt, an unhappy couple who live on Oak Street with their two kids, Brian (Christian Convery) and Audrey (Maisy Stella). Greg is ashamed of his failure as a breadwinner, having a humiliating side-job delivering pizzas. Denise is secretly writing an autobiographical novel about a woman planning to abandon her family.At the height of their discontent, the family are perplexed by a sudden change in the atmosphere. It becomes unbearably hot and humid; a plant thought to have been extinct for millennia springs up in someone’s garden; a pile of mysterious ordure materialises in the mean neighbour’s yard. Then, we see glimpses of alien-looking scales and claws vanishing behind fences. It appears that a dinosaur-infested part of the prehistoric era has landed in the Platts’ neighbourhood – or that their part of modernity has been transported back to that time. The key to this mystery appears to be a glowing ball of light that vanishes and reappears in various locations. “Maybe this will take us home!” says Greg, presciently.Are the dinosaurs symbolic of the family’s suppressed passions and concealed rage? Or is this the displaced seismic eruption that their domestic frustrations have been leading up to? Maybe – but these emotions feel less real than the dinosaurs. Either way, Mitchell can hardly resist shooting a shocking moment without cutting to a framed family photo showing a happier time. And he has a weakness for the eerie “split diopter” shot, much beloved of Brian De Palma, depicting a foregrounded face and background detail in the same dreamlike sharp focus. There’s a moment of fatal violence that is rather tamely cancelled out, and the element of jeopardy is missing. The End of Oak Street is fun at first, but it feels like Mitchell doesn’t really believe in any of it.The End of Oak Street is in UK cinemas from 14 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmScience fiction and fantasy filmsAnne HathawayEwan McGregorJJ AbramsAction and adventure filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Wrong Girls review – Kristen Stewart fumbles through forgettable stoner comedy | Comedy films | The Guardian
description: First time director Dylan Meyer’s female twist on the genre is let down by silly stereotypes and jokes that land with a thud
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: First time director Dylan Meyer’s female twist on the genre is let down by silly stereotypes and jokes that land with a thud
Content: Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat in The Wrong Girls.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonView image in fullscreenKristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat in The Wrong Girls.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonComedy filmsReviewThe Wrong Girls review – Kristen Stewart fumbles through forgettable stoner comedyFirst time director Dylan Meyer’s female twist on the genre is let down by silly stereotypes and jokes that land with a thudOwen MyersWed 12 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 15.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWant to feel old?Superbadturns 20 next year. It’s been decades since the stoner comedy ruled the box office. In fact, the genre’s best theatrically released film of recent years – the hilarious buddy movieOne of Them Days– didn’t feature any weed smoking at all despite hitting all the usual outlandish beats of a stoner flick. If the streaming success of Hulu’s recent R-rated bong-ripperPizza Movieis anything to go by, audiences would rather watch this particular strain of movie on the couch where they can spark up in peace.The End of Oak Street review – suburban dino-survival romp is more turkey than T-rexRead moreThe Wrong Girls aims to reverse that trend with a nationwide US theatrical rollout by Neon, the arty distributor which propelled Parasite and Anora to Oscar glory. Best friends Molly (Alia Shawkat) and Frankie (Kristen Stewart) live in a PeeWee’s Playhouse-coded stoner cave with macrame decor, a life-size cutout of Céline Dion, multiple cat towers and a contraption called the bong-o-tron – a complex rig of tubes and bubbling conical flasks – that fills the entirety of their coffee table. Being high all the time gives them a daffy kind of magical thinking, as they drive around town belting out power ballads and imagine that they are under the ocean with all manner of friendly sea creatures.After being mistaken for her lookalike at a punk show, Frankie is entrusted with a briefcase full of experimental drugs which give the pair Matilda-like telekinetic powers, the ability to talk to their pet cats (voiced bySeth RoganandKumail Nanjiani), and sets off a chain of chaotic, intermittently funny events as the pair are pursued across Los Angeles by baddies who want their property back.It’s clear that first-time director Dylan Meyer (also Stewart’s wife) has studied the stoner comedy. The Wrong Girls has all the touchstones of the genre, with slacker roommates at its center (Half Baked), rent that is due (Friday) and a novelty bong set-up (take your pick). But she might not have taken the best lessons from them. The Wrong Girls has far too few laughs and a surprising lack of memorable set-ups. You can spot its jokes a mile off, like a sitcom’s Thanksgiving dinner episode that you know isn’t going to go well after someone leaves their weed gummies next to mom’s chewable vitamins.Initially, it’s fun to watch the pair at its centre. Stewart’s character Frankie is the plucky one: she worked out how to steal the neighbours’ cable, helps the pair get out of whatever stoned scrapes they get into and has a tattoo on her left arm that reads “cool boobs”. Shawkat’s Molly has vague aspirations of being a chef, but the closest she comes to it is making fussily arranged plates of food for her roommate at the local all-you-can eat buffet. At a certain point I wondered just how high you would have to be to appreciate Meyer’s humor, which leans heavily on scenes where Mollie and Frankie get the munchies, or are too stoned to parallel-park.Other instances seem like blatant plays for meme-able moments: there’s no real reason for a character to put his penis in hummus apart from a punchline about “dick dip”, while another is named Herr Koch in what initially seems like a nod to Carol Reed’sThe Third Manbut turns out to just be an excuse to say a word that sounds like “cock”. What semblance of a plot there is begins to feel especially thin as the film spirals from one silly set piece to another daft cameo, with a third act that plods despite the film’s relatively short 99-minute run-time. Most eye-rolling of all is Kate McKinnon’s mad Danish scientist, who the actor portrays with a risible accent seemingly modeled on Austin Powers’s Frau Farbissina.The scenes where the characters trip are beautifully tactile with a DIY charm, as Frankie and Molly imagine themselves as mermaids with stunning cinematography from DP Todd Banhazl, who worked onHustlersas well asrecentvideosfor Olivia Rodrigo and Bruno Mars.The best stoner comedies give you the sense of being let in on private in-jokes built on years of shared history (Broad Cityis the north star here). But Meyer’s characters feel underwritten with generic-feeling recurring bits about blue cheese brownies or the majesty of Dion. I am sure the movie was fun to make. But for those of us who weren’t on set, The Wrong Girls just feels high on its own supply.The Wrong Girls is in US theaters from 14 August with UK and Australia release dates to followExplore more on these topicsComedy filmsKristen StewartAlia ShawkatComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: My Brilliant Career review – Netflix’s take on this Australian classic is sassy and steamy – but a tad syrupy | Television | The Guardian
description: Philippa Northeast is entertaining as Sybylla Melvyn in this adaptation of Miles Franklin’s 1901 novel that has more erotica and a more pronounced love triangle
Author: Luke Buckmaster
Headline: Philippa Northeast is entertaining as Sybylla Melvyn in this adaptation of Miles Franklin’s 1901 novel that has more erotica and a more pronounced love triangle
Content: ‘A very entertaining high-voltage performance’: Philippa Northeast as Sybylla, pictured with Jake Dunn as Frank, in My Brilliant Career.Photograph: Netflix/PAView image in fullscreen‘A very entertaining high-voltage performance’: Philippa Northeast as Sybylla, pictured with Jake Dunn as Frank, in My Brilliant Career.Photograph: Netflix/PATV reviewTelevisionReviewMy Brilliant Career review – Netflix’s take on this Australian classic is sassy and steamy – but a tad syrupyPhilippa Northeast is entertaining as Sybylla Melvyn in this adaptation of Miles Franklin’s 1901 novel that has more erotica and a more pronounced love triangleLuke BuckmasterWed 12 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 22.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s difficult to believe that Miles Franklin’s wonderfully lively and rebellious novel My Brilliant Career is 125 years old: its prose crackles with life and energy, and the words leap off the page. Notwithstanding some inevitably dated turns of phrase (though I, for one, feel it’s time to return “what the deuce!” to daily conversations), the book feels like it could have been written yesterday. The story is centred around Sybylla Melvyn, a bullheaded author determined to write her own story – literally and otherwise – in a deeply patriarchal world that would prefer her to settle down, shut up and take a man’s hand in marriage.My Brilliant Career: inside Netflix’s horny, ‘bonkers’ take on an Australian classic the world is about to loveRead moreWhereas Gillian Armstrong’s1979 film adaptationis a class act, elegant and stately, Netflix’s new six-part series is, perhaps predictably, steamier and more juiced up, with at times Mills & Boon-ish vibes. There’s more erotica, a wilder tone and a more pronounced love triangle for Sybylla, played by Philippa Northeast. Unfortunately, it’s also a tad syrupy and wishy-washy, particularly towards the end (this review encompasses every episode) – the show even deploys one of those cloying photo album-like montages of key moments: the visual equivalent of Green Day’s Good Riddance.But this new take – created and co-written by Liz Doran, and co-directed by Alyssa McClelland and Anne Renton – still has plenty of pluck and sass, an appealingly messy kind of gusto, and a very entertaining high-voltage performance from Northeast.Sybylla leaves her modest, rural family life in Possum Gully to join her wealthy aunt (Anna Chancellor) at the more salubrious estate of Caddagat. The family hopes she’ll find a husband there, though the protagonist – who wants nothing more than to be an author – views her relocation through a different lens, rationalising that she must “fully experience the world before I can write about it”.Sybylla soon encounters a potential suitor, Harry Beecham (Christopher Chung), who, in this version, is Chinese Australian and totally ripped; the first episode features him shirtless, Sybylla admiring the view from behind a tree. The Beechams are “colonial royalty” and Harry’s aunt Augusta (Kate Mulvany) a “raving suffragist”, who immediately likes the cut of Sybylla’s jib and becomes something of a mentor. She implores her to ditch poetry – “a fast track to a wedding ring” – and instead write “stories that sell”. Before too long another potential suitor emerges in Caddagat’s foreman, Frank (Jake Dunn).View image in fullscreenHarry Beecham (Christopher Chung) is ‘totally ripped’ in this version of Miles Franklin’s lively and rebellious novel.Photograph: Ian Routledge/NetflixMy Brilliant Career continues the now familiar technique, popularised in shows such asDickinsonandBridgerton, of anachronistically throwing contemporary music into the mix. I have mixed thoughts about this technique, which can reduce our sense of time and place, though the point is certainly made that historical fidelity and period authenticity aren’t high on the show’s agenda.The past can only ever be viewed through the lens of the present. But here modern sensibilities can be felt everywhere, including the series’ diverse casting and added focus on stories of historically underrepresented people. There’s now a subplot involving a gay couple, Caddagat’s “golden boy” Julius (Alexander England) and Alex (Everard Grey), who are keeping their romance secret. And another involving young First Nations horse trainer Nell (Sherry-Lee Watson, so great in the under-watchedThou Shalt Not Steal), whose dream is to be Caddagat’s foreman but whose storyline feels tacked on and tangential.View image in fullscreenGenevieve O’Reilly as Helen Bossier and Northeast as Sybylla in My Brilliant Career.Photograph: Ian Routledge/NetflixThe supporting cast are all pretty good, though nobody brings much gravitas so fun lines (such as “I think no man should have to defend anything he says after midnight”) don’t tend to land with much force. Though that’s not the case with Northeast: she’s a delight, channelling the essence of the source material while bringing something different to the party. There’s a youthful energy and impishness to her performance that captures the spirit of the series at its most compelling.My Brilliant Career is onNetflixworldwide from 13 AugustExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewAustralian televisionAustralian booksNetflixreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Don’t Say Good Luck review – high-school musical weepie puts Sunny Sandler in the spotlight | Movies | The Guardian
description: A mother’s illness threatens to overshadow a stagestruck teen’s big break in a school production
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: A mother’s illness threatens to overshadow a stagestruck teen’s big break in a school production
Content: Anguish … Sunny Sandler, left, and Melanie Lynskey.Photograph: Netflix Inc/PAView image in fullscreenAnguish … Sunny Sandler, left, and Melanie Lynskey.Photograph: Netflix Inc/PAMoviesReviewDon’t Say Good Luck review – high-school musical weepie puts Sunny Sandler in the spotlightA mother’s illness threatens to overshadow a stagestruck teen’s big break in a school productionPeter BradshawWed 12 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo you, like me, have a soft spot for both high-school angst and Broadway showtunes – and maybe Douglas Goodhart’s amusing Master It! Insta reels on how to make it in musical theatre? Then you might find yourself giving a pass to this sugary but heartfelt teen weepie from director and co-writer Julia Hart, co-produced byAdam Sandlerand starring his daughter Sunny Sandler.She plays Soph, the shy theatre kid who unexpectedly gets the lead in her school production of the musical Waitress. Her devoted mom Elizabeth (Melanie Lynskey) has cancer, and thinks she should maybe wait until after the run to tell Soph the awful truth, so as not to spoil her big moment. But will that be ... too late?There’s a shrewd and entertaining scene at the very beginning when Soph gets a first inkling from her phone that something is terribly wrong with her mother just as she is about to go on stage to audition for a lesser role; she almost backs out but can’t bear for her mean-girl blonde rival to think that this is just a humiliating bout of nerves. So she goes on stage and channels her anguish into her singing, thereby impressing the director Ms Parker (Stephanie Beatriz, from TV’s Brooklyn Nine-Nine) that she gets the lead.Ms Parker has of course seen something in Soph; something real, something above and beyond mere stage histrionics. Yet Soph finds herself having to do some embarrassing onstage kissing with her dreamboat male co-star (Jack Champion) on whom she naturally has an excruciating crush. Fans of the 90s TV classic My So-Called Life might enjoy their Angela Chase/Jordan Catalano energy (although accusations made againstJared Letomean that this comparison has rather lost its innocence).I slightly regretted the absence of the comedy and satire that the movie’s opening act appeared to promise in modest quantities; for that, you’ll have to go toMolly Gordon and Nick Lieberman’s acerbic Theater Camp. The keynote here is serious. There’s nice support from Bebe Neuwirth and Steve Buscemi as Soph’s grandparents and Jon Lovitz as the grumpy serving guy in the deli her dad owns. You’ll need a sweet tooth for this kind of emotional sugar rush.Don’t Say Good Luck is on Netflix from 14 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsAdam SandlerSteve BuscemiMusicalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A History of the Novel in Britain by Philip Hensher review – a masterpiece of criticism | Books | The Guardian
description: This joyous book takes readers on a literary adventure across 300 years of fiction, from Defoe to Zadie Smith
Author: Kathryn Hughes
Headline: This joyous book takes readers on a literary adventure across 300 years of fiction, from Defoe to Zadie Smith
Content: ‘That blustery old fogey’ … Evelyn Waugh.Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveView image in fullscreen‘That blustery old fogey’ … Evelyn Waugh.Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveBook of the dayBooksReviewA History of the Novel in Britain by Philip Hensher review – a masterpiece of criticismThis joyous book takes readers on a literary adventure across 300 years of fiction, from Defoe to Zadie SmithKathryn HughesWed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his opening paragraph, Philip Hensher declares that a novel not only “tells a good story” but is a good story in itself. We could extend that neat formula to include this book, which is not only a masterful account of fiction since 1719, when Daniel Defoe set Robinson Crusoe down on his desert island, but is itself a wonderful read. There is nothing dreary here; no sense of being back in the seminar room taking notes. Instead it is 600 pages of deep pleasure, an excuse to revisit old literary loves and be reminded of ones that have slipped from view.Hensher is smart enough to know why his book works so well and vain enough to tell us. The usual methodology for a survey is to assemble a roster of academics and invite them to trot out a chapter on their specialism, whether that be “Thomas Hardy” or “High Modernism”. The result is a series of silos, with little sense of historical connection or intellectual unfolding. Hensher, by contrast, gives us a joined-up account of creative call and response. Equally crucial to this project’s success is Hensher’s own experience as a novelist. He brings a practitioner’s informed eye to such questions as why some chapters in Dickens’s Dombey and Son are in the present tense or how Henry James pulls off free indirect speech in What Maisie Knew.After setting out the novel’s origin story, we are plunged into the inky churn of the middle-18th century. Samuel Richardson writes Pamela in 1740, Henry Fielding shoots back with his snarky parody, Shamela (1741), followed by the more sustained inversion of Joseph Andrews (1742). Richardson, in turn infuriated by the lack of moral purpose in Fielding’s Tom Jones (1749), storms back with The History of Sir Charles Grandison (1754).double quotation markOne of the delights of Hensher’s capacious narrative is being alerted to authors and books that never got their proper dueHensher is brilliant on the warring duo’s finances, giving us a forensic account of the risk and reward of their different publishing models. Richardson was a printer before he was an author and hung on to his own copyrights. This allowed him the autonomy to shape the fledgling genre in ways that he wanted which, in the case of Clarissa (1748), meant 1m words written entirely in epistolary form. Fielding, no less lucky, had a patron and printer who supported him no matter how eccentric his artistic choices.Few authors were so favoured. Jane Austen chose to sell Pride and Prejudice for a flat fee to Thomas Egerton in 1812, having previously lost money on Sense and Sensibility when she insisted on retaining copyright and paying for the printing. Under the new arrangement, Egerton was under no obligation to spend more than the minimum on production. When Pride and Prejudice eventually appeared in 1813 it was in such tiny print and scrappy paper that disgruntled readers decreed it “almost unintelligible”.That sort of thing can kill a career, but Austen went on to rise above it, even if it took until the 1940s before the literary establishment caught up with her glory. One of the delights of Hensher’s capacious narrative is being alerted to authors and books that never got their proper due. Hannah More, usually written off as a Sunday school prig, turns out to be “a beautiful and graceful writer”, while Tobias Smollett, who generally gets dismissed these days as an unfunny hack, is rehabilitated as an inventive craftsman with supreme control over narrative voice. Arnold Bennett, characterised as a dreary bore thanks to Virginia Woolf’s unkind take-down of 1924, is lovingly restored as the author of the incomparable Old Wives Tale (1908), which “ought to be acknowledged among the 20 greatest novels in English”.If Hensher is generous with plaudits, he is equally vigorous in his loathing. Ann Radcliffe, author of the hugely popular and preposterously gothic The Mysteries of Udolpho (1794) “was (and remains) a simply terrible writer”. DM Thomas, Booker nominated in 1981 for The White Hotel, is “patently untalented”. And poor David Lodge, who tried so hard with modish literary pastiche in Changing Places (1975), is simply “not up to the task”.Hensher never falls into crankiness, but he is unafraid to point out home truths. Such as the fact that so much of the pleased-with-itself “experimentalism” of the 1960 to 1980 period was merely a retread of things that had been done better before. Tickled by the clever wheeze of having central characters with no name? Fanny Burney was already doing that in 1814. Keen on using fragmentary collage to signal modernity? That blustery old fogey Evelyn Waugh got there first with Vile Bodies (1930). As for self-reflexivity, that device by which the novelist comments on the process of writing a novel, you should go back to Fielding.Hensher doesn’t bring his account right up to date, preferring to stop in 2000 – at Zadie Smith and her “wonderful ear for speech” – on the grounds that it is impossible to form a proper critical judgment until plenty of time has passed. It is a wise decision and a tactful one, underscoring the moral seriousness of this master­piece, quite aside from its buoyant joy. Reader, I could not put it down.A History of the Novel in Britain by Philip Hensher is published by Pelican (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Something Like Happiness by Tom Newlands review – a tender take on hard times, anger and autism | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A twentysomething Scottish couple care for their autistic son in the bleak follow-up to Only Here, Only Now
Author: Suzi Feay
Headline: A twentysomething Scottish couple care for their autistic son in the bleak follow-up to Only Here, Only Now
Content: Tom Newlands.Photograph: Sophie DavidsonView image in fullscreenTom Newlands.Photograph: Sophie DavidsonFictionReviewSomething Like Happiness by Tom Newlands review – a tender take on hard times, anger and autismA twentysomething Scottish couple care for their autistic son in the bleak follow-up to Only Here, Only NowSuzi FeayWed 12 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrazer and Caitlin have been emotionally entwined since schooldays. Now in their mid-20s, and parents of a five-year-old, they live in a grotty flat in a Scottish new town – the faded posters read “Happiness, Here” – that has crumbled into decay. Jobs are scarce and unrewarding; little Jamie, who has autism, is silent; and the pressure is starting to tell.Frazer’s adored Caitlin is “beautiful and driven”, fit, petite – and a rageaholic. At her mildest she’s irritated and unreasonable, at her worst violent and intimidating. She is incensed at Frazer’s refusal to move from their mould-infested block to the new council house they’ve been assigned. Apex Court is where he was brought up, filled with relics of his dead parents, and it’s the only home his son has ever known. “You’ve become the sad sack guardian of a bunch of shite that belonged to your parents, including their hovel of a flat,” Cait sneers.Caitlin’s shrewish mother Janetta also thinks Frazer is the problem, and is forever scheming to separate him from Jamie. Weighted towards Frazer’s dazed perspective, Nothing Like Happiness would seem a better title for the novel. Why doesn’t he leave?Tom Newlands’s 2024 debutOnly Here, Only Nowcentred on vivacious teenager Cora Mowat, tenderly depicted in the manner of fellow Scot Alan Warner’s brilliantly realised portraits of young women. Cora’s physical “fizziness” turns out to be ADHD. For his follow-up, Newlands, himself billed as a “neurodivergent writer”, focuses on a troubled young man. The plot concerns the aftermath of the punch by Cait that fells Frazer during one particularly vicious row.This novel feels thinner in texture than the exuberant Only Here, Only Now, leaving the reader largely to infer the characters’ motivation. Grief-stricken at the loss of his mother, indecisive Frazer could have PTSD or a variant of the autism experienced by his son, while Cait’s hair-trigger fury could be a result of growing up with a violent father, her gruesome amateur boxing bouts a bid to impress him. At least the pair are united in caring for their small son; the concern they devote to a mostly oblivious child is heartrending. Cait screams abuse at teachers and other parents for what she sees as their violation of Jamie’s norms and boundaries. The question looms: is their protectiveness stopping him integrating with peers?Beyond Jamie’s welfare, the pair’s love of childhood pets – Frazer’s budgie Sequin, Cait’s iguana Natasha – hints at a softer connection, but their significance isn’t fully explained. Frazer does have potential confidants, but stubbornly resists seeking help until he reaches the point of breakdown. Hoping to dissolve his shame, one helpful contact avers that one in six domestic abuse cases involve a female perpetrator and male victim. There are angels in unlikely places, the novel proposes, if you look for them.Frazer can get riled himself, bristling at a description of the Apex as “this grey shithole”. Seeing through his eyes, Newlands conjures a bleak poetry in descriptions of the estate: “The wind had changed, and rain was drifting through the gap in the breezeblocks now. Over on Donaldson Drive someone was dragging a wheelie bin with a broken wheel.” Whether the rowing couple’s relationship will ever amount to “something like happiness” is once more left to the reader to decide.Something Like Happiness by Tom Newlands is published by Phoenix (£20).
