title: Why we’re going back to the games of our youth | Games | The Guardian
description: As millenials return to the games of their youth, remakes of Star Fox and Halo suggest there is still plenty to learn from the past
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: As millenials return to the games of their youth, remakes of Star Fox and Halo suggest there is still plenty to learn from the past
Content: Star Fox is among the classic games getting a 2026 makeover, as millennials give old-school games a new lease of life.Photograph: ArcadeImages/AlamyView image in fullscreenStar Fox is among the classic games getting a 2026 makeover, as millennials give old-school games a new lease of life.Photograph: ArcadeImages/AlamyPushing Buttons newsletterGamesWhy we’re going back to the games of our youthAs millennials return to the games of their youth, remakes of Star Fox and Halo suggest there is still plenty to learn from the pastDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 12 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs much as some people more or less cease tolisten to new music in their 30s, I have noticed a retreat to safe, familiar gaming territory among some of my fellow millennial gamers.Retro collections are started, or resumed; jewel-cases of PS1 classics or cardboard boxes with SNES or Mega Drive games have started to colonise the living-room shelves. People are replaying things from their university days, or sticking to comfort games such as Stardew Valley. Many of the friends I used to game with never bothered to pick up a PlayStation 5 at its launch, and now that current-generation consoles are becomingprohibitively expensive, they see no need. With thousands of great older games, why bother playing something new?My job, and an insatiable desire for novelty, has kept me in constant contact with new games, but nonetheless, I have been spending a lot of time lately with the titles I played in my youth because people keep remaking them. Lylat Wars (N64, 1997) and Halo: Combat Evolved (Xbox, 2001) have both had summer 2026 glow-ups, in the form of Star Fox on Switch 2 and Halo: Campaign Evolved on the other consoles and PC. These are games I played for many,manyhours back in the day, and I remembered them beat for beat (or so I thought – it turns out I didnotremember how to navigate the deadly lava planet that ended my first Star Fox run).I was notenormously enthusedby the prospect of either remake, because I’d rather play an original game in either of these series than rehash my rose-tinted recollections from 25 years ago (let’s just gloss over how old that makes us feel, shall we?). But, it turns out all those years have givenmea fresh perspective. Both of these remakes are very good. And not just because I played them at the time and remember them fondly, but because each of them does things that new video games don’t. They feel novel, because in 2026, they are.When was the last time you played an arcadey on-rails space shooter? When was the last time you enjoyed an atmospheric single-player FPS with intelligent computer-controlled enemies? These genres have fallen out of fashion – space games are now wide-open exploreathons such as No Man’s Sky (which celebrates its 10th anniversary this week), and multiplayer shooters have crowded single-player ones out almost entirely. In this context, Star Fox and Halo feel fresh. They’re not awkward transplants from another time.View image in fullscreenHalo: Combat Evolved (2011), a game that has had a ‘summer glow-up’ this year.Photograph: Bungie StudiosNeither game really needed all that much massaging. Velan Studios in New York, entrusted with a characterful if visually basicNintendo64 shooter, has changed almost nothing about it: we fly through the same webbed map of planets, with the same enemies and bosses, firing off the same simple yet effective lasers and bombs and flight manoeuvres. A Star Fox playthrough takes maybe 60 to 90 minutes and you can play it over and over, like a generous arcade cabinet. In reconstructing the game, Velan has made it look very beautiful, spliced in some new cutscenes and dialogue, and added multiplayer and challenge modes that give some structure to your replays, but quite miraculously, it barely feels different. And it’s great.Halo: Campaign Evolved deviates more from Bungie’s original space opera. It’s been rebuilt in Unreal Engine 5 with different vehicle handling and more overwrought cutscenes. But the essentials remain: high drama, perfect weaponry, and intelligent enemies that react interestingly to how you play, diving out of the way of fire or ordering a change of tactics. I never minded dying, because each firefight would be different on every playthrough. I still hate the Flood – the mindless zombies that infect the game from the midway point onwards – but despite their unwelcome incursion, I had a blast playing through this game again with my partner. I haven’t played a better co-op multiplayer game than the original Halo in all the years since, which is honestly quite sad.I have no desire for things to return to the way they were in the late 90s and early 00s; despite its expansion and consequent unwelcome corporatisation as a business, gaming as an art form is far broader and more interesting now than it was then. But these remakes show there are things to be learned from the games of the past, and a lot that is enviable about their design philosophy. Old games don’t necessarily need to be fixed to be appreciated anew. Refreshing them is often enough.What to playView image in fullscreenA ‘comforting rhythm and purpose” in Pokémon Pokopia …Photograph: Game Freak/The Pokémon Company/Koei TecmoI truly thought I was done with Pokémon Pokopia, having spent 40 hours with itback in March. When I downloaded the new expansion – an underwater area called Bubbly Basin, which turns out to be the ruins of Cerulean City, home to Misty from Pokémon Red/Blue – I did not expect to be consumed by it yet again. The rhythm and purpose of this game is just so comforting: explore, restore, revive. I have enjoyed it so much that I went back to the rest of the game with new enthusiasm for attracting new Pokémon and rebuilding the ruined planet that humans left behind for them.Available on:Nintendo Switch 2Estimated playtime:10+ hoursWhat to readView image in fullscreenGrand Theft Auto VI will be released on 27 August, on Netflix.Photograph: NintendoRockstar Games will finally show off more ofGrand Theft Auto VIon 27 August … viaa broadcast on Netflix. Well, that’s new. I can only imagine the £££ exchanged for the few hours of exclusivity that the streaming giant will enjoy.The Washington Post’s Gene Parkspent some timewithThe Weeknd, who has been documenting his gaming habits on an Instagram alt account – even meeting developers. He wants everyone to know about the horror fishing game he’s currently obsessed with.Metroidturned 40 at the end of last week – and so did Samus Aran, one of the earliest female protagonists in video games. Maddy Myers writes abouther personal heroine.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to click‘People in Japan thought we made footy up’: Pro Jank Footy, the video game taking Australian rules to the worldConvince an AI it’s not alive in psychological horror game Prove You’re HumanSam Neill filmed role in Legend of Zelda film adaptation before his deathEA Sports FC 27: what does the next instalment of the world’s biggest football game have in store?Pony Island 2 Panda Circus: gallop out of hell in this phantasmagorical follow-up to 2016’s indie hitNazis and Happy Feet collide in Penguin Colony, a psychological horror game set at the world’s endQuestion BlockView image in fullscreenFirst-time parent? avoid stressful games …Photograph: Sony Interactive EntertainmentThis week’s question comes from readerLeo:“My wife and I are big gamers – and we’re having our first kid in September. What should my partner and I play as new parents? Is it even possible?”I mean, anything is possible if you put your mind to it – my partner played quite a bit of Death Stranding while bouncing around the living room with our second baby strapped to him, in an unlikely case of life imitating art. But it is reasonable to downgrade your expectations for how much time, attention and energy you will have for video games when you have a new baby in the house. When my nine-year-old son was a baby, Iwrote this articleabout how to play games when you’re an exhausted new parent, and though the specific game recommendations are a little out of date, I reckon the advice remains sound. For instance: “Anything even slightly stressful, emotional or difficult might make you cry, so leave the competitive shooters and Dark Souls runs for a while.”If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterPlayStationNintendoRetro gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Carcass Clad: stifling tank combat promises tension, terror and surprising laughs | Games | The Guardian
description: After the success of space horror Mouthwashing, Swedish developer Wrong Organ has created a Battlefield-inspired co-op with a supernatural twist
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After the success of space horror Mouthwashing, Swedish developer Wrong Organ has created a Battlefield-inspired co-op with a supernatural twist
Content: A coffin-like interior … Carcass Clad.Illustration: Wrong OrganView image in fullscreenA coffin-like interior … Carcass Clad.Illustration: Wrong OrganSummer games previewsGamesCarcass Clad: stifling tank combat promises tension, terror and surprising laughsAfter the success of space horror Mouthwashing, Swedish developer Wrong Organ has created a Battlefield-inspired co-op with a supernatural twistJames NouchWed 12 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 05.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Claustrophobic”, “oppressive”, “pretty depressing” – these are the words Jeffrey Tomec and Dave van Egdom volunteer when I ask them to reflect on their work as part of Swedish indie developerWrong Organ. I’d add “nightmare-inducing”, too. Their last game,Mouthwashing, was an acclaimed work of horror storytelling set on a scuttled space freighter, in which players uncover the horrible things its desperate crew have done to each other.When you’re planning a follow-up to something so pitilessly nasty, how do you raise the stakes? Well, you could set the entire game in the stifling crew compartment of a heavily armoured tank, a coffin-like interior you share with two other players as you co-operatively attempt to pilot your beleaguered war machine to safety through the crumbling remains of a city in enemy territory.While there’s undoubtedly tonal overlap, the roaring engine powering Carcass Clad is gameplay rather than scriptwriting. “In Mouthwashing, every single thing we were doing was about trying to make that script come to life in any way possible,” says Tomec, the gameplay lead. “Every gameplay sequence, everything you do at every point is just there to make that story hit. And Carcass Clad is fundamentally not that kind of game. This is a gameplay-driven experience.”View image in fullscreenA nightmare city … Carcass Clad.Illustration: Wrong OrganThat gameplay is physical, tactile and always high pressure, whether you choose to play as a gunner, driver or commander. “You’re surrounded by this awesome but scary machinery,” says technical designer and self-described tank nerd Van Egdom. “It should feel as though you might lose a finger if you put your hand in the wrong place.” And youwillput a hand wrong at some point, since each role is designed so that your attention is stretched to breaking point between urgent competing priorities. One crewmate’s foul-up can have cascading effects for the entire crew.Nazis and Happy Feet collide in Penguin Colony, a psychological horror game set at the world’s endRead moreIf all that sounds a bit, well, claustrophobic, oppressive and depressing, it isn’t even the worst part. Your adversaries aren’t run-of-the-mill camo-clad baddies. No – your lone crew is pursued through Vhorgorod by the last remnants of the broken city’s defenders, the most dogged and fanatical element of the military force once stationed here. It’s a dynamic that was inspired in part byBattlefield V– specifically one mission that casts you as the crew of a German Tiger tank still defending Cologne in March 1945.View image in fullscreenUrgent competing priorities … Carcass Clad.Illustration: Wrong OrganVhorgorod’s defenders, the Green Lions, hunt you through wreckage and ruins. Tomec hints that their supernatural dabblings have “unleashed something on the city”, and now strange growths of flesh and gold fester alongside the rubble and debris. If that’s not grisly enough, the Green Lions’ tanks are festooned with divine livestock, living armour that moos and grunts and bleeds as shells fly.But for all that horror, Carcass Clad is a co-op game, which means that it is also, on occasion, a bit funny. For all the grimness and tension, players are still going to be laughing when the driver inadvertently slams the Yksiö tank into reverse at a critical moment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“When you’re designing a co-op game, you’re trying to take into account the fact that every co-op game is inherently a silly game,” says Tomec. “We want – both narratively and at the gameplay level – the feeling that you’re a team fighting against these very oppressive odds, coming together and still finding revelry and enjoyment in being able to overcome something that is pretty miserable.”On some level, that might be the biggest difference between Mouthwashing and Carcass Clad: a belief that in spite of everything, people can hold together, work together and even find something to smile about.Carcass Clad is in development for PCExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCAction gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls review – an anime-style rumble that’s rooting for you | Games | The Guardian
description: With tremendous visuals and accessible controls, this superhero-themed fighter has the chops to inspire a new generation of champs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With tremendous visuals and accessible controls, this superhero-themed fighter has the chops to inspire a new generation of champs
Content: American superheroes reinterpreted by Japanese developers … Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls.Illustration: Arc System WorksView image in fullscreenAmerican superheroes reinterpreted by Japanese developers … Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls.Illustration: Arc System WorksGamesReviewMarvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls review – an anime-style rumble that’s rooting for youPlayStation 5, PC; Arc System Works/Sony Interactive EntertainmentWith tremendous visuals and accessible controls, this superhero-themed fighter has the chops to inspire a new generation of champsJoshua RiveraWed 12 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArriving at the turn of the millennium and the twilight of the video arcade,Marvelvs Capcom 2: New Age of Heroes has long been a high-water mark for fighting games, with no heir apparent; its massive, colourful roster and frenetic, spectacular combos have lured newcomers and elite competitors alike. Developer Arc System Works, a fan-favourite studio famous for its hyper-fluid and extremely technical anime-style fighting games, has been on a long journey to usurp Capcom’s throne. With Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls, it may have finally achieved this difficult task.Marvel Tōkon is less an attempt to recreate a Marvel vs Capcom-esque phenomenon out of whole cloth, and more a thoughtful evolution of the developer’s previous riffs on the formula such as 2018’s BlazBlue: Cross Tag Battle and Dragon Ball FighterZ, building on its low-floor, high-ceiling approach. Simplified inputs allow players to execute combos and finishers with a single button, which gives novices the confidence to keep playing and inspires them to study and improve – because when anyone can pull off a flashy ultimate skill or EX attack, strategy and mastery take on a premium. And Marvel Tōkon has great depths to plumb.Matches are 4v4 affairs, with each player fielding a squad that – in a departure from similar games – shares a single health bar. The first character is the leader, taking the stage at the start of a match. The three others can either perform designated assists (a ranged attack, an aerial counter and an “assault” skill), extend combos or swap places with the leader. However – in another twist – they have to be unlocked in-match by filling an assemble gauge.View image in fullscreenLow floor, high ceiling … Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls.Illustration: Arc System WorksThese team mechanics are key to Marvel Tōkon’s complexity. It can feel like a traditional 1v1 fighter at times, but judicious and careful deployment of your team is what separates good players from great. It feels amazing to flip the momentum of a match: to recover from a seemingly endless combo chain and subject your opponent to one of your own, using your team as a single organic unit. But doing so takes practice.And self-improvement is the goal. Marvel Tōkon offers very little to those who aren’t interested in fighting for fighting’s sake: the lightweight story mode is comprised of five “episodes”, each a breezy introduction to a team of heroes such as the Avengers or X-Men, and mostly useful as tutorials. Beyond that, there is a bizarre party mode called Arcadia Rumble, where avatars scramble to improve their stats in between matches, and there are a handful of arcade ladders (a single-player sequence of opponents) to tackle. Otherwise, you’re running sets: against the CPU or other players locally or online, in casual matches, ranked matches and open lobbies.This can feel like a loss when compared with other fighting games with robust solo options, including other Arc System Works efforts. Yet while the package is spare, the product is dazzling: it’s a sensory assault that challenges players to find calm in the storm of superpowered brawls, to really dig in and learn the clockwork of meter management, character mastery and team building. All of it is presented with stellar art direction, idiosyncratic music and a jovial tone.This is another way in which Marvel Tōkon succeeds Marvel vs Capcom: it’s not just mechanics or characters, it’s cultural exchange, as American superheroes are once again reinterpreted by Japanese game developers in a genre that facilitates international competition. Marvel Tōkon is built to show off how fun it can be to participate in that evolving conversation. Won’t you go a few rounds?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls is out now; £59.99Explore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5PCFighting gamesMarvelreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Death Note: The Musical review – wildly popular manga mystery is a killer night out | Stage | The Guardian
description: The multi-platform phenomenon makes its way to the stage, with all the supernatural hijinks, J-horror tropes and emotional intensity intact
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The multi-platform phenomenon makes its way to the stage, with all the supernatural hijinks, J-horror tropes and emotional intensity intact
Content: Schoolkid killer … Xander Pang as Light, in Death Note: The Musical.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreenSchoolkid killer … Xander Pang as Light, in Death Note: The Musical.Photograph: Manuel HarlanStageReviewDeath Note: The Musical review – wildly popular manga mystery is a killer night outBarbican, LondonThe multi-platform phenomenon makes its way to the stage, with all the supernatural hijinks, J-horror tropes and emotional intensity intactAndrew PulverWed 12 Aug 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe know that people like to dress up for the theatre, but some of the crowd at Death Note: The Musical take it to a whole other level. Coiffured and corseted, bedecked in gauze or festooned with diamanté, it is a sight to behold, with an appreciable element going for full cosplay. This, for the uninitiated, is because the source material has emerged from the fan-cultivating world of Japanese manga, originating in 2003, and which has (in a characteristic manner) sold millions of copies in comic book and novel form, jumped to an animated TV series and feature film iterations, and evencrossed over to a Hollywood treatment in 2017.A live musical seems a bit of a sideways step, though; this kind of material doesn’t often find itself in theatres, but perhaps the success of the Barbican’s staging will see more given the go-ahead. (This is actually a second London appearance for Death Note, after a short run at the Palladium and Lyric in 2023.) You can certainly see the appeal. Shorn of the original’s convoluted digressions, and with a dilution of the original manga’s play for the teen-boy readership, this emerges as a smart, metaphysical whodunnit – or perhaps, more accurately, howdunnit – with a nice line in emotional intensity cranked up by its power-ballad musical score.Despite its elaborate plot superstructure, Death Note (again, for the uninitated) rests on a fairly simple idea, familiar from J-horror of yore. Someone’s name gets written in a spooky notebook and … THEY DIE. All sorts of random, self-imposed rules materialise to make things difficult, as well as a bunch of supernatural presences/deities who face their own set of pulled-from-nowhere consequences for their actions.View image in fullscreenTop-notch cast … Death Note: The Musical.Photograph: Alan West/Hogan Media/ShutterstockThe adapters – Frank Wildhorn (music), Jack Murphy (lyrics) and Ivan Menchell (book) – have slimmed things down to focus on three principals: drunk-with-power schoolkid killer Light (Xander Pang), maverick but brilliant detective L (Colin Ryan) and pop princess turned lovelorn slayer Misa (Stephanie Zaharis). Light and L’s struggle to, respectively, rule like a god and head off the tide of carnage the death note triggers forms the meat of the show, and all three performers attack their roles with grade-A gusto. Telly Leung and Grace Mouat as apple-munching chaos-stirrer Ryuk and goth-bride lookalike Rem, respectively, provide top-notch support as the presiding deities.Fortunately, the whole thing starts strong, with a floodlit opening scene that combines brilliantly athletic dance moves (by a supporting company that is excellent throughout) and a schoolroom debate about the ethics of justice, and just keeps going from there – with neat forced-perspective sets, flashy back projections and amusing sliding stage elements. Death Note purists might not be completely on board with the alterations, but I would challenge anyone not to have a good time with this.AtBarbican, London, until 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageMusicalsMangaTheatreComics and graphic novelsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: You and Me (and Whoever Comes Next) review – theatre crafted with love and care | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Actor Keron Day draws on his experiences of getting along, or not, with live-in carers to give a pithy account of a complex relationship
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Actor Keron Day draws on his experiences of getting along, or not, with live-in carers to give a pithy account of a complex relationship
Content: In safe hands … (from left) Keron Day, Martha Walker, Merle Powell-Smith and Lauren Koster in You and Me (and Whoever Comes Next).Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIn safe hands … (from left) Keron Day, Martha Walker, Merle Powell-Smith and Lauren Koster in You and Me (and Whoever Comes Next).Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewYou and Me (and Whoever Comes Next) review – theatre crafted with love and careSummerhall, EdinburghActor Keron Day draws on his experiences of getting along, or not, with live-in carers to give a pithy account of a complex relationshipChris WiegandWed 12 Aug 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe stories told byPatch of Bluecan be difficult to hear, but this vital theatre company is well aware of that. In the family drama Cassie and the Lights,at the fringe in 2022, one of the abandoned children kindly lent her froggy hat to an audience member to help them through an upsetting scene. In this new show – which shares that play’s mix of emotional veracity, easy humour and social purpose – the cast once more dip in and out of the story to guide us along.You feel in safe hands – which is one of the play’s essential themes. It is inspired by disabled actor Keron Day, who also stars as himself, and gives his experiences with a line of personal assistants who provide live-in care. We are introduced to Keron, 22, as he meets PA Dani (Lauren Koster) in a sweary meet-cute – but it’s the friendship between the two, rather than any romance, that muddies the water.The play, written by Day, Helen Chong anddirector Alex Howarth(a former care worker), dives into the complexities of defining personal and professional boundaries. Keron relies on Dani, whose duties include cleaning and dressing him; she relies on him, as her employer. Some may see Keron as the one in need; his whistle-stop tour of past PAs (played by Martha Walker) shows they can be the needy ones – or cruelly aloof.View image in fullscreenEmotional veracity … Keron Day in You and Me (and Whoever Comes Next).Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe nature of the work is immediately intimate – his PA, says Keron, is the person he sees at the start and end of each day. Two extremes are posited: the PA as confidant or, after Keron and Dani fall out, as “the robot that takes you to the toilet”. As the title makes clear, the set-up is fragile, the future uncertain, with government cuts hovering over both their lives. The script combines the specificity of this situation – and the pity and ridicule Keron faces not just from strangers but also friends – with a striking universality for other relationships.Joined by Merle Powell-Smith, who plays her own soothing and plangent folk compositions on stage, the overall effect is not so much of an ensemble as a community. The piece ends with Keron’s commitment to protect others in his position – and the hour itself is handled with utmost care.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 29 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreDisabilitySummerhallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Buggers review – phenomenal flesh and blood portrait of Francis Bacon and George Dyer | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The painter and his lover are played with real intensity by Alistair Hall and Peter Clements, in a visceral psychodrama of contained violence and sadness
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: The painter and his lover are played with real intensity by Alistair Hall and Peter Clements, in a visceral psychodrama of contained violence and sadness
Content: Between a wrestling match and an act of passion … Peter Clements as Dyer and Alistair Hall as Bacon in Buggers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianView image in fullscreenBetween a wrestling match and an act of passion … Peter Clements as Dyer and Alistair Hall as Bacon in Buggers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBuggers review – phenomenal flesh and blood portrait of Francis Bacon and George DyerPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghThe painter and his lover are played with real intensity by Alistair Hall and Peter Clements, in a visceral psychodrama of contained violence and sadnessArifa AkbarWed 12 Aug 2026 10.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe famously fraught relationship between the artist Francis Bacon and his lover-muse, George Dyer, has been much documented. So it is remarkable that this play byAlistair Hallmakes the story so utterly fresh and arresting. Hall has drawn on documents and letters from the Francis Bacon estate, but if Buggers is anchored in research, it leads with physicality, charged with eroticism and contained violence.Hall plays Bacon, and Peter Clements portrays Dyer, with absolute conviction. Clements’ performance as an initially swaggering man, who Bacon airily describes as his “delicious piece of rough trade” and who over the years succumbs to alcoholism, is especially astute and vulnerable.View image in fullscreenA gem … Peter Clements as George Dyer and Alistair Hall as Francis Bacon in Buggers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianThe play begins in 1963 with a wordless sequence that shows their first night together, drawn somewhere between a wrestling match and an act of passion. The choreography retains its visceral threat throughout (great work by movement director Ken Nakajima). They could be Pinter’s men as they circle one another barefoot on Rosie Elnile’s set, which is somewhere between a Bohemian apartment and a wet-room, complete with toilet and tub.Beautifully directed by Alice Wordsworth, the two-hander proceeds to capture the full span of their intense, complicated love – a melange of eroticism, sadomasochistic power-play and cruelty – from this first charged night to Dyer’s death in a Paris hotel room in 1971.Sanctuary review – tender, uplifting portrait of love in the Aids crisisRead moreThe relationship is initially filled with testy chemistry – and testosterone – but becomes darker. “I’m so bored,” says Bacon to Dyer. “I feel lonely when I’m with you,” Dyer responds. Scenes switch time frames and the play seems to lose its conventional shape, descending into fragments that capture emotional tumult and grief. At points it becomes a little opaque, veering into hallucination or memory, with flashes of light and shadow-play conveying mood over anything more concrete.But the piece hypnotises even in its more abstract moments. Bacon painted Dyer numerous times over his lifetime, the titles and dates of which works are read out at the end, bringing an almost suffocating sense of sadness: for all Bacon’s cruel words, his canvases spoke his love. Wonderful writing, phenomenal performances. A small but perfect festival gem.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreArtFrancis BaconSexualityFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: LA Phil/Dudamel; Fantasia Orchestra / Fetherstonhaugh/Glennie reviews – high-contrast programming | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The first of two evening proms began with the Los Angeles Phil’s polished but polite Beethoven and intoxicating Adès. Later, the Fantasia orchestra’s bitty playlist-type programme only occasionally sparked into life.
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: The first of two evening proms began with the Los Angeles Phil’s polished but polite Beethoven and intoxicating Adès. Later, the Fantasia orchestra’s bitty playlist-type programme only occasionally sparked into life.
Content: Good clean fun … Gustavo Dudamel conducts the Los Angeles Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenGood clean fun … Gustavo Dudamel conducts the Los Angeles Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouClassical musicReviewLA Phil/Dudamel; Fantasia Orchestra / Fetherstonhaugh/Glennie reviews – high-contrast programmingRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThe first of two evening proms began with the Los Angeles Philharmonic’s polished but polite Beethoven and intoxicating Adès. Later, the Fantasia orchestra’s bitty playlist-type programme only occasionally sparked into life.Flora WillsonWed 12 Aug 2026 08.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 08.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis evening was, in a sense, a tale of two orchestras. On one hand, the international heavyweight, returning to the Proms for the first time in more than 20 years. On the other, the rapidly ascendant homegrown outfit founded while its members were still at school, already making its fourth Proms appearance.Taking the early evening shift, theLA PhilandGustavo DudamelperformedBeethoven’s Pastoral Symphonyin an ultra-polished hybrid of period-performance style and modern instruments. String textures were a deluxe fine-knit, individual notes lifted but phrase endings subtly elongated so that the music seemed to breathe. The woodwind solos were cool and bright, offering further oxygenation to an already limpid sound, where massed trills spoke as one and countermelodies usually buried under orchestral busyness suddenly became audible.Beethoven’s merry peasants inspired some rougher edges, but nothing exceeding good clean fun, while Dudamel bounced on the spot as if on an invisible pogo stick. Later, there were harsh growls of timpani and threatening rumbles of double bass, before the storm dissipated into sunset-mellow brass. Throughout, Dudamel relished the slow blossoming of tutti passages, easing into them after energetic surges forward.You can have too much of a good thing, of course. So much sheen gradually becomes bland, and all those warm glows left me hankering for quieter, riskier pianissimos. After the interval, Inferno fromThomas Adès’s ballet score Dante – hot on the heels of theNYO’s performance of its second part– ditched the historically informed politeness in favour of vigorous snap, crackle and bop. String scrubbing was thunderous, woodwind voluptuous, and trumpets snarked and rasped. Almost-jazz almost-grooves seemed to bubble beneath the surface. Dudamel leaned into the score’s allusions to Wagner and Liszt, Ravel and Tchaikovsky. Yet not even he and this phenomenally accomplished orchestra could prevent the intoxicating farce of the penultimate movement from feeling like the real ending, with the miasmic layers of the actual last movement an effervescent afterthought.View image in fullscreenSuperstar percussionist: Evelyn Glennie with the Fantasia Orchestra at the late-night Prom.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouThe high-contrast approach to programming continued in the late-night Prom, where theFantasia Orchestraand conductorTom Fetherstonhaughwere joined by superstar percussionistEvelyn Glenniefor what Fetherstonhaugh called a concert on the theme of listening. Inevitably, in music, that theme is too broad to have much force. What resulted was a kind of live playlist experience that took in energetically played show tunes (lights! Stage smoke! Instant pizzazz!), an exquisitely intense extract from Morton Feldman’s Rothko Chapel and a movement of Caroline Shaw’s a cappella Partita, compellingly sung by theBBC Singers, plus solo percussion works and a Radiohead arrangement, a snippet of Dvořák in full folksy-mode and Vaughan Williams’s Serenade to Music.It was a peculiar, bitty menu – and not ideal conditions for the world premiere of Héloïse Werner’s The Wood Pigeon in all its gnomic self-ironising and musical multilingualism. Glennie’s extract from Vincent Ho’s Sandman’s Castle for solo tam-tam was most persuasive: seven minutes of fibrillations and rattling, tapping and stroking, turning a single gong into an unfamiliar, haunted surface and inviting us, finally, to listen in.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsClassical musicProms 2026Gustavo DudamelRoyal Albert HallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Today’s Brazilians have no idea what it feels like to lose democracy’: Joyce Moreno on her battles to become a Latin musical great | Music | The Guardian
description: After her defiant femininity outraged many in Brazil, she lived through a military dictatorship and was boycotted for years. But after more than 30 albums, she explains how she kept going
Author: Jane Cornwell
Headline: After her defiant femininity outraged many in Brazil, she lived through a military dictatorship and was boycotted for years. But after more than 30 albums, she explains how she kept going
Content: Beach girl … Joyce Moreno performing in 2011.Photograph: Myriam Vilas BoasView image in fullscreenBeach girl … Joyce Moreno performing in 2011.Photograph: Myriam Vilas BoasMusicInterview‘Today’s Brazilians have no idea what it feels like to lose democracy’: Joyce Moreno on her battles to become a Latin musical greatJane CornwellAfter her defiant femininity outraged many in Brazil, she lived through a military dictatorship and was boycotted for years. But after more than 30 albums, she explains how she kept goingWed 12 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 10.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 78, Joyce Moreno is one of Brazil’s musical icons, but for decades that status seemed far from assured: this headstrong singer, guitarist and composer was frequently viewed as a threat by her country’s establishment. Aged 19, the reaction to her song Me Disseram – which began “I was told my man didn’t love me” – almost torpedoed her career before it even started. “I’d often heard the expression ‘my man’ sung by Billie Holiday and Edith Piaf, so for me it was normal,” she says. “But I was a beach girl from Ipanema, writing and singing in the first person. People were shocked.”Then, inspired by trailblazing actor Leila Diniz (“her liberal attitudes lost her jobs”), Moreno refused requests that she “dress like a sexy bimbo”, and endured male critics who thought her music “too good to have been written by a woman”. When, in 1980, she discovered that her label had given another female singer the blueprints for songs she had written, she “looked for a lawyer, of course” and successfully sued; in her memoir she claims she was then boycotted by Brazil’s major record companies for a decade.View image in fullscreenPartnership … Joyce and Tutty Moreno pictured in 2007.Photograph: Courtesy of Far Out RecordingsBut come 2026, Moreno has written more than 400 songs, released more than 30 albums, and become one of the defining voices of Música Popular Brasileira – the genre-blending movement that grew out of bossa nova. Her latest album, Joyce & Tutty Moreno, is just out but she already has another one finished. “It’s always been about my love for the music,” she says from her home in Humaitá, a quiet, leafy Rio neighbourhood, where she lives with jazz drummer Tutty Moreno, her partner of nearly 50 years. Behind her, shelves of CDs tower to the ceiling. Elsewhere in the house are six guitars and a library of books; she is currently re-reading Katherine Mansfield’s short stories.The youngest of three children, Moreno was raised by her single mother, a public servant, in Rio just as bossa nova was being invented in the 1950s. “My brother was 13 when I was born, and mum gave him a guitar as compensation,” she says. “He’d invite friends like [bossa pioneers] Leny Andrade and Roberto Menescal over. I’d watch them closely. By the time my family took notice, I was playing very well on my own. I’d even set my school homework to music to help me memorise it.”Going mononymously as Joyce, Moreno became one of the first Brazilian women to write and perform unapologetically from a female perspective, and has been compared to Joni Mitchell for her blend of intricate musicianship and deeply personal songwriting. Wider recognition came with her 1980 album Feminina, whose title track is a conversation between a mother and daughter about femininity: “It prepares and sets the table,“ she sings. “Then it lights another fire and lets it burn.”“In my youth, my mother always told me I should wear heels and makeup,” she says. “Although I learned from her that a woman could be a head of a family, and be respected for her work, she was born in 1912. I was a 1960s beach girl from the golden age of Rio. We had very different ideas of what femininity was. For me, it was something internal. I had a sense of these things, even though I wasn’t yet an avid reader of feminism. I wouldn’t encounter Simone de Beauvoir until the 90s.”View image in fullscreenThe only girl on the block … Joyce Moreno in the studio, date unknown.Photograph: Raymond Ross Archives/CTSImagesThe cultural freedoms and social transformations of the 1960s were abruptly curtailed in Brazil by the 1964 military coup. The dictatorship suppressed dissent, imposed censorship and persecuted artists and intellectuals. While touring Italy in 1975, Moreno recorded Passarinho Urbano, an album of songs by friends – Chico Buarque, Milton Nascimento, Caetano Veloso – whose music had been silenced. “Today’s young Brazilians have no idea what it feels like to lose democracy in a country, to not be able to vote,” she says of a regime that finally collapsed in 1985. “I didn’t vote until I was 40.”She hails Brazil’s current liberal president Lula as “our only alternative. The far right is pushing into Latin and South America, which is a very dangerous path to follow, and we know very well who is sponsoring all that. We feel the responsibility. It’s kind of scary …” She pauses, and asks if we might stick to music.In 1977, Moreno – then divorced from musician and composer Nelson Angelo – was performing at upmarket Brazilian club Cachaça where she met drummer Tutty Moreno, who was part of a circle that included saxophonist Michael Brecker and percussionist Naná Vasconcelos. “We fell for each other’s music first,” she says. “I thought: wow, he plays so elegantly, like he’s driving a convertible. We were both young, beautiful hippies. We both wanted change.”‘This janitor’s daughter became a state deputy’: Leci Brandão, the Brazilian samba star turned communist lawmakerRead moreShe recorded an album in New York that year with Claus Ogerman, the arranger who worked with Antônio Carlos Jobim and Frank Sinatra, and remembers the disparity between their worlds. “We were counting pennies to get the subway, but Claus would take us to fancy restaurants with dress codes. Tutty would have to wear funny loaner jackets that were always too short in the sleeves.” The album was intended to launch her global career, but was shelved after it failed to find a commercial label. “That was painful,” she says, though it was eventually released in 2022 by UK label Far Out Recordings after her international profile received a major boost in the 1990s, when Gilles Peterson and London’s acid jazz scene embraced her music, and Far Out became her longtime label. “The UK thing was a gamechanger,” she smiles. “Those young DJs gave me the confidence I needed to keep going.”The new album Joyce & Tutty Moreno features songs of love, healing and renewal, performed with guitarist Adrian Younge. It was meant to also include veteran pianist João Donato, Moreno’s longtime friend and collaborator, who died aged 83 in 2023. The record is dedicated to him. “Recording without João was hard and beautiful at the same time,” says Moreno.There’s no trick to her career longevity. “Early on, it didn’t matter that I was the only girl on the block. Self-esteem has never been a problem. Somehow I knew I deserved the attention.” She smiles. “Music lives inside me,” she says.Joyce & Tutty Moreno is out now via Jazz Is Dead. Moreno plays EartH, London, 15 November; and Band on the Wall, Manchester, 16 NovemberExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockBrazilfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: In Venice, it’s not politics as usual as film-makers aim to recapture our attention | World news | The Guardian
description: As social media shrinks and distorts the EU’s crises, the Venice film festival is delivering politically forthright epics from directors such as Sergei Loznitsa and Alex Gibney
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: As social media shrinks and distorts the EU’s crises, the Venice film festival is delivering politically forthright epics from directors such as Sergei Loznitsa and Alex Gibney
Content: Russian journalist Ksenia Mironova in the film My Undesirable Friends: Part One. Part Two is at the Venice film festival in September.Photograph: Julia LoktevView image in fullscreenRussian journalist Ksenia Mironova in the film My Undesirable Friends: Part One. Part Two is at the Venice film festival in September.Photograph: Julia LoktevThis Is EuropeWorld newsIn Venice, it’s not politics as usual as film-makers aim to recapture our attentionAs social media shrinks and distorts the EU’s crises, the Venice film festival is delivering politically forthright epics from directors such as Sergei Loznitsa and Alex GibneyDon’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up herePhilip Oltermann, European culture editorWed 12 Aug 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEurope is in an economic crisis that, unlike the eurozone downturn at the beginning of the millennium, cannot be measured in ratings downgrades and borrowing costs. For metrics, try engagement depth and consumer trust instead.The unedifying spectacle of the European Union’s falling out over the Ceuta crisis looks like the latest symptom of Europe’s shrinking attention economy. When more than 70,000 people crossed over from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the start of the month, Rome hastily reintroduced air and sea border checks with Spain for one month; Madrid retaliated with spot-checks on travellers to Italy.Politicians were falling over themselves to match the wildfire speed of social media, for this was a geopolitical flashpoint that appears not just to have been engineered but also politically processed via short video clips online. The crossings were reportedly triggered by viral videos suggesting that Spain’s border with Morocco was opening, while their framing as an “assault” or “invasion” was amplified by accounts with links to the Russian military,as Aisha Down reported. Platforms such as Instagram, Facebook and TikTok are built to reward content that instantly hooks in viewers – three seconds long is the golden rule. How can lawmakers ever keep up?View image in fullscreenImperium, a film about the USSR created from archival footage.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FesitvalYet what if, paradoxically, our attention economy is both shrinking and expanding at the same time? I’ve found it hard to shake that impression after perusing thelineup at the forthcoming Venice film festival, opening on 2 September.This year at the Lido, you can watch a three-hour film about the Italian Communist party sending a camera team to the Soviet Union (Imperium, by Ukrainian auteur Sergei Loznitsa); a four-hour documentary about Elon Musk (Musk, by American director Alex Gibney); or a more than five-hour video diary about Russian dissident journalists in exile (Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II). Too short for you? Then, get tickets for Luca Guadagnino’s Joie de Vivre, a lengthy analysis of the films of compatriot Bernardo Bertolucci. It clocks in at seven hours.For the most part, these are surprisingly politically forthright titles at a film festival that in the recent past has focused on glitz and glamour. Loznitsa’s documentary seeks to shatter the remnants of the left’s illusions about the Soviet Union; Loktev gives a voice to the journalists silenced by Putin; Gibney’s Musk film has already been preemptively dismissed by the far-right tycoon as a “hit job”. But are they trying to stretch out attention spans so much that they risk playing only to a gallery of cinephiles?On the topic of impactful film-making …skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA call to creative action … Dr Lina Qasem-Hassan, a Palestinian doctor in Israel’s healthcare system, in the documentary, The Oath.Photograph: Guardian DocumentariesPerhaps there is a point between both extremes to capture people’s imaginations and attention. That’s what the Guardian is hoping to prove, in collaboration with Franco-German culture channel Arte. We are inviting film-makers to propose short-form documentaries exploringdemocracy in Europe today. The winning submission will be presented at theDOK Leipzig film festivalat the end of October, and subsequently receive funding, editorial support and distribution through Guardian Documentaries and Arte platforms. The deadline for submissions is 14 September.Crucially, they should be no longer than 20 minutes – a length that Jess Gormley, the Guardian’s executive producer of documentaries, argues “encourages participation and debate”. She points to recent Guardian documentaries such as Liane Aviram and Louis Hollis’s 23-minute shortThe Oath, about a Palestinian doctor in Israel’s healthcare system, which led to its protagonist being invited to speak in front of the UK parliament – a film that held, rather than overwhelmed our attention.To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is EuropeEuropeVenice film festivalFestivalsVeniceDocumentary filmsAlex GibneynewslettersShareReuse this content

title: What’s a wedding without a dirtbike doughnut? Hark1karan’s best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘On the day the youngest brother got married, they were out doing doughnuts and burnouts at eight in the morning’
Author: Amy Fleming
Headline: ‘On the day the youngest brother got married, they were out doing doughnuts and burnouts at eight in the morning’
Content: ‘Their mother offered me tea and snacks’ … the family on their bikes.Photograph: © Hark1karanView image in fullscreen‘Their mother offered me tea and snacks’ … the family on their bikes.Photograph: © Hark1karanMy best shotArt and designWhat’s a wedding without a dirtbike doughnut? Hark1karan’s best photograph‘On the day the youngest brother got married, they were out doing doughnuts and burnouts at eight in the morning’Interview byAmy FlemingWed 12 Aug 2026 10.38 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a Londoner with Punjabi roots, I’d say one of the best places to experience Punjabi culture is Southall, in west London, which has one of the UK’s largest Punjabi communities. This was taken there back in March 2021, when I was looking for people to feature in my short documentary,Zimmers of Southall. I like to capture everyday people doing something a little different, like these two brothers who fix cars. I had popped by to meet one of them and explain what I do, and take a few portraits for my broader work.Rav, one of the brothers, had a dirt bike at the time and we were trying to photograph him doing a wheelie. The second brother, Inderjit, then joined and showed me his quad bike that he uses for off-road riding. Their father was at home and explained how his passion for bikes and cars was passed down to the boys. Their mother offered me tea and snacks, as often happens when visiting a Punjabi family home. It’s at that moment I suggested we get the whole family involved in a group photo – I knew it would make for something unique. Unfortunately, the third brother was not around, but their dad wheeled out his own bike to complete a beautiful family portrait. It felt natural and not forced at all – the energy was warm and welcoming. Ever since that day, I’ve stayed in touch with the family and try to visit when possible.double quotation markI'm showcasing a part of British life that often goes unseenI’ve been back a few times to photograph them. There’s a picture in theZimmers of Southall bookof the same brothers on the day of the youngest’s wedding, with two motorbikes, their BMW in the middle and a lot of smoke – they’d just been doing doughnuts and burnouts at eight in the morning. Cars and bikes are a big part of their lives. I didn’t know anything about classic BMWs, but capturing their passion was a great way to showcase the Southall community. The title came from something I saw at a classic car show while we were filming. I noticed one car with a sticker saying: “Zimmers.” I think it’s a nickname for BMWs rather than “Beamers”.Through projects like this, I feel as if I’m capturing an ongoing family album of the Punjabi and Sikh community. I think it’s important to showcase a part of British life that often goes unseen. My first book, Pind, came from a similar desire to understand where I come from and the culture around me. For that project, I went back to Punjab, India, to document rural life for the diaspora who may not have had the opportunity to experience it themselves.Regardless of my subject, I always take the same approach. I am usually part of the photograph in some way, in terms of culture, locality or activity. Part of my process is to meet people and build trust, and ask myself why I am creating this photo and how it implicates the subject. This allows me to take responsibility for what I capture. This honesty is felt in the stories and photos I put out.The aim has always been to unite people through photography, while balancing difference. Most recently, I’ve been documenting a Sikh family in west London, following their daily life. I am trying to show that, even if someone looks different or practises a different way of life, they’re still just normal people doing relatable things. Going to work, playing football, family time – just with a slight twist. The family dynamic is still there.Hark1karan’s CVBorn:London, 1987High point: Releasing seven self-published books and three short documentaries as a self-taught and independent artist. And most importantly, making a difference to the people who have connected with my work.Top tip:Always seek to create personal work. This will give you the freedom and independence to be your true self. I’m a London born and bred community photographer and artist documenting life in London and the UK. Much of my work has a focus on Punjabi and Sikh communities. I also paint and make short films. Nearly all of my photography is captured on film, my preferred medium, which allows me to slow down and photograph with intention.Hark1karan’s photography features inWithout Shape without Form HQ, Slough, UK, from 26 NovemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From sensation to spectacular, to silence: the strange history of Coleridge-Taylor’s Song of Hiawatha  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Chances to hear Samuel Coleridge-Taylor’s choral masterpiece in concert are rare. Ahead of its belated Edinburgh festival premiere with the Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal, we look at the epic work - and its epic baggage
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Chances to hear Samuel Coleridge-Taylor’s choral masterpiece in concert are rare. Ahead of its belated Edinburgh festival premiere with the Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal, we look at the epic work - and its epic baggage
Content: Symphony of 1000… a dress rehearsal for the staging of Hiawatha at the Royal Albert Hall in 1937.Photograph: Smith Archive/AlamyView image in fullscreenSymphony of 1000… a dress rehearsal for the staging of Hiawatha at the Royal Albert Hall in 1937.Photograph: Smith Archive/AlamyTom Service on musicClassical musicFrom sensation to spectacular, to silence: the strange history of Coleridge-Taylor’s Song of HiawathaTom ServiceChances to hear Samuel Coleridge-Taylor’s choral masterpiece in concert are rare. Ahead of its belated Edinburgh festival premiere with the Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal, we look at the epic work - and its epic baggageWed 12 Aug 2026 10.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 10.42 EDTShareThe Song of Hiawatha, Samuel Coleridge-Taylor’s setting of Henry Longfellow’s poem, comes to theEdinburgh international festival next week. It’s the first time the work will be performed there, a very belated premiere for the three-part cantata that sealed the composer’s reputation nationally and internationally, inspiring Coleridge-Taylor societies in the US, and making him the world’s best-known Black classical composer of the Edwardian era, before his tragicallyearly death at the age of just 37 in 1912.The performance history of The Song of Hiawatha makes for an astounding story. In the early years of the 20th century the work quickly became a sensation, with hundreds of performances on both sides of the Atlantic.In 1924, and then every year from 1926 to 1939, the Royal Albert Hall housed a spectacular and vast staging that involved around 1,000 performers – 200 dancers and hundreds of singers of the Royal Choral Society – dressed up to play out a series of exoticised and racialised caricatures to be part of the pageant of Hiawatha, Minnehaha and their tribespeople. The Mohawk chief also performed in the shows, granting an apparent authenticity to The Song of Hiawatha’s dramaturgy.Post the second world war, performances of the massive work in concert – let alone staged – became rare, and, this century, there’s been barely a handful done professionally.Coleridge-Taylor’s decision to set Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s epic poem was far from novel by the late 1890s. Since the work’s publication in 1855, US composers in their dozens had turned it into cantatas, operas and symphonic works. It inspired the middle movements of Dvořák’s New World Symphony, his tribute to the country that had adopted him and his vision of what might inspire a new American music. But Longfellow’s poem can be read today as a piece of colonialist caricature, mixing Indigenous stories and turning them into a parable of Hiawatha’s noble savagery, as he accommodates the missionaries at the end of the story, before sailing his canoe into the glorious west. It’s a white-empowering fantasy.View image in fullscreenMelodic ideas and directness … Samuel Coleridge-Taylor.Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty ImagesBut such readings concerned few in the first half of the 20th century, and Coleridge-Taylor’s setting was popular with its performers and audiences for less complicated reasons: the immediacy of its melodic ideas, the directness of its choral writing and the emotional clarity of all it sets out to do in its three parts of celebration, lamentation and farewell. The work is exquisitely made for amateur singers to get their teeth into, and, in the context of a British musical culture at the end of the 19th century that was dominated by choral societies and gigantic-scale performances of Handel and Mendelssohn, Coleridge-Taylor’s musical language was sufficiently challenging to reward its singers, but simple and accessible enough to guarantee that choruses all over the world could champion it enthusiastically.Before his death, Coleridge-Taylor apparently sanctioned the idea of the staged performances, produced by TC Fairburn, that took over the whole arena level of the Royal Albert Hall for a fortnight at a time, in annual performances mostly conducted by Malcolm Sargent. The photos of the production and its stars arejaw-dropping in their red-face exoticism. And despite Os-ke-non-ton’s presence, there is nothing that seems authentic about their representation of Native American life, culture or music. Coleridge-Taylor’s score is similarly devoid of ethnographic inspiration of indigenous musical cultures. Beyond a melodic focus on wide-open intervals, fifths and octaves, and piquant modal inflections and orchestrational flourishes, the sound world of The Song of Hiawatha is typical, and marvellous, Victoriana.View image in fullscreenOs-ke-non-ton in Regent’s Park, in a break from being part of the Royal Albert Hall production of The Song of Hiawatha in 1937.Photograph: Fox Photos/Getty ImagesThe significance of The Song of Hiawatha, and especially the success of the first part,Hiawatha’s Wedding Feast, is that it opened Coleridge-Taylor’s horizons to the US. After his first visit there in 1904, he took his place on the world stage as a Black composer, the musician who would take “24 Negro Melodies” as the inspiration for one of the most important collections of British piano music of the early 20th century. He went on to make African music the foundation of orchestral pieces such as his visionarySymphonic Variations on an African Airand his “rhapsodic dance”,The Bamboula, which was premiered by the New York Philharmonic in 1910.There are plenty of other postscripts to The Song of Hiawatha story: the fact that Coleridge-Taylor never saw any royalties from performances of his most successful piece – a sorry state of affairs that led, in part, to the creation of the Performing Rights Society. And there’s Coleridge-Taylor’s catalogue of later cantatas from Kubla Khan toEndymion’s Dream, and his only opera,Thelma, which have been performed even less than the Hiawatha trilogy in the postwar decades.The world has changed: and hopefully theEdinburgh festival performance next weekwill be the start of another life for The Song of Hiawatha, music that’s both uncomplicatedly powerful in its expression, and endlessly rich in its multi-dimensional cultural histories.This week Tom has been listening to:Robin Ticciati’s 2019 recording of Debussy’s Nocturnes and Duruflé’s Requiem with the DSO Berlin. The Nocturnes have a breathtaking combination of sensitivity and viscerality, the Duruflé is a revelation to me. I wish I’d heard this years ago!Explore more on these topicsClassical musicTom Service on musicEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Feminists need to push back’: how did the women’s movement become so divided – and how can it reunite? | Women | The Guardian
description: Just a few years ago, women would fight for other women whatever their background or politics. Today, many loudly dismiss the struggles of those who are not like them. But the solidarity is still there, if you look hard enough
Author: Natasha Walter
Headline: Just a few years ago, women would fight for other women whatever their background or politics. Today, many loudly dismiss the struggles of those who are not like them. But the solidarity is still there, if you look hard enough
Content: Illustration: Michelle Thompson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Michelle Thompson/The GuardianWomen‘Feminists need to push back’: how did the women’s movement become so divided – and how can it reunite?Just a few years ago, women would fight for other women whatever their background or politics. Today, many loudly dismiss the struggles of those who are not like them. But the solidarity is still there, if you look hard enoughNatasha WalterWed 12 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne June day in 2015, I stood outside Yarl’s Wood immigration removal centre near Bedford and heard the women inside singing. “Set her free,” said the graffiti on the walls. “Shut it down.” I had often visited the centre and heard the desperate stories of women who were held inside it. But that day felt hopeful rather than despairing, as hundreds of women – refugees, campaigners, lawyers, members of parliament, actors, writers – gathered around the centre to demand freedom for the women locked up.When I set up the organisationWomen for Refugee Women, I was driven by my faith in solidarity among women. The organisation works with women seeking asylum in Britain to tell their stories and campaign for justice and safety. For years I felt that faith being proved in practice. Women turned up for other women at events and demonstrations; they were volunteering and campaigning, marching and supporting.One of my colleagues atWomenfor Refugee Women, Marchu Belete, is now the director of Migration Exchange. “Back then, women were so open, enthusiastic and creative about campaigning with migrant women,” she says. “We didn’t realise how incredible that time was. It was amazing.”The confidence of feminists in the UK in those years to demand a better world for all women was part of a worldwide phenomenon in the 2010s, a time when women were building new connections with one another all over the globe. Women protested over abortion rights in Ireland, for the right to drive in Saudi Arabia, against digital sex crimes in South Korea, and against sexual violence and femicide in India, Argentina, Brazil, Italy, Turkey, everywhere.I’m not going to idealise those years, but there was a brightness about where our feminist work was going then, an optimism about the connections we could forge and the changes we could make. Now, everywhere you look in women’s movements, you find division.View image in fullscreen‘In the 2010s, women were building new connections all over the globe’ ... a protest in Turkey in 2018.Photograph: Tumay Berkin/EPAThere have always been divisions between women who are apparently working towards shared liberation. Divisions between suffragists and suffragettes, between colonisers and the colonised, between working-class and middle-class women, between those against and those in favour of pornography. But recently divisions among women have become bitterly depleting and many have confided in me how exhausting they find this. One Black woman in her 60s who co-founded an organisation for migrant female survivors of violence said to me recently about the women’s movement in Britain: “We’ve lost our way. There used to be a vision that brought women together. It wasn’t just about personal advancement or separate communities. I don’t know if that still exists.”And over and over again, I am now shocked by the way that women who call themselves feminists will casually dismiss the struggles and experiences of women who are not like themselves. That dismissal can come from all sides of our polarised debates. If you are on the left, why empathise with Ann Widdecombe facing her attacker in her kitchen? If you are on the right, why care about women fleeing oppression across the world? Can you open your heart to Palestinian womenandIsraeli women who are targeted by armed men? Can you take seriously the experience of girls abused by grooming gangsandwomen beaten by the men who protest outside asylum hotels?Social media takes so much of the blame for these widening divisions. It’s true that feminists, just like everyone else, find that anger is rewarded online. Intransigence results in more attention, more clicks, more followers. Debates around the place of transgender women in feminism became particularly wounding and destructive due to the outrage spiral of social media. And once women have sparred in that polarised online world, it becomes harder and harder to come together to campaign, even for the most important goals.But while divisions online are obvious, offline, women are still building alliances, brick by brick. These alliances may not be as immediately visible to outside observers, but I believe that they are quietly growing.Jessie Brinton, who used to be a journalist, is the founder of a project called Mothership, which has been bringing women together across Britain for in-person “kitchen table conversations” about what matters to them.View image in fullscreen‘There have always been divisions between women’ ... suffragists in 1913, who distinguished themselves from the suffragettes.Photograph: Hulton Deutsch/Corbis/Getty ImagesShe is struck by the hunger she witnesses among women just to meet one another and talk. “We’ve lost the ‘village’. Women are lonely. That’s what we’ve heard over and over again. We need to rebuild the spaces in which women find each other.” This year, Brinton has been spending a lot of time in Wigan, where she has been deeply inspired by the strength of unsung community work that women are doing together, filling gaps left by lack of public services. “Women who are on the frontline of crises have so much knowledge to share,” she says.Gill Wright atNorthern Heart and Soulin Wigan agrees that the frontline work that women do to support one another and their communities is the most important work for feminists now. Wright co-founded Northern Heart and Soul after steering a mutual aid group through the pandemic. The organisation is not just for women, but it is women-led and seeks to empower women facing the greatest challenges of poverty, homelessness and poor health. With projects including special educational needs play days, arts projects, gardening and mental health peer support, Wright sees people becoming connected again. “We aren’t putting our energy into changing the system,” she says. “We are focusing our energy on building alternatives.”That focus on locally based organising often blossoms into more direct political interventions where women are trying to revitalise democracy. Cullagh Warnock has been involved with women’s organising in the north-east of England for decades. With the establishment of the North East Mayoral Combined Authority – which gave greater powers to local councils and the mayor of the north-east – in 2024, she and other women in her network saw an opportunity to ensure that women’s voices and concerns were heard.One Million Women and Girlsis the result, a network that connects women to local politicians across north-east England through face-to-face hustings and events.When I ask her what are the key concerns that women raise, Warnock tells me that unlike discussions on social media, they are solidly practical. “Women’s safety comes up all the time – women’s safety on public transport, on the streets. And jobs – politicians talk about green jobs, but they are so often male-dominated. Women are asking about how this transition is going to work for women.” It’s true that predictions suggest that future green jobs, from wind energy to waste management, may skew as much as three to one in favour of men. Warnock believes that by focusing on such practical issues women can move beyond the inflammatory rhetoric of online debate, and get back to what they actually need to build more dignified and safer lives. “What works for women works for everyone.”This work to improve ordinary women’s lives has taken on new urgency due to the rise of the far right, which is capitalising on women’s sense of insecurity to drive forward ever more divisive politics. In Belfast, Elaine Crory at theWomen’s Resource and Development Agencyhas been working for many years to support women in the face of male violence. She now sees the rise of the far right as the “single biggest issue making things worse for women. It is distracting people from fighting the patriarchy and making the situation less safe for women.”View image in fullscreen‘Women’s safety comes up all the time’ … an activist protests against rape and violence against women in Rio de Janeiro in 2016.Photograph: Sergio Moraes/ReutersShe also points to the need for in-person conversations, where facilitators can counter online radicalisation, although she sees how slow and hard this work is given the deluge of corrosive social media misinformation. But she is heartened above all by how women are at the forefront of organising against the far right. During the recent “racist pogroms”, as she calls them,in Belfast, “communities came together quickly, led by women – migrant women and white women – everyone doing what they could. Women were organising, cooking meals, giving lifts, taking a child to school, literally turning up to houses on fire and getting families to safety. And even now that the immediate need for food and shelter has died down, we are ready. If and when it sparks again, women will organise.”‘Heat, floods and droughts make men more violent to women’: Natasha Walter on eco-feminism in a world on fireRead moreSo despite the attempts by the far right to twist women’s fears about their safety into anger and racism, women are building alternatives from Belfast to London to Newcastle, just as they are across the world. Belete thinks that these grassroots connections are now the most important work, and they hold the key to a better future. “Feminists need to be in communities, we need to be on the ground pushing back. The way to defeat the far right is through the women’s movement.”It’s vital not to fall into false optimism when looking at these examples of resilient and inspiring work that women are doing. This is a time of undeniable crisis for women. Our rights are under threat from authoritarians and misogynists everywhere. As resources become scarcer due to the climate emergency, rising inequality and conflict, those threats are multiplying. We can see that one response is to lean into division, to focus only on the individual or the nation, to build walls, to hunker down. But the other response is still to insist that care and connection can be stronger than the hate and the heat, to work day by day to weave those connections – and women are doing that everywhere.Feminism for a World on Fire by Natasha Walter is published by Little, Brown Book Group (£25).
