title: Nipple tape, pickle juice and dinosaurs: how I learned to love running, the unorthodox way | Running | The Guardian
description: The usual advice was getting me nowhere. If I really wanted to embrace running, I’d need to go off-piste. It was a journey that took me to some very strange places …
Author: Ioan Marc Jones
Headline: The usual advice was getting me nowhere. If I really wanted to embrace running, I’d need to go off-piste. It was a journey that took me to some very strange places …
Content: Getting the side-eye … Ioan Marc Jones tests out his hydration system.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGetting the side-eye … Ioan Marc Jones tests out his hydration system.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianRunningNipple tape, pickle juice and dinosaurs: how I learned to love running, the unorthodox wayThe usual advice was getting me nowhere. If I really wanted to embrace running, I’d need to go off-piste. It was a journey that took me to some very strange places …Ioan Marc JonesWed 12 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve always hated running. I’ve tried several times in the past, even made it work for a week or two, then stopped. I hated the excess of pain, the minimal gain. I never experiencedrunner’s high, only runner’s low. I despised the weather, come rain or shine, and the fact I had to be out in it. But most of all I hated the plodding, the tedium, the sheer mundanity of the run. Is that really how I’d choose to spend my one precious life?Then an old football injury returned, with a vengeance. Doctors had previously rebuilt my kneecap, added titanium and rendered me bionic. But they’d not anticipatedNatasha Bedingfield, come midnight at a wedding, and the extremity of my dance moves. My kneecap went a-wandering. It started to catch and click-clack, like castanets. A physio soon gave me the news I’d always dreaded: I had tostart running, outside, properly, and often.Typical running advice had always failed me. I’d tried carb-loading, but I just gained a stone (14lb, or about 6kg). I’d downloaded all the apps, played all the playlists. I’d stretched, warmed down, the whole nine yards. But nothing worked.So this time I decided I’d reach out to seasoned runners and ask for unorthodox advice. I’d learn to love running, via the road less travelled.Week 1: brineFor my first run I left my flat in an M&S T-shirt, swimming trunks (the only shorts I owned) and scruffy Reebok Workouts. I instantly learned that Workouts are terrible for workouts. I learned that Penge High Street in south London is not the best place to jog, with its dreary pavements and immovable crowds, and that swimming trunks tend to slide down. But I managed to finish the run, with a little walking, and recorded my time: 1.51km in 11 minutes and 57 seconds. I was pleasantly surprised.Now for the improvement. “I went to a sports store and purchased running gear and decent shoes,” writes Haruki Murakami, novelist and author ofWhat I Talk About When I Talk About Running. “This is how you become a runner.” Following his lead, I hovered awkwardly around the local sports shop and asked the closest employee for all the help I could get. I soon found myself shoeless, as the man conducted an ocular gait analysis.View image in fullscreenIf the shoe fits …Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian“You have flat feet,” he said. “And they’re exceptionally wide.” I nearly apologised. After trying on a few pairs, like a fat-footed Cinderella, I found the perfect shoe. My glass slipper was the Brooks Adrenaline GTS25.I bought new running tops and short shorts, because runners wear short shorts. I wanted to fit in. And I bought a hydration vest, after reading advice fromrunners online. It seemed akin to a beer helmet but proved a godsend, preventing the jingle of keys and the bounce of my phone, even if the plastic straw kept slapping my face.I made some unusual purchases, too, on the advice of Sarah Hartley, a presenter onThe Running Channel Podcast. “I want to help you avoid pain,” she told me. That’s how I ended up online, in incognito mode, buying nipple tape. And found myself rubbing anti-chafe balm on the area my nan once described as an undercarriage. I was all in. I’d run just once and suddenly felt as if I was prepping for the world’s most choreographed orgy.I asked a friend about nutrition. Alex Revell has run a half marathon or full marathon every month of 2026 and his unfortunate advice was a shot of pickle juice on the day of the run (supposedly as good as any shop-bought electrolytes). So, committed to the experiment, with nipple tape on nipples, I opened a jar of pickles. It felt over the top, verging on absurd, but I took a hefty swig and shivered.I flew on that second run, over 2km. Perhaps nipple tape is aerodynamic. Maybe I’ve previously been slowed by chafe. More likely, the combination of the right gear, the right stretches and the right brine-based hydration instantly elevated me. The pre-run rituals pumped me up, too, forcing me to make the run count. Who knew that preparation actually worked?Week 2: sexy paceI did not run the streets of Penge, but I ran around them. And after a few runs I found the streets incredibly boring. I decided to take advice from Martinus Evans, founder of theSlow AF Run Club: “There is something about awe-inspiring views that helps take your mind off running.” So I decided to search for some awe. And I realised that few things in this world are more awe-inspiring than dinosaurs.The dinosaurs in Crystal Palace park, just down the road from Penge, are absurdities. They are ridiculous things – a point of pride to locals, apoint of moderate confusion to outsiders, but somehow important in thehistory of dinosaurs. Dating from 1854, they were the first full-scale reconstructions, based on crude inaccuracies of early palaeontology, and the results are hilarious. They are creepy, overweight and their smiles will make you smile. It’s fun, running with dinosaurs.View image in fullscreenA couple of Crystal Palace park’s famously inaccurate dinosaurs.Photograph: Jack Dredd/ShutterstockNew surroundings made the runs less tedious and more fun, but in this second week, my distances stalled. Two kilometres felt easy enough, but then I’d suddenly feel wiped.Based on my research, the problem was my pacing. Learning to run slowly is thebest advicefor new runners. Evans recommends the “sexy pace”, so named because it’s like running slow motion on the beach, à la Baywatch. I slowed down to the extent that walkers lapped me, but my distance grew: I ran 3km on the first attempt, in 26 minutes.Week 3: zombiesI had all the right gear, the right pacing, the pickle juice and the dinosaurs, but then came the greatest challenge: existential dread. That had been a thorn in my side in the past. I’d always managed a few runs, even felt encouraged, then the acute boredom and discontent would hit me. And it arrived, right on cue, as I entered my third week.Runners typically turn to music. I trialled strange playlists, as per recommendations: Detroit techno, grime, even classical. Techno definitely helped, with its repetitive beats, but the best was the high energy of early grime records. However, music failed to hold my attention for longer periods.I followed advice fromDr Chloe Bedford, a psychologist and running advocate, and listened to the same song on repeat. This is meant to create a rhythm, but it just made me despiseEye of the Tiger. I needed to find something to better occupy my mind, something to push away the tedium and dread.So I turned to Shakespeare. “Running is a great activity to do while memorising,” Murakami writes. “As I move my legs, I line the words up in order in my mind.” A study in theInternational Journal of Exercise Sciencefound memorising while exercising improved recall, so you can escape boredom while learning something new. I’ve always loved Hamlet and never had a party trick, so I decided to memorise the soliloquies.View image in fullscreenLegs against a sea of troubles.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThis is what running is all about. I started the run, listened to two lines ofRichard Burtonreciting the “To be or not to be” speech and started the track again. I let the track play a little further, concentrated and learned a few more lines. Much of my run was spent pressing my headphones. By the end, I remembered little of the soliloquy, but attempts to memorise had taken my mind off the tedium. I went slowly and covered more than 3km, my best run to date.The lesson is not to listen to Hamlet necessarily, but to find something that helps you focus. Bedford offered a few interesting suggestions that might capture your attention. One was to listen to an audiobook only on your runs, ideally one that ends on cliffhangers, so you’ll want to return to the story as soon as possible. Another is to pretend you’re an MI5 agent on a secret mission: “Works best when it’s raining, as it adds a bit of drama.”Or you can turn to apps for drama. My partner’s cousin, Sarah, usedZombies, Run!to do aCouch to 5k. The app feels like an intense audiobook, with narratives perpetually hanging on cliffs. You pick up strange items, complete missions and work towards zombie-based goals. It was perhaps a little too intense for me – the first episodes consist of a crashed helicopter, a zombie apocalypse, and drawing the undead from a township – and I often felt more confused than frightened. But it certainly got my heart racing.Week 4: rancourBy now, I was struggling to find my motivation. Putting on shoes felt like a gargantuan task, something I could not tolerate. The heatwave did not help, nor did the early-morning starts, even though it was cooler. I started searching desperately for excuses and kept finding them: niggle in my toe, the risk of missing a parcel delivery, Mercury in retrograde.Revell, who has run at least 5k every day this year, says success depends on removing any excuses. “Get everything ready the night before,” he told me. He lays out running clothes and shoes, preps all pre- and post-run food, even grinds his coffee beans before going to bed. It’s a matter of leaving nothing to chance, ensuring minimal barriers prior to leaving the house.Bedford suggests bribery: “Give yourself a reward when you’ve completed a run.” I’d love a ciggie, I thought, having quit five years ago. Perhaps I could smoke my way to good health. Not sure that’s what Bedford had in mind. Typically, these rewards are things like chocolate, cake, maybe a spot of retail therapy, but I have learned to tailor the advice to the person. I tried to think about what I’d actually like.View image in fullscreenBliss.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianSo I started sitting under a tree. At the end of the run, I’d grab a coffee and I’dread for a bit, having stashed a book in my hydration vest. My reward was a sense of quiet early in the morning, surrounded by birds. It made putting my trainers on less daunting. I looked forward to the ambush of calm, enough to drag me out of the flat.Alternatively, you can take motivation from your enemies. Evans recalls how a doctor once called him fat and said running would kill him. For more than a decade he has proved the doctor wrong, all the way to thecover of Runner’s World. In the acknowledgments of his book, Slow AF Run Club: The Ultimate Guide for Anyone Who Wants to Run, Evans addresses the doctor: “I still think you’re a fucking dick and an asshole for saying what you said to me.” You can take that energy and find your own worst enemy.I thought of a thing a person said years ago and I dwelled on it. And I mean I spent hours, dwelling. That dwelling helped me put on my shoes when I really wanted to stay home. If you don’t have enemies, create one. Run against him or her. Run in spite. Let the disdain drive you.Week 5: bapsOrthodox advice suggests avoiding advice from people on the internet. But I was not looking for the orthodox. On the fifth week, leaving no stone unturned, I found an “unhinged running tips that actually work”thread on Redditand started putting them into practice.One Redditor suggested I shout “Fuck!” whenever the run got hard. I did it in the name of science. Any time I felt pain, I shouted, “Fuck!” It was bad enough that I wore a little backpack, with a straw slapping my face, and probably stank of pickle, but now I was cursing in public, amid dinosaurs, like a pirate.View image in fullscreenWhat happens when you ditch your headphones.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe interesting thing: it worked. But not as expected. Shouting “Fuck!” in the middle of the park, in the school holidays, made me run faster, not longer, because I was sprinting away from a succession of dirty looks.“Rawdogging” was perhaps the worst advice I tried to follow. It means no music, no zombies, no Hamlet. I was left to run alone with my thoughts. So I grappled with my mortality. It was the worst run of my life. I ran very fast and not very long and I arrived home like a sweaty Schopenhauer, afraid of existence.One final bit of advice from Reddit worked a treat. It called for a mid-run breakfast. I ran 3km with the dinosaurs, then stopped in the cafe. I ate a veggie bap drowning in brown sauce, drank some fancy lemonade, then read my book for a bit. It was perhaps too relaxing. Then I stood up, put my vest back on, and ran the final kilometre back to my flat.It was fun, but spending a tenner every time is unsustainable in this economy. I might do it as a treat on weekends, though, especially once I start reaching longer distances.Week 6: the finish lineFor the first time in my life, I’ve run consistently for more than a month. A rhythm has taken hold. My last run was just over 4km. Now I need to figure out the long term – how to make running a constant in my life.The best long-term advice I’ve heard, which I’m putting into practice, comes from Hartley. She says success depends on defining your running personality.Hartley offers a few possibilities: Lover of the Plod, Trail-running Mountain Goat,RunningClub Fanatic, Person Who Jogs to Find Pastries. Finding your running identity makes running part of you. It is an act of empowerment, open to everyone. You are a runner. You just need to decide the sort of runner you wish to be.It is too simplistic to suggest I now love running. But the experiment has pushed me to leave my flat, helped me to tie my shoes in the mornings. I am learning. I am making progress. And I am enjoying my trip on the road less travelled. Because I am a runner now – one who relies on historically inaccurate dinosaurs, nipple tape, pickle juice and Hamlet. I like that.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: How to use up parmesan rind to make pesto – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Why waste the tastiest bit of the cheese?
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Why waste the tastiest bit of the cheese?
Content: Parmesan rind pesto drizzled on a roast chicken and baked vegetables.Photograph: Matt Austin/PRView image in fullscreenParmesan rind pesto drizzled on a roast chicken and baked vegetables.Photograph: Matt Austin/PRWaste notFoodHow to use up parmesan rind to make pesto – recipeWhy waste the tastiest bit of the cheese?Tom HuntWed 12 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlthough parmesan rind is tough, it has just as much, if not more flavour than the cheese from inside the wheel itself. It can be used just as it is to flavourstockorrisi e bisi(Venetian pea risotto), but grating it opens up a whole range of other uses, such as in mymac and cheese “rinds” and today’s parmesan rind pesto. The flavour is very powerful, though, so add it to taste: you may find that you need a lot less than you think you do.Parmesan rind pestoWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appParmesan rind is a powerful ingredient that creates a more flavourful and robust sauce that holds up especially well against big flavours such as wholegrain pastas or barbecued meat and vegetables. Pesto is quick to make whether you do so in a blender or with a pestle and mortar, but I find that the latter produces a more interesting texture and, if anything, a more powerful flavour, because all that crushing and bruising releases more flavour compounds and volatile oils than the sharp blade of a blender. That said, to make it in a blender, simply pulse-blend all the ingredients bar half the pine nuts, until the pesto is smooth but textural.4 tbsp pine nuts1 small garlic clove, peeled1 pinch coarsesea salt75g bunchfresh basil, including the stalks2 tbsp finely grated parmesan rind– I use a Microplane100-150ml extra-virgin olive oilToast the pine nuts in a dry pan until golden brown, then tip out and leave to cool. Put the garlic and salt in a mortar and grind to a smooth puree. Work in half the pine nuts, crushing them into small pieces (save the rest to add at the end, for extra texture).Grind in the basil a handful at a time, working quickly to preserve its vivid green colour, then pound in the grated parmesan rind.Slowly grind in the extra-virgin olive oil, until the pesto is of a consistency that’s to your liking, then finish by stirring in the remaining whole pine nuts and adding more salt to taste, if need be.Serve fresh, or keep in a sealed container in the fridge for up to two days.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteCheeseSauces and graviesItalian food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: All-British chocolate bar made by scientists using Reading-grown cocoa | Chocolate | The Guardian
description: Master’s student made first bar with 100% UK ingredients since 1932 to highlight effect of climate crisis on cocoa plants
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Master’s student made first bar with 100% UK ingredients since 1932 to highlight effect of climate crisis on cocoa plants
Content: Maha Khan, the University of Reading food security master’s student who created the chocolate bar.Photograph: University of ReadingView image in fullscreenMaha Khan, the University of Reading food security master’s student who created the chocolate bar.Photograph: University of ReadingChocolateAll-British chocolate bar made by scientists using Reading-grown cocoaMaster’s student made first bar with 100% UK ingredients since 1932 to highlight effect of climate crisis on cocoa plantsHelena HortonWed 12 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 03.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe late queen was the only person in history to have ever eaten a chocolate bar made with 100% British ingredients, after she was given one as a six-year-old in 1932 by the confectioner Rowntree’s.The bar was created from a glasshouse-grown cocoa plant, at Rowntree’s headquarters in York.But now, others could have the same experience after scientists at the University of Reading created a bar with cocoa beans grown inBerkshire.Raw cacao beans are coated in a white flesh ‘that tastes like lychee’.Photograph: University of ReadingThe bar was crafted to celebrate the university’s 100th anniversary, made with cocoa grown from plants in the institute’s collection.The UK makes some of the world’s best chocolate in a market worth £10.4bn, but the industry is entirely reliant on imported cocoa.Maha Khan, a master’s student at the university, decided to make a bar with cocoa fromReading. She harvested, fermented, and processed the beans at the university’s food department.Why hot weather and chocolate can go togetherRead moreShe said: “It has been amazing to follow the entire chocolate-making process, from pod to bean to bar, without leaving Reading.“This British bar of chocolate highlights the precarious nature of our food supplies. Cocoa plants are very sensitive to changes in temperature and rainfall, and climate changeis already causing problems in countriesthat produce most of the world’s cocoa. Protecting different varieties is vital if farmers need hardier plants that can cope with a changing climate.“I hope this shows people just how much work goes into the chocolate we enjoy, and how important it is to protect cocoa farmers and communities around the world.”She said the chocolate is “delicious”, adding that it had a very rich flavour: “It’s incredible to taste the complexity of the flavour profiles as the cocoa is made from plants originating from over 300 varieties grown here. It was also really interesting to taste the raw cacao before it gets processed – the beans are coated in a white flesh that tastes like lychee and isn’t something many people in this country get to try.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCocoa pods in the University of Reading’s international cocoa quarantine centre.Photograph: Oliver SirrellAs well as being somewhat of a stunt, the university hopes that this can highlight the importance of its work in preserving different varieties of cocoa, which could be resistant to changes in weather brought by climate breakdown, as well as pests and diseases made more common by a heating planet.Reading has more than 300 types of cocoa plant at its international cocoa quarantine centre, which handles 97% of the world’s international movement of cocoa plants.Chocolate prices haverisen in recent yearsas high temperatures in regions where cocoa is grown have stunted the growth of plants. Extreme rainfall made more likely by climate breakdown has also drowned crops across Africa.The bar is currently a limited edition, with only six made so far, but Khan said there are hopes to ramp up production, depending on the availability of the beans – a single cocoa pod can take six months to grow.She hopes to give one to the Princess of Wales: “We haven’t decided yet who will get to eat the chocolate. As the last British chocolate made was eaten by the future queen in 1932, it would be fitting if the next bar was a gift to another future queen, the Princess of Wales, who, like the chocolate, was also born in Reading.”Explore more on these topicsChocolateReadingBerkshireClimate crisisFoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tarte tatin, spicy pork chops and crumble: Ravinder Bhogal’s gooseberry recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: The gooseberry makes itself welcome in both sweet and savoury settings: in a tarte tatin, in a lively salad for spicy, herby pork chops and in a crumble custard cake
Author: Ravinder Bhogal
Headline: The gooseberry makes itself welcome in both sweet and savoury settings: in a tarte tatin, in a lively salad for spicy, herby pork chops and in a crumble custard cake
Content: Ravinder Bhogal’s pork chop with fennel, tarragon and gooseberry salad.Photograph: Beca B Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.View image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s pork chop with fennel, tarragon and gooseberry salad.Photograph: Beca B Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Isobel Clarke.FoodTarte tatin, spicy pork chops and crumble: Ravinder Bhogal’s gooseberry recipesThe gooseberry makes itself welcome in both sweet and savoury settings: in a tarte tatin, in a lively salad for spicy, herby pork chops and in a crumble custard cakeRavinder BhogalWed 12 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the summer glut of saccharine fruits such as strawberries and peaches, gooseberries may not be the ones you reach for first. But behind their strange burr of fine fuzz, these translucent, marble-like fruits offer a complex, defiant flavour. They are juicy, fragrant, a little sweet (especially the red ones that come along later in the season), but, overall, they are raspishly sour. Like rhubarb, they need sweetening if you’re using them in compotes or desserts, but their natural tartness offers a wonderful contrast and cuts through cheese, fatty meat such as pork or oily fish such as mackerel.Spiced pork chops with fennel, tarragon and gooseberry salad (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appThe addition of tart fruit in the salad helps to cut through the fattiness of the meat.Prep15 minMarinate20 minPickle10 minCook30 minServes42tsp sea salt2tsp fennel seeds2 tbsp coriander seeds1tsp black peppercorns1tsp caster sugar½tsp paprika1tsp dried oregano4pork chops2tbsp olive oil25g butter4garlic cloves, unpeeled and bashed flatFor the salad3tbsp white-wine vinegar1tbsp caster sugar, or honeySea salt and black pepper1tsp coriander seeds, toasted and very lightly crushed2 fennel bulbs, trimmed and very finely sliced from top to base (preferably with a mandoline)1 cucumber, peeled and sliced into long ribbons with a vegetable peeler or mandoline1 banana shallot, peeled and very finely sliced200g gooseberries25g tarragon, leaves picked25g mint, leaves picked and finely chopped3tbsp extra-virgin olive oilPut the salt, fennel seeds, coriander seeds, pepper and sugar in a mortar and grind to a fine powder. Add the paprika and oregano, and grind again. Pat the chops dry with kitchen paper, then press the spice mix all over the meat. Leave to marinate at room temperature for 20 minutes.Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/350F/gas 6. Heat the oil and butter in an ovenproof frying pan and add the garlic. Using tongs, hold the chops skin-side down in the pan for five minutes to crisp up and render the fat. Once the fat is a lovely amber colour, fry the chops for three minutes on each side, basting as you go, then transfer to the oven for six minutes, or until cooked all the way through. Rest the meat for five minutes.Meanwhile, make the salad. Mix the vinegar and caster sugar in a mixing bowl until the sugar has dissolved, then season well with salt and pepper. Add the coriander seeds, fennel, cucumber and shallot, and set aside to lightly pickle for 10 minutes. Finally, add the gooseberries and herbs and drizzle over the olive oil. Toss well and serve with the pork chops.Gooseberry tarte tatin with goat’s cheeseWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s gooseberry tarte tatin.A savoury take on the classic apple tarte tatin. This version features a wonderful partnership between tart gooseberries and funky goat’s cheese. Serve with some dressed salad leaves and toasted hazelnuts for crunch.Prep10 minCook55 minServes640g butterA few sprigs of thyme2½tbsp runny honey3tbsp apple cider vinegarSea salt and black pepper750g gooseberries,topped and tailedPlain flour,for dusting500g blockpuff pastry150g soft goat’s cheeseHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/425F/gas 6. Put a 20cm ovenproof frying pan on a medium heat and melt the butter. Once the butter has completely melted, add the thyme and fry briefly for 30 seconds, then stir in the honey and vinegar and season well.Once the glaze has thickened and caramelised, remove the pan from the heat and leave to cool for eight to 10 minutes. Add the gooseberries and stir to coat.On a floured work surface, roll out the pastry to 3mm thick, then cut out a circle slightly larger than the pan. Cover the gooseberries with the pastry, using your fingers to carefully tuck it in at the edges. Bake for 30-35 minutes, or until crisp and golden on top.Remove from the oven and leave to cool for at least five minutes before carefully inverting on to a serving plate. Serve hot or cold, scattered with crumbled goat’s cheese and more black pepper.Gooseberry crumble custard cakeWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s gooseberry crumble custard cake.The sour fruit offers a welcome respite in this nursery-sweet cake layered with custard. Raspberries would also work well here.Prep5 minCook1 hr 20 min, plus coolingChill4 hrServes12300g unsalted butter, plus extra to grease tin300g golden caster sugar5 medium eggs300g plain flour2 tsp baking powder150ml milk400ggooseberries500ml fresh vanilla custardFor the crumble200g plain flour125g chilled butter125g golden caster sugarA fat pinch of sea salt70g flaked almondsFinely grated zest of 1 lemonHeat the oven to 160C (140C fan)/325F/gas 3. For the crumble topping, rub the flour and butter between your fingertips to a breadcrumb-like consistency, then mix in the sugar, salt, almonds, and lemon zest. Chill until needed.Grease a 20cm x 30cm rectangular cake tin with butter, then line it with baking paper.In a stand mixer or with an electric whisk, beat the butter and caster sugar until light and fluffy. Add the eggs one at a time, beating each one in thoroughly, then sift in the flour and baking powder. Pour in the milk, gently fold in, then add half the gooseberries.Spread half the gooseberry batter evenly into the lined tin, then pour the custard on top. Carefully spread the rest of the batter on top, then dot with the remaining gooseberries.Sprinkle with the crumble mixture, then bake for about an hour, until golden but still a bit wobbly in the centre. Leave to cool in the tin, then chill for at least four hours, and ideally overnight. Cut into 12 rectangles and serve.Explore more on these topicsFoodFruitSummer food and drinkPieMain courseStarterSaladrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Sali Hughes on beauty: a shortcut to glass skin? Try these one-step moisturisers | Beauty | The Guardian
description: Three new products – and one old favourite – achieve a glazed sheen in one easy application
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: Three new products – and one old favourite – achieve a glazed sheen in one easy application
Content: Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianSali Hughes on beautyBeautySali Hughes on beauty: a shortcut to glass skin? Try these one-step moisturisersThree new products – and one old favourite – achieve a glazed sheen in one easy applicationSali HughesWed 12 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.As you will no doubt have noticed, “glass” skin – that is, a complexion with a smooth, glazed sort of sheen – has been fashionable for ages. Until now, however, it has only come as the result of a meticulous, umpteen-step Korean skincare routine. But the new glass skin moisturisers attempt to mimic the look in one simple application.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Erborian’sGlow Moisturiser(from £9, all skin types) is a Goldilocks’s porridge sort of face cream. Not too heavy, not too light, just dewy enough without looking oily, and with lasting hydration that never becomes wet. I must advise the glimmer-avoidant that it does have a smidge of pearlescence, but I find that flattering.double quotation markI’ve rarely changed my mind about a product so quickly. It went on sticky and stiff – but then transformedMac’sFaceglass Hydrating Skin Gloss(£30) is, as you might expect from an artistry brand, a more definite “look”. I’ve rarely changed my mind about a product so quickly. On first application, I found the cloudy gel sticky and stiff, but seconds later it behaved very differently – smooth, spreadable and silky, with a lasting, glitter-free reflection. It gives true – not just cosmetic – skin hydration, thanks to a heavy load of glycerin and squalane, and while it has a strong fruity scent, it doesn’t have that jammy teenage lipgloss finish. Makeup goes over it nicely, and the more I experimented, the more versatile I found it. This is more than an-all over moisturiser – it can be applied locally to cheekbones, brow bones and lips, and its thickness prevents unwanted migration to other areas.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSali Hughes on beauty: behold the power of the long-wearing liquid eyeshadowRead moreOne of this summer’s most impressive launches is Rhode’s “luminizing”Highlight Milk(£28), a liquid moisturiser I use often as a last layer before sunscreen. Unlike the bestselling colourless original,Glazing Milk, this version is tinted (there are four shades that between them cover everyone). The two are otherwise identical – soothing, milky moisture with a glazed-doughnut sort of finish. I love shade 02 so much I’ve been dispensing with foundation altogether.I’ve recommended it before, but it bears repeating:L’Oreal Paris’sRevitalift Filler Glass Skin Face Moisturiser(£17.99, but frequently on offer) gives a subtle glassy sheen for those who don’t want to overcommit. It’s a milky serum that hydrates, plumps and leaves just enough dewiness so you look vital and healthy without ever seeming sweaty or sticky. I find a matte-ish makeup over the top looks more natural and effortless for it, and even dry skin stays lubricated. It’s a terrific – but oddly overlooked – buy.Explore more on these topicsBeautySali Hughes on beautyWomenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Katendrecht: Rotterdam’s sailors’ quarter reinvented as cultural hub | Rotterdam holidays | The Guardian
description: The regeneration of historic warehouses has transformed this former red-light district into one of the port city’s most vibrant areas
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The regeneration of historic warehouses has transformed this former red-light district into one of the port city’s most vibrant areas
Content: The viewing platform of the Tornado staircase in Fenix in Katendrecht, Rotterdam.Photograph: Barbara Laborde/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe viewing platform of the Tornado staircase in Fenix in Katendrecht, Rotterdam.Photograph: Barbara Laborde/AFP/Getty ImagesZoning inRotterdam holidaysKatendrecht: Rotterdam’s sailors’ quarter reinvented as cultural hubThe regeneration of historic warehouses has transformed this former red-light district into one of the port city’s most vibrant areasPat RiddellWed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy go now?A thin peninsula just south of Rotterdam’s centre, Katendrecht was once at the heart of the world’s busiest port, home to continental Europe’s first Chinatown and a lively sailors’ quarter. Its later reputation as a red light district has been shrugged off – part of the city’s wider reinvention in the aftermath of extensive second world war bombing.Still Europe’s largest port, Rotterdam’s maritime history is very much evident today, with the former headquarters of the Holland-America Linenow a hoteljust a short hop across the Rijnhaven Bridge. The 2012 opening of this pedestrian and bicycle bridge finally connected cut-off Katendrecht to Wilhelminapier, which was a jumping off point for transatlantic migration, and is today a major cruise terminal, with more than 100 ships departing every year.double quotation markOriginally home to the first Chinese restaurant in the Netherlands, Delistraat is buzzing from morning to nightThe opening of theFenix museum of migrationlast year and the reopening of theNederlands Fotomuseumin a new location here in February have accelerated Katendrecht’s rise in status, following on from the entrepreneurs and creatives who have introduced craft breweries, food halls and design boutiques in recent years.Former warehouses have been transformed – into the aforementioned museums among other venues – and a lively cultural and arts scene has grown as the neighbourhood has seen new residents rediscover the formerly downtrodden area.With more big construction projects under way, Katendrecht will be transformed further over the next five years, with apartments, shops, a five-star hotel, an urban beach and, notably, the Rotterdam Centre for Dance,Danshuis, on the horizon.Where to eat and drinkView image in fullscreenDeliplein in Katendrecht.Photograph: Iris van den BroekDeliplein is the place to begin – the tree-lined square lies at the heart of the old sailors’ quarter and houses more than 20 restaurants and bars. Originally home to the first Chinese restaurant in the Netherlands, Delistraat is buzzing from morning to night.Start atJordy’s Bakery, where flaky pastries, vegan muffins, sourdough sandwiches and speciality coffees will fuel you for the morning. Across the road in the Fenix atrium,O: Anatolian Caféis run by the Michelin-starred chef Maksut Aşkar; on the menu are all-day Turkish breakfasts, meze platters, sandwiches and salads at extremely reasonable prices.Kaapse Brouwersin the Fenix Food Factory is where the post-work crowd heads. Sit on the terrace, admire the waterfront view and explore its range of more than 20 craft beers on tap – from Belgian blonds and New England IPAs to pilsners and sours. And back on Delistraat,Café de Ouwehoeris a classic old-style pub with a nod to the area’s past – and a huge range of whiskeys to boot.A few doors down, finish your evening at the small but perfectly formed fine-dining establishmentDe Matroos en Het Meisje(The Sailor and the Girl), which offers a changing daily menu. With the option of choosing from four to six courses, dependent on season and produce, dishes could be charred carrot, cured Japanese fish, creme fraiche and onion, or chicken breast with mushroom beurre blanc, blackberries and crisped rice.Cultural experiencesView image in fullscreenThe Suitcase Labyrinth at Fenix.Photograph: Image Broker/AlamyFenixis the obvious first stop. Funded by the philanthropic foundationDroom en Daad(Dream and Do), the museum of immigration opened last May in a renovated historic warehouse and finally gave Katendrecht a real focal point for visitors.Formerly part of the world’s largest warehouse for cargo transfer, the museum reflects the fact that millions of migrants arrived at and departed from the port in search of a new life. At its heart is the Tornado, a spectacular mirrored spiral staircase, which offers 360-degree views across the neighbourhood, docks and the city. It symbolises the central theme, with architect Ma Yansong describing it as “a metaphor for the journeys of migrants”.double quotation markThe exposed brick, rough-edged concrete and steel girders offer a striking contrast to the impressive photography on displayThe industrial space is used sparingly to display photography, art and sculpture that communicate the experience of immigration, movement and displacement of peoples. It’s humbling and moving. The exhibitionAll Directionsfeatures more than 100 artists, with stories of the war in Kyiv and refugee camps in Tunisia, Jordan and Lebanon, as well as a lifesize New York bus made from fabric.The Family of Migrantsexhibition showcases more than 200 photos from around the world, depicting the story of migration from the late 19th century to the present day. And theSuitcase Labyrinthhas about 2,000 donated cases, dating from 1898 to today, with 30 audio stories detailing the unique past of some of them.Farther down the waterfront, the newly openedNederlands Fotomuseumis also in a renovated warehouse – formerly used to store coffee from Brazil – and is topped with a modern anodised aluminium structure. Inside, the exposed brick, rough-edged concrete and steel girders offer a striking contrast to the impressive photography on display.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenNederlands Fotomuseum.Photograph: Iwan BaanThe original museum opened in 2003, and the collection now comprises more than six million negatives, transparencies, prints, photo albums and other archival matter – visitors are encouraged to look in the depots and studios. Every week, thousands of images are digitised and made available online, while old and damaged photography is conserved and restored.On the first floor, theGallery of Honour of Dutch Photographyshowcases 99 distinguished photographs, selected by a group of experts, spanning 1842 to the digital era. And as you go up the central staircase, which leads all the way to the rooftop restaurant, a mosaic of projected images merely hints at the breadth and depth of photography in storage.Where to shopIn the Bay House development, close to the Nederlands Fotomuseum, there are a number of designer fashion and vintage furniture stores.Selected With Lovehas “upcycled” clothing,Caesarsells designer menswear, whileThe Gallery by Collectors Networkis a space for numerous independent dealers selling vintage design pieces – Vintage Hoarder, for example, has 1980s Belgian floor lamps, a 1970s French slate table and 1960s Italian dining chairs.The museum shops offer the best range of unique purchases. Fenix has items created in collaboration with artists and designers as well as chocolates from Rotterdam, slippers from Greece and tea from small family-run plantations in China.Don’t missVerhalenhuis Belvédèreis perhaps the best place to get a sense of where Katendrecht has come from. Dating from 1894, the building was originally a cafe then a jazz club – saved from demolition, it became a cultural centre, community hub and exhibition space in 2009.As part of its cultural programmes, community meals and storytelling events, Belvédère collects and shares the stories of Rotterdam residents, from the first Cape Verdean migrants to Jewish families and Chinese seafarers.Where to stayView image in fullscreenHotel New York in Rotterdam.Photograph: Edwin Muller/AlamyOfHotel New York’s72 rooms, the suites in the former offices of the Holland-America Line’s directors, overlooking the Nieuwe Maas river, and the two tower rooms are the ones to book. Rooms from €110.On the western tip of Katendrecht, the former cruise shipSS Rotterdamis permanently moored and is now a 254-room hotel that retains much of its original styling, with wood panelling throughout, and the public spaces – bars, restaurants, theatre – are like stepping back in time. Tours are available. Rooms from €73. The five-starEurostarshotel is expected to open in the autumn, next door to the Nederlands Fotomuseum and right by the Rijnhaven metro station, which connects easily to Rotterdam Centraal train station.The trip was hosted by theNetherlands Board of Tourism & ConventionsExplore more on these topicsRotterdam holidaysZoning inNetherlands holidaysCity breaksEurope holidaysShort breaksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: One flower here is thriving, defying the drought | Environment | The Guardian
description: Frome, Somerset: While other plants are withering or skeletal, tansy is growing in great profusion, and it rewards close observation
Author: Derek Niemann
Headline: Frome, Somerset: While other plants are withering or skeletal, tansy is growing in great profusion, and it rewards close observation
Content: Tansy on the banks of the River Frome.Photograph: Sarah NiemannView image in fullscreenTansy on the banks of the River Frome.Photograph: Sarah NiemannCountry diaryEnvironmentCountry diary: One flower here is thriving, defying the droughtFrome, Somerset:While other plants are withering or skeletal, tansy is growing in great profusion, and it rewards close observationDerek NiemannWed 12 Aug 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 04.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt first light, the scent of ’76 hangs in the air, a reminder of that endless summer burning itself into autumn, just like this one. I first caught a sniff of it walking home one sweltering evening in the June heatwave and said: “Too soon, too soon.”Now the toasted aroma of spent grass is everywhere – on crispy playing fields, straw village greens, and these scorched tawny meadows of the combe. Scattered groups of cattle have their heads down here. For them I think eating the grass must be like consuming a Pot Noodle before the water is poured in.And then I find the outflow of one of the hillside’s springs. Though it registers nothing more than a seep, it is nevertheless a pocket oasis of comparative lushness, a blessing to a heifer’s eyes.Country diary: The eyebright paradox: a sunny healer and tiny parasitic thief | Paul EvansRead moreThese cows know a thing or two; against the fiercest sun in that hottest spell, they fashioned themselves a long awning on the riverbank, chomping the trees, twigs and all, up to a browse line, then sheltered under the canopy. Clearly barely palatable, the alders survived this first onslaught, but even they were stripped out by mid-July. Cow licks tugged out the grass from below, hooves pounded the ground to bare earth. The adjoining path still wears a dried cowpat crust.Beyond the gate, beyond the cows, one plant in particular defies the drought, striking for its sprinkling of vivid colour against the skeletons of umbellifers and wilting greens.Tansygrows in such localised profusion that it gives the immediate impression of great sprays of primary yellow buttons. Close observation confirms a dual identity in appearance. From the neck down, it displays fern-like leaves. But the aster family is there in its little bunched-together disc florets, each about a centimetre across, bobbled like compound eyes.Richard Mabey’s magisterialFlora Britannicaattests to tansy’s medieval lineage as an all-purpose, largely medicinal herb, ranging from the mildly toxic and purgative to its inclusion as bitter flavouring for an omelette. Another source claims tansy leaves were garlanded into an embalming wreath for thecoffined first president of Harvard University. I think I might leave them for other mouths to sample.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentCountry diaryRural affairsPlantsDroughtAnimalsFarmingWaterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘If we exhibited all the Balkan jokes, we wouldn’t have opened’: a trip to Slovenia’s Bullshit Museum | Museums | The Guardian
description: In the heart of old Ljubljana, a mannequin with a bucket on its head welcomes visitors to a new and ambitious project – a museum focusing on the varied and sometimes antagonistic humour of the former Yugoslavia
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In the heart of old Ljubljana, a mannequin with a bucket on its head welcomes visitors to a new and ambitious project – a museum focusing on the varied and sometimes antagonistic humour of the former Yugoslavia
Content: Bucket cred … the mannequin welcoming visitors to step into Ljubljana’s new museum of Balkan humour.Photograph: Veronika SnojView image in fullscreenBucket cred … the mannequin welcoming visitors to step into Ljubljana’s new museum of Balkan humour.Photograph: Veronika SnojMuseums‘If we exhibited all the Balkan jokes, we wouldn’t have opened’: a trip to Slovenia’s Bullshit MuseumIn the heart of old Ljubljana, a mannequin with a bucket on its head welcomes visitors to a new and ambitious project – a museum focusing on the varied and sometimes antagonistic humour of the former YugoslaviaVeronika SnojWed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the main promenade along the river that runs through Ljubljana, Slovenia’s capital, tourists stop to photograph a mannequin with a bucket on its head. Dressed in a pistachio jacket and red leggings, the figure sits at a table in front of one of the houses in the historic Old Town, staring at a spilled cup of Turkish coffee, popular with Slovenes and with the other Balkan and central European citizens with whom they shared a country, until it collapsed in the early 1990s. A large sign in the background reads: “Bullshit Museum: The world is off the rails, and so are we.Yebiga!”Yebiga, which can be loosely translated as “fuck it”, or “screw it”, is the red thread running through the museum that was launched in May and consists of five small rooms filled with mannequins wearing odd accessories, AI-generated images of laughing characters and scenes accompanying some of the jokes, framed or displayed on cardboard screens. The word encompasses the heart of Balkan humour, says the museum’s founder, Borut Kokelj, who wears a T-shirt emblazoned with the words: “What part of yebiga don’t you understand?”View image in fullscreenThe Bullshit Museum is spotted with mannequins wearing various odd accessories.Photograph: Veronika Snoj“Even when there’s no money, when there are no jobs, when nothing is settled, everything can be solved with humour,” he says. “And for that to work, humour must have no filter”.Although it presents itself as the home of “Balkan” humour, the museum is primarily centred on the joke culture of the former Yugoslavia, the socialist federation that included the Balkan Peninsula countries that are now Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kosovo.Formed out of the wreckage of the first world war, Yugoslavia was a political project to unite southern Slav and some non-Slavic minorities under a common identity and language, then officially known as Serbo-Croatian. But the genocidal wars that accompanied Yugoslavia’s disintegration in the early 1990s demonstrated that the idea of a single Yugoslav nation lacked deep foundations. The region’s different nations have since continued to define themselves through distinct religious identities, including Catholicism, Orthodoxy and Islam, but also separate dialects and languages.View image in fullscreen1. Good morning! 2. What is he saying? 3. He said Good morning, but in Cyrillic …  a cartoon at the Bullshit Museum.Photograph: Veronika Snoj“Balkan” humour, the museum suggests, may have been the glue that held Yugoslavia’s cultural bric-a-brac in place, and it is fitting that some of the jokes on display play directly on the issue of language. “A fool is a fool in both the Cyrillic and the Latin alphabets,” reads a large poster at the entrance, using both scripts: Cyrillic, being associated with Serbs and Orthodox Christianity, and the Latin alphabet being used by other, mostly non-Orthodox nations of the dissolved state.The armed conflicts that have shaped the region are also reflected in the exhibition, albeit indirectly. There is wordplay on the title of the controversial 1996 Serbian drama Lepa Sela Lepo Gore (literally “pretty villages burn nicely”), about a group of surrounded Serbian soldiers during the Bosnian war, here adapted into the absurdist lineLepa jela lepo goje(“Fine food fattens you up well”).View image in fullscreenDisplays and inverted mannequin at the museum.Photograph: Veronika SnojThe role and power of women in society also seems to be a unifying factor. “Starleta is the first Balkan mythical being with the body of a woman and the head of a turkey”, reads an “encyclopedic” definition of a “starleta” – a woman who seeks fame and wealth through no other achievements than her (plastic surgery-assisted) beauty. “She wanted to marry a prince, but a horse had more money,” reads another, playing on the wordkonj(horse), which is used in many former Yugoslav nations to describe a “man”.Kokelj, who has collected about 25,000 jokes from the region over the years, said he resisted freighting the exhibition with politically loaded humour. “If we were to exhibit all the truly ‘Balkan’ jokes, we likely wouldn’t have opened,” he admits, referring to jokes that directly address religion, ethnicity, or national symbols.The selection also avoids jokes that mock a specific group or feature characters identified with a particular ethnic group. There are no jokes here mocking the supposed “laziness” of Montenegrins (such as this from the humour section of a local magazine: “What does a Montenegrin say before going to bed? ‘Rise, earth, so that I may lie down,’”). I find only one AI-generated “ethnic” meta-joke: it plays on the stereotype of Slovenes as a nation eager to present itself as the most “elegant” and “European”, thereby distancing itself from the rest of the region: a Slovenian man tells a joke “the Slovenian way”, using innocent euphemistic curses such as “three hundred hairy bears”, while his “Balkan” counterpart has no restraint when it comes to colourful insults.Overall, most of the jokes address everyday issues and the absurdities of life. “Life is neither nail polish nor acetone,” reads one. “We had it better, and we still complained. Now that things are getting worse, we’re complaining again,” says another. Others focus on romantic relationships: “Love is when you look like a sack of potatoes, but she sees you as fries.” Another recurring theme is the ability to laugh at oneself: “Amateurs make mistakes, but we, the experienced ones, create catastrophes.”There seems to be one element that holds the exhibition together to this day, though: rakija, the celebrated Balkan fruit brandy. It is served to visitors as they enter the museum and is described in one of the exhibits as “the first aid of every Balkan household”. It is also central to the definition of the infamousyebiga, which one exhibit describes as follows: “The Balkan way of saying: what are you going to do? Maximum feeling, minimum energy. It usually goes with rakija, a cigar and a song that hurts more than it should.”Explore more on these topicsMuseumsComedyExhibitionsSloveniaSlovenia holidaysEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Drowned the day her visa came through: the tragedy of a Moroccan footballer trying to reach Ceuta | Global development | The Guardian
description: Struggling on her meagre pay, Faten Ben Omar El Azizi dreamed of reaching Europe. Then she joined thousands trying to reach a better life in Spain
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Struggling on her meagre pay, Faten Ben Omar El Azizi dreamed of reaching Europe. Then she joined thousands trying to reach a better life in Spain
Content: Faten Omar Ben El Azizi, a 26-year-old football player in Morocco’s regional league, died with at least at least 141 others while trying to reach Ceuta.Photograph: HandoutView image in fullscreenFaten Omar Ben El Azizi, a 26-year-old football player in Morocco’s regional league, died with at least at least 141 others while trying to reach Ceuta.Photograph: HandoutRights and freedomGlobal developmentDrowned the day her visa came through: the tragedy of a Moroccan footballer trying to reach CeutaStruggling on her meagre pay, Faten Ben Omar El Azizi dreamed of reaching Europe. Then she joined thousands trying to reach a better life in SpainSupported byAbout this contentSoraya Aybar Laafou in Tétouan, MoroccoWed 12 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFootball was the life Faten Ben Omar El Azizi had wanted. She had long played in Morocco’s regional league for Moghreb Atlético Tetuán, whose striking kit replicates the colours of the famous Spanish club Atlético Madrid.And in the cruellest of ironies, on the day that she drowned last month, one of nearly 150 people who died in the illegal mass crossing into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, her mother was told that her daughter had just been granted a visa to go toSpain.El Azizi loved training, says her coach: Tuesdays on the pitch and Thursday at the beach, near the city of Tétouan in northern Morocco, where the 26-year-old lived with her mother and the rest of her family.But making a living from playing in a women’s football league in Morocco had proved impossible for El Azizi. She received only a small payment of about 260 dirham (£21) when her team won and nothing when it lost – not enough to support her mother, two siblings and other relatives. Her father died when she was 12.Alongside her football, she had been working in Tétouan’s oldest cemetery, cleaning graves and selling mourners bunches ofrayhan(basil), which is associated with blessings in Muslim funeral traditions.“She dreamed of reachingEuropethrough football,” says her mother, Jamilla. Instead, El Azizi is now buried in the cemetery she once worked in after she drowned on 30 July while trying to swim from Morocco to Ceuta, the Spanish exclave near Tétouan.View image in fullscreenJamilla, Faten Ben Omar El Azizi’s mother.Photograph: suppliedShe was among at least 141 people whodied during last month’s extraordinary mass crossingto the Spanish territory in north Africa, according to the migrant rights group Caminando Fronteras. It is believed most of those who died – drowning or crushed at the land border – were under the age of 35.Their deaths have come less than a year after awave of youth-led demonstrations swept across Morocco– the biggest since the2011 Arab spring. The protesters had criticised underfunding of healthcare and education amid spending on expensive stadiums as the country gears up to co-host the 2030 World Cup with Spain and Portugal.For Morocco, the 2030 World Cup has become a symbol of national ambition, although it has also sharpened the debate over public priorities. Nearly 40% of young people aged 15 to 24 were unemployed in Morocco last year, while for those who do find work, wages can be low – Morocco’s gross minimum wage in the non-agricultural private sector is about £270 a month.Simo, 20, who recently returned to Morocco after the mass crossing into Ceuta last month, says: “Like Faten, many of my friends and myself cannot find work in our country. It’s difficult to build a future here.”Jamilla says her daughter dreamed of training and developing as a player, but the family could not afford to help her.On the morning of 30 July, Jamilla says she received a phone call from someone who asked to speak to Faten. “No, I am her mother,” Jamilla replied. An official then told her that her daughter’s Spanish visa had been approved and that Faten should travel to the consulate in Tangier with her identity card to collect it.View image in fullscreenEl Azizi playing for Moghreb Atlético Tetuán.Photograph: SuppliedJamilla says she had not known her daughter was applying for a visa or, given she had applied for one, why she spontaneously decided to try to reach European territory by crossing to Ceuta.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHer mother believes Faten had been applying for a visa informally and did not expect to get it approved. She does not know what type of visa it was or where her daughter intended to travel.‘I sit alone and talk to myself’: a family ripped apart by Europe’s migration crisisRead moreIn recent weeks, she says, her daughter had become unusually quiet, sad and distant. “She seemed switched off,” Jamilla says.After Faten disappeared, her family says they searched through the night. A young man eventually came to the house and asked whether she had been wearing a tracksuit. He said that she had struck her head during the crossing.Jamilla says she could not bring herself to enter the room where the bodies of those who died were being kept. “I did not want that image engraved in my memory,” she says. Instead, her sister went in to identify the body.For Jamilla, the heartache continues. After learning that Faten had made the crossing, she found out that her other two children had gone, too.Her eldest son reached Ceuta and phoned her, but Jamilla is still awaiting news of her 14-year-old daughter, who is also believed to have reached Ceuta. “Now I am alone without my children,” she says.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentRights and freedomMoroccoAfricaMiddle East and north AfricaMigration and developmentMigrationSpainfeaturesShareReuse this content
