title: At least 44 dead after overcrowded ferry capsizes on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe | Zimbabwe | The Guardian
description: Operation under way to rescue people after boat overturned by waves at world’s largest human-made lake
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Operation under way to rescue people after boat overturned by waves at world’s largest human-made lake
Content: Passengers rescued from the ferry that capsized on Tuesday on Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba.Photograph: Maxton Kanhema/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPassengers rescued from the ferry that capsized on Tuesday on Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba.Photograph: Maxton Kanhema/AFP/Getty ImagesZimbabweAt least 44 dead after overcrowded ferry capsizes on Lake Kariba in ZimbabweOperation under way to rescue dozens missing after boat overturned by waves at world’s largest human-made lakeRachel Savageand agenciesWed 12 Aug 2026 08.21 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 06.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 44 people have diedafter an overcrowded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba inZimbabwe, police said.The boat had a capacity of 90 people, but was carrying 114 adult passengers, five crew members and an unknown number of children, Zimbabwe’s civil protection unit (CPU) said earlier on Wednesday, citing ticket sales.A crew membertoldthe national broadcaster ZBC that there were 153 people onboard when the ferry overturned on Tuesday after it hit large waves. A passengertoldZBC that the boat began taking on water about 30 minutes after it left the lakeshore town of Kariba, heading for islands and fishing camps.A specialised underwater team was flown to the area, the CPU said, as search and rescue continued on Wednesday. At the time, the CPU said the death toll was 15, with 27 known to be missing.Zimbabwe’s police updated the death toll on Wednesday afternoon inposts on Xtwice in the space of 32 minutes. In thefirst post, it said the death toll was 38, adding: “The bodies have been retrieved from the lake.” Then it said that 44 people were now known to have died.Avideoshared by ZBC on Tuesday showed several people appearing to be sitting on the upturned ferry, while at least four speedboats came to their aid and a helicopter circled overhead.Maxwell Kanhema Page, who describes himself as a media practitioner and originally posted the video shared by ZBC,reshareda video on his Facebook page filmed from the shore, in which he had noted that the lake was “angry”.He said: “A few moments later I get over 200 calls about [the ferry] sinking. A sad day indeed.”Lake Kariba is theworld’s largest human-made lake by volume,stretching about 150 miles along Zimbabwe’s northern border with Zambia. It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people. The Kariba dam supplies at least a third of both countries’ electricity.It is not uncommon for boats to overturn on the lake. In 2014, 26 people, 24 of them children,drownedin Zambia’s part of the lake, when the boat meant to transport them to independence day celebrations capsized.On the Zimbabwean side, five drowned in a 2021 incident and three werefeared deadin an October 2023 capsizing. The month before, apolice boat overturnedalthough no one died.Agence France-Presse contributed to this report.Explore more on these topicsZimbabweAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Halting the march of the African armyworm: a natural cure offers hope to farmers | Global development | The Guardian
description: South African scientist’s breakthrough research shows soil fungus could be used in fight against devastating crop pest
Author: Kaamil Ahmed
Headline: South African scientist’s breakthrough research shows soil fungus could be used in fight against devastating crop pest
Content: Finding dead African armyworms in a field set entomologist Letodi Luki Mathulwe on a path that may finally lead to a way to control the dreaded pest.Photograph: Letodi Luki MathulweView image in fullscreenFinding dead African armyworms in a field set entomologist Letodi Luki Mathulwe on a path that may finally lead to a way to control the dreaded pest.Photograph: Letodi Luki MathulweGlobal developmentHalting the march of the African armyworm: a natural cure offers hope to farmersSouth African scientist’s breakthrough research shows soil fungus could be used in fight against devastating crop pestSupported byAbout this contentKaamil AhmedWed 12 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 10.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHearing about fields full of dead caterpillars enveloped in a mysterious white substance intrigued the South African scientist Letodi Luki Mathulwe. Something was killing off the African armyworm – one of the most devastating pests for farmers in east and southern Africa.The white substance was a naturally occurring fungus and it was wiping out the caterpillar, which gained its name from its march-like advance through fields of crops.An outbreak of African armyworm (Spodoptera exempta) in 2025 had started in northern SouthAfricaand by April had reached the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal, where Mathulwe was working for the agriculture department. Every day she was getting panicked calls from local farmers who were finding the caterpillars in their fields.Mathulwe went out to the KwaZulu-Natal countryside to see for herself and it was there, in the fields of Kikuyu grass – crucial grazing for livestock – that she realised she had made an important discovery.View image in fullscreenArmyworms eating grass. A soil fungus could offer a new way to tackle the hugely destructive caterpillars where chemical controls have fallen short.Photograph: Letodi Luki Mathulwe“Something was killing the insects naturally. I was intrigued because in other areas the insects were alive and destroying the grass but as soon as they come here, there’s something that is killing them,” she said.As an entomologist who had studied the use of fungi to kill insect pests, Mathulwe immediately gathered samples of the dead armyworms and the fungus to test at her laboratory in Pietermaritzburg.Herteam’s results, nowpresented in a peer-reviewed research paper, showed she was right in her hunch that the fungus could be used in the fight against the armyworms.It was a major breakthrough, said Mathulwe, because while there are chemical treatments for dealing with the caterpillars in the early stages of life, nothing has proven effective against mature populations.The African armyworm not only eats staple crops such as maize and sorghum but also releases a chemical compound in grass that can make cattle sick.The impact can be brutal for farmers. One outbreak in 2017 was estimated to have destroyedup to 40% of Zambia’s maizeproduction.View image in fullscreenMajor outbreaks of armyworms have threatened the food security of some African countries.Photograph: Courtesy of Letodi Luki MathulweIt also sends food prices soaring and puts strain on government budgets.Last year’s outbreak caused problems for farmersin countries such as Zimbabwe, where inflation hadhit 736% in 2024, and Malawi, where itreached 35% in 2024.The African armyworm causes the most damage in its caterpillar stage but is also hard to control when it develops into a moth, allowing populations to migrate.“When we discovered this fungus, we realised we could develop this into a product that can be eventually used when the next outbreak happens,” said Mathulwe.“I think it will be a great thing – it will eventually eliminate the fear for farmers that the insect creates because once it’s present within grazing fields, farmers start to panic.”Mathulwe said there was still more work and more testing to do in developing a product for use by farmers.“I think it will create a lot of hope for farmers, because it will mean that their animals won’t get sick if the farmer is able to control the presence of the insects within their field,” she said.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentFarmingInsectsSouth AfricaAfricaZimbabweMalawinewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Mexican governor charged in case of 43 students who vanished in 2014 | Mexico | The Guardian
description: Ángel Aguirre indicted in case that rocked Mexico and became symbol of its brutal cartel violence
Author: Oscar Lopez
Headline: Ángel Aguirre indicted in case that rocked Mexico and became symbol of its brutal cartel violence
Content: Ángel Aguirre speaking at a news conference in 2014. He is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice.Photograph: Jorge Lopez/ReutersView image in fullscreenÁngel Aguirre speaking at a news conference in 2014. He is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice.Photograph: Jorge Lopez/ReutersMexicoFormer Mexican governor charged in case of 43 students who vanished in 2014Ángel Aguirre indicted in case that rocked Mexico and became symbol of its brutal cartel violenceOscar LopezWed 12 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former governor of Guerrero state inMexicohas been formally charged over his alleged involvement in the disappearance of 43 students in 2014, a case that has become a symbol of the country’s brutal cartel violence and government impunity.Ángel Aguirre, who wasarrested last week, is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice for ordering the destruction of surveillance tapes that may have shed light on what happened to the students from the Ayotzinapa teacher training college on the night of 26 September 2014.On Wednesday, a judge ruled Mexico’s attorney general had presented enough evidence to formally charge Aguirre with forced disappearance and ordered that he remain in a maximum security prison awaiting trial.A lawyer for Aguirre denied his client’s wrongdoing. Guillermo Baradas told reporters: “We presented evidence demonstrating a high-level meeting attended by Mr Ángel Aguirre at the time the videos were allegedly handed over to him.”Aguirre’s indictment is the biggest breakthrough in the Ayotzinapa case since the 2022 arrest of Jesús Murillo Karam, who served as Mexico’s attorney general at the time of the students’ abduction.The brutality of the case rocked Mexico and continues to haunt the country more than a decade on. With the remains of only three students identified, it is not known what happened to the 40 others.On the night that they were abducted, the students from the Raúl Isidros Burgos teacher training college in the village of Ayotzinapa had commandeered several buses in the city of Iguala to get to a protest in Mexico City.But before they could leave Iguala, in Guerrero state, the students were attacked by a local criminal gang working with municipal police. A years-long international investigation determined that federal forces, both police and military, were also involved either by participating directly or failing to intervene as the students were taken away and presumably killed.The government at the time orchestrated an elaborate coverup, attempting to place blame for the attack solely on the criminal gang and local police. Suspects were tortured into giving false confessions and crime scene evidence was manipulated.Meltión Ortega, a spokesperson for the 43 students, said: “We want no more deception; we want to be told the truth and for those responsible to be punished. The victims from Guerrero deserve to have the actual perpetrators and the masterminds punished, rather than just seeing a charade, as has happened in serious cases of human rights violations.”Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has vowed to get to the bottom of what happened to the students and formedan investigative unitto dig into the case last year. “I’m going to put all my effort, all my energy, all my willpower [towards obtaining truth and justice],” she told reporters at a news conference last week.Explore more on these topicsMexicoAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Canadian airline WestJet agrees to settle flight attendants’ sexual harassment class action  | Canada | The Guardian
description: Female staff alleged company failed to maintain safe workplace, after allegations of sexual assault against pilot
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: Female staff alleged company failed to maintain safe workplace, after allegations of sexual assault against pilot
Content: The suit followed allegations by Mandalena Lewis (pictured), a former flight attendant, that a pilot had sexually assaulted her and a colleague but that WestJet kept the pilot flying, thereby putting other employees at risk.Photograph: Mandalena LewisView image in fullscreenThe suit followed allegations by Mandalena Lewis (pictured), a former flight attendant, that a pilot had sexually assaulted her and a colleague but that WestJet kept the pilot flying, thereby putting other employees at risk.Photograph: Mandalena LewisCanadaCanadian airline WestJet agrees to settle flight attendants’ sexual harassment class actionFemale staff alleged company failed to maintain safe workplace, after allegations of sexual assault against pilotOlivia Bowdenin TorontoWed 12 Aug 2026 10.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Canadian airline WestJet has agreed to pay C$4.5m (£2.4m) to settle a decade-long sexual harassment class action lawsuit levelled by its female flight attendants, who alleged the company failed to maintain a safe workplace.The suit followed allegations by Mandalena Lewis, a former flight attendant, that a pilot had sexually assaulted her and a colleague, but that WestJet kept the pilot flying, thereby putting other employees at risk.A British Columbia judge on Monday approved the terms of the settlement, which were finalised on 22 June after months of negotiation. The payment will be distributed among the 3,452 flight attendants in the class action after expenses are removed, including legal fees.WestJet agreed to hire a third-party to conduct a workplace inquiry that will examine the prevalence of harassment, the extent of underreporting and how reporting systems can be made more effective.The suit had called on WestJet to implement mandatory anti-harassment training for pilots, along with an admission of wrongdoing and an admission of a breach of employee contract. None were included in the settlement.Lewis filed the initial class action against the airline in April 2016. She said she was dismayed by the results, especially given that two years ago WestJet paid out$12.5min a baggage fee class action, nearly three times the amount agreed to in the sexual harassment suit.“I’m glad it’s over … but I’m just exhausted. I’m shaking my head,” she said, adding that she was advised the amount was the most that could be achieved given that legalexpenses were piling up.Under BC law, the suit included all female flight attendants who worked for the company between 4 April 2014 and 28 February 2021, because Lewis’s suit alleged that all of them had their contracts violated by WestJet during that period because its employee policy promised that the workplace would be free from harassment.The suit claimed WestJet broke its policy by not taking enough steps to address reports of assault or to prevent harassment in the first place.Lewis said she was sexually assaulted by a WestJet pilot while on a layover in Hawaii in 2010 when she was 25 years old. In court documents, she said the same pilot had also assaulted another flight attendant in 2008.Though she reported the assault to WestJet, the pilot remained at the company and Lewis was eventually fired in 2016 for “gross insubordination”, according to court documents submitted by WestJet that year, which she and her legal team allege was retaliation for trying to hold the airline accountable internally.She said she abandoned an individual civil claim and instead created the class action after learning other flight attendants had also experienced harassment.Lewis said she reported the assault to police in Maui but alleges WestJet rerouted the pilot so he would not face questioning in Hawaii.She said fellow members of the class action suit were also disappointed with the result. Eight of them had already asked the province’s supreme court not to approve the settlement in February when some of the details first emerged, citing a low payout and a lack of accountability by WestJet.“We didn’t get justice here,” said Lewis.The case garnered national attention for exposing pilot behaviour toward female flight attendants and the vulnerability of the scores of young women who have historically been the target demographic for the job.A 2018 survey of more than 3,500 flight attendants by the US Association of Flight Attendants found that 68% had experienced sexual harassment in their careers while only 7% had reported an incident to their employer.WestJet did not respond to questions about Lewis’s claims of assault, and the allegations that it failed to keep the workplace free of harassment and does not properly investigate alleged sexual assaults.In a statement, the company said it was “pleased to have reached a mutually agreed upon settlement”. It said: “We are committed to strengthening our operations and training, focused on the safety and wellbeing of all WestJetters and we are focused on advancing a culture of empowerment.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaSexual harassmentAir transportAirline industryAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thailand suspends gun licences as teen shooter and grandparents he killed are cremated | Thailand | The Guardian
description: Prime minister Anutin Charnvirakul calls for tighter gun controls and ‘decisive penalties’ after nine dead in school shooting
Author: Natasha May
Headline: Prime minister Anutin Charnvirakul calls for tighter gun controls and ‘decisive penalties’ after nine dead in school shooting
Content: People pay their respects at the Tem Rak Samakkhi Buddhist temple in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok, in front of the caskets of the grandparents shot dead by their 14-year-old grandson.Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople pay their respects at the Tem Rak Samakkhi Buddhist temple in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok, in front of the caskets of the grandparents shot dead by their 14-year-old grandson.Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty ImagesThailandThailand suspends gun licences as teen shooter and grandparents he killed are crematedPrime minister Anutin Charnvirakul calls  for tighter gun controls and ‘decisive penalties’ after nine dead in school shootingNatasha Mayin Bangkok and agenciesWed 12 Aug 2026 01.28 EDTFirst published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThailand has suspended firearms licences afterthe deadly Nonthaburi school shooting, as the bodies of the teenage attacker and the grandparents he killed were cremated.The prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, said he had ordered the interior ministry and police to stop issuing licences to possess, purchase and carry firearms, and called for “tighter controls and decisive penalties”. The measures are temporary until a new gun control law is in place, according to government operated news-channel NBT World.Anutin had vowed to implement changes on Friday when earlier that morning a 14-year-old boy shot dead the grandparents who raised him at their home in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok, before killing six others at his school and then turning the gun on himself.At a temple in Thailand, parents mourn a 12-year-old mass shooting victim, and a father pleads for forgivenessRead moreAnutin had aimed for reforms in previous roles as minister for the interior and health after gun violence in 2022 and 2023. In2023, a shootingsaw a boy of the same age kill two people at a shopping mall using a modified pistol intended to fire blanks that police said was likely ordered online. Anutin ordered a raft of gun control measures, including a short-term ban on new licences, import restrictions and the banning of people under 20 years old from shooting ranges.However, past promises of tightening gun laws have not preventedrecent shootings.While Thailand’s licensing laws appear tough on paper, the reality is the country has millions of unregistered guns.The most recent data from theSwitzerland-based Small Arms Surveyin 2017 showed that with over 10m civilian-owned firearms, Thailand had the highest number in south-east Asia – a rate more than one gun for every seven people – and over 4m were unregistered.The government plans to establish a designated period for people to surrender illegal firearms or inherited weapons that cannot be legally transferred, during which they may be exempt from penalties, according to government operated news-channel NBT World.Commissioner General Kitrat Phanphet of the Royal Thai police has also ordered tighter oversight of government-issued police firearms.The widely criticised “welfare gun” scheme allows eligible public officials to obtain weapons at steep discounts, but theBangkok Post reportsmany of these guns end up being resold.Deputy Commissioner General Thana Chuwong will be responsible for targeting illegal weapons possession and trafficking, including illegal weapons sales through social media and other online platforms.A new school safety plan has also been introduced by the ministry of education, including stricter entry screening with guards to check for weapons before anyone enters school premises, and increased mental health counselling.View image in fullscreenThe wife of a teacher killed in the Debsirin Nonthaburi school shooting weeps.Photograph: Rungroj Yongrit/EPAThe reforms were foreshadowed as multi-day Buddhist funerals for the victims continued to take place.The white caskets of the first victims, the shooter’s grandparents, were laid out at the Tem Rak Samakkhi Buddhist temple on Tuesday, alongside their portraits, ahead of their cremation capping a funeral lasting several days.The boy’s smaller casket was placed to the side at the same temple, surrounded by white flowers.Among the mourners was Tawee Piewphong, who paid tribute to his brother-in-law – the grandfather – as “a man of few words, but a very kind person”.Tawee expressed shock at the killings, saying he had no idea what motivated the teenager, but also offered compassion. “I want to tell him that being 14 is just a small fraction of your entire life, and every problem has a solution. Not everything is the end of the world,” the 70-year-old said.Investigators were still seeking a motive for the shooting, but police said on Sunday that the boy had watched violent videos online and once brought an air gun to school. Officials said previously that he faced academic-related stress, and a classmate said he was bullied.“Of course I feel bad for the innocent people who were killed,” said Somjai Poosod, whose grandchildren attend the school attacked. “But I feel there is an issue of mental health that we may need to address to prevent incidents like this from happening again.”The shooting has resonated across the country, with the king and Anutin leading an outpouring of grief.On Monday, the attacker’s fathertold the Guardianhe still did not understand why his son did it, but was left to reckon with the violence his own flesh and blood had committed. “I’m experiencing so many emotions all at once. I feel guilty and heartbroken because I’ve suffered a loss too. I’ve lost my child, as well as my parents.”The shooter used his grandfather’s gun to kill his grandparents before heading to the school.There, he shot dead five teachers and staff and wounded a 12-year-old girl who died in hospital on Saturday.With Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsThailandGun crimeAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mass evacuations in Beijing as Typhoon Dolphin brings more torrential rain to China | China | The Guardian
description: Forecasters warned the Chinese capital could receive more than one-third of its average annual rainfall over 24 hours
Author: Yu-chen Li
Headline: Forecasters warned the Chinese capital could receive more than one-third of its average annual rainfall over 24 hours
Content: 1:52Typhoon Dolphin hits east China with heavy rainfall and strong winds – videoChinaMass evacuations in Beijing as Typhoon Dolphin brings more torrential rain to ChinaForecasters warned the Chinese capital could receive more than one-third of its average annual rainfall over 24 hoursYu-chen Liin TaipeiWed 12 Aug 2026 00.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of people have been evacuated from areas at risk of flooding and landslides in Beijing, as the remnants of Typhoon Dolphin continue to bring torrential rain to northern and centralChina.Forecasters warned on Tuesday that theChinese capital could receive more than 150mm of rainover the following 24 hours, with some districts forecast to exceed 200mm – more than one-third of Beijing’s average annual rainfall of 528mm.Beijing remained under an orange rainstorm warning, the second-highest level, on Wednesday, with the heaviest rainfall expected across the morning.Floods, storms and landslides: Typhoon Dolphin ravages China – in picturesRead moreAuthorities closed hundreds of tourist attractions and campsites on Wednesday, with more than 1,300 tourists evacuated or turned away. Meanwhile, over 5,000 elderly people were moved from care facilities and about 1,800 people living around construction projects in mountainous or riverside areas were relocated.View image in fullscreenA person rides an electric scooter on a flooded street while avoiding fallen bicycles in Xiangyang, Hubei province.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersThe rain also disrupted Wednesday morning’s commute. Official local media reported that 250 bus routes had been suspended and trains were running at reduced speeds on 10 metro lines.Dolphin, thestrongest typhoon to hit China so far this year, has weakened after making landfall in the eastern province of Zhejiang on Sunday, but its remnants have continued to draw large amounts of tropical moisture deep inland and drench central and northern parts of the country.The neighbouring Hebei province was also on alert for mountain floods, landslides and other geological hazards. Authorities said they had dispatched 623 teams to mountainous areas and equipped more than 2,100 at-risk villages with satellite phones or satellite messaging terminals to maintain communications during emergencies, according to state media.View image in fullscreenCars drive on a flooded street following heavy rain brought by Typhoon Dolphin in Taizhou, Zhejiang province.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesIn the central province of Henan, authorities raised the warning for torrential rain to the highest-level red alert on Wednesday morning, as downpours continue to batter large swathes of the province. More heavy rain was forecast through Thursday morning, with 24-hour rainfall totals of up to 350mm expected in some areas.Classes, business operations and non-essential outdoor activities have been suspended in the affected areas of Henan. Residents were told to avoid deep flood waters and evacuate immediately if vehicles stall in water, state media reports.China, the world’s second-largest economy, is increasingly exposed to destructive ‌weather events that scientists link to climate change. This year is proving particularly tough due to the ​emergence of the El Niño weather pattern that is driving up temperatures and fuelling more frequent and intense typhoons.Rainfall records have alsobeen broken elsewhere in central China. Wugang in Henan received 209.5mm in a day and Xiangyang in neighbouring Hubei recorded 169.1mm, both the highest single-day rainfall totals for August, according to state media.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsChinaExtreme weatherFloodingAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Passenger jet billed as China’s answer to Boeing and Airbus prepares to make first international flight | China | The Guardian
description: The Comac C919 will fly from Beijing to Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia, although experts say it could take generations for it to challenge the west’s dominance of the industry
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: The Comac C919 will fly from Beijing to Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia, although experts say it could take generations for it to challenge the west’s dominance of the industry
Content: China's C919 takes off on a test flight in Shanghai in July. The passenger jet built by Comac is scheduled to make its first international flight on Wednesday.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChina's C919 takes off on a test flight in Shanghai in July. The passenger jet built by Comac is scheduled to make its first international flight on Wednesday.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesChinaPassenger jet billed as China’s answer to Boeing and Airbus prepares to make first international flightThe Comac C919 will fly from Beijing to Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia, although experts say it could take generations for it to challenge the west’s dominance of the industryAmy HawkinsSenior China correspondentTue 11 Aug 2026 22.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 22.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChina hopes to break into the world of commercial aviation with the first international flight of a Chinese-made passenger jet scheduled for Wednesday.The Comac C919 will take off from Beijing capital international airport at 3pm, landing in Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, just over two hours later.It has been billed as China’s alternative to the Boeing-Airbus duopoly that dominates global aviation, particularly in Asia, but analysts say it could take generations before a Chinese aircraft could meaningfully challenge their global dominance.The C919 is made by the Chinese state-owned aircraft manufacturer Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (Comac) and is similar in size to the Boeing 737.Chinese EV sales surge to new high in Europe putting tariffs under scrutinyRead moreThe C919 has been flying on domestic routes operated by Chinese airlines since 2023. But Wednesday’s Air China flight to Ulaanbaatar will be the first time that the narrow-body jet is used on a commercial international route.“This is essentially a public relations move,” said Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. “Ulaanbaatar was likely chosen because of how close it is to Beijing. It doesn’t change the fact that the plane was years overdue, is composed of western components, and is less efficient than its Boeing and Airbus cousins.”China has long dreamed of building its own jet. When the C919 wasunveiled in 2015, Li Jiaxiang, the head of China’s civil aviation authority, said: “A great nation must have its own large commercial aircraft.”But progress has been slow, even while China has whizzed ahead in other hi-tech fields, such asroboticsandelectric vehicles(EVs).That is because aviation requires the integration of many different types of advanced science and engineering, as well as parts sourced from overseas. Ananalysisby the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in 2020 found that more than half of the C919’s suppliers were in the US.View image in fullscreenChina’s C919, its first self-developed large passenger jetliner, is unveiled in Shanghai in November 2015.Photograph: ChinaFotoPress/Getty Images“Large passenger aircraft and jet engines are extremely complex and challenging to manufacture. They require precision components, complex electro-mechanical control systems, and the ability to coordinate a vast global supply chain,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at Brookings focused on China’s industrial policy.“There’s a reason there are basically only two major commercial aircraft makers in the world. Building large passenger jets that are safe and reliable is an order of magnitude more difficult than making EVs,” Chan said.Last year Comacreportedlydelivered only 15 units of the C919 to customers, well short of its target of 75.Comac did not respond to a request for comment.Comac primarily serves Chinese domestic airlines. In 2023, the Brunei-based airline GallopAir signed a $2bn deal to purchase 30 planes from Comac, including 15 of the C919, but the airline is not operating commercially yet. The C919 has not been approved by European or American regulators.Last year the USreportedlysuspended the export of some products to Comac for use in the C919 jet amid the tit-for-tat restrictions that Beijing and Washington used against each other during theUS-China trade war.The two countries later agreed a trade war truce that is set to expire in November.When US president Donald Trump visited Beijing in May for astate visit, one of thefew takeawaysfrom the trip was an agreement from China to buy 200 jets from Boeing.In return, the US provided supply guarantees for aircraft engine parts and components for its own manufacturing.China sees being able to build its own commercial aircraft as a national security priority.In a recent interview with Chinese state media, Zhang Yanzhong, an academic of the Chinese Academy of Engineering and a leading aviation expert who worked on the C919, said reliance on other countries for large aircraft technology would “threaten national strategic security”.However, there was still “a long way to go before achieving commercial success”, Zhang said.Experts have pointed out that Comac’s dependence on foreign suppliers goes beyond the supply of individual components. International suppliers have also provided guidance about how to integrate complex components and software together into sky-worthy commercial aircraft.Kennedy argued it was misleading to describe the C919 as a Chinese plane because so many of its parts were imported. He said it was “very unlikely” for Comac to become a serious challenger to Boeing and Airbus, “even a generation from now”.Chan said Comac could still face “a long road to gaining trust among airlines and passengers”.Zhang called on China’s young engineers to contribute their talents to China’s aviation ambitions, saying: “Though the journey may be fraught with difficulties, a fledgling eagle can soar faster than its parent.”Explore more on these topicsChinaAsia PacificAir transportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cook Islands election: PM Mark Brown speaks on the diplomatic crises that defined his year | Pacific leaders: in their words | The Guardian
description: The prime minister tells the Guardian that last year’s diplomatic rift with ally New Zealand could be on voters’ minds as they head to the polls
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The prime minister tells the Guardian that last year’s diplomatic rift with ally New Zealand could be on voters’ minds as they head to the polls
Content: Cook Islands prime minister speaks to the Guardian ahead of the Pacific island nation’s general election.Photograph: Carly Earl/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCook Islands prime minister speaks to the Guardian ahead of the Pacific island nation’s general election.Photograph: Carly Earl/The GuardianPacific leaders: in their wordsCook Islands election: PM Mark Brown speaks on the diplomatic crises that defined his yearThe prime minister tells the Guardian that last year’s diplomatic rift with ally New Zealand could be on voters’ minds as they head to the pollsRashneel Kumar in RarotongaTue 11 Aug 2026 20.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 20.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs voters in the Cook Islands prepare to head to the polls in a high-stakes general election, they will have much to reflect on. Over recent years, politics in this small island nation has been defined by fierce debates aboutdeep-sea mining, diplomatic rifts with ally New Zealand and a major reshaping of the country’s foreign partnerships.In an exclusive interview with the Guardian, days before Wednesday’s poll, Cook Islands prime minister Mark Brown defended his four-year term and the decisions he made that have seen this South Pacific nation of 17,000 people pushed into the international limelight, turning it into abattleground for influence between Beijing and western powers.In 2025, Cook Islands struck strategic partnership deals with Beijing, sparking severe alarm in Wellington. The rift was formally patched after the signing of anew bilateral agreement with New Zealand in April.Brown acknowledged the diplomatic fallout “does have bearings” on voters, saying “our people are quite mindful and aware of what happens in the geopolitical space”.View image in fullscreenCook Islands prime minister Mark Brown on the sidelines of the G7 Summit leaders’ meeting in 2023.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty Images“For us in theCook Islands, it’s important that these engagements are on our terms … and that their collaboration with us is on areas that we’ve identified as priorities for the Cook Islands.”According to a poll conducted by Cook Islands News, Wednesday’s election will be a close race between Brown’s Cook Islands party and challenger the Cook Islands United party, led by Teariki Heather, who organised a public protest against the partnership agreement withChinalast year.That partnerships agreement significantly affected Cook Islanders at home and in New Zealand, Heather said, adding that Brown should have been transparent from the start about the documents signed on behalf of the country.“What prime minister Mark Brown did has upset the people. It is not the way to act,” Heather said. “For us, the Cook Islands people, humility is most important. We respect that relationship with New Zealand – it has been set in concrete since 1965.”The economy and cost of living pressures are key issues for voters. When Brown took office in 2020, the Cook Islands faced major economic uncertainty amid the Covid-19 pandemic. Two years later, as he led his party to victory in the 2022 general election, the country was still reeling from border closures that decimated its primary economic engine – tourism – which traditionally accounts for roughly 70% of GDP. Debt swelled as the government struggled to “keep things alive, keep businesses going”.View image in fullscreenLeader of the Cook Islands United party, Teariki Heather, speaks to protesters at a rally in 2025.Photograph: MELINA ETCHES/Cook Islands News“Today our economy is the strongest it’s ever been in its history,” Brown said. “We’ve managed to halve the debt that we took on in 2022. We’ve had significant year on year growth exceeding 10% per annum.”Like other small island states in the South Pacific, the Cook Islands has been hit hard by inflation and global energy shocks caused by chaos in the Middle East.“When this fuel price spike occurred as a result of the conflicts in Iran, immediately we saw the impacts of that with unstable fuel supply, huge spikes and increases,” he said. The administration established a fund to absorb extreme swings in energy prices.Brown’s foreign policy moves have also triggered intense domestic debate and ruffled feathers across the Pacific.After Cook Islands struck deals with China in 2025, New Zealand – which maintains constitutional “free association” ties and provides citizenship to Cook Islanders – temporarily halted millions in aid. Wellington accused Rarotonga of a lack of transparency, and Brown called the reaction patronising.Map of south pacificHowever, he said the signing of the Defence and Security Agreement “really allayed a lot of fears that people had about our relationship with New Zealand”.Brown insists that establishing defence boundaries with New Zealand allows the Cook Islands to freely pursue economic relationships elsewhere without compromising security ties.“In matters of security and defence, our partner is New Zealand – that’s clear in everybody’s minds, not just our people, but internationally as well.”Developing relationships with other countries “and not relying just on one country is important for us as a country, to maintain and build our economic resilience”.China remains a cornerstone of that strategy, particularly for infrastructure programmes, alongside expanding engagements with India, South Korea, Japan and the United States.“China remains an important partner, not just for the Cook Islands, but right across the Pacific,” Brown said.“It’s the largest trading partner of Australia and New Zealand and some of our other Pacific Island countries.”He said China has a “huge development programme” which supports many countries in the Pacific, including in infrastructure.The deep-sea mining questionThe US is showing heightened strategic and economic interest in the country’s deep-sea polymetallic nodules, which are rich in critical minerals needed globally for the transition to renewable energy technologies.Environmental groups and some regional leaders warn thatseabed extraction could cause irreversible damage to fragile marine ecosystems. Brown, however, maintains that research must precede any definitive verdict.View image in fullscreenA bed of manganese nodules, deep offshore of the Cook Islands.Photograph: USGS“The exploration phase is still being undertaken,” Brown said. “There is no mining that is taking place right now. And there will be no mining that takes place until and unless we can be satisfied that its impacts will not affect our marine environment.”Tonga PM welcomes US deal to explore deep-sea minerals amid environmental concernsRead moreBrown said ongoing research is building a significant body of data that is attracting interest from global research institutes. This knowledge, he noted, will deepen understanding of the deep ocean, facilitate potential mineral extraction to diversify the economy and position the Cook Islands within the global transition toward renewable energy.Cook Islands political analyst William Numanga said the outcome of the election would be closely watched by international partners, particularly New Zealand and China.However, he emphasised that the election should not be seen simply as the Cook Islands choosing between the two.“New Zealand remains our closest constitutional partner, with deep family, historical and economic ties, while the Cook Islands will continue to build relationships with China and other international partners where they support our national interests,” Numanga said.He said the challenge for the next government will be to maintain the relationship with New Zealand while pursuing an “independent foreign policy that puts the interests of Cook Islanders first.”Explore more on these topicsPacific leaders: in their wordsCook IslandsChinaDeep-sea miningPacific islandsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pay with a glance at a screen as biometric technology company begins push into Australian retail | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Customers will be able to pay using face and palm scans, potentially speeding up transactions – but rollout of the technology is likely to be slow
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Customers will be able to pay using face and palm scans, potentially speeding up transactions – but rollout of the technology is likely to be slow
Content: New point of sale technology will enable customers to pay using facial recognition technology, but requires new terminals to be installed by retailers.Photograph: Verifone image of a POS screen showing camera image of a woman's face/SuppliedView image in fullscreenNew point of sale technology will enable customers to pay using facial recognition technology, but requires new terminals to be installed by retailers.Photograph: Verifone image of a POS screen showing camera image of a woman's face/SuppliedAustralia newsPay with a glance at a screen as biometric technology company begins push into Australian retailCustomers will be able to pay using face and palm scans, potentially speeding up transactions – but rollout of the technology is likely to be slowFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterWed 12 Aug 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 18.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe company behind 300,000 Eftpos terminals across Australia is hoping shoppers will want to make payments by simply glancing at a screen, as biometric technology pushes further into retailing.Verifone is selling the innovation as “pay for your coffee with a smile”, promising faster checkouts for people who opt in to having their face or palm-vein – the veins in people’s hands – biometrics used for Eftpos transactions in Australia.It may take a long time before the technology is widely available, however, with cafes, restaurants and retailers required to upgrade their existing equipment.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe head of product for Asia Pacific at Verifone, Ben Hughes, said the biometric payments will ease the “friction” of slow transactions.“If you go to a grocery store and you have to tap a loyalty card, plus tap a payment card, that’s the kind of thing that now we’d be able to speed up,” he said.He said the company was expecting retailers to deploy the Verifone Victa devices, which launched last month, incrementally as their current terminals reached their end of life.Hughes said the technology will need buy-in from banks and other organisations that want to allow their customers to pay using biometrics.Biometrics are converted into tokens on the device, he said, meaning images are not stored by Verifone, but biometric profiles are managed by merchants, banks or digital wallet providers.Customers will be able to continue to use contactless payments on their card or phone.Hughes said the company had measures in place to avoid users “spoofing” other people’s hands or faces, as has been seen in the rollout of facial verification technology, similar to that used in age assurance technology for Australia’s social media ban.The company is expecting some pushback on the shift to biometrics, but compared it to initial wariness over contactless payments.“This is continuous evolution, if you remember when contactless first came out, the amount of negative press we actually got from that initiative,” Verifone’s Asia Pacific president, Paris Tsounias, said.AI agents aren’t legally responsible for any harm that they cause, experts say. So who is?Read more“If you look at today, the stats, it’s over 90% of transactions are all contactless.“Now, no one even thinks of the risk around it. And we’ve covered the risk through the multitude of different type of certifications and compliance.”Card-related fraud losses were $2.2bn in the 2024-2025 financial year, according to theAustralian Bureau of Statistics, which did not break down the number of incidents related to contactless payment fraud, when people unknowingly have their cards tapped for payment.Part of the acceptance of contactless may have been that, according to the ABS, nearly 78% of people who reported card-related fraud did not lose any money after reimbursements.There has also been a shift away from using physical cards.In March, the Reserve Bank of Australia reported that, in 2025, the number of people paying by tapping a card had declined from a peak in 2022 of nearly 80% to under 60%, with payment by devices such as phones or smartwatches increasing to nearly 40%.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsBiometricsConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cruise ships, quiet towns and an all-day festival: millions flock to eclipse viewing spots across Europe | Solar eclipses | The Guardian
description: Beginning in Russia’s remote Arctic north, the eclipse traced an arc over much of western Europe – with the best views in Spain, Iceland and Greenland
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Beginning in Russia’s remote Arctic north, the eclipse traced an arc over much of western Europe – with the best views in Spain, Iceland and Greenland
Content: Prague Castle is silhouetted against a partial solar eclipsePhotograph: Martin Divíšek/EPAView image in fullscreenPrague Castle is silhouetted against a partial solar eclipsePhotograph: Martin Divíšek/EPASolar eclipsesCruise ships, quiet towns and an all-day festival: millions flock to eclipse viewing spots across EuropeBeginning in Russia’s remote Arctic north, the eclipse traced an arc over much of western Europe – with the best views in Spain, Iceland and GreenlandAshifa Kassamin Madrid,Miranda BryantandChris Michaelin LondonWed 12 Aug 2026 15.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt was a moment of awe shared by millions across Europe: an eclipse that blocked out the sun, plunging parts of the continent into a daytime darkness in which temperatures dropped and birds suddenly went quiet.Wednesday’s eclipse began in Russia’s remote Arctic north, going on to trace an arc over much of western Europe. From the UK to northern Italy, tens of millions of people turned to the sky as the light of the setting sun was almost completely blocked out.The most sought-after experiences were in Greenland,Icelandand Spain along with a small strip of Portugal. It was in parts of these countries that totality – referring to when the moon completely covers the sun’s light – was on offer, drawing millions of local people and thousands of tourists from across the globe into the path of the eclipse.“It was one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever seen in my life,” Sara García Alonso, a reserve astronaut for the EuropeanSpaceAgency, told broadcaster RTVE. “It gave me goosebumps.”Standing next to her, the astronaut Pablo Álvarez Fernández nodded in agreement: “It had been described to me so many times, but it was much more beautiful than what I had expected.”In Iceland, people flocked by air, land and sea to take in the country’s first total solar eclipse in 72 years. Amid concerns that clouds would block the view, a record 31 cruise ships plied the waters off the western part of the country, hoping to secure a top view for about 53,000 passengers and crew.View image in fullscreenThe sun during a partial solar eclipse and partially obscured by clouds, the International Space Station silhouetted as it transits at roughly five miles per second.Photograph: Nasa Handout/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople gather to observe the total solar eclipse, as clouds cover the sky, in ReykjavikPhotograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenPassengers on board the Ambassador cruise ship Ambition watching the start of the total solar eclipse off the coast of GreenlandPhotograph: Owen Humphreys/PAThe eclipse-themed activities included a day-long music festival hosted by the Icelandic artist Björk in Víðistaðatún park, offering a DJ-curated backdrop as people took in the eclipse. The 10-hour set list included two minutes set aside for totality, the artist said on social media, while the festival website noted that every ticket included a pair of approved solar eclipse glasses.Those watching from Iceland included the US space agency, Nasa, which followed the moon’s shadow using a high-altitude WB-57 aircraft while Nasa-funded teams launched balloons to study the atmospheric impact of the sudden darkness and cooling.View image in fullscreenA WB-57 Canberra aircraft is pictured during a media visit ahead of a Nasa-supported missionPhotograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenCary Klemm, sensor equipment operator, and pilot John Gustine of Nasa’s Johnson Space Centre pose in front of a WB-57 Canberra aircraftPhotograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenA WB-57 Canberra aircraftPhotograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenA gyroscopic sensor system aboard a WB-57 Canberra aircraftPhotograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersIn Spain, wheresome of the best viewsof the total eclipse were expected, the hours leading up to the celestial alignment were filled with frenzied debate about weather forecasts and where best to watch the phenomenon.More than 450,000 tourists had arrived in the country from as far as Canada and Australia, crisscrossingSpainby train, bus and caravan to stake out the perfect viewing spot.View image in fullscreenThe sun’s corona glows as the moon completely blocks the sun during the totality phase of the total solar eclipse as seen from San Asensio, La Rioja region, SpainPhotograph: Ander Gillenea/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople wait for a solar eclipse at the beach in A Coruña, SpainPhotograph: Lavandeira/EPAView image in fullscreenA beachgoer wearing special eclipse glasses looks up during the beginning phase of a solar eclipse at Puerto de Sagunto beach near Valencia, SpainPhotograph: Alberto Saiz/APView image in fullscreenThe sun’s corona glows as the moon completely blocks the sun during the totality phase of the total solar eclipse as seen from Arenal beach in Llucmajor, on the Balearic island of MallorcaPhotograph: Jaime Reina/AFP/Getty Images“Our car was cancelled,” one woman, who had travelled from Brazil with her sister to take in the eclipse, said on social media. After her appeals to hitch a ride to their chosen site were met with no response, they took matters into their own hands. “So we took a three-hour bus, a 20-minute taxi and two-hour hike. Arrived at the location!”About 10,000 metres above sea level, the Spanish airline Iberia livestreamed the moment when the sun, moon and Earth aligned from a special charter flight. “Some flights take us to new destinations. Others allow us to see the world from a different perspective,” the airline said as it announced the charter flight.Spanish officials estimated that as many as 6 million people were expected to flock to the path of the eclipse, which stretched about 124 miles (200km) from A Coruña in Spain’s north-west to the Mediterranean island of Mallorca. On Wednesday, just hours before the eclipse, officials reported traffic jams on the major thoroughfares out of Madrid and Barcelona.Others took their chances in the cities. In Madrid’s Parque del Oeste, hundreds gathered in hopes of catching a good view of the eclipse, cheering as they watched the moon cover the sun – plunging the park into darkness – and gasping as the outer corona left a glowing halo around the moon. Just over a minute later, when daylight returned to the park, the crowd burst into raucous cheers.It was, in the words of César González, an astronomer and science communicator at the Madrid Planetarium, “a spectacular experience”. He had left Madrid early in the morning to set himself up in a field in northern Spain to watch the eclipse. “Until one goes and experiences it, there’s no way to explain what it is to see an eclipse.”View image in fullscreenMario Garrido, a member of the Los Taraos amateur astrophotography group, waits to shoot a total solar eclipse in Berlanga de Duero, central SpainPhotograph: Bernat Armangué/APView image in fullscreenThe moon completely covers the sun during a total solar eclipse as seen from the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory in Arcos de las Salinas, near Teruel, SpainPhotograph: Christian Hartmann/ReutersView image in fullscreenArtists use self-made artefacts to observe a solar eclipse before totality near the small village of Castell de Cabres, SpainPhotograph: Eva Manez/ReutersView image in fullscreenA composite image of seven separate photographs taken with a single fixed camera shows stages of a solar eclipse before, during and after totality, as seen from Arija, SpainPhotograph: Borja Suárez/ReutersHe was able, however, to explain the impact. “In broad daylight, all of a sudden the light dims to a point where you can see the brightest stars in the sky. When totality starts, the temperature drops several degrees. If you’re in a field and surrounded by animals, their behaviour often changes. The birds stop singing because they think it’s nightfall. And all of this lasts for a few minutes – in this case around 1 minute and 45 seconds.”In Spain, most eclipse watchers were heading to rural areas, filling often quiet villages and towns clogged with skygazing tourists. The eclipse had helped putsome parts of “empty Spain”on the map; this week people linked to Nasa turn up in northern Spain’s Villalibado to set up a live broadcast for millions of people around the world, breathing new life into a municipality whoselast two residentsleft in 1998.Throughout human history, eclipses have sparked amazement, fear and reverence. In villages and cities across Europe, the eclipse forged ad hoc communities, as people came together to witness one of nature’s great wonders.In Camberwell, south London, an impromptu crowd of all ages gathered in Brunswick Park to experiment with different methods of seeing the eclipse, which reached 92% totality. Some held up colanders, others a spatula with holes, still others makeshift pinhole cameras made of old candy boxes.Ludmila, a Ukrainian woman in her 70s, said she had worked at an observatory in Crimea for 30 years. “What a surprise to find an actual refractor,” she said, pointing to a telescope with a solar filter taped on the end brought out by a resident. “It’s like a wonderful gift.”Later, as the eclipse passed its zenith and the sun began to set for real, dozens of neighbours who had never previously spoken to each other stayed on picnic blankets to drink beer and swap photos.

title: In Venice, it’s not politics as usual as film-makers aim to recapture our attention | World news | The Guardian
description: As social media shrinks and distorts the EU’s crises, the Venice film festival is delivering politically forthright epics from directors such as Sergei Loznitsa and Alex Gibney
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: As social media shrinks and distorts the EU’s crises, the Venice film festival is delivering politically forthright epics from directors such as Sergei Loznitsa and Alex Gibney
Content: Russian journalist Ksenia Mironova in the film My Undesirable Friends: Part One. Part Two is at the Venice film festival in September.Photograph: Julia LoktevView image in fullscreenRussian journalist Ksenia Mironova in the film My Undesirable Friends: Part One. Part Two is at the Venice film festival in September.Photograph: Julia LoktevThis Is EuropeWorld newsIn Venice, it’s not politics as usual as film-makers aim to recapture our attentionAs social media shrinks and distorts the EU’s crises, the Venice film festival is delivering politically forthright epics from directors such as Sergei Loznitsa and Alex GibneyDon’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up herePhilip Oltermann, European culture editorWed 12 Aug 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEurope is in an economic crisis that, unlike the eurozone downturn at the beginning of the millennium, cannot be measured in ratings downgrades and borrowing costs. For metrics, try engagement depth and consumer trust instead.The unedifying spectacle of the European Union’s falling out over the Ceuta crisis looks like the latest symptom of Europe’s shrinking attention economy. When more than 70,000 people crossed over from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the start of the month, Rome hastily reintroduced air and sea border checks with Spain for one month; Madrid retaliated with spot-checks on travellers to Italy.Politicians were falling over themselves to match the wildfire speed of social media, for this was a geopolitical flashpoint that appears not just to have been engineered but also politically processed via short video clips online. The crossings were reportedly triggered by viral videos suggesting that Spain’s border with Morocco was opening, while their framing as an “assault” or “invasion” was amplified by accounts with links to the Russian military,as Aisha Down reported. Platforms such as Instagram, Facebook and TikTok are built to reward content that instantly hooks in viewers – three seconds long is the golden rule. How can lawmakers ever keep up?View image in fullscreenImperium, a film about the USSR created from archival footage.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FesitvalYet what if, paradoxically, our attention economy is both shrinking and expanding at the same time? I’ve found it hard to shake that impression after perusing thelineup at the forthcoming Venice film festival, opening on 2 September.This year at the Lido, you can watch a three-hour film about the Italian Communist party sending a camera team to the Soviet Union (Imperium, by Ukrainian auteur Sergei Loznitsa); a four-hour documentary about Elon Musk (Musk, by American director Alex Gibney); or a more than five-hour video diary about Russian dissident journalists in exile (Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II). Too short for you? Then, get tickets for Luca Guadagnino’s Joie de Vivre, a lengthy analysis of the films of compatriot Bernardo Bertolucci. It clocks in at seven hours.For the most part, these are surprisingly politically forthright titles at a film festival that in the recent past has focused on glitz and glamour. Loznitsa’s documentary seeks to shatter the remnants of the left’s illusions about the Soviet Union; Loktev gives a voice to the journalists silenced by Putin; Gibney’s Musk film has already been preemptively dismissed by the far-right tycoon as a “hit job”. But are they trying to stretch out attention spans so much that they risk playing only to a gallery of cinephiles?On the topic of impactful film-making …skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA call to creative action … Dr Lina Qasem-Hassan, a Palestinian doctor in Israel’s healthcare system, in the documentary, The Oath.Photograph: Guardian DocumentariesPerhaps there is a point between both extremes to capture people’s imaginations and attention. That’s what the Guardian is hoping to prove, in collaboration with Franco-German culture channel Arte. We are inviting film-makers to propose short-form documentaries exploringdemocracy in Europe today. The winning submission will be presented at theDOK Leipzig film festivalat the end of October, and subsequently receive funding, editorial support and distribution through Guardian Documentaries and Arte platforms. The deadline for submissions is 14 September.Crucially, they should be no longer than 20 minutes – a length that Jess Gormley, the Guardian’s executive producer of documentaries, argues “encourages participation and debate”. She points to recent Guardian documentaries such as Liane Aviram and Louis Hollis’s 23-minute shortThe Oath, about a Palestinian doctor in Israel’s healthcare system, which led to its protagonist being invited to speak in front of the UK parliament – a film that held, rather than overwhelmed our attention.To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is EuropeEuropeVenice film festivalFestivalsVeniceDocumentary filmsAlex GibneynewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Iran war and high living costs fuelling last-minute holiday bookings, Tui says  | Tui Travel | The Guardian
description: Middle East conflict has cost Europe’s largest travel firm €60m so far, and timing of decisions over trips has shifted
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Middle East conflict has cost Europe’s largest travel firm €60m so far, and timing of decisions over trips has shifted
Content: Tui’s markets and airlines division swung to a €17m loss in its third quarter as it was hit by weaker demand for holidays, high fuel prices and a competitive travel market.Photograph: Mark Waugh/AlamyView image in fullscreenTui’s markets and airlines division swung to a €17m loss in its third quarter as it was hit by weaker demand for holidays, high fuel prices and a competitive travel market.Photograph: Mark Waugh/AlamyTui TravelIran war and high living costs fuelling last-minute holiday bookings, Tui saysMiddle East conflict has cost Europe’s largest travel firm €60m so far, and timing of decisions over trips has shiftedJoanna PartridgeWed 12 Aug 2026 06.45 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 05.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHolidaymakers are waiting until the last minute to book their trips because of the continuing uncertainty caused by the war in Iran and the cost of living crisis, according toTui, Europe’s largest travel company, which said the war had cost it €60m (£51m) so far.In the weeks after theoutbreak of the warat the end of February, Tui recorded a temporary drop-off in customers wanting to travel to Cyprus or Turkey, in what the company called a “volatile market”.Tui’s chief executive, Sebastian Ebel, said: “Travel remains highly relevant to people’s lives, but the timing of travel decision has shifted. Wars and geopolitical tensions, consumer caution, economic weakness and rising inflation in Europe’s core markets – all these factors have influenced consumer sentiment and the timing of purchasing decisions.”Two of Tui’s cruise ships – Mein Schiff 4 and 5 – were in the Gulf in Dubai and Qatar when the conflict in Iran broke out. They were unable to continue their journeys through thestrait of Hormuz, leading to the ships being out of service for 12 weeks. The cost of these “bad luck incidents”, as the company called them, ofrepatriating customersand the lost income from the ships was €40m.Hotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipseRead more“We had to repatriate all customers, 5,000 customers on board, which was a significant cost. And of course, when the ship is not cruising, you don’t have the income,” Ebel told reporters.The company reported a 43% slide in pre-tax profits to €153m (£131m) between April and June, down from €267m a year earlier, while it reported a 3% fall in customers during the period to just under 10 million.Tui’s markets and airlines division swung to a €17m loss in its third quarter from a €50m profit a year earlier as it was hit by weaker demand for holidays, high fuel prices and a competitive travel market.Tui usually makes most of its money between July and September, and the company said demand for summer holidays had picked up in the past four weeks as the peak summer season got under way.This was despite thestring of heatwavesthat have hit western Europe, and Ebel told reporters that “destinations were quite often cooler, significantly cooler than the weather here in Germany”.He added that hotel owners had been investing in air conditioning, “not only in their rooms, but also in the common facilities, from the dining room to the spa”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEurope’s changing climate is prompting some holidaymakers to fly outside peak holiday times in the “shoulder season” – which typically includes March to May and September to November – to take advantage of cooler temperatures.“It’s important to build the offers also for November, December, February, March, because we do see there is opportunity,” Ebel said, adding the company now flies to Heraklion in Crete in November and discussed with local organisations whether restaurants would stay open during this month to serve tourists.He said: “From a weather standpoint, it’s supporting this trend. The hotels need to support that and some have invested not only in cooling but also in heating; that has helped customers feel comfortable even if there is cooler weather.”Explore more on these topicsTui TravelTravel & leisureUS-Israel war on IranEuropeUK cost of living crisisCost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Germany approves lifting curbs on spy agencies in security ‘revolution’ | Germany | The Guardian
description: Reforms comply with wishlist of intelligence services which say Germany lags behind allies and enemies
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Reforms comply with wishlist of intelligence services which say Germany lags behind allies and enemies
Content: The BND headquarters in Berlin will gain new powers to confront threats from state actors such as Russia and China, using the help of AI.Photograph: Michael Sohn/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe BND headquarters in Berlin will gain new powers to confront threats from state actors such as Russia and China, using the help of AI.Photograph: Michael Sohn/ReutersGermanyGermany approves lifting curbs on spy agencies in security ‘revolution’Reforms comply with wishlist of intelligence services which say Germany lags behind allies and enemiesDeborah Colein BerlinWed 12 Aug 2026 06.43 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 06.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe German government has approved a draft law aimed at lifting many of the restraints on its spy agencies imposed during the postwar period as the country reels from two attacks in a month that have exposed serious security gaps.The controversial changes, which must still pass parliament, largely comply with a wishlist pulled together by the foreign and domestic intelligence services, which have long complainedGermanylags behind its allies and enemies.“We are turning our intelligence services into genuine secret services,” the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, told Bild newspaper, which called it a security “revolution” and “historic”.He said: “It is high time we positioned ourselves to be competitive and on an equal footing with our partner services around the world. This requires operational capabilities and active powers to tackle modern state terrorism and extremist groups more effectively.”Adeadly car rammingin late July at Berlin’s huge annual Pride parade by aGerman-born Islamist known to the authoritieswas followed by the discovery last week of adrone laden with explosivesnear a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport, a key defence transport hub.Friedrich Merz’s unpopular centre-right, centre-left coalition government is under pressure to demonstrate it can modernise to keep its citizens safe, while preserving rights and principles laid out in Germany’sBasic Law.View image in fullscreenThe federal minister of the interior, Alexander Dobrindt, called the approval of the draft laws ‘historic’.Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/ShutterstockThe intelligence services reform plans have been in the offing for months and were repeatedly fine-tuned before being presented to the cabinet on Wednesday.The federal foreign intelligence service (BND), which turned 70 this year and is run by a former ambassador to Ukraine, Martin Jäger, will gain new powers to confront emerging threats from state actors such as Russia and China with fewer impediments, and with the help of AI.German authorities say the threat level has soared since Russia’s full-scale invasion ofUkrainein 2022 as agents linked to Moscow have allegedly carried outrepeated sabotage, spying and hacker attacksagainst critical infrastructure and military equipment manufacturers.Jäger said Germany must be able to show adversaries “that we’re in a position to do similar things so the other side also feels the pain”.The BND has until now overwhelmingly had a defensive position, making it largely a repository for information with few operational powers.According to the draft law’s more than 700-page text, German spies will have permission to manipulate or delete data known as “hack-back” cyber-attacks.Other options include, altering instructions on how to build weapons or rendering arms harmless during production.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUS intelligence ‘believes Russia was behind Leipzig airport drone bomb’Read moreDigital payments tolow-level “disposable” agents, employed on a one-off basis by foreign governments, could be blocked to thwart attacks.The use of force by intelligence personnel abroad will remain forbidden – keeping it far out of the league of the CIA, the Mossad in Israel or the DGSE in France. But agents will be able to carry weapons for self-defence more often without explicit permission.The law, which the government hopes will be in place by 1 January 2027, would loosen rules around data protection,widely mocked as exaggerated and self-defeating.The BND and the domestic security watchdog, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), will be unshackled to collect, store and analyse more information for longer with the help of AI. It will also be easier to gain permission for online searches and home surveillance against criminal suspects.Germany will also beef up oversight of the BND and the BfV by an independent board, in addition to powers already granted to parliament’s intelligence control committee.Although reforms were widely seen as necessary and overdue, some politicians warned of overreach.The federal commissioner for data protection, Louisa Specht-Riemenschneider, said her office would be stripped of oversight powers over the BND and criticised the expanded access to CCTV footage in public spaces in Germany and abroad.Konstantin von Notz, the opposition Green party’s spokesperson on intelligence oversight, called the changes “urgently needed” and said he backed “stronger powers” for the BND. But he said the draft law “overshoots the mark”.He was particularly critical of the powers granted to the BfV, which he said were “difficult to reconcile” with the principle of separation between the powers of the intelligence services and the police – a lesson drawn from the darkest chapters of German history.The legislation could face court challenges mounted by its critics.Faced with rising geopolitical uncertainty and doubts about the role of the US as guarantor of the country’s security, Germany is also in a major rearmament drive. Merz took office last year pledging to turn Germany’s armed forces, or Bundeswehr, into“Europe’s strongest conventional army”.Explore more on these topicsGermanyEuropeFriedrich MerzEspionagenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli militants besiege two Palestinian families in their West Bank homes | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Settlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terror
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Settlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terror
Content: Refqa Hassan watches as Israeli settlers besiege her family home for the fourth consecutive day in the town of Qusra.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAView image in fullscreenRefqa Hassan watches as Israeli settlers besiege her family home for the fourth consecutive day in the town of Qusra.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAWest BankIsraeli militants besiege two Palestinian families in their West Bank homesSettlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terrorEmma Graham-Harrisonin QusraWed 12 Aug 2026 17.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 18.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli militants have besieged two Palestinian families in their homes since the weekend, aiming to take over their properties in theWest Bankvillage of Qusra through a campaign of terror.A group of settlers and soldiers set up a tent outside the home of Yousef Hassan on Sunday afternoon, trapping him inside with his wife and two young daughters.The Israeli men gathered just metres away from the spot where 28-year-old Amir Moatasem Odeh waskilledby a settler in March. Another attacker stabbed his father. No one has been arrested over the murder and assault.“Every night, the settlers throw stones, use obscene language and shout during the night. We are living in a state of terror,” Hassan said. His mother, brother and sister, and three neighbours have also been blockaded inside, and their power and water have been cut off.View image in fullscreenIsraeli soldiers stand guard next to settlers in front of Palestinian homes that they have blockaded in the village of Qusra.Photograph: Nidal Eshtayeh/APSettlers used thesame tacticsto steal another Palestinian home in neighbouring Jalud village, driving the al Tubasi family out in July after a months-long siege.They cut off water and electricity to the homes, although a solar panel allows Hassan to keep some devices charged in Qusra. They have also blocked medical care.When his younger daughter, a two-year-old, fell ill with vomiting and a high fever on Monday, settlers blocked an ambulance from reaching the house. The girls and their mother were eventually evacuated on Tuesday.They are short on food and are drinking water and juice delivered by the ambulance that came to collect his daughter. “The situation is extremely dire,” Hassan said.On Wednesday morning, the commander of Israeli forces in the region, Gen Avi Bluth, visited the families and promised to lift the siege, an Israeli military spokesperson said. Hassan confirmed the visit.“Today, the area commander came and spoke with us and assured us that he would evacuate the settlers. For the first time, I feel that there is some seriousness on the part of the army in dealing with the settlers,” Hassan said, but added that it had not yet produced tangible results.Soldiers took the tent but not bedding and other possessions and, after brief clashes with the settlers, withdrew. “The settlers are still there in front of the house, and we are still unable to leave.”View image in fullscreenYousef Hassan said Israeli settlers throw stones, use obscene language and shout during the night.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAAn Israeli military spokesperson said commanders were “gravely concerned” about the settlers’ actions and that soldiers who supported them would face disciplinary action, but declined to give a timeline for lifting the siege.On Wednesday evening, chief of the general staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Eyal Zamir, met other senior commanders to discuss the situation in Qusra. He ordered a battalion of infantry reservists back from leave to reinforce troops in the West Bank.“The battalion, which is currently undergoing a period of refreshment and training, will be deployed to the sector in order to strengthen operational control. Furthermore, additional soldiers will remain on standby for deployment as necessary,” a military spokesperson said.The military is working with the police to bring “those responsible for the disturbances to justice”, the spokesperson added.Israeli militants target Palestinians with neartotal impunityin the occupied West Bank. Since 2020, Israeli civilians and soldiers have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians there, and there has been only oneindictmentover those deaths.Violence isdeployedas part of a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing. Israel has forcibly displaced 64 Palestinian communities over the past three years, rights group B’Tselem said. Fifteen other communities have lost residents, with more than 4,800 people driven from their homes.View image in fullscreenAn Israeli settler leads his sheep as settlers besiege a Palestinian home.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA“What is happening in Qusra is not an isolated incident,” said B’Tselem’s executive director, Yuli Novak.“Settler militias, backed by the Israeli military, are expanding their attacks into Palestinian villages and towns – seizing land, attacking homes and forcing families out.
