Westbrook also holds the NBA mark for most triple-doubles in a season with 42 in 2016-17, when he earned his only MVP award. He averaged double figures for points and assists in five of six seasons starting in the 2015-16 season.Westbrook also played for Houston, Washington, the Lakers and Clippers – splitting the 2022-23 season between the Los Angeles teams and Denver.Last season, Westbrook started 58 of the 64 games he played for Sacramento. He averaged 15.2 points and 6.7 assists.Explore more on these topicsNBABasketballOklahoma City ThunderSacramento KingsLos Angeles LakersHouston RocketsWashington WizardsShareReuse this content

title: Doué seals Super Cup glory for PSG after Madjo makes history for Aston Villa | Uefa Super Cup | The Guardian
description: After Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s opener was cancelled out by the teenage striker Brian Madjo, Désiré Doué curled in a second-half winner to give PSG a 2-1 victory against Aston Villa in Salzburg
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: After Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s opener was cancelled out by the teenage striker Brian Madjo, Désiré Doué curled in a second-half winner to give PSG a 2-1 victory against Aston Villa in Salzburg
Content: Paris Saint-Germain's Marquinhos lifts the Super Cup after victory over Villa.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersView image in fullscreenParis Saint-Germain's Marquinhos lifts the Super Cup after victory over Villa.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersUefa Super CupDoué seals Super Cup glory for PSG after Madjo makes history for Aston VillaUefa Super Cup: Paris Saint-Germain 2-1 Aston VillaKvaratskhelia 20, Doué 62; Madjo 45Ben Fisherat Red Bull ArenaWed 12 Aug 2026 18.48 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 17.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLuis Enrique says it doesn’t matter which sport he is playing – football, tennis, padel or parchis, a board game – he wants to win all of the time. InParis Saint-Germain, he has built a winning machine, the back-to-back Champions League victors maintaining a useful habit by conquering Aston Villa in an absorbing Super Cup contest in Salzburg. For PSG, after the joy of Munich and Budapest, three months ago, does a three-peat in Madrid in May beckon?Aston Villa more than played their part in an enthralling showpiece, Brian Madjo becoming the competition’s youngest scorer after the 17-year-old cancelled out Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s opener. They could have taken the game to a penalty shootout, Warren Zaïre-Emery’s extraordinary block preventing João Gomes a near-certain debut goal and Emi Buendía heading wide in stoppage time.Kvaratskhelia and Madjo show us that the beautiful game can wash away Infantino’s stain | Nick AmesRead moreVilla will take plenty of encouragement from a fearless display, Désiré Doué’s well-taken winner ultimately the difference. The goal was initially disallowed but, after a VAR review, Omar Artan – the Somali referee handed the game by Uefa after being denied entry to the US to officiate at the World Cup – awarded it after replays showed Matty Cash played Doué onside.Before kick-off, the sights and sounds were in effect an extension of Villa’s victory in Istanbul, a party atmosphere raining down from the 6,000-strong Villa following. There were huge cheers when Unai Emery’s face appeared on the big screens in opposite corners after the teams were read aloud and hearty roars for the £38m arrival Gomes and Madjo, the hulking forward who made his presence felt on his full Villa debut. Madjo’s inclusion felt particularly ominous for Tammy Abraham, the striker signed seven months ago, his £18.25m arrival yet to pay dividends.“We won’t be in our best moment,” Emery warned on the eve of the game but, after a summer of change, the future looks bright. Emery could finally unleash Madjo in a competitive game for the first time since his £10m arrival from Metz in January, Villa winning an appeal at the court of arbitration for sport (Cas) to register him after Fifa prohibited him from playing. Chelsea’s João Pedro is the only Premier League player to have outscored Madjo in pre-season and his equaliser here was on the grandest stage yet after goals against Walsall, Real Sociedad and Indonesia All Stars. Madjo occupied Willian Pacho and Marquinhos, one of the most decorated defenders in the world. The 19-year-old George Hemmings played the full game and kept Achraf Hakimi on his toes.Only five players from Villa’s memorable victory over Freiburg remained in the XI though Emi Martínez, Ezri Konsa and Ollie Watkins are still on holiday. Emery told Watkins to rest after the striker volunteered to play here. Boubacar Kamara made his first start since sustaining a serious knee injury against Tottenham in January. More new faces will join, with Villa in advanced talks to sign João Palhinha from Bayern Munich and the Atlético Madrid left-back Matteo Ruggeri expected to undergo a medical in the next 48 hours. “Overall we can feel proud of everything we’ve done,” Emery said. “Some changes will be needed but we are confident.”View image in fullscreenBrian Madjo punches the air after scoring for Aston Villa on the stroke of half-time.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersPSG seized the lead on 20 minutes through Kvaratskhelia, who had the summer off. Madjo’s clunky control allowed Vitinha to claim the ball and locate Doué. Then Kvaratskhelia took charge, jinking inside Cash and blasting his shot in at Marco Bizot’s near post. Six minutes later, it should have been 2-0 after more Kvaratskhelia brilliance, but PSG could not apply the finishing touch. Nuno Mendes galloped on to Kvaratskhelia’s flipped pass but the full-back’s cutback from the left flank evaded the £43m summer buy Maghnes Akliouche and three other blue and red shirts.Madjo had a hat-trick of chances from John McGinn’s cunning crosses before levelling. He glanced at the screens showing a replay of him misdirecting a free header. Then he overcooked a shot when looking for the far corner after Hemmings beat Hakimi. Another flunked header followed after McGinn twirled clear of Kvaratskhelia. But with the half-time whistle looming, Madjo made amends, dispatching a side-footed volley into the roof of Matvey Safonov’s net after meeting another brilliant cross from McGinn. As the ball flew towards the back post, Pacho clung to Madjo for dear life, but the teenager kept him at arm’s length to ripple the net.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOusmane Dembélé replaced Akliouche at half-time. Fabián Ruiz, the only other player missing from the XI that began against Arsenal in Budapest in May, arrived late on. Villa kept hunting, McGinn working Safonov after Madjo spread play. But PSG regained the lead just after the hour when Dembélé’s pass unlocked Villa’s defence, exposing an imperfect offside line. Dembélé zipped the ball into the right channel and, while Ian Maatsen and Pau Torres raised their hands and Doué’s goal was initially ruled out, semi-automated offside exposed Cash.Villa still had chances to level. Zaïre-Emery slid across the turf to thwart Gomes. Safonov repelled Hemmings’s strike from close range and the substitutes Alysson and Abraham almost combined to devastating effect but Abraham did not gamble in the box, much to Emery’s frustration. Perhaps Villa will, as McGinn suggested this week, prove everybody wrong – again.Explore more on these topicsUefa Super CupParis Saint-GermainAston Villamatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Jack Draper: ‘When you reach rock bottom like that you can come back up again’ | Jack Draper | The Guardian
description: Jack Draper tells Tumaini Carayol how he is rebuilding after the most difficult period of his career and explains his emotional reaction in Canada
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Jack Draper tells Tumaini Carayol how he is rebuilding after the most difficult period of his career and explains his emotional reaction in Canada
Content: Jack Draper has spent the past year desperately trying to find solutions to his arm injury.Photograph: Minas Panagiotakis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJack Draper has spent the past year desperately trying to find solutions to his arm injury.Photograph: Minas Panagiotakis/Getty ImagesJack DraperInterviewJack Draper: ‘When you reach rock bottom like that you can come back up again’Tumaini Carayolin CincinnatiFormer world No 4 reflects on emotional reaction in Canada and rebuilding after the most difficult period of his careerWed 12 Aug 2026 16.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThose painful images have relentlessly spread to all corners of the internet. Deep in the final set of the first-round match at the Canadian Open against Térence Atmane just over a week ago, 15 months of pent up emotion erupted. Two games from defeat,Draper spent the entire changeover in tears.This was a devastating and alarming sight. Injuries had already defined so much of Draper’s career, but the uncertainty of trying to recover from a bone bruise injury to his left arm over the past year has been more challenging than anything he has experienced. All of his efforts since last July have been focused on trying to find a way to compete consistently at the highest level again, to no avail.Arthur Fery ready to test himself at Masters level after Wimbledon runRead moreIt was reasonable to wonder if his tears represented the realisation he may never recover, but the 24-year-old was seen on the practice court the following day in Montreal and his name did not shift from the entry list of the Cincinnati Open, where he is a wildcard recipient.Ahead of Thursday’s first-round match against Martín Landaluce, Draper speaks with admirable vulnerability and optimism about this most difficult period. “I don’t get emotional often,” he says. “There was once I got emotional in practice in May when I had really bad knee tendinitis and my arm was really sore as well. I was in so much pain. I was running and my knee [hurt] and my hitting the balls and my arm was sore.“Last week came from a place of, I think I had so much to focus on and manage, so much change going on in my tennis. I got to [No]4 in the world through doing the same things, the consistent work, the differences, and then went through this whole process of a lot of setbacks and a lot of struggle.“That’s taken a lot out of me. But then at the same time, I’m in a position where I’m having to start again. That reality is difficult sometimes.“The reason I got emotional was that through all the challenges, you can forget who you are on the court. And last week I felt like I couldn’t give any more. I was emotional because I didn’t recognise the player I was out on the court due to my injuries and due to probably the way I’ve been feeling for a long time.“When you reach rock bottom like that you can come back up again. Since then I’ve practised really well, I’ve had amazing support from the people around me and you get to a point more and more of acceptance. We’ve definitely reached that acceptance phase now.”View image in fullscreenJack Draper has reached the acceptance stage after more than a year of uncertainty due to his injury problems.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockDraper has spent the past year desperately trying to find solutions to this injury. After retreating on some of his earlier changes to his racket strings and technique,his retirement from Wimbledonon the eve of the tournament forced him to make even more extreme changes in his attempts to reduce the strain on his arm.Not only has he returned to a hybrid gut string setup, he is playing with a completely different, more flexible racket. Draper appears to be using a frame from a company other than his sponsor, Dunlop, which he declined to comment on.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“After this long period, my shift has gone away from performance,” he says. “I’m changing my string. I desperately don’t want to. I desperately know it’s hopefully not something that I’m going to have to do moving forwards, but it’s something I have to do for the nature of my injury. Same with the racket.“It’s a difficult one because I’m a winner. I’m out there, I want to perform. But I have to accept reality, which is that I have to find a way in very uncomfortable circumstances right now. But if that can get me to the end of the year where I’m feeling really good again and my body’s in a great place and my mind’s in a great place, then that’s only going to help me to move completely past this injury. But there is a way out and I’m seeing that on a day-to-day basis.”A year ago, Draper stood at a career-high ranking of No 4. Now he is ranked No 143 and the stop-and-start nature of his injury struggles mean he is not eligible for protected ranking. He is reliant solely on wildcards to compete on the ATP tour rather than in qualifying draws or on the ATP Challenger circuit.“At the very start of my injury, if I was to say to myself: ‘Right, I’m four in the world now, what’s the worst outcome?’ It would probably be where I’ve got to,” he says, smiling. “But there’s a certain peace in that and acceptance because I have to start again. And what a challenge.”Explore more on these topicsJack DraperTennisinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Fever’s White says critics can ‘go to hell’ over handling of Sophie Cunningham controversy | Indiana Fever | The Guardian
description: Stephanie White has pushed back on those who have criticized how she has handled the controversy that erupted after Saturday’s game
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Stephanie White has pushed back on those who have criticized how she has handled the controversy that erupted after Saturday’s game
Content: Stephanie White and Sophie Cunningham during Tuesday’s win over the New York Liberty.Photograph: Michael Conroy/APView image in fullscreenStephanie White and Sophie Cunningham during Tuesday’s win over the New York Liberty.Photograph: Michael Conroy/APIndiana FeverFever’s White says critics can ‘go to hell’ over handling of Sophie Cunningham controversyCoach was booed by sections of Fever fanbaseFever’s success on court continues despite distractionsGuardian sportand agenciesWed 12 Aug 2026 07.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 09.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndiana Fever coach Stephanie White has pushed back on those who have criticized how she has handled the controversy that erupted after Saturday’s game between her team and the Chicago Sky.Sky’s DiJonai Carringtonwas ejected for a Flagrant 2 foulafter she struck Fever’s Sophie Cunningham in the head and neck during Saturday’s game. Afterwards, White, – who previously coached Carrington at ⁠the Connecticut Sun – said she did not believe Carrington intentionally aimed for Cunningham’s neck. White was booed by some Fever fans before Tuesday’s win over the New York Liberty, while Indiana’s lieutenant governor has called for her to be fired.Does Sophie Cunningham benefit from white privilege? Of course she does | Etan ThomasRead moreAfter Tuesday’s game, White briefly addressed the ⁠media as ​she pounded her fist on the table multiple times, and declined to take questions from journalists.“The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that’s trying to hijack our league will not win. It won’t win. We are united. We are ‌connected. We will not be divided,” White said. “Every day, these women put their ass on the line. Every day. When ​they go low, we go high. Love will win. Grace will win. Humility will win, and kindness will win. I stand by them. I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell.”White said she had not seen Carrington’s foul in real time before her comments on Saturday, and rebutted suggestions that she did not “100% always have my players’ back.”“Our players’ success, our players’ health and wellness, our players’ safety is always a top priority for me,” she said after Tuesday’s game. “One of the things I pride myself on is my relationships with players. I didn’t see the play in real time. I went straight to a press conference. I thought the play got called right. Thankfully, Sophie’s OK. Was it egregious? Absolutely. When you have a chance to watch that over and over and over on replay, you can see that. I didn’t have that in real time.”Cunningham expressed her support for White, who is in her second year in charge of Indiana.“Our locker room in there, it’s tight, and we have each other’s backs,” Cunningham said on Tuesday. “Coach loves us. She didn’t see the clip ... and that’s OK. Me and Steph are great. Steph is great with all of us, and so it’s really the outside noise that’s trying to distract us, but we’re good.”The Fever have been under scrutiny this season. They have the WNBA’s most prominent player, Caitlin Clark. Cunningham has frequently come to Clark’s defense after physical play by opponents and has becomeone of the higher-profile playersin the league. In an ESPN article published last month, she voiced support for barring transgender girls and women from girls’ and women’s sports, which led to small protests and rallies outside Fever games in Seattle and Portland. After Saturday’s game, Carringtonposted the words “white privilege”on social media, although she denied it was a comment on her ejection from the game.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe off-court storylines do not appear to be affecting the Fever’s play. They have the best record in the Eastern Conference and the fourth-best in the league. Tuesday’s win was Indiana’s ninth win in their last 12 games.“We really did play with joy, and with everything going on, that’s kind of been hard to do,” Cunningham said. “Tonight was the night that we all just clicked and we had fun. We did it for Steph and we did it for everyone in the locker room.”Explore more on these topicsIndiana FeverWNBABasketballUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: High school football player in Arkansas practices with 2ft viper in helmet | US sports | The Guardian
description: An Arkansas high school player wore his helmet for nearly an hour before a two-foot cottonmouth was discovered beneath the padding during practice
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An Arkansas high school player wore his helmet for nearly an hour before a two-foot cottonmouth was discovered beneath the padding during practice
Content: A venomous cottonmouth snake like the one found in a high school football player’s helmet last week in Arkansas is seen at Fort Bragg in North Carolina.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APView image in fullscreenA venomous cottonmouth snake like the one found in a high school football player’s helmet last week in Arkansas is seen at Fort Bragg in North Carolina.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APUS sportsHigh school football player in Arkansas practices with 2ft viper in helmetTwo-foot venomous snake found inside helmetPlayer wore gear for nearly an hour without a biteOfficers used water to force reluctant reptile outAgenciesWed 12 Aug 2026 00.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA high school football player inArkansashad every right to be rattled after finding a venomous snake inside his helmet during practice.The Maumelle High student felt unusual movement inside his headgear following warmups last week and brought his helmet to an assistant coach for inspection. A slithering two-foot cottonmouth was discovered behind some padding.The pit viper was so reluctant to exit the helmet that police officers had to pour water into the headgear to force the snake out and into a bag. Animal services technicians arrived a few minutes later, identified the snake as a deadly cottonmouth and took the animal to a wooded area far from the school.Cottonmouths are the second-most venomous snakes found in Arkansas.Allow Facebook content?This article includes content provided byFacebook. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueMaumelle animal services director Chris Davis said the player wore the helmet for nearly an hour and was fortunate he wasn’t bitten.“It was unreal,” Davis said. “You had to kind of be there and take pictures to say this was real.”The player grabbed a different helmet and continued practice. But the situation caused the head coach to reiterate to his team that players should examine their equipment carefully before using it, checking for insects – or maybe something larger and more dangerous.“One of the officers noticed that it, due to it being big and fat, may have recently ate a couple of days before,” Davis said. “It probably was trying to find a dark spot to digest the food, and when it was coming across, it saw a helmet lying on the ground.”Explore more on these topicsUS sportsSchool sportsArkansasShareReuse this content

title: Lionel Messi has ‘quite a few doubts’ about football future after death of his father | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: Lionel Messi said on Wednesday that he is having doubts about continuing his career following the death of his father last week
Author: John Ashdown
Headline: Lionel Messi said on Wednesday that he is having doubts about continuing his career following the death of his father last week
Content: Lionel Messi in action for Inter Miami in August.Photograph: Dax Tamargo/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLionel Messi in action for Inter Miami in August.Photograph: Dax Tamargo/ShutterstockLionel MessiLionel Messi has ‘quite a few doubts’ about football future after death of his fatherMessi’s father, ⁠Jorge, died last week at age of 68Argentinian suggests he may not play on much longerJohn AshdownWed 12 Aug 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLionel Messi has hinted that the end of his career may be near after ­admitting to “quite a few doubts” about his football future following the death of his father.Jorge Messidied last week at the age of 68in Rosario, Argentina, after a long illness, with his health during this summer’s World Cup appearing to take a toll on Argentina’s 39-year-old captain.In a tribute on Instagram on Wednesday, Messi wrote: “I don’t know what I’m going to do without you. I don’t know how ​to move forward. I only played football and now I have quite a few doubts about whether I’m going to keep doing it for much longer.Jorge Messi, father and agent of Argentina great, dies aged 68Read more“You were by my side from the beginning; there was so little left until the end. Why couldn’t you hold on just a little longer so we could finish it together?”Messi ​spent time with his ‌father after the tournament, where Argentina were beaten in the final by Spain, before rejoining his club side,Inter Miami, making his Major League Soccer return against Columbus at the start of this month.Jorge had been a constant presence during his son’s career from his earliest days at Barcelona, with the World Cup the first time he had been absent from a major tournament. Messi revealed that his father, despite his deteriorating condition, had urged him to play forLa Albicelestein their ultimately unsuccessful attempt to defend their title.“You always asked me to play in the last World Cup and a few days before it started was when you got worse,” he wrote. “It was the first time you weren’t going to be at a tournament … Every time a match ended, I would ‌wait and hope for your message. That’s when I realised how real the situation was.”After tearfully celebrating the opening goal of his hat-trick against Algeria in the group stage, Messi had explained he was going through “a few difficult, complicated days” because of “something unrelated to football”. he said he ran out of energy in final.“My legs couldn’t go on any more,” he wrote. “This time I tried to push myself beyond my ​physical limits, but I couldn’t. ​I never felt well … We weren’t champions, ​but you don’t know how much we enjoyed every match. Once again, you were ​right: I had to ‌be there and play ​it.”Messi has earned 207 caps forArgentinasince making his debut for his country in August 2005. He captained the side to World Cup glory in 2022, matching the achievement of Diego Maradona in 1986, though like Maradona he fell at the final hurdle when attempting to win back-to-back titles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMessi did, though, break the record for total World Cup goals, with his strike against Egypt in the last 16 his 21st at the tournament and his 125th in all for Argentina. His World Cup tally was later surpassed by France’s Kylian Mbappé in the third-place playoff.With his future uncertain it remains to be seen whether he will add to his remarkable CV of honours, which includes 10 La Liga titles, four Champions Leagues and eight Ballons d’Or in addition to that World Cup triumph in Qatar.But he promised to honour his father’s memory through his own children: “I’m going to miss you so much, but you will always be present, especially in the upbringing of my children, because I will teach them and raise them the way you raised me.”Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiArgentinaInter MiamiUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: CBS Sports chief says ‘no timetable’ on Tony Romo’s future after OWI arrest | NFL | The Guardian
description: CBS Sports president David Berson says the network is still assessing the lead NFL analyst’s future following last month’s arrest
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: CBS Sports president David Berson says the network is still assessing the lead NFL analyst’s future following last month’s arrest
Content: CBS Sports play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz (left), analyst Tony Romo (center) and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson look on at a Super Bowl press conference in February 2024.Photograph: Kirby Lee/USA Today SportsView image in fullscreenCBS Sports play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz (left), analyst Tony Romo (center) and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson look on at a Super Bowl press conference in February 2024.Photograph: Kirby Lee/USA Today SportsNFLCBS Sports chief says ‘no timetable’ on Tony Romo’s future after OWI arrestAnalyst on indefinite leave after Wisconsin arrestCBS Sports president says network ‘still assessing’JJ Watt to join Jim Nantz on lead broadcast teamAgenciesTue 11 Aug 2026 20.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 08.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCBS Sports president David Berson said Tuesday he does not have a timeline for a decision about Tony Romo’s future.Romo, the network’s leadNFLanalyst, is on leave following his arrest last month in Wisconsin on suspicion of operating a vehicle while under the influence.“It’s an evolving situation, and therefore we’re still assessing,” Berson said during a network event. “There is no timetable or final decision at this time.”Tony Romo placed on leave from CBS Sports after OWI arrest in WisconsinRead moreBerson also told reporters the decision to place Romo on indefinite leave was intended to shift attention toward the games and away from his legal situation.“We we had to consider the impact on our image and on our brand. That’s very important to us. Whether the games, marketing, PR, social, the focus should and needs to be on our presentation and not on any other factors,” he said.Analyst JJ Watt will join play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson on CBS Sports’ lead NFL team during Romo’s absence. Their first game will be on 13 September, when the Minnesota Vikings host the Green Bay Packers.View image in fullscreenTony Romo appears in bodycam footage obtained by the Guardian documenting his OWI arrest in Milwaukee.Photograph: Milwaukee county sheriff’s officeWatt joined CBS in 2023. He was an analyst on The NFL Today for two seasons before teaming with Ian Eagle on the network’s No 2 crew beginning last season. Ross Tucker has been moved up to the No 2 team. He has previously teamed with Eagle on radio broadcasts for Westwood One.Romo, 46, has been the lead game analyst for CBS’ NFL coverage since 2017 after making four Pro Bowl appearances during a playing career that ran from 2004-16 and was spent entirely with Dallas.Hewas arrested on 23 Julyafter he was stopped while driving south on Interstate 43 in Wisconsin. According to the Milwaukee county sheriff’s office, Romo performed poorly on field sobriety tests before getting arrested, booked and released.He has a court date set for 21 September.Romo went to high school about 35 miles southwest of Milwaukee in Burlington, Wisconsin.Explore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsUS televisionShareReuse this content

Content: Rodri in action for Spain in the World Cup final last month.Photograph: Image Photo Agency/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRodri in action for Spain in the World Cup final last month.Photograph: Image Photo Agency/Getty ImagesManchester CityBarcelona make improved £51m bid for Rodri as Manchester City target FernándezLatest offer close to City’s valuation for Spain midfielderChelsea’s £120m price for Fernández may be too highJamie JacksonWed 12 Aug 2026 06.57 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 06.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarcelona have made an improved bid toManchester Cityof around €60m (£51m) for Rodri. title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 7: Coventry | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: After 25 years away, can Coventry make their return to the top division stick under Frank Lampard?
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: After 25 years away, can Coventry make their return to the top division stick under Frank Lampard?
Content: Eyebrows were raised when Frank Lampard replaced the popular and long-serving Mark Robins, but his success at Coventry cannot be argued with. Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesAfter 25 years away, can Coventry make their return to the top division stick under Frank Lampard?ByBen FisherWed 12 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:18th (NB: this is not necessarily Ben Fisher’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:1st (Championship)Prospects“We are back”, as the banners proudly state. It is 25 years since, after relegation was confirmed, Match of the Day cameras lingered on a message held aloft by a Coventry City supporter named John Mullaney. “We’ll be back,” were the words he inked – in sky blue, of course – on a scrap of wallpaper. When Coventry celebratedreturning to the top flightandlifted the Championship trophyin front of a capacity crowd, thousands of supportersheld aloft new-look signswith a tweaked slogan to symbolise the journey coming full circle: “We are back”.It has not been without painalong the way; nine years ago they were preparing for their first season in the fourth tier for 59 years, and from 2019 to 2021 they had to share St Andrew’s with the landlords Birmingham. That was not even their first spell of homelessness; in 2013-14, they played “home” games 35 miles away in Northampton. Many supporters will recall those harder times when Frank Lampard’s side kick off the new season in the Premier League curtain-raiser at champions Arsenal a week on Friday. Many will also rememberthe work of Mark Robins, who across two spells spent more than eight years in charge, en route to this point.The biggest challenge will be adapting to the level. Lampard is aPremier Leaguegreat but only seven of his squad count experience of the division on their CVs, the returning maverick Gus Hamer boasting the most starts among them (34) from his season in the top flight with Sheffield United. “Part of that is a good thing: we’re excited, hungry and the players want to show they deserve to be here,” Lampard said. “But we also have to work to help the squad to bridge the gap.”Coventry’s recruitment has been superb under the sporting director, Dean Austin, andthe club-record £23m arrivalof Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi from the Danish side FC Nordsjælland is particularly exciting. Some of those who flourished upon joining in the second tier also look capable of stepping up, including Milan van Ewijk, Jack Rudoni and Carl Rushworth,who has signed permanentlyafter a successful loan from Brighton. Goals were no problem last season: Coventry were the highest scorers in English football’s top four tiers with 97.Aside from a playoff semi-final defeat to Sunderland last year and a bumpy start to this one, it has been largely smooth sailing since Lampard succeeded Robins in November 2024. Coventry lost seven league matches last season, only two at home, and the going will be tougher in the top tier. “We’ve won a lot of games at this club in the last year – it’s going to be much harder to do that in the Premier League,” Lampard said. “I’m not scared of that. We have to be excited by it.”Past five seasonsOff-field pictureCoventry launched a “storytelling space” at the club’s stadium to celebrate promotion and the path to this point. The first exhibition in the club’s museum is titledThe Journey Back, which tells the club’s story from homelessness to the Premier League and showcases artefacts donated by supporters, players and managers and the owner, Doug King, opened last month. Promotion means abiding by Premier League regulations and the Coventry Building Society Arena, as it is now known, has dropped in capacity by about 300 seats in order to accommodate camera gantries and other changes to ensure compliance.Owner-fan relationshipKing angered supporters when sacking Robins but his decision was ultimately vindicated. King is never too proud to get involved: see him fist pumping the crowd, belting out the Enemy’s We’ll Live and Die in These Towns, the club’s de facto pre-match anthem, from the directors’ box, or swaying to Take That, who performed a trio of gigs at the stadium he bought 12 months ago – another big tick. Such is King’s popularity, supporters chant his name and a couple last season donned fancy dress to masquerade as him, wearing lanyards, sky-blue ties and bouffant wigs. “They tried to blag themselves into the boardroom ... but I’m way more handsome than them,”Kingsaid.The managerPromotion to the Premier League, Lampard says, marked the proudest moment of his managerial career. He went to work on his coaching badges after retiring and, 12 months after taking charge of Derby, he achieved his ultimate goal in double-quick time: managing Chelsea.A lot has happened since, including a stint “babysitting” the Blues when put in interim charge in April 2023. That seven-week period was his last exposure to the top flight as a manager but the familiar voices of his assistants Joe Edwards and Chris Jones remain. After 20 months in charge, he is comfortably the longest-serving ofthe three English managers in the division(Michael Carrick, eight months; Gary O’Neil, three months). Fresh from being named the League Managers Association manager of the year, an award presented to him by Thomas Tuchel, this summer Lampard signed fresh terms until 2029.Star signingNever fall in love with a loan player? Coventry did not just score goals last season, they kept them out, too, Rushworth claiming the Championship golden glove for 17 clean sheets. An ever-present in the league, his performances earned him three end-of-season club awards. On Coventry’s open-top bus parade, Rushworth, handed a pen by the captain, Matt Grimes, signed a placard that read “Sign here Carl” in block capitals. Then, this month, he signed a real contract to join permanently from Brighton, who inserted a buyback clause. “He was this close to getting kicked out of the group chat,” the defender Jake Bidwell joked after embracing Rushworth on his return. Before his season at Coventry, he had enjoyed loans across the league pyramid with Walsall, Lincoln, Swansea and Hull, but now the highly-regarded 25-year-old will test himself at the highest level.View image in fullscreenCoventry valued Carl Rushworth so highly they spent a club-record £22.5m to sign him permanently from Brighton.Photograph: Richard Hammersley/ShutterstockStat attackArsenal were not the only champions to make good use of dead-ball situations last season. Coventry led the Championship for set-piece goals, with 29. Only Bayern Munich (0.65 goals per game) bettered their average (0.63) in the top divisions in England, France, Germany, Italy and Spain. The issue is whether they will win enough corners and free-kicks in the Premier League to exploit this ability.StatSet for a breakthroughPromotion makes the jump from the academy to the first team that little bit bigger but Kai Andrews has at least made a dent in the senior squad. The 20-year-old, who made his debut aged 17, made seven substitute appearances last season before being loaned to Hibernian. Competition has only got fiercer since but Andrews has plenty of admirers. “There’s just something more about this kid; he has a presence – and that excites me,” said Craig Bellamy, who played for Coventry at the beginning of his career and handed an 18-year-old Andrews a shock call-up to the Wales squad approaching 18 months ago.World Cup impactDid Yirenkyi have an inkling that he would soon call Brandon Thomas-Asante a clubmate after the striker set him up to score his first World Cup goal for Ghana? Thomas-Asante, one of five players to reach double figures for Coventry last season, made inroads down the left flank and then squared the ball to the six-yard box, where Yirenkyi was on hand to strikea 95th-minute winner against Panamain their opener in Toronto. Haji Wright, Coventry’s top scorer last season, made two late substitute appearances for the USA, while Aurèle Amenda was part of the Switzerland squad that reached the last 16 but did not play a minute.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27Coventry CityPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Atlético Madrid agree £34.1m deal for Tottenham’s Cristian Romero | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: Centre-back Cristian Romero is closing on a move to La Liga while Hull have broken their transfer record to sign Nobel Mendy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Centre-back Cristian Romero is closing on a move to La Liga while Hull have broken their transfer record to sign Nobel Mendy
Content: Cristian Romero endured a troubled last season at Spurs.Photograph: George Wood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCristian Romero endured a troubled last season at Spurs.Photograph: George Wood/Getty ImagesTottenham HotspurAtlético Madrid agree £34.1m deal for Tottenham’s Cristian RomeroCentre-back closes on move to La Liga sideHull break their transfer record to sign Nobel MendyPA MediaWed 12 Aug 2026 18.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 19.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTottenham have reached an agreement withAtlético Madridover the sale of their captain, Cristian Romero. Romero was given the green light by the club and Roberto De Zerbi to depart Spurs this summer after a turbulent 2025-26 campaign in which he served four separate suspensions.Inter initially led the chase for the Argentina centre-back, but after talks with Spurs stalled, long-term admirers Atlético swooped in and a package of €40m (£34.1m) is set to secure Diego Simeone his target.Barcelona make improved £51m bid for Rodri as Manchester City target FernándezRead moreIt will bring a rollercoaster five-year spell in north London to an end for Romero, who joined in 2021 and enjoyed mixed success under Antonio Conte before a strong bond was formed with Ange Postecoglou.Romero wore the captain’s armband when Tottenham ended a 17-year trophy drought with victory over Manchester United in the2025 Europa League finaland produced a fine performance to ensure Postecoglou’s promise of silverware in his second season came true.However, Postecoglou’s dismissal weeks later was met with a thinly veiled social media post in the direction of Spurs’ hierarchy by Romero and more followed during a chaotic last season where only a final-day win against Everton avoided relegation.Romero, who was made captain by Thomas Frank ahead of the 2025-26 campaign, was in Argentina days before Tottenham’s 1-0 success over Everton to receive treatment on a knee injury before he got a flight back to be present in the stands. The return of Romero for the relegation decider only occurred after widespread criticism from Spurs supporters and it proved the final nail in the coffin for many fans.The World Cup winner will exit Spurs after 156 appearances and link up with his compatriot Simeone, who has repeatedly talked up the quality of the Argentinian in recent seasons and will finally get his man this summer.Tottenham have inserted a 15% sell-on clause in the deal and this imminent departure continues a summer of mass changes with De Zerbi overseeing a huge revamp of a squad which has finished 17th in consecutive seasons.Newly promotedHullhave broken their transfer record to sign the Senegal defender Nobel Mendy from Spanish side Rayo Vallecano. They also signed Australia international Lucas Herrington on Wednesday.View image in fullscreenLucas Herrington became Australia’s youngest player to make a World Cup appearance this summer.Photograph: Alex Livesey/Fifa/Getty ImagesThe Tigers have not disclosed the fee for the 21-year-old Mendy but it exceeds the reported £20m they paid for the Greece goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis last week. Mendy, who has one international cap and previously played for Paris FC and Real Betis, has signed a five-year deal, with an option for a further 12 months. He finished his only season with Rayo Vallecano with an appearance in May’sConference League final loss to Crystal Palace.“I have wanted to play in the Premier League since I was little, so it’s a great challenge to face and I am ready for it,” Mendy told Hull’s website.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHerrington, 18, became Australia’s youngest player to start a World Cup game for the Socceroos this summer, and arrived from MLS side Colorado Rapids on a five-year deal.Crystal Palacehave re-signed Aston Villa’s Evann Guessand on loan for the season with an option to buy. The Côte d’Ivoire international made 14 appearances after moving to Selhurst Park in January until the end of last season, but in July Palace opted against making the move permanent.The 25-year-old joined Villa from Ligue 1 side Nice for £30m last summer but failed to win a regular place in Unai Emery’s side.Celtichave signed the Egypt winger Haissem Hassan from Spanish club Real Oviedo, subject to international clearance. The 24-year-old, who impressed at this summer’s World Cup, joins the Scottish champions on a four-year deal, with the option of a further 12 months.“When I heard about Celtic being interested in me, I had to get here and be part of the club,” Hassan told the club’s website. Manager Martin O’Neill said Celtic had done “really well” to secure a player of Hassan’s quality amid interest from other clubs.“He is someone who I think has the ability and experience to do very well for us, performing at a high level in domestic and international football,” said O’Neill.Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurAtlético MadridTransfer windowHull CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Anderson still pained by England defeat but ready to shine at Manchester City | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: New Manchester City midfielder Elliot Anderson has said England’s World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina still pains him
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: New Manchester City midfielder Elliot Anderson has said England’s World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina still pains him
Content: Elliot Anderson hopes his performances at the World Cup for England can inspire him at Manchester City.Photograph: Nathan Ray Seebeck/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersView image in fullscreenElliot Anderson hopes his performances at the World Cup for England can inspire him at Manchester City.Photograph: Nathan Ray Seebeck/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersManchester CityAnderson still pained by England defeat but ready to shine at Manchester CityMidfielder takes confidence from World Cup performancesAnderson intent on making impact for CityWill UnwinWed 12 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElliot Anderson has admitted ­England’s World Cupsemi-final defeat to Argentinastill pains him, but is hoping to use the confidence from his performances at the ­tournament to inspire the start of his Manchester City career.Anderson will probably make his debut when City play ­the Premier League winners, Arsenal, on ­Sunday at the Principality ­Stadium in ­Cardiff for the Community Shield.Lionel Messi has ‘quite a few doubts’ about football future after death of his fatherRead more“It’s really hard,” Anderson said of England’s loss. “I’m still sort of ­struggling with that. There are highs and lows in football. It’s about how you bounce back.“I’ve had three weeks to reflect on it, but now is a new season, you have to move forward.I take huge confidence knowing I can perform on a World Cup stage. I hadn’t played in anything as big as that yet. That was a really good test for me.”The 23-year-old is likely to become a significant figure in City midfield because ofBarcelona’s interest in signing Rodri. A new £51m bid was made by the La Liga side on Wednesday, as they try to seal a deal for the 30-year-old. If the Ballon d’Or ­winner does depart, City’s new No 5 will be expected to be part of the plan to replace him in the middle of the park. Asked if he is similar in style to the Spaniard, Anderson said: “I think so. I can do various things within ­midfield and I’ll see where I get used.“I’ll play anywhere. Creating things, driving forward or the other role if they ask me to do that.”Andersonjoined from Nottingham Forestfor what was briefly a record £116m fee [Morgan Rogers’s £117m move to Chelseasoon eclipsed it] for a British player – City had a ­longstanding interest in him while Pep Guardiola was in charge. Due to his extended World Cup exertions with England, the former ­Newcastle midfielder is yet to feature for City under their new head coach, Enzo Maresca.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGuardiola’s departure, though, did not made him debate his decision. “It’s such a huge club and the players they have are the best. I want to be surrounded by these sorts of ­players, proving myself on a daily basis.“[Kevin] De Bruyne was always the player I looked up to over the last 10 years. I loved watching him. To be here at the same club and playing where he played is special.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United enjoy trip to Dublin with penalty shootout win over Leeds | Friendlies | The Guardian
description: Manchester United beat Leeds 5-4 on penalties at Croke Park after the game finished 1-1
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Manchester United beat Leeds 5-4 on penalties at Croke Park after the game finished 1-1
Content: Noussair Mazraoui is congratulated by Bruno Fernandes after winning the penalty shootout for Manchester United in the pre-season friendly against Leeds at Croke Park.Photograph: David Fitzgerald/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNoussair Mazraoui is congratulated by Bruno Fernandes after winning the penalty shootout for Manchester United in the pre-season friendly against Leeds at Croke Park.Photograph: David Fitzgerald/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesFriendliesManchester United enjoy trip to Dublin with penalty shootout win over LeedsManchester United 1-1 Leeds (5-4 on pens)First game between two ­English clubs at Croke ParkJamie Jacksonat Croke ParkWed 12 Aug 2026 17.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith blazing sunshine fading over a hot Dublin day, this penultimate friendly forManchester Unitedand Leeds United felt like a pre-season game on a far continent, not one staged a few hundred miles from the teams’ home across the Irish Sea.The phoney-war element is always present whatever the locale, as ­players sharpen technique and fitness, so when Joshua Zirkzee’s instant left-foot shot met Diogo Dalot’s zipped-in cross and James Trafford saved low, all involved could be satisfied.‘It is just smelling football’: Tielemans says adjusting to life at United has come naturallyRead moreEven better for Michael Carrick’s men ensued: Bryan Mbeumo raced along the left and served the ball to Zirkzee who, again, hit a first-time effort that this time beat Trafford to his right.Leeds had been scythed open, their right-side defenders, Jayden Bogle and Sebastiaan Bornauw, rendered awol by a lightning attack straight from the Carrick-Steve Holland ­training ground playbook.Daniel Farke’s switch to a 3-5-2 at half-time of November’s 3-2 loss at Manchester City is credited, rightly, with saving their top-flight status, and the manager’s job.Yet it can cause a retroactive-mode if the wingbacks retreat into a five-man rearguard. After Bogle and Rhys Chadwick did so, Mbeumo’s attempt, after one more United foray, underlined the problem.More proactive, then, were two Ao Tanaka throw-ins that dipped into the area and posed those in red to scramble. When Leeds came straight back at them, a Tyler Fletcher shimmy backfired, and they profited.The midfielder was robbed by Dan James who flipped the ball into the area where Brenden Aaronson stroked past Senne Lammens, who was helpless. So, too, Trafford when a Mbeumo rocket beat him, the bar saving Leeds, as, along the touchline, replacements prepared to enter for the second period.Quick GuideLewis-Skelly scores in Arsenal friendly as transfer speculation continuesShowMyles Lewis-Skelly appeared to underline his commitment to Arsenal by setting aside transfer speculation to score in Wednesday’s 1-1 friendly draw with the Italian club Como. The 19-year-old has been linked with Chelsea and Manchester United amid uncertainty over his future.Starting in midfield, he capitalised on an error from the Como goalkeeper, Jean Butez, to put the hosts ahead in the 33rd minute at Emirates Stadium. Lewis-Skelly then made a heart sign to the crowd as he celebrated before tapping the club badge on his shirt on his way back to the centre circle.The England international signed a five-year contract with Arsenal last summer but his long-term future has come under scrutiny since he fell behind Riccardo Calafiori and Piero Hincapié last term to become Mikel Arteta’s third choice left-back. While he started only five Premier League games across the course of the campaign, he enjoyed an end-of-season resurgence in centre midfield.Arsenal, however, are well-stocked in that position after signing Bruno Guimarães to join Declan Rice, Martin Ødegaard and the World Cup winners Martín Zubimendi and Mikel Merino.Guimarães, who joined from Newcastle in a £75m deal, was introduced at half-time against Como to make his debut, while Lewis-Skelly was replaced in the 62nd minute by Merino.The Premier League champions were pegged back by Champions League-bound Como, who are managed by the former Arsenal midfielder Cesc Fàbregas, when Martin Baturina equalised in the 43rd minute. But Arsenal won the penalty shootout 4-3, with Guimarães and his fellow summer signing Christos Tzolis on target.PA MediaWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Before the game, Carrick had issued an update on those not involved. “Marcus [Rashford], Licha [Martínez] and Kobbie [Mainoo] aren’t quite ready yet,” he said. “We’re ­preserving them for this weekend [against Milan in Wroclaw].”Missing, too, were Mason Mount, as a precaution, Tom Heaton, whose problem is being assessed and Harry Maguire, who joined training on Wednesday.“Tonight is going to be ­historical,” screeched the enthusiastic PA announcer when billing this ­inaugural meeting between two ­English clubs at the cavernous stadium.View image in fullscreenBrenden Aaronson slots home Leeds’s first-half equaliser.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesBut Carrick’s three half-time changes were hardly stellar names to please the capacity crowd. Off went Patrick Dorgu, Andrey Santos and Mbeumo for the fringe players, Toby Collyer, Daniel Armer, an 18-year-old debutant, and Tynan Thompson, given a first outing since joining recently.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFarke’s changes ran to 10, with only Bornauw surviving, so now the question was how disjointed the contest might be. Encouragingly, Harry ­Wilson and Alfie Cresswell tested Lammens, then slick Zirkzee footwork took him in on goal.But further disruption followed when Carrick made six more changes, including the introduction of his captain, Bruno Fernandes, Youri Tielemans, his new £35m midfielder, and Matheus Cunha, who spearheaded the 4-2-3-1.The result: a long lull before ­Lammens repelled a James Justin rasper, a Fernandes strike was ruled offside and the same player clipped the bar before penalties, to decide the Boyle Sports Cup, arrived.Before the final whistle five fans rushed on for selfies with Fernandes and Tielemans – youngsters, sure, but a concerning security breach, ­especially as a sixth followed.View image in fullscreenA capacity crowd of more than 80,000 turned up at Croke Park.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesUnited won the shootout 5-4, Noussair Mazraoui netting the decisive kick, and the teams wandered away offering scant clue how their 2026-27 season will be.The pre-season results of United now read this victory, 1–1 against Paris Saint-Germain on Saturday, 2–1 (Atlético Madrid), 5–0 (Rosenborg) and the 1–0 loss to Wrexham on 18 July. After this defeat, Leeds’s record is 2-0, against RB Leipzig, 4-2 (Liverpool), 1-0 win (Sunderland), and the 3-2 defeat, also to Wrexham, on 26 July.Leeds finish their preparation by hosting Augsburg, while United make the trip to Poland. Last term they ended third, 24 points ahead of Leeds in 14th. Given the former’s thus far underwhelming transfer window – only Tielemans and Santos as major signings – they would take the same finish, as would Leeds, surely, as survival will be their priority.Explore more on these topicsFriendliesManchester UnitedLeeds UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Xavi Hernández appointed head coach of the Netherlands on four-year contract | Netherlands | The Guardian
description: The 46-year-old Spaniard has agreed a contract to lead the team through to the 2030 World Cup in Saudi Arabia
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The 46-year-old Spaniard has agreed a contract to lead the team through to the 2030 World Cup in Saudi Arabia
Content: Xavi Hernández won the World Cup as a player with Spain in 2010.Photograph: Enric Fontcuberta/EPAView image in fullscreenXavi Hernández won the World Cup as a player with Spain in 2010.Photograph: Enric Fontcuberta/EPANetherlandsXavi Hernández appointed head coach of the Netherlands on four-year contractFormer Barcelona coach given deal until 2030 World CupSpaniard has been out of management since 2024PA MediaWed 12 Aug 2026 16.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 17.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former Barcelona head coach Xavi Hernández has been appointed the new head coach of theNetherlands. The 46-year-old Spaniard has agreed a contract to lead the team through to the 2030 World Cup.He replaces Ronald Koeman, whostepped downfollowing the Netherlands’ last-32 defeat by Morocco at this summer’s World Cup.Lionel Messi has ‘quite a few doubts’ about football future after death of his fatherRead moreFormer Barcelona midfielder Xavi won the World Cup as a player with Spain in 2010 and also lifted the European Championship in 2008 and 2012. He guided Barça to the La Liga title in 2023 after beginning his managerial career with Qatari club Al Sadd.“I consider it a tremendous honour to become head coach of the Dutch national team,” he said in a statement released by the Dutch Football Association (KNVB).“As someone who received his training at the FC Barcelona academy, with strong influences from Johan Cruyff and Rinus Michels, among others, I feel a special connection to Dutch football. You could say that I am a bit of a son of Dutch football.”Xavi’s appointment marks his first return to management since leaving Barcelona in 2024. He took over the Catalan club in November 2021, also succeeding Koeman, after making 767 appearances for the club.“The Netherlands has a rich football culture and a clear vision that also appeals to me enormously: attacking football, based on possession, with creativity, passion, and conviction,” he said. “Of course, the most important goal is and always will be to win, but I prefer to do so in a way that reflects those characteristics and that people can enjoy. The potential for this is there, as well as a solid foundation to build upon.”Former Liverpool head coach Arne Slot walked away from talks about replacing Koeman after saying he wants to remain in club football. His link to the role did not get beyond an initial approach.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“At this stage in my career, I prefer to see myself on the training pitch with my players every day, something that is simply not possible in the same way with a national team,” Slot told Voetbal International. “And [it is] why I chose not to continue the talks and not to start negotiations on what a possible contract might look like.“I have enormous respect for the national team and for the KNVB [Dutch Football Association] and can only be positive about the professional manner in which the talks proceeded that week. For now, I believe club football still has a lot to offer me.”Explore more on these topicsNetherlandsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Championship angst: why the sense of rejuvenation in EFL is not universal | Championship | The Guardian
description: The lineup of Championship teams this season is fearsome, leaving some supporters fearing a long slog to come
Author: Dominic Booth
Headline: The lineup of Championship teams this season is fearsome, leaving some supporters fearing a long slog to come
Content: Blackburn are among the sides facing a battle to avoid a difficult season.Photograph: Craig Galloway/ProSports/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBlackburn are among the sides facing a battle to avoid a difficult season.Photograph: Craig Galloway/ProSports/ShutterstockChampionshipChampionship angst: why the sense of rejuvenation in EFL is not universalThe lineup of Championship teams this season is fearsome, leaving some supporters fearing a long slog to comeDominic BoothWed 12 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnew season is supposed to be about renewed hope and optimism, a fresh campaign opening up a world of possibilities, a clean slate. But with the English Football League due to kick off on Friday night when Wolves host Blackburn in theChampionship, the sense of rejuvenation is not universal.The lineup of Championship teams this season is fearsome. Wolves and West Ham, hitherto established Premier League clubs, have dropped into the second tier. Others such as Burnley, Middlesbrough and Southampton anticipate a promotion push. So perhaps supporters of those who are not enjoying parachute payment riches and squads still packed with top-flight talent are wise to feel cautious. Some fear a long slog of a season to come.League One 2026-27 preview: the contenders, hopefuls and strugglersRead moreBlackburn fans, for example, saw their side scrape to the safety of a 20th-place finish last season, therefore would be forgiven for tempering their expectations before the trip to Molineux. Tony Mowbray has been brought back to Ewood Park as an experienced guiding hand, but the 62-year-old has a huge task to avoid a relegation battle.Fans believe the Rovers owners and the club’s head of football operations, Rudy Gestede, have sold Mowbray short on players heading into the season, particularly in midfield. The 34-year-old Sam Morsy – described by Mowbray as “a real man, a soldier” – has added steel to that area of the pitch with his free transfer, but after Moussa Baradji and Jayden Fevrier he is only the third addition at Blackburn this summer. Mowbray wants and needs more.“I’m a bit greedy for good players,” he said. “I keep saying to Rudy: ‘I just want good players, doesn’t really matter where they come from, what age they are.’ I want to see personality on the pitch, players who are desperate to win.”Blackburn edged past Burton 2-1 in the Carabao Cup first round last week, though they required late goals from Andri Gudjohnsen and Fevrier, who Mowbray believes can bring “magic” on the right wing after signing from Stockport.View image in fullscreenBolton Wanderers celebrated victory in the League One playoff final but a tricky season lies ahead.Photograph: Nigel French/PADown the road, there are two other Championship clubs feeling a similar sense of trepidation before the new campaign, and they meet at the Toughsheet Stadium on Saturday lunchtime, a game that could set the tone for their seasons. Bolton should still be on cloud nine; they finished last season with a4-1 demolition of Stockportin the League One playoff final. Yet as the football world has witnessed this summer at York – where the manager, Stuart Maynard, was sacked and replaced by Scott Lindsey, despitewinning the National League with 108 points– the afterglow of promotion can be short-lived. Reality bites quick.And such is the chasm between the second and third tiers nowadays, the need for Steven Schumacher’s side to strengthen fast became paramount after that glorious day at Wembley. David Watson, Ben Davies, Akin Famewo, Luca Stephenson, Kyliane Dong and Gaizka Larrazabal have all arrived, but there is a feeling among the fanbase that a marquee addition is needed, especially in attack where they risk asking too much of the striker Sam Dalby. Schumacher’s admission last week that Bolton “can’t afford to waste money” rang alarm bells with the fanbase. There is not an embarrassment of riches in the pot but forward players must be signed.“We know we’re short, especially at the top end of the pitch,” Schumacher said. “Our budget isn’t massive so we need to make sure we get the right players in, rather than just signing anybody to fill numbers. We need to try and consolidate this year, rebuild, get some more finances behind us, bring in a better squad that can keep us at this level, and then kick on.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSchumacher said that “this part of the journey is an exciting one” but it seems negativity among some fans has kicked in before a Championship ball has been kicked. A 1-0 defeat against Sheffield Wednesday in the Carabao Cup reinforced concerns around goalscoring, or the lack of it. Max Dean of Gent is coveted, but the striker is just 22 and his English football experience is limited to a short spell at MK Dons.Preston will hope to take advantage of the uncertainty around Bolton on Saturday, but Paul Heckingbottom has endured his own problems in the transfer market this summer. A public spat with Ben Whiteman over the midfielder’s desire to join Wrexham left a cloud hanging above the club and saw the Lilywhites lose their club captain. Heckingbottom said Whiteman “crossed a line” and was frustrated by the saga.Money has been spent at Deepdale this summer with Alfie Devine brought in from Tottenham for a fee in the region of £6m, while Callum Lang “feels like a new signing” according to Heckingbottom, having arrived in January for around £2m before getting injured. So the pressure is on Heckingbottom perhaps like never before. A run of just four wins from their final 20 matches of last season prompted a few fan murmurs of discontent towards the manager. With Preston almost investing £1.5m to install a modern hybrid pitch at Deepdale, the club expect better than last season’s 14th-place finish, but expectations can weigh heavy.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s a nice hobby’: Manchester United’s Janina Leitzig on goalkeeping and gardening | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: The former Leicester player’s focus has moved from runner beans to running drills as the season approaches, she tells Tom Garry
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: The former Leicester player’s focus has moved from runner beans to running drills as the season approaches, she tells Tom Garry
Content: Janina Leitzig will challenge Phallon Tullis-Joyce for the No 1 role at Manchester United.Photograph: Molly Darlington/WSL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJanina Leitzig will challenge Phallon Tullis-Joyce for the No 1 role at Manchester United.Photograph: Molly Darlington/WSL/Getty ImagesMoving the Goalposts newsletterWomen's Super LeagueInterview‘It’s a nice hobby’: Manchester United’s Janina Leitzig on goalkeeping and gardeningTom GarryThe former Leicester player’s focus has moved from runner beans to running drills as the season approachesWed 12 Aug 2026 06.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 09.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith some parts of England gearing up for a fifth heatwave of 2026 the new Manchester United goalkeeper Janina Leitzig, a keen gardener, is sympathetic to the precarious health of this reporter’s tomato plants. “You’re not used to so little rain, are you?” she observes. For the time being, after her summer move to Manchester, the former Germany youth international does not have a garden of her own but she reveals that, during her three-and-a-half-year spell at her former club Leicester, homegrown vegetables were her pride and joy.“I love to do some gardening. Back home, everyone has their own vegetables and it’s just better, it tastes better,” she tells the Guardian. “Being away from home and away from family, of course you have your football friends, but still it can be quite lonely sometimes if you come home from training, so it was really nice to have a garden and to spend time outside. It’s not too much effort, it’s just a nice hobby.”The 27-year-old got her outdoor fix with a spot of surfing in Cornwall this summer during the off-season, but now the serious business of pre-season is well under way. Her new club Manchester United are heading to La Manga for a training camp between 14 and 19 August, where the focus will have to be less on runner beans and more on running drills.Leitzig, the former Bayern Munich and Hoffenheim keeper, was sitting down for an interview before it was known that the Spanish coachEva Olid was to become United’s new manager, but explained why swapping Leicester for United was appealing to her. “It’s such a big club and it’s such a big honour to be here,” Leitzig says.“I think, for every player, it’s really interesting if you have an offer from Manchester United. First of all, the team is so nice. The characters in here – you can tell it’s a really good and strong team. The training quality is really high. The building and the facilities [at Carrington] are really good; it’s really professional here. [When] the conversations were going on [with United], they just gave me a really good feeling.”View image in fullscreenJanina Leitzig during a training session at Carrington.Photograph: Poppy Townson/MUFC/Getty ImagesLeitzig has signed a contract with United until 2029, after the disappointment of relegation with Leicester last season, but says she has nothing but fond feelings about her former club, who she initially joined on loan in January 2023 before signing permanently that summer.Looking back at what she learned in the East Midlands, she says: “It was such a special time for me. It was supposed to be only half a year and then it ended up being three-and-a-half. I think that says a lot about how much I liked it there. The people are great and the club is great.“Obviously we had some tough times and unfortunately the relegation last season was really, really tough and it really hurt, because the club deserves to be in a better position, but I really hope that the girls will do well and I see them soon back in the WSL. It would be great if they could come back up quickly.”During her time in England, Leitzig has observed an evolution in goalkeeping styles, and she is in a thoughtful mood when discussing what the future might look like for keepers, tactically. On the modern trend of keepers playing out from the back, she says: “To be fair, there was one phase where everyone wanted goalkeepers to play with the feet and I think it’s still really important, but I think there was a phase where it was too much. I think it was a bit overexaggerated at times, so I think it’s coming back now to be more about the basic stuff.“Obviously you have to switch play and you have to be good with your feet under pressure, but I think the game is going to be more [about] trying to get the ball as quick as possible in the opposite half to then keep the pressure up there and not to try to take such a high risk. It’s going to be interesting.“I think, because I’m German and Manuel Neuer [her idol] is German, I learned quite early to play with both feet and I was an outfield player initially, so I’m feeling confident about playing with the ball. But saving shots is the best part of goalkeeping.”The USA keeper Phallon Tullis-Joyce played in 21 of United’s 22 matches in the Women’s Super League last season and Leitzig says they will enjoy working together and helping each other. “They [United] said it’s like a competition [to start in goal]. Obviously it’s really important to have strong goalkeepers, because you never know what happens in the season.“I will just give my best, I’ll try to bring quality, and then it’s the manager’s decision to decide who’s going to play. But it’s really important that we are a good goalkeeper team, that we support each other and push each other because then everyone can get better.”United, who finished fourth last season, will get the new WSL season under way on the opening night, at London City Lionesses on 4 September. Leizig concludes by looking ahead to that showdown and says, with fire in her eyes: “To have the first game of the season Friday evening, 7pm, floodlights, it’s just something you’re really excited for. Working in the pre-season you think: ‘When can the [games] finally start,’ so I’m really excited for that game.”Get in touchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailmoving.goalposts@theguardian.com.This is an extract from our free email about women’s football, Moving the Goalposts. To get the full edition,visit this page and follow the instructions.
