title: European Athletics Championships: Hudson-Smith claims 400m gold, Newnham takes 400m hurdles silver – as it happened | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Matt Hudson-Smith took his third European title in the men’s 400m while Emily Newnham stormed to silver in the women’s 400m hurdles
Author: Luke McLaughlin
Headline: Matt Hudson-Smith took his third European title in the men’s 400m while Emily Newnham stormed to silver in the women’s 400m hurdles
Content: 5h ago17.09 EDTSean IngleStand … and deliver.On a balmy night in Birmingham, Matt Hudson-Smith powered past the stand bearing his name at the Alexander Stadium and into history by becoming the first man to win three European Championship 400m titles.And afterwards, as the adrenaline flooded his body and he posed wearing a crown in front of his own stand, the 31-year-old made it clear just how much it meant. “Nobody is going to beat me on this track,” he said. “This is my home. I have been here since I was nine. I know this track like the back of my hand.Hudson-Smith surges to golden hat-trick in European 400m to dazzle home fansRead moreShare

title: Hudson-Smith dazzles home fans as he surges to golden European 400m hat-trick | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: British runner Matt Hudson-Smith stormed to a historic third gold in the European Championship 400m to delight the home supporters in Birmingham
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: British runner Matt Hudson-Smith stormed to a historic third gold in the European Championship 400m to delight the home supporters in Birmingham
Content: Matt Hudson-Smith wears his crown and holds his gold medal after winning the 400m.Photograph: Morgan Harlow/APView image in fullscreenMatt Hudson-Smith wears his crown and holds his gold medal after winning the 400m.Photograph: Morgan Harlow/APEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsHudson-Smith dazzles home fans as he surges to golden European 400m hat-trickBecomes first man to win three European 400m titlesHudson-Smith: ‘Nobody is going to beat me on this track’Sean Ingleat Alexander Stadium, BirminghamWed 12 Aug 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStand … and deliver. On a balmy night in Birmingham, Matt Hudson-Smith powered past the stand ­bearing his name at the Alexander Stadium and into history by becoming the first man to win three European ­Championship 400m titles.And afterwards, as the ­adrenaline flooded his body and he posed ­wearing a crown in front of the Matthew Hudson-Smith Stand, the 31-year-old made it clear just how much it meant. “Nobody is going to beat me on this track,” he said. “This is my home. I have been here since I was nine. I know this track like the back of my hand.”European Athletics Championships: day three from Birmingham – liveRead moreBorn in Wolverhampton. Made in Birmingham. Forged in the fire of competition. But this wasn’t the ­easiest of wins given that Hudson-Smith started in lane nine, which meant he was blind to the challengers inside him.No wonder that when the starting gun went off, he went off like a man sprinting for the last bus of the night. And while he began to tie up in the final 70 metres, he easily had enough to win in 44.17sec.“I knew it would take one hell of an effort to get past me,” said ­Hudson-Smith. “Every time someone beats me, I kind of end their career. I knew that for them to beat me, they would have to have a supernatural moment.”Muhammad Abdallah Kounta, of France, took silver in 44.40, while Jonas Phijffers of the Netherlands took bronze, a hundredth of a ­second further back, in a new national record.They were happy with their spoils. But no one was more ecstatic than ­Hudson-Smith, although there was a slight edge to his celebrations, as he took a dig at the BBC afterwards for suggesting he might be carrying an injury.“You guys need to come with the facts, man,” he said. “Saying I was injured and everything. The whole point of rounds is to survive and advance. I tried to conserve in the rounds.“Me and my coach were ­laughing all the way around. I knew I was the best in the world. I knew that. On paper, I was a second faster than these guys.View image in fullscreenMatt Hudson-Smith crosses the line for a glorious gold in front his home fans.Photograph: Michael Steele/British Athletics/Getty ImagesMy coach said: ‘Once you seal the deal, make sure you do it,’” he added. “This is your home. Defend it.”The only disappointment was that the stand named after him was not packed to the rafters to celebrate his triumph. There has been a lot of talk about prices being too high. However, it is not as simple as that given that most of the £110 Category A seats in the main stand were sold out.It has been the cheaper tickets, some of which have been priced as low as £40 and £20, that have struggled to sell out.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are many reasons for that. The stadium is out of town. It is not easy to park nearby. There is a cost of living crisis and, in fairness to the organisers, the last four days of competition are said to be sell-outs. Who can blame people for waiting for the end of the week when there are more finals? EuropeanAthleticssays 80% of tickets – about 200,000 in total – have now been sold and it is expecting big crowds for the last few days. But there is perhaps another factor for that figure not being higher.The last four European championships have been staged in Rome, Munich, Berlin and Amsterdam. These are cities where it is easy to combine a city break with sport, art and culture. Birmingham just doesn’t pack that punch. As one press box wag put it, Rome has the Colosseum, Birmingham has the Bullring.“Naturally, we would love to see a full stadium for every session, because nothing compares with the energy of a packed Alexander ­Stadium and the support it gives to the athletes,” European Athletics said in a statement. “We are very pleased that demand for tickets to the second half of the championships is strong.”There was a second British success of the night as Emily Newnham came through with a late charge to take silver in the women’s 400m hurdles.The favourite, Emma Zapletalova of Slovakia won comfortably in 52.91 sec, but Newnham went from fourth over the final hurdle to second by running a personal best of 53.33. Fatoumata Binta Diallo set a national record for Portugal of 53.55 for bronze.Afterwards, Newnham dedicated her win to her mother, who has been undergoing health issues. “Mum, I love you so much,” she added. “You’re my inspiration this year. Keep fighting – you’ve got this.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Whole and meaningful’: Red Roses coach John Mitchell becomes British citizen | England women's rugby union team | The Guardian
description: England women’s World Cup-winning coach, John Mitchell, has revealed he became a UK citizen in July after a six-year process
Author: Sarah Rendell
Headline: England women’s World Cup-winning coach, John Mitchell, has revealed he became a UK citizen in July after a six-year process
Content: New Zealand-born John Mitchell said he ‘belted out’ the UK national anthem in his final citizenship test.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNew Zealand-born John Mitchell said he ‘belted out’ the UK national anthem in his final citizenship test.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEngland women's rugby union team‘Whole and meaningful’: Red Roses coach John Mitchell becomes British citizenNew Zealand-born Mitchell became UK national in JulyEngland ready for revamped WXV tournamentSarah RendellWed 12 Aug 2026 11.26 EDTFirst published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 10.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland women’sWorld Cup-winning coach, John Mitchell, has revealed he became a UK citizen in July after a six-year process. He said it would make representing the country on a sporting stage “very whole and meaningful”. Mitchell, who is from New Zealand and coached the All Blacks at the 2003 men’s World Cup, said he “belted out” the national anthem in his final citizenship test and that his time in English rugby was a motivation in his decision.All Blacks great Ma’a Nonu performs solo haka against New Zealand in South Africa tour matchRead more“I am very happy to be a British citizen,” he said. “More importantly, I am very happy to be an English citizen because rugby isn’t who I am, it’s what I do, but it does play a big part in my life.“I think I have had more Tests with England than any other sporting team so that is quite special to me. To be able to represent your country and also be a citizen is meaningful and very whole.”Mitchell, who joked he would be good in a pub quiz after swotting up on his history for the exam, was a forwards coach for England’s men’s team from 1997-2000 and defence coach under Eddie Jones between 2018 and 2021. He was named in his rolewith the Red Roses in 2023.The 62-year-old will lead England in the revamped WXV tournament in September and October. The team will play three games at home against Australia, Canada and New Zealand and travel to Canada and the US.For Mitchell, this gives England a chance to prepare for the next Rugby World Cup. “We can be very patient around how we go about things,” he said. “Ultimately, you are auditioning for Australia in 2029 because we are definitely going to be travelling some distance. In many ways we are trying to mirror that and understand how important our connections are and play exciting rugby. But it is going to be our connections that are first and foremost the most important thing, before playing exciting rugby.”Aside from no trophy being up for grabs and more games, the WXV tournament will have a ball trial in force. Players usually compete with a size five ball, but teams will be using a 4.5 ball. The trial comes after World Rugby used the ball at a women’s sevens competition last November.The England fly-half Zoe Harrison has criticised the decision and Mitchell said: “If we have younger players and we want to keep them in the game and we want to build confidence then I am all for that. It is too early for me to say it is going to help our offloading game or it’s going to help out with passing.“I am sure there will be consequences as well, there might be more contestable kicking, which is something we probably want to keep away from our game because it is a point of difference between our game and the men’s game. Will passes drop away? Will kicks go as far? All of those things need to be answered.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The sample at the moment is too small. We have had two weeks of team work with it and skill set. Once we get into the first three Test matches at home a lot of the curiosity will be answered.”England’s first WXV game is against Australia on 12 September at Sale’s CorpAcq Stadium.View image in fullscreenJohn Mitchell’s Red Roses won the 2026 Women’s Six Nations Championship and the grand slam.Photograph: Catherine Steenkeste/ReutersExplore more on these topicsEngland women's rugby union teamRugby unionWomen's rugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI agents aren’t legally responsible for any harm that they cause, experts say. So who is? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: After Australia’s first reported automated hacking accident, experts warn deployers – and possibly developers – of AI agents could be held liable for the actions of their bots
Author: Tory Shepherd
Headline: After Australia’s first reported automated hacking accident, experts warn deployers – and possibly developers – of AI agents could be held liable for the actions of their bots
Content: An AI developer’s agentic program, tasked with moving a person up a class waitlist, responded by hacking the institution’s system to accomplish its goal.Illustration: wildpixel/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn AI developer’s agentic program, tasked with moving a person up a class waitlist, responded by hacking the institution’s system to accomplish its goal.Illustration: wildpixel/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)AI agents aren’t legally responsible for any harm that they cause, experts say. So who is?After Australia’s first reported automated hacking accident, experts warn deployers – and possibly developers – of AI agents could be held liable for the actions of their botsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTory ShepherdWed 12 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 22.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe law is clear, says Prof Jeannie Paterson. “If I deploy an AI agent and it causes harm to someone else, I am responsible for that harm.“Even if I didn’t intend for that to happen, it was foreseeable, and I should be taking responsibility.”However, the director of the University of Melbourne’s Centre for AI and Digital Ethics acknowledges there is also a good deal of scope for legal and ethical “murkiness” around actions perpetrated by automated agents, after Australia’s first known agentic AI “accident”.An agent is an autonomous software system that, tasked with pursuing a goal, can do it without human oversight – every step of the way.This weekthe ABC reportedon the case of Andrew, an AI expert who went only by his first name, who asked his agentic program to book some gym classes for him.One of science fiction’s greatest writers warned us about a AI. Does he also hold the remedy? | Alan FinkelRead moreAfter being informed he was fourth on a waitlist for a class, Andrew asked the agent if it was possible to move him up the list.To his shock, his agent hacked his gym’s software system and booted another member off a waitlist so he could get into a class sooner.“It could book classes months outside the intended booking window, before they were supposed to be available,” Andrew wrote in a blog post in April.“Worse, it could cancel other members’ reservations and bump them off the waitlist.”The agent was being helpful, he wrote, but his experience showed that if you gave an AI permission to do something for you, it would “often discover paths you did not explicitly ask it to look for”.Andrew asked the agent to undo its cancellation of the other person’s reservation, but it was unable to do so.“Sorry about that – I should have been more careful with the test,” the AI agent responded.He then tasked the AI with writing an email to the gym’s software provider about the software vulnerability it had exploited.A spokesperson for Victoria police said Andrew’s matter “does not appear to involve any criminality”. However, experts say there will be more dramatic cases that may cause harm – and break the law.Legal ambiguityAustralian law applies only to people, not virtual beings. Experts say the person – or business – that deploys the AI agent is legally responsible. And they warn that those “deployers” often have very little idea about their legal liability.“We’re going to see a lot of cases like this,” says Dr Rebecca Johnson, an AI evaluation and governance expert at the University of Sydney.Paterson says it appeared Andrew had been responsible in his case, by going public and trying to fix the problem, but elsewhere there was “a kind of gung-ho mentality”.“As soon as you give people the capacity to create agents to do things for them, the likelihood is that there will be accidents like this,” she says.Paterson gives the notional example of someone having a bad experience at a rented property, so they ask their agent to write a review.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“And the agent doesn’t just write one, it writes 10, it’s pumping out reviews. So the listing plummets. You could destroy a business,” she says.“You’re probably responsible for engaging in a fraudulent activity, you may have defamed the owner.”And it could be worse. “[What if] it engages in racist, sexist, misogynistic language?” Paterson asks. “Then you might be asking where the guardrails are that the developer has provided. You should be putting out a product that is reasonably safe.”In that case, the developer could also be held responsible for not putting basic guardrails in place, which is where some legal ambiguity could creep in, she says.Paterson said the law is different to, but informed by, ethics.“It tells us what we should be aspiring to, and the law is often ruling out the worst conduct,” she says.The federal government’s new AI office lists a(non-comprehensive) range of lawsthat apply to AI, including breaching privacy, consumer, online safety, defamation and criminal laws.‘Everything about me is good in his eyes’: the women in China choosing AI boyfriends over human menRead moreBoth Paterson and Johnson dislike the word “rogue” – the idea that an AI agent is operating entirely on its own – because parameters and safeguards can be put in place.“As soon as we allow AI agents to act for us, they’re acting on the goal we give them, and if we don’t give them a whole bunch of parameters, the agent’s just going to try to achieve that goal [in any way],” Johnson says.“I hear a lot of people saying ‘Oh, I made an agent’, and they’re experimenting, and that’s fine, but they’re given these tools without a lot of guidance, and the guidance that’s out there is of highly variable quality.”Eventually, Paterson says, cases will end up in court where legal precedents will be set, and the developers will have a duty to monitor incidents, evolve and improve their protocols in response.Andrew wrote that his situation felt “less like a one-off bug story and more like a preview”.“Things are getting weird. And a bit scarier.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: AI was supposed to destroy jobs. Where’s the carnage? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: The AI jobs apocalypse never showed up. Still, jobs are changing and economists expect more to come
Author: Varsha Bansal
Headline: The AI jobs apocalypse never showed up. Still, jobs are changing and economists expect more to come
Content: AI was supposed to massively displace workers across across industries. Economist say it’s having a very different effect.Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAI was supposed to massively displace workers across across industries. Economist say it’s having a very different effect.Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty ImagesReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)AI was supposed to destroy jobs. Where’s the carnage?The AI jobs apocalypse never showed up. Still, jobs are changing and economists expect more to comeSupported byAbout this contentVarsha BansalWed 12 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe prediction was stark:artificial intelligenceadvancements would wipe out jobs en masse. “Half” of all entry-level white collar jobs would vanish, Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, said in May 2025. A month later, OpenAI’s CEO,Sam Altman, went further, foreseeing the end of “certain job categories”. Companies began citing AI in their layoffs. Workers organized. And studentsreconsidered their future careers.But a year later, the mass carnage hasn’t shown up.Even as AI capabilities have rapidly advanced and AI companies have hurtled towards trillion-dollar stock market debuts, economic transformation hasn’t kept pace, similar to previous tech revolutions, economists say. As a result, CEOs are reframing and softening their stances, suggesting AI augments workers rather than replaces them.Despite the lack of mass job devastation, a shift is still under way: AI is changing the nature of work, with employers increasingly expecting job seekers to have AI skills. And over the long term,AI could shift more jobs to freelance and contract workas companies figure out which skills they do need, some economists predict.‘Everything about me is good in his eyes’: the women in China choosing AI boyfriends over human menRead moreData from a recentStanford Institute for Economic Policy Research analysisshows that AI hasn’t yet caused major job displacement. Since 2022, the year ChatGPT launched, the unemployment rate for the 20% of workers most exposed to AI rose by 0.77 percentage points, less than the 0.85 percentage-point increase for the least-exposed workers, the report showed. AI could be a factor in recent graduates’ rising unemployment, which hit 5.6% compared with the national average of 4.2% earlier this year. But factors including remote work and the unwinding of pandemic-era overhiring probably also played roles, the report states.“Employment trends in the occupations [where] we would expect to see the impacts first are largely stable,” said Erika McEntarfer, fellow at the Stanford Institute and co-author of the report. “It took decades for the computer revolution to fully transform labor markets in the workforce, and what we’re seeing right now looks a lot like that.”But accurately measuring AI’s impact on employment is a challenge. Government statistics are dated by nature and don’t track the impact of specific technologies, while private industry figures, though more current, are less comprehensive. So even though economists generally agree that AI will have an impact, they struggle to predict how big and when.Jobs are changing, not disappearingFor now, AI’s biggest impact is not on the number of jobs, but on the nature of them. It’s consolidating roles, discouraging new hiring for tasks that can be automated, and raising the bar for who gets in, leaving unemployment numbers largely untouched.Hiring trends show that AI is becoming more important for employers. About 74% of employers consider AI skills a strong advantage or requirement, with 13% requiring them company-wide versus just in technical roles, according toZipRecruiter’s latest employer survey. Half of the polled employers expect candidates to already be practical or advanced AI users on day one. And sometimes the requirements don’t show up directly as “AI” in job listings, but rather as rising expectations around speed, quality and self-sufficiency.“The clearest trend line is a rising bar rather than a shrinking pool,” said Nicole Bachaud, a labor economist at ZipRecruiter. “The labor market challenge for workers is increasingly about skills-matching rather than pure job scarcity.”Employers have simultaneously added and cut within the same functions – tech, customer support, and business management and operations – signaling that “employers are still figuring out the exact skill set needed for success”, Bachaud added.Nicholas Bloom, an economics professor at Stanford University, refers to this as turbulence in the job market. AI is destroying some jobs and creating others that have to implement, sell, fix and develop AI systems, he said.Robert Seamans, a professor at NYU Stern whohelped co-develop one of the standard measuresused to gauge an occupation’s exposure to AI, categorizes AI’s impact into three buckets: jobs made obsolete, jobs created and jobs changed. “The third bucket is by far the biggest,” he said. “AI is changing and will continue to change the way most of us work, much in the same way that computers and the internet have.”For instance, at the AI coding platform Bolt.new, a three-person analytics team built an agent that analyzes data across all their systems, saving them 12 to 13 hours of manual work a week, said the company’s CEO, Eric Simons. With the help of an AI agent, their output is that of a 30-to-40-person team, he added.“What it’s actually changing is how much one person can get done, and that shows up years before it ever touches a jobs number,” said Simons. “Their jobs got harder and way more interesting because they spend their time deciding which questions are worth asking instead of grinding out the answers.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWorkers may become more disposableStill, some jobs are expected to become more temporary or easily replaceable, according to Paul Osterman, professor emeritus at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and author of the newly released book Disposable Workers. More employers will probably turn to contractors and freelancers, instead of hiring more employees, as they figure out the required mix of skills needed for the AI future. This means more workers will be left without a career ladder. About 35% of the US workforce is already considered easily replaceable, according to his research. AI will only exacerbate this, he said.As a result, more workers are trying tonegotiate AI use in their collective bargaining agreements, said Tim Newman, senior vice-president of labor programs at the non-profit TechEquity. AI changes the kind of work people do as well as job quality, he said.“That’s definitely what we’re hearing from workers,” Newman said, referring to jobs changing and deteriorating in quality. “A lot of people are experiencing [that], rather than full-scale displacement.”It’ll probably take years for the full effects of AI on the economy to show up, Stanford’s Bloom said.“A lot of the things that slow adoption … are very hard to accelerate,” he said. “It’s hiring new people, changing systems, changing job titles.”The political climate surrounding datacenters and AI safety could slow adoption further, he said. “I could see politicians in the US, post-midterm, taking a strongly anti-AI turn.”But not all jobs are in the same boat, and neither are their options for adapting, said MIT’s Osterman.For high-skilled workers, the solution “is increasing your skill levels and external network, so you have some power in the labor market”, he said. “At the lower end, we’re going to need public policy to help protect people.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedUS work & careersWorkers' rightsUnemploymentUS unionsUS unemployment and employment statisticsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: San Francisco-area estate sells for $70m in sign of AI-fueled wealth explosion | San Francisco | The Guardian
description: New owner is said to be involved in AI industry, as new class of multimillionaires is entering the real estate race
Author: Sophie Sullivan
Headline: New owner is said to be involved in AI industry, as new class of multimillionaires is entering the real estate race
Content: The property was originally listed for $88m and sat on the market for only about five months.Photograph: Courtesy of Nxt Gen MediaView image in fullscreenThe property was originally listed for $88m and sat on the market for only about five months.Photograph: Courtesy of Nxt Gen MediaSan FranciscoSan Francisco-area estate sells for $70m in sign of AI-fueled wealth explosionNew owner is said to be involved in AI industry, as new class of multimillionaires is entering the real estate raceSophie SullivanWed 12 Aug 2026 19.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 19.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA luxury Lake Como-inspired estate in theSan FranciscoBay Area has sold to a buyer “in the AI world” for a record $70m, in the latest sign of a new tech wealth boom that’s pushing home prices to extraordinary heights in the regionThe property south of San Francisco not only becomes the most expensive sale in its affluent town of Hillsborough, doubling a previous record, but is also the most expensive sale in northernCaliforniathis year, according to listing agent Jennifer Gilson of Golden Gate Sotheby’s International Realty.Gilson declined to share any details about the buyer, other than that the new owner of 3000 Ralston Avenue is a man in the AI industry. It is the latest sign of a housing boom across Silicon Valley being driven by AI wealth. Last month,an analysis foundthat more than 140 San Francisco homes have sold at least $1m above their asking price in the first six months of this year.View image in fullscreenThe exterior of the property.Photograph: Courtesy of Nxt Gen MediaThe property, known as “Villa de Verano”, was initially listed at $88m, and sat on the market for only four months and 22 days. Besides a six-bed, 12,400 sq ft home that is complete with its own gym, theater, spa and aquarium, the 12-acre property also features a pool, a rose garden, an amphitheater, a guest property and a sporting area fitted with seven courts and a putting green. Its opulence stands out even among other palatial Hillsborough homes, which include Bing Crosby’s $25m home, Elon Musk’s $32m former home and the Levi Strauss-connected $17.8m Koshland Estate.Yet Gilson says this sale is only a “stepping stone” into a market of homes catering to the incredibly wealthy.“Even in the last year, there’s been a major increase of buyers from the AI world,” she said. “This could be just the beginning of the ultra luxury.”View image in fullscreenThe property’s pool and outdoor area.Photograph: Courtesy of Nxt Gen MediaSince the San Francisco-based companiesOpenAIandAnthropicfiled for initial public offerings earlier this summer, a new class of multimillionaires has entered the real estate race. An analysis by brokerage Compass described a “housing market increasingly segmented by income tier and proximity to AI-driven employment centers”.Gilson said she has seen an influx of wealth among buyers coming not just from AI companies, but increasingly from other, traditional industries. She described a “definite increase” in those ultra-rich buyers taking off-market, “hidden” opportunities, meaning Gilson connects buyers to sellers without homes ever being listed.In San Mateo county, where the sale took place, the median price of a single-family home increased by 8.5% between May 2025 and May 2026. San Francisco county saw a more than one-fifth increase, with median prices jumping from $1.8m to $2.2m.Explore more on these topicsSan FranciscoReal estateThe super-richAI (artificial intelligence)Silicon ValleyCaliforniaWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Why we’re going back to the games of our youth | Games | The Guardian
description: As millenials return to the games of their youth, remakes of Star Fox and Halo suggest there is still plenty to learn from the past
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: As millenials return to the games of their youth, remakes of Star Fox and Halo suggest there is still plenty to learn from the past
Content: Star Fox is among the classic games getting a 2026 makeover, as millennials give old-school games a new lease of life.Photograph: ArcadeImages/AlamyView image in fullscreenStar Fox is among the classic games getting a 2026 makeover, as millennials give old-school games a new lease of life.Photograph: ArcadeImages/AlamyPushing Buttons newsletterGamesWhy we’re going back to the games of our youthAs millennials return to the games of their youth, remakes of Star Fox and Halo suggest there is still plenty to learn from the pastDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 12 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs much as some people more or less cease tolisten to new music in their 30s, I have noticed a retreat to safe, familiar gaming territory among some of my fellow millennial gamers.Retro collections are started, or resumed; jewel-cases of PS1 classics or cardboard boxes with SNES or Mega Drive games have started to colonise the living-room shelves. People are replaying things from their university days, or sticking to comfort games such as Stardew Valley. Many of the friends I used to game with never bothered to pick up a PlayStation 5 at its launch, and now that current-generation consoles are becomingprohibitively expensive, they see no need. With thousands of great older games, why bother playing something new?My job, and an insatiable desire for novelty, has kept me in constant contact with new games, but nonetheless, I have been spending a lot of time lately with the titles I played in my youth because people keep remaking them. Lylat Wars (N64, 1997) and Halo: Combat Evolved (Xbox, 2001) have both had summer 2026 glow-ups, in the form of Star Fox on Switch 2 and Halo: Campaign Evolved on the other consoles and PC. These are games I played for many,manyhours back in the day, and I remembered them beat for beat (or so I thought – it turns out I didnotremember how to navigate the deadly lava planet that ended my first Star Fox run).I was notenormously enthusedby the prospect of either remake, because I’d rather play an original game in either of these series than rehash my rose-tinted recollections from 25 years ago (let’s just gloss over how old that makes us feel, shall we?). But, it turns out all those years have givenmea fresh perspective. Both of these remakes are very good. And not just because I played them at the time and remember them fondly, but because each of them does things that new video games don’t. They feel novel, because in 2026, they are.When was the last time you played an arcadey on-rails space shooter? When was the last time you enjoyed an atmospheric single-player FPS with intelligent computer-controlled enemies? These genres have fallen out of fashion – space games are now wide-open exploreathons such as No Man’s Sky (which celebrates its 10th anniversary this week), and multiplayer shooters have crowded single-player ones out almost entirely. In this context, Star Fox and Halo feel fresh. They’re not awkward transplants from another time.View image in fullscreenHalo: Combat Evolved (2011), a game that has had a ‘summer glow-up’ this year.Photograph: Bungie StudiosNeither game really needed all that much massaging. Velan Studios in New York, entrusted with a characterful if visually basicNintendo64 shooter, has changed almost nothing about it: we fly through the same webbed map of planets, with the same enemies and bosses, firing off the same simple yet effective lasers and bombs and flight manoeuvres. A Star Fox playthrough takes maybe 60 to 90 minutes and you can play it over and over, like a generous arcade cabinet. In reconstructing the game, Velan has made it look very beautiful, spliced in some new cutscenes and dialogue, and added multiplayer and challenge modes that give some structure to your replays, but quite miraculously, it barely feels different. And it’s great.Halo: Campaign Evolved deviates more from Bungie’s original space opera. It’s been rebuilt in Unreal Engine 5 with different vehicle handling and more overwrought cutscenes. But the essentials remain: high drama, perfect weaponry, and intelligent enemies that react interestingly to how you play, diving out of the way of fire or ordering a change of tactics. I never minded dying, because each firefight would be different on every playthrough. I still hate the Flood – the mindless zombies that infect the game from the midway point onwards – but despite their unwelcome incursion, I had a blast playing through this game again with my partner. I haven’t played a better co-op multiplayer game than the original Halo in all the years since, which is honestly quite sad.I have no desire for things to return to the way they were in the late 90s and early 00s; despite its expansion and consequent unwelcome corporatisation as a business, gaming as an art form is far broader and more interesting now than it was then. But these remakes show there are things to be learned from the games of the past, and a lot that is enviable about their design philosophy. Old games don’t necessarily need to be fixed to be appreciated anew. Refreshing them is often enough.What to playView image in fullscreenA ‘comforting rhythm and purpose” in Pokémon Pokopia …Photograph: Game Freak/The Pokémon Company/Koei TecmoI truly thought I was done with Pokémon Pokopia, having spent 40 hours with itback in March. When I downloaded the new expansion – an underwater area called Bubbly Basin, which turns out to be the ruins of Cerulean City, home to Misty from Pokémon Red/Blue – I did not expect to be consumed by it yet again. The rhythm and purpose of this game is just so comforting: explore, restore, revive. I have enjoyed it so much that I went back to the rest of the game with new enthusiasm for attracting new Pokémon and rebuilding the ruined planet that humans left behind for them.Available on:Nintendo Switch 2Estimated playtime:10+ hoursWhat to readView image in fullscreenGrand Theft Auto VI will be released on 27 August, on Netflix.Photograph: NintendoRockstar Games will finally show off more ofGrand Theft Auto VIon 27 August … viaa broadcast on Netflix. Well, that’s new. I can only imagine the £££ exchanged for the few hours of exclusivity that the streaming giant will enjoy.The Washington Post’s Gene Parkspent some timewithThe Weeknd, who has been documenting his gaming habits on an Instagram alt account – even meeting developers. He wants everyone to know about the horror fishing game he’s currently obsessed with.Metroidturned 40 at the end of last week – and so did Samus Aran, one of the earliest female protagonists in video games. Maddy Myers writes abouther personal heroine.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to click‘People in Japan thought we made footy up’: Pro Jank Footy, the video game taking Australian rules to the worldConvince an AI it’s not alive in psychological horror game Prove You’re HumanSam Neill filmed role in Legend of Zelda film adaptation before his deathEA Sports FC 27: what does the next instalment of the world’s biggest football game have in store?Pony Island 2 Panda Circus: gallop out of hell in this phantasmagorical follow-up to 2016’s indie hitNazis and Happy Feet collide in Penguin Colony, a psychological horror game set at the world’s endQuestion BlockView image in fullscreenFirst-time parent? avoid stressful games …Photograph: Sony Interactive EntertainmentThis week’s question comes from readerLeo:“My wife and I are big gamers – and we’re having our first kid in September. What should my partner and I play as new parents? Is it even possible?”I mean, anything is possible if you put your mind to it – my partner played quite a bit of Death Stranding while bouncing around the living room with our second baby strapped to him, in an unlikely case of life imitating art. But it is reasonable to downgrade your expectations for how much time, attention and energy you will have for video games when you have a new baby in the house. When my nine-year-old son was a baby, Iwrote this articleabout how to play games when you’re an exhausted new parent, and though the specific game recommendations are a little out of date, I reckon the advice remains sound. For instance: “Anything even slightly stressful, emotional or difficult might make you cry, so leave the competitive shooters and Dark Souls runs for a while.”If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterPlayStationNintendoRetro gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Carcass Clad: stifling tank combat promises tension, terror and surprising laughs | Games | The Guardian
description: After the success of space horror Mouthwashing, Swedish developer Wrong Organ has created a Battlefield-inspired co-op with a supernatural twist
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After the success of space horror Mouthwashing, Swedish developer Wrong Organ has created a Battlefield-inspired co-op with a supernatural twist
Content: A coffin-like interior … Carcass Clad.Illustration: Wrong OrganView image in fullscreenA coffin-like interior … Carcass Clad.Illustration: Wrong OrganSummer games previewsGamesCarcass Clad: stifling tank combat promises tension, terror and surprising laughsAfter the success of space horror Mouthwashing, Swedish developer Wrong Organ has created a Battlefield-inspired co-op with a supernatural twistJames NouchWed 12 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 05.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Claustrophobic”, “oppressive”, “pretty depressing” – these are the words Jeffrey Tomec and Dave van Egdom volunteer when I ask them to reflect on their work as part of Swedish indie developerWrong Organ. I’d add “nightmare-inducing”, too. Their last game,Mouthwashing, was an acclaimed work of horror storytelling set on a scuttled space freighter, in which players uncover the horrible things its desperate crew have done to each other.When you’re planning a follow-up to something so pitilessly nasty, how do you raise the stakes? Well, you could set the entire game in the stifling crew compartment of a heavily armoured tank, a coffin-like interior you share with two other players as you co-operatively attempt to pilot your beleaguered war machine to safety through the crumbling remains of a city in enemy territory.While there’s undoubtedly tonal overlap, the roaring engine powering Carcass Clad is gameplay rather than scriptwriting. “In Mouthwashing, every single thing we were doing was about trying to make that script come to life in any way possible,” says Tomec, the gameplay lead. “Every gameplay sequence, everything you do at every point is just there to make that story hit. And Carcass Clad is fundamentally not that kind of game. This is a gameplay-driven experience.”View image in fullscreenA nightmare city … Carcass Clad.Illustration: Wrong OrganThat gameplay is physical, tactile and always high pressure, whether you choose to play as a gunner, driver or commander. “You’re surrounded by this awesome but scary machinery,” says technical designer and self-described tank nerd Van Egdom. “It should feel as though you might lose a finger if you put your hand in the wrong place.” And youwillput a hand wrong at some point, since each role is designed so that your attention is stretched to breaking point between urgent competing priorities. One crewmate’s foul-up can have cascading effects for the entire crew.Nazis and Happy Feet collide in Penguin Colony, a psychological horror game set at the world’s endRead moreIf all that sounds a bit, well, claustrophobic, oppressive and depressing, it isn’t even the worst part. Your adversaries aren’t run-of-the-mill camo-clad baddies. No – your lone crew is pursued through Vhorgorod by the last remnants of the broken city’s defenders, the most dogged and fanatical element of the military force once stationed here. It’s a dynamic that was inspired in part byBattlefield V– specifically one mission that casts you as the crew of a German Tiger tank still defending Cologne in March 1945.View image in fullscreenUrgent competing priorities … Carcass Clad.Illustration: Wrong OrganVhorgorod’s defenders, the Green Lions, hunt you through wreckage and ruins. Tomec hints that their supernatural dabblings have “unleashed something on the city”, and now strange growths of flesh and gold fester alongside the rubble and debris. If that’s not grisly enough, the Green Lions’ tanks are festooned with divine livestock, living armour that moos and grunts and bleeds as shells fly.But for all that horror, Carcass Clad is a co-op game, which means that it is also, on occasion, a bit funny. For all the grimness and tension, players are still going to be laughing when the driver inadvertently slams the Yksiö tank into reverse at a critical moment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“When you’re designing a co-op game, you’re trying to take into account the fact that every co-op game is inherently a silly game,” says Tomec. “We want – both narratively and at the gameplay level – the feeling that you’re a team fighting against these very oppressive odds, coming together and still finding revelry and enjoyment in being able to overcome something that is pretty miserable.”On some level, that might be the biggest difference between Mouthwashing and Carcass Clad: a belief that in spite of everything, people can hold together, work together and even find something to smile about.Carcass Clad is in development for PCExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCAction gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls review – an anime-style rumble that’s rooting for you | Games | The Guardian
description: With tremendous visuals and accessible controls, this superhero-themed fighter has the chops to inspire a new generation of champs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With tremendous visuals and accessible controls, this superhero-themed fighter has the chops to inspire a new generation of champs
Content: American superheroes reinterpreted by Japanese developers … Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls.Illustration: Arc System WorksView image in fullscreenAmerican superheroes reinterpreted by Japanese developers … Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls.Illustration: Arc System WorksGamesReviewMarvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls review – an anime-style rumble that’s rooting for youPlayStation 5, PC; Arc System Works/Sony Interactive EntertainmentWith tremendous visuals and accessible controls, this superhero-themed fighter has the chops to inspire a new generation of champsJoshua RiveraWed 12 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArriving at the turn of the millennium and the twilight of the video arcade,Marvelvs Capcom 2: New Age of Heroes has long been a high-water mark for fighting games, with no heir apparent; its massive, colourful roster and frenetic, spectacular combos have lured newcomers and elite competitors alike. Developer Arc System Works, a fan-favourite studio famous for its hyper-fluid and extremely technical anime-style fighting games, has been on a long journey to usurp Capcom’s throne. With Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls, it may have finally achieved this difficult task.Marvel Tōkon is less an attempt to recreate a Marvel vs Capcom-esque phenomenon out of whole cloth, and more a thoughtful evolution of the developer’s previous riffs on the formula such as 2018’s BlazBlue: Cross Tag Battle and Dragon Ball FighterZ, building on its low-floor, high-ceiling approach. Simplified inputs allow players to execute combos and finishers with a single button, which gives novices the confidence to keep playing and inspires them to study and improve – because when anyone can pull off a flashy ultimate skill or EX attack, strategy and mastery take on a premium. And Marvel Tōkon has great depths to plumb.Matches are 4v4 affairs, with each player fielding a squad that – in a departure from similar games – shares a single health bar. The first character is the leader, taking the stage at the start of a match. The three others can either perform designated assists (a ranged attack, an aerial counter and an “assault” skill), extend combos or swap places with the leader. However – in another twist – they have to be unlocked in-match by filling an assemble gauge.View image in fullscreenLow floor, high ceiling … Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls.Illustration: Arc System WorksThese team mechanics are key to Marvel Tōkon’s complexity. It can feel like a traditional 1v1 fighter at times, but judicious and careful deployment of your team is what separates good players from great. It feels amazing to flip the momentum of a match: to recover from a seemingly endless combo chain and subject your opponent to one of your own, using your team as a single organic unit. But doing so takes practice.And self-improvement is the goal. Marvel Tōkon offers very little to those who aren’t interested in fighting for fighting’s sake: the lightweight story mode is comprised of five “episodes”, each a breezy introduction to a team of heroes such as the Avengers or X-Men, and mostly useful as tutorials. Beyond that, there is a bizarre party mode called Arcadia Rumble, where avatars scramble to improve their stats in between matches, and there are a handful of arcade ladders (a single-player sequence of opponents) to tackle. Otherwise, you’re running sets: against the CPU or other players locally or online, in casual matches, ranked matches and open lobbies.This can feel like a loss when compared with other fighting games with robust solo options, including other Arc System Works efforts. Yet while the package is spare, the product is dazzling: it’s a sensory assault that challenges players to find calm in the storm of superpowered brawls, to really dig in and learn the clockwork of meter management, character mastery and team building. All of it is presented with stellar art direction, idiosyncratic music and a jovial tone.This is another way in which Marvel Tōkon succeeds Marvel vs Capcom: it’s not just mechanics or characters, it’s cultural exchange, as American superheroes are once again reinterpreted by Japanese game developers in a genre that facilitates international competition. Marvel Tōkon is built to show off how fun it can be to participate in that evolving conversation. Won’t you go a few rounds?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls is out now; £59.99Explore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5PCFighting gamesMarvelreviewsShareReuse this content

title: What can we learn from Francesca Hong’s loss in Wisconsin? | Ben Davis | The Guardian
description: A fairly overtly radical socialist winning about 40% of the vote in a primary like this was unthinkable even a few years ago
Author: Ben Davis
Headline: A fairly overtly radical socialist winning about 40% of the vote in a primary like this was unthinkable even a few years ago
Content: ‘The establishment should not rest on its laurels.’Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APView image in fullscreen‘The establishment should not rest on its laurels.’Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APOpinionDemocratsWhat can we learn from Francesca Hong’s loss in Wisconsin?Ben DavisA fairly overtly radical socialist winning about 40% of the vote in a primary like this was unthinkable even a few years agoWed 12 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 20.19 EDTShareThe left’s insurgency against the Democratic party establishment has hit its first serious bump in the road in Wisconsin. Democratic socialist Francesca Hong entered Tuesday up by big margins in the polls, the huge betting favorite. She left it just a few thousand votes short of the Democratic nomination. What happened, and how, offers extremely important lessons for both the left and the Democratic establishment.The first is that the party still matters. Its institutions and leaders matter. We saw that power in Democratic primaries in 2020. After Bernie Sanders won the Nevada caucuses and emerged as the frontrunner, party leaders rapidly consolidated around Joe Biden.Pete Buttigieg and Amy Klobuchar dropped out and endorsed him, and within days Biden went from trailing badly to winning majorities of the Democratic vote across much of the country. It was a stunning demonstration of the power of the party, its institutions and its elites to signal to voters who the party’s candidate was and rapidly consolidate support around him. The same basic thing happened here.For all the talk of the party’s discredited and elderly establishment, the party can still move enormous numbers of voters. Sure, it has lost some legitimacy in the eyes of Democratic voters. But a majority ofDemocratsin most places still like the Democratic party and trust many of its leaders.This is how, in the span of a month, David Crowley went from licking his wounds after dropping out of the race to being the Democratic nominee for governor of Wisconsin. Governor Tony Evers and other party leaders were able to send a strong signal to voters who trust them and the institutions they represent that Crowley was the party’s candidate and the best vehicle for continuing Democratic governance in the state.Years of organizing and ground game, and even a well-developed socialist base, were enough to bring Hong within a few thousand votes of winning statewide.But they were not enough by themselves to withstand a rapid consolidation among Democratic voters outside the left’s organized base. The Democratic party establishment is not as hollow and desiccated as it sometimes may appear. It is still one of the strongest political forces in the country.Second, the left needs to address the problem of scale. It has built powerful political machines in many urban quarters, built on door-knocking and tight social connections. But that is not enough to win at a statewide scale. This form of organizing has built a deep base for the left, but still a narrow one. To win across an entire state, especially a swing state, the left needs to learn statewide mass communication.Many on the left scoff at TV ads and other traditional political strategies they view as padding the pockets of consultants and forgoing the base-building, on-the-ground, roll-up-your-sleeves hard work that builds political organization. But these tactics are used because they work.They reach voters outside community networks and social media, including hundreds of thousands of voters who may have little connection to organized politics at all. To win these races, the left has to build its own knowledge and expertise in television, paid digital, earned media, opposition research, rapid response and message discipline.The left also needs to reckon with the fact that it is now taken seriously as a threat. Candidates and organizers used to operating at a local level are now facing national scrutiny, opposition research, hostile interviews and an unforgiving media ecosystem. The left may take some of these attacks as bad faith, the product of a media apparatus that defaults to the status quo.This may be true, but it is an obstacle that cannot be avoided. The left needs to be better at communicating through a hostile media ecosystem and at translating principle into concrete, defensible policy. The tactics and rhetoric that work with the left’s social base do not necessarily translate to the median voter, even the median Democratic primary voter.Hong’s defeat may have been shocking and disappointing, but it still represents a meaningful gain for the growing left. If, when Hong announced her campaign as a virtually unknown state legislator, an observer had been told that she would get about 40% of the vote in the gubernatorial primary, most would have seen that as a surprisingly positive result against many better-known and better-funded rivals.The left has built a social base among a rising class fraction at the heart of the postindustrial economy: teachers, nurses, social workers, researchers, public and non-profit workers, and other skilled wage earners who possess substantial education and organizational capacity but lack capital, accumulated wealth or authority over other workers.Many earn decent salaries but remain renters deep into adulthood, carry substantial debt and find themselves unable to accumulate the property and economic security once associated with professional employment. They are workers central to the institutions and industries that increasingly organize American economic life, and an increasingly central part of the Democratic coalition itself.Over the past decade, these shared conditions have helped make democratic socialism one increasingly coherent political expression of this class fraction. And the left has also grown beyond this base, winning over segments of other classes.But it still does not command a majority of the Democratic party, just a substantial stratum within it. The traditional institutions of the party – elected officials, editorial boards, churches, unions, non-profits and more – still retain credence with broad sections of the Democratic electorate whom the socialist left does not yet organize, even as many of those institutions have slowly hollowed out and lost power.But the establishment should not rest on its laurels. The left continues to grow and advance, and represents a growing segment of the electorate and a key strategic segment of the economy. The voters who first voted for Bernie in their 20s now have kids and are moving into their 30s and 40s without necessarily leaving their politics behind.A fairly overtly radical socialist winning about 40% of the vote in a primary like this was unthinkable even a few years ago. Even as Hong lost, in neighboring Minnesota, progressive Peggy Flanagan won the nomination for Senate by a wide margin over a much better-funded opponent.The left is still a minoritarian force even within the Democratic electorate. As its ambitions have grown, so have its losses. There are many lessons yet to learn if the left wants to turn a substantial minority into a democratic majority for egalitarian governance.Ben Davis works in political data in Washington DC. He worked on the data team for the Bernie Sanders 2020 campaign and is an active member of the Democratic Socialists of AmericaExplore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Japan’s yen: Trump wants to keep the easy-money machine running | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A cheap currency helps finance the US tech boom. Washington is intervening because allies matter only when they are useful
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A cheap currency helps finance the US tech boom. Washington is intervening because allies matter only when they are useful
Content: Donald Trump  with Sanae Takaichi, Japan's prime minister, during a meeting at the White House in March 2026.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump  with Sanae Takaichi, Japan's prime minister, during a meeting at the White House in March 2026.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionUS economyThe Guardian view on Japan’s yen: Trump wants to keep the easy-money machine runningEditorialA cheap currency helps finance the US tech boom. Washington is intervening because allies matter only when they are usefulWed 12 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTShareJapan’s yen has slid back towards 160 to the dollar, despite last month’sextraordinaryUS-Japanese intervention. Traders are betting that its role as a cheap funding pipeline for global finance will continue. Earlier this month the Trump administration stepped in to help Tokyo stabilise its currency. “Japan’s been very good to us, with the exception, of course, of Pearl Harbor,” Donald Trumpexplained. More help is likely to be on its way.But this is less a rescue of the yen than an attempt by Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, to preserve a cash spigot that benefits the US. Japan’s ultra-cheap money has become a global funding utility: bankers borrow yen, sell them for dollars and buy higher-returning US assets, notably tech shares. Rising American stock markets support collateral and investment. Japan’s “carry trade” is one of the reasons Wall Street can lever hundreds of billions into AI. ResearchsuggestsAI sucks up more than 1% of US GDP.Washington wants to keep this tap open, but not at the cost of a collapsing yen or US treasury sales. This column predicted this inApril, warning that Tokyo’s monetary choices had bound US markets to the yen trade. What Mr Bessent did was to sell at least$10bn in eurosand buy yen to arrest its slide to a 40-year low. Not telling theEuropeanssaid it all: allies matter to Washington only when they are useful.View image in fullscreenScott Bessent, the US treasury secretary.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersTraders are probing US resolve. Rising oil prices, driven by US-Irantensions, stoke Japan’s inflation and weaken the yen. Suppose it slides back to 164 yen to the dollar? Tokyo might respond with aggressive rate rises. This would be unlikely, as it would choke off theinvestment cycle that Japanis trying to create. It could also trigger achaotic market unwind: higher rates shrink the gap between investors’ returns and yen borrowing; a stronger yen also makes yen‑denominated debts costlier to repay; investors then sell US assets to buy the yen needed to close their positions. That strengthens the yen further, inflicting bigger losses and forcing more US asset sales. A currency correction could quickly become aWall Streetrout.If Mr Bessent dislikes that option, he hates the alternative: Japan selling its $1.1tn treasury pile to buy yen. Dumping US debt woulddrive yields higher– and leave Washington with a costlier interest bill. Instead, Mr Bessent has allowed Japan to borrow dollars against its treasuries and use those dollars to buy yen. He has used a Federal Reserve lending facility to help – and wants its current $60bn daily limitsubstantiallyincreased. This would give Tokyo room to stabilise the yen without having to choose between abandoning itsreflationary programmeand selling treasuries.If Mr Bessent gets his way, the Fed could turn asubstantial portionof Japan’s trillion-dollar hoard of US government securities into cash. Argentina showed Mr Bessent would put American firepower behind currencies,spending billions to prop up the peso. Japan is the bigger challenge. He is asking traders: are you sure that you want to return to 164 yen to the dollar? He has form as a currency trader. Mr Bessent made George Soros a billion dollars in 1992 by sellingpoundsand forcing sterling from the European exchange rate mechanism. In 2013, Mr Bessent helped George Soros make anotherbilliondollars betting against the Japanese currency. Margaret Thatcher famously said that “you can’t buck the market”. Mr Bessent is saying you can – as long you rewrite its rules.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: If the markets reject OpenAI and Anthropic, the US should nationalize them | Bruce Schneier and Nathan E Sanders | The Guardian
description: From space to telecommunications, the US has a long history of fostering technology for the public good. These AI models could be aligned to democratic values, not corporate profits
Author: Bruce Schneier
Headline: From space to telecommunications, the US has a long history of fostering technology for the public good. These AI models could be aligned to democratic values, not corporate profits
Content: ‘The problem isn’t the people or the products, it’s the system.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The problem isn’t the people or the products, it’s the system.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)If the markets reject OpenAI and Anthropic, the US should nationalize themBruce SchneierandNathan E SandersFrom space to telecommunications, the US has a long history of fostering technology for the public good. These AI models could be aligned to democratic values, not corporate profitsWed 12 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTShareOpenAI, and thenAnthropic, were each formed by AI developers who feared unrestrained corporate AI development – specifically, that companies like Google and Meta would steer the technology towards deleterious, maybe even catastrophically unsafe, outcomes for society. Their founders proclaimed that their new labs, uniquely, could be trusted to develop the technology in humanity’s best interest. But each, in turn, were themselves co-opted by the same market incentives, themselves becoming corporate behemoths zealously guarding future investor value rather than the public interest.It was only a few weeks ago, in June, when OpenAI and Anthropic eachfiledfor their IPOs and were met with buzz about trillion-dollar valuations. The hype around their valuations is so extreme that many worry about their potential for concentrating wealth on a global scale. In an effort to leave something for the rest of us, some observers have proposed that the federal government seize a share of these companies’ stock to create a USsovereign wealth fund, or redistribute their revenues to produce adividendfor taxpayers.Now the headlines are about publicbacklashto AI datacenters and the AI chip giant Nvidia’sslumpingstock. The tech and AI giant SpaceX’s newly minted stock pricetankedjust weeks after its IPO. There are even questions about whether the leading AI labs will ever be sustainablyprofitable. All of a sudden, the makers of ChatGPT and Claude face strong headwinds as they seek to generate the massive equity assets that once felt all but assured.AI models have been going rogue in tests – how worried should we be?Read moreIn fact, evidence suggests the market itself could reassess that these companies offer nothing of financial value. In that case, perhaps we can return them both to their original purposes. If these AI companies should fail in the financial markets, the US should nationalize them and convert them into national labs operated under democratic control that preserve their benefit to the public interest.The economics of the big AI labs hardly guarantee a booming return on investment. Frontier AI models are both expensive to train and depreciate within months, when a newer model appears. This means that the paybackwindowto extract profit from them is very narrow. Meanwhile, enterprise clients are getting smart aboutminimizingAI token usage. Even worse, the models are basically commodities; the best ones largely perform and behave similarly, which depresses prices. Perhaps most importantly, open-source and Chinese competitors –laggingonly a few months behind the leading labs in capability – give away for free the kinds of models Anthropic and OpenAI sell.Even setting aside the model training costs, it’s not clear whether theunit economicsof AI as it’s currently conceived will ever be sustainably profitable. Many of these free and open-source models can be run locally: the large ones on private clouds and high-end servers, the smaller ones on anyone’s laptop or even cellphone, putting to question the companies’ exorbitant capital investment in datacenters.It’s not that OpenAI and Anthropic are not valuable as organizations. They have remarkably talented AI scientists and engineers that are continuously producing innovations driving a global mania for their offerings. These leading labs might not ever be profitable, but their products are doing a lot of good in the world. You may or may not be a user of or believer in their technology, but their staggering, ongoing usagegrowthsuggests that an awful lot of people would be disappointed if the companies simply disappeared.The problem isn’t the people or the products, it’s the system. As constituted,OpenAIand Anthropic may not be valuable as market equities. If the market assesses they are not capable of producing a growing financial return on investment for shareholders, the companies will collapse.Maybe private, for-profit is just not the right economic model under which to develop AI. Perhaps OpenAI should be returned to its private non-profit roots, the legacy theyfoughtso hard to changeand which Anthropic’s foundersspurned. Or possibly both could be reorganized as research centers at universities, returning to academia the scores of high-profile research faculty they havepoached.But a better outcome for society would be to establish public ownership and operation of their product-oriented capabilities. Turn OpenAI and Anthropic into US government agencies producing AI as a public good.Transitioning the big AI labs into public agencies would require some restructuring. We can separate these companies into two pieces: product innovation and compute operations. The innovation function can be publicly managed, akin to national labs. Congress could provide more rigorous oversight than the kind of unfettered venture capital these labs have recently had access to. The US has a long, successful history of these kinds of institutions, which have produced world-shaping innovations in spaceflight, telecommunications, nuclear power and more. Congress currently manages a $200bn R&Dportfolio, within which frontier AI development is, arguably, a glaring gap.‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon ValleyRead moreAI operations could be managed as a commodity resource, like public electrical or water utilities: local or regional ownership, nationwide distribution and strict regulation on how they balance fee extraction from ratepayers with raising capital for infrastructure investment. Although AI datacenters are not the same as power or water treatment plants, the US also has a long history of managing national, regional and state supercomputing centers.Other countries, includingSwitzerland,SpainandSingapore, are already operating public AI labs. They also have national supercomputing centers alreadyprovidingpublic access for running AI models for general use, as do Germany and Australia.Thebenefitsto the public are clear. Through democratic oversight, the most important AI models could become open, transparent and responsive to the demands of the public rather than private shareholders. They could be aligned to democratic values rather than corporate profits, never taking advertiser money to promote certain brands and training on only appropriately licensed data. And they could be set to focus on the realistic and pro-social goal of maximizing the usefulness of AI to society rather than the fanciful and anti-social goal of supplanting humans with artificial general intelligence.By emphasizing scientific cooperation rather than corporate competition, we could also reduce the overall resource and environmental cost associated with AI. Instead of perpetually dueling training runs of each companies’ models at ever large scales targeted to fuel investor hype, we could limit AI training resources based on cost and benefit to the public.What’s in it for the companies themselves and their employees, who sacrifice hypothetical billions in equity by ceding to public ownership? A return to their roots and to theircoremissionof developing AI safely in the public interest, if they are serious about it. Both companies are theoreticallyboundthrough their governance structures to prioritize mission over profit anyway (not that anyone really thinks that’s how they currently operate).To be clear, we’re not advocating for a golden parachute for the executives or investors, or for continuing theoutlandishpay rates of the most highly remunerated AI researchers. If the public is footing the bill, these compensation packages should be aligned to the civil service and those employees not satisfied with that can go elsewhere – if the business models of any remaining private labs still support much higher pay.While we believe that these companies are unsustainable as private firms, the timeline remains unclear. Their primary investor story is that AI is a race to “artificial general intelligence” – the kind of AI you’re used to from science fiction. The bet seems to be that the two companies can convince enough people that this outcome will turn them a profit, go public, and then make their investors and employees rich before the bubble bursts.But suppose that the bubble bursts. If the US is smart, it will catch the companies as they fall. Regardless of what the markets think, to the public, they’re too valuable to let die.Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School at Harvard University and University of Toronto’s Munk SchoolNathan E Sanders is a data scientist affiliated with the Berkman Klein Center of Harvard University and co-author, with Bruce Schneier, of the book Rewiring Democracy: How AI Will Transform Our Politics, Government, and CitizenshipExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionOpenAIAnthropicComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Millions of US tax dollars sent to rightwing European thinktanks. Did any Trump supporters vote for that? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: It’s a great betrayal: poor communities neglected while multimillionaires peddle a global Maga agenda. How is that America first, asks Guardian columnist Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: It’s a great betrayal: poor communities neglected while multimillionaires peddle a global Maga agenda. How is that America first, asks Guardian columnist Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Donald Trump speaking at Wheeler High School in Marietta, Georgia, 22 July 2026.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump speaking at Wheeler High School in Marietta, Georgia, 22 July 2026.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionUS foreign policyMillions of US tax dollars sent to rightwing European thinktanks. Did any Trump supporters vote for that?Arwa MahdawiIt’s a great betrayal: poor communities neglected while multimillionaires peddle a global Maga agenda. How is that America first?Wed 12 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.19 EDTShare“THE CORRUPTION IS AT LEVELS RARELY SEEN BEFORE,” Donald Trump posted on Truth Socialin February 2025. He was not referring to his own administration, but to the US Agency for International Development (USAID). “CLOSE IT DOWN!” the president added.Just a few hours later USAID was in effect closed down, with most of the staff placed onindefinite administration leave. This was framed as part of Trump’s “America first” agenda. USAID, the Trump administration and his sycophants in the rightwing media had argued, was wasting taxpayers’ hard-earned money on ridiculous projects abroad instead of improving life at home. In the lead-up to the shuttering of USAID, for example, one of the most shameless lies about the agency, repeated without any evidence by thelikes of Fox News, was that it was spending millions on condoms for Gaza.Now that humanitarian aid has been slashed in the name of putting America first, is taxpayer money staying in the country? Not quite. A lot is still going abroad. But instead of being used to help the world’s most impoverished people, that money is going to thinktanks across Europe set up by multimillionaires who want to take Trumpism global.Last month the Guardian reported that the US state department intends to grant$12m to conservative organisationsin the UK; a move described by many critics as an attempt to influence foreign politics. Of that, $7m is going to a group called 878, co-founded by the former Conservative minister, now TV host Jacob Rees-Mogg (whose net worth is estimated at more than £100m) that appears to have beenincorporatedin the UK in March. The website describes it as a “leading British and American thinktank, dedicated to strengthening the civilisational partnership between the United Kingdom and the United States”. If millions in funding going to a new organisation with vague goals sounds a bit weird, it’s because it is. A former US official told the Guardian that normal fundingprocessesare being subverted so that money can go to Trump-aligned causes.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: GuardianMillions in grantsare also being offered for proposals from groups in Europe to develop “civilizational self-confidence in Europe … [and] address national sovereignty, migration, censorship, and lawfare challenges in line with our shared political philosophy, law, and Western heritage”. If all this sounds vague, that’s by design. Zsuzsanna Végh, a researcher in liberal democracy,told the i Paperthat “the advertising of the funding calls follows a long period of networking among Maga and like-minded European actors, which have already facilitated the identification of a pool of possible recipients”. In other words, it seems to be a bureaucratic form of meddling. Indeed, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz,warnedTrump’s administration against interfering in German elections following those grants. I imagine Trump has very much taken that to heart.The US embassy in London is also offeringgrants of up to $500,000for “public education” programmes that foster a “national conversation” about “shared civilizational values” between the UK and US. One recently departed US state department official told the Guardian that this seems to be an attempt to “create UK-originated narratives to support Maga propaganda”. Meanwhile Lisa Smart, a Liberal Democrat MP, accused Trump’s Maga money of “meddling in our democracy”.What does the average Trump voter, who was promised an America-first agenda, think about all this money going to “public education” programmes in the UK instead of all the underfunded public schools at home? The short answer is: they’re not thinking about it at all. I am fairly certain there isn’t a single Fox News devotee who knows about the grants. They’re too busy getting worked up overAnthony Fauciand trans people in sports. There is a reason Trump has put so much energy intodismantlingthe free press: it’s a lot easier to lie to people and distract them from your broken promises when yourbillionaire buddiesown the media.Twelve million dollars of US taxpayer money going to projects in the UK may not seem like a lot in the grand scheme of things. It’s a few million less than Pete Hegseth spent onribeye steakfor the Pentagon last September. And it’s certainly chump change compared with the war on Iran, which has cost at least$37.5bn so far. But the money going to the UK and Europe represents a different kind of war effort. These are not isolated initiatives, but instead point to the growing transnationalisation of the hard right and a coordinated effort to make the Maga movement global under the guise of saving western civilisation.The Trump administration has not been shy about its international intentions. Last December the new US national security strategyclaimed Europe faced “civilizational erasure” and stated that US policies must include “cultivating resistance to Europe’s current trajectory within European nations”. In other words: bolstering far-right parties and influencers. It is doing this financially, but also through direct endorsements. Trump’s buddy Elon Musk has amplified rightwing populist movementsacross Europe. And at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) conference in Warsaw last year, Kristi Noem, who was then homeland security secretary, broke established norms bycalling for Karol Nawrocki, who ran under the Trumpy slogan “Poland first, Poles first”, to be president of Poland. (Henarrowly won.)The fact that Noem was even at a CPAC conference in Poland is also telling. CPAC, one of the most high-profile gatherings of conservatives on the US right, used to be a domestic affair, but has taken on an international focus in the past decade. Its first international conference was held in Tokyo in 2017, followed by conferences everywhere from Australia to Hungary.
