Last month also saw theinaugural British franchiseof CPAC, called CPAC GB, spearheaded by the former Conservative prime minister Liz Truss, who ran the country for just 49 days. “We believe the fight for freedom and conservative values doesn’t stop at America’s borders,” CPAC’s chair, Matt Schlapp, told Axios last year.All this brazen meddling in foreign affairs is alarming. However, the US hard right may have overreached by trying to take Maga global without actually addressing American problems first. The average person in the US cares less about this crusade to “save” western civilisation than about whether they can afford petrol and groceries. And trying to square America first promises and Trump’s pledge not to startany new warswith rising costs thanks to the Iran war is starting to get tricky.Last month a Politico pollfound that just a third of Trump’s Maga base thought the war in Iran was worth the cost, down from half in May. Influential Trump supporters such as the podcaster Joe Rogan have also turned on the presidentbecause of Iran.Trump, for his part, has brushed off cost-of-living concerns, declaringlast year: “I don’t want to hear about the affordability.” But the president, who made an estimated$2.2bn last year, should start listening. The average Trump voter may not know anything about all the grants their taxpayer money is funding in Europe. But it’s becoming more obvious to even the most diehard Maga fan that they are being put last.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUS foreign policyOpinionTrump administrationUSAIDDonald TrumpThe far rightJacob Rees-MoggUS-Israel war on IrancommentShareReuse this content

title: Isn’t it amazing what a policy that actually tackles the cause of outrageous house prices can do? | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: Labor has shown what a government can do to improve housing affordability, exposing how pathetic previous attempts had been
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: Labor has shown what a government can do to improve housing affordability, exposing how pathetic previous attempts had been
Content: ‘“Property recession” is not a thing,’ writes Greg Jericho. ‘Let’s not make up terms just because real estate agents’ profits have taken a hit.’Photograph: Diego Fedele/AAPView image in fullscreen‘“Property recession” is not a thing,’ writes Greg Jericho. ‘Let’s not make up terms just because real estate agents’ profits have taken a hit.’Photograph: Diego Fedele/AAPGrogonomicsAustralian economyIsn’t it amazing what a policy that actually tackles the cause of outrageous house prices can do?Greg JerichoLabor has shown what a government can do to improve housing affordability, exposing how pathetic previous attempts had beenGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 12 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 19.29 EDTShareFor the first time in 25 years, an Australian government actually did something about housing based on the idea that the only way to make houses more affordable is for house prices to fall. They stopped pretending there was another way.For years, politicians liked to talk about how, if incomes rise faster than house prices, housing becomes more “affordable”.But let’s cut through all the shrubbery.When the median house price in Sydney at the end of last year was $1.56m – that’s $605,000 (63%) higher than it was in the middle of 2020 – getting income to rise a bit faster than prices was not going to do much at all.Prices needed to fall.The way the market was set up was just helping those with property and those making stonks of money lending out ever larger mortgages. There’s a reason why Commonwealth Bank yesterdayreported a bumper $10.9bn profitfor 2025-26 (up 7%) and yet was warning things might not be so good for 2026-27.And that’s because,after three interest rate rises and a government finally willing to undo the damage of the 50% capital gains tax (CGT) discount and negative gearing,prices have actually begun to fall.Homes in Australia are now cheaper – why can’t the government sell this good news story? | Saul EslakeRead moreIt speaks to just how pathetic every attempt since 2000 to address the decline in housing affordability has been that only now, after tackling the CGT discount and negative gearing, are there headlines about price falls.The big one this week is ANZ research suggesting that by the end of next year prices in capital cities across the country will have fallen 10.6%, with falls of 14.5% in Sydney.Horror show!Or so the leader of the opposition,Angus Taylor, would have you believe.On Tuesday he opened the first question time of this sitting period by asking the prime minister: “The ANZ bank today reports Sydney house prices could fall by almost 15%, the worst crash in more than four decades. Will the prime minister finally admit Labor’s broken promises on capital gains tax and negative gearing have made millions of Australian homeowners worse off?”My goodness, the worst “crash” in four decades!Not to be outdone, oneproperty agentsuggested we are in a “property recession”.I guess it’s time to start getting the kids to gather at the feet of gen Xers to hear them talk about the dark days of the early 1990s.Please.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailFirst off, “property recession” is not a thing. Let’s not make up terms just because real estate agents’ profits have taken a hit.But more seriously, let’s look at those price fall projections by the ANZ that have Taylor’s jimmies so rustled.ANZ on Tuesdayforecast Sydney house prices over the next two years would fall 14.5% from the peak at the start of this year, 12.8% in Melbourne, 7.9% in Brisbane, 9.8% in Adelaide and 5.2% in Perth.Using the ABS figures for median house prices, that would take the median price for a house in Sydney from $1.56m at the end of last year to $1.33m.That’s all the way back to 2023 prices – and still $379,000 (40%) higher than they were in June 2020.The projected fall in Brisbane wouldn’t even take away a year’s worth of price increases, and in Adelaide the price drop would still leave the median price 80% higher than they were in the middle of 2020.If the graph does not display click hereWhen prices have risen so fast for so long, a 10.6% average price fall over two years across the country is not something to panic about. Rather it is finally an end to madness.But here’s the thing: yes, ANZ forecast prices will fall 10.6% over 2026 and 2027, but then in 2028 they forecast a 4.3% increase.If the graph does not display click hereIn the grand scheme of things it is barely a dip, let alone a crash or recession.But it will mean the cost of a house in terms of household incomes will finally begin to go down.On Tuesday the Reserve Bank’slatest Statement on Monetary policycontained its predictions out to the end of 2028.Using these together with ANZ’s projections we can make a decent estimate for what the cost of the average dwelling in Australia will be in terms of years of average household disposable income.From a height of 17.3 years’ worth of annual income in the March quarter this year, we could see average dwelling prices fall to 14.7 years’ by the end of 2027 (before slightly rising in 2028).That would be the biggest two-year improvement in housing affordability going back to 1970:If the graph does not display click hereIsn’t it amazing what a housing policy that actually tackles the cause of house prices can do?Obviously, it doesn’t undo 25 years of damage but it’s a nice start. And it’s a heck of a lot better than what we have seen before.For a government battling in the polls, it might be worth it pondering that showing what a government can do is rather more impressive than coming up with excuses for why it can’t.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsAustralian economyGrogonomicsLabor partyHousingTaxAustralian politicsAnthony AlbaneseAngus TaylorcommentShareReuse this content

title: Farage has turned Clacton into a human zoo. Here’s the truth about what’s happening here | Sarah Elizabeth Cox | The Guardian
description: When I moved to the town in 2022 I loved the beach walks, cheap drinks and panoramic coastal views. Now it feels like a never-ending circus, says historian Sarah Elizabeth Cox
Author: Sarah Elizabeth Cox
Headline: When I moved to the town in 2022 I loved the beach walks, cheap drinks and panoramic coastal views. Now it feels like a never-ending circus, says historian Sarah Elizabeth Cox
Content: Clacton pier, 6 August 2026.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenClacton pier, 6 August 2026.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersOpinionClacton byelection August 2026Farage has turned Clacton into a human zoo. Here’s the truth about what’s happening hereSarah Elizabeth CoxWhen I moved to the town in 2022 I loved the beach walks, cheap drinks and panoramic coastal views. Now it feels like a never-ending circusWed 12 Aug 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTShareClacton town centre is bustling, the beaches are packed and the pier’s raking in cash. We can credit the weather, but no doubt press coverage and Count Binface’s promotional videos have got us on radars too. The tourists look like they’re having a lovely time.I moved to Clacton in 2022 and the first year was brilliant. It started with beach walks, cheap drinks and decorating a flat with panoramic sea views, and ended fat and happy from chips and ice-cream, a newborn baby in tow. Privileged with my health and stable income, albeit strained by aTruss-era mortgage, it was a place I loved, and was proud of.ThenNigel Faragetargeted us, and shit hit the fan.With the general election in 2024, the world’s press descended, and then came thousands of social media comments that left me embarrassed, sad and fuming. You’re all thick, racist, gullible, hateful, toothless, jobless old fools, we were told. You deserve him. The worst of the snobbery was, sadly, on my lefty social media platform of choice, Bluesky.Farage was elected with 46% of a 58% turnout. Fine,somepeople actually are gullible fools. But the other parties rolled over and failed to bother, treating us with contempt. I didn’t support, but I understood, why 46% voted as they did. I still loved Clacton, but it got harder to defend. Then things died down and we were forgotten again by everyone, including our new MP.The gag about Farage not knowing where we are isn’t exactly true – he pops by for photo opportunities like a ceremonial mayor – but he seemsless keen on surgeries, or representing Clacton in the Commons. Snaps for the local newspaper’s Facebook make fans think he’s doing great things for businesses and charities. It’s smoke and mirrors. Check Hansard for “Clacton” and see how many times he’s raised a Clacton issue in parliament (six times). Then do “Colchester” for Pam Cox and “Ipswich” for Jack Abbott. Compare and contrast.We wanted him to actually be an MP. To notice the homeless people, freezing all winter in closed bank doorways, and now lining the coastal paths in tents. To notice how we’ve been priced off the railways – the commuter trains are empty. The worsening health, declining life expectancy. The low employment rates and lack of affordable homes. We don’t have an A&E. We don’t have maternity care after 5pm. It would have been nice too, if he’d spent more time doing what he said he would, and what Binface has achieved instead – promoting our towns and villages’ positives. There are many, I promise.Nobody wanted a byelection. For the many people struggling here, there is little energy for another awful circus. Clacton didn’t need yet more focus on Farage, Farage, Farage, while the area’s entrenched and complex problems continue to be ignored by him and by the government.This summer, the media presence has been even bigger than in 2024. Content creators and reporters continually vox pop outside Wetherspoons, cherrypicking quotes about how great Nigel is, how persecuted Nigel is. Well, we’re being swarmed with migrants, aren’t we? Getting put up in hotels while we struggle. It’s not like it used to be round here. The Turks, they’re taking over with the barber shops. Or, I don’t really do politics. They’re all the same as each other. A welcome few, it has been pleasing to see, have started to notice the slipperiness, the back of fag packet policies and his absence.The “Migrants Out” leaflets were pushed into our homes, a turquoise Reform bus did the rounds and sad men with silly hats and placards yelled things in the town square. I’ve seen anti-racism campaigners told to F off, and can’t leave my flat without the smug face of a British Democratic party candidate leering down at me from giant poster boards. It has all felt surreal, hostile, dividing. Generally bad vibes.The nasty, stereotyping, hurtful comments about us continue. With some exceptions – like Tim Burrows’thoughtful portrait of Clacton– we’re a human zoo, and the butt of a joke. Farage used us as a pawn, and the media treats us as clickbait.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYet in shops, the gym, pubs, on the beach, in the street, at the park, at nursery drop off, I’ve not overheard a single conversation about any of it, unless it was between a reporter and a local. Not one. The leaflets started getting left in the hallway, unread. Few of my family or neighbours plan to vote. We’re angry at him, but we are also bored, and exhausted.My prediction: It’ll be a low turnout, Farage way ahead, with Binface second but the only real winner. I’ll read about how we wasted the chance for a hilarious outcome, you idiots. You gullible, racist fools. You deserve him. And so on. Then it’ll die down again, briefly, and we can get back to what’s left of the summer, the lives Farage has no clue about or interest in and keep talking about the things that really matter in Clacton: litter, landlords, potholes, parking and whether there’ll be a second series ofSecret Lives of Gypsy Wives.Sarah Elizabeth Cox is a historian, and communications manager for a science charityExplore more on these topicsClacton byelection August 2026OpinionNigel FarageReform UKImmigration and asylumVoter apathycommentShareReuse this content

title: Heard about the ‘luteal uglies’? Women know more about our hormones than ever – and that’s beautiful  | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: When I was younger, female biology was seen as something to be overcome. Now we can talk about the reality of living in our bodies, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: When I was younger, female biology was seen as something to be overcome. Now we can talk about the reality of living in our bodies, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: ‘Women’s hormones have become trending topics.’Photograph: d3sign/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Women’s hormones have become trending topics.’Photograph: d3sign/Getty ImagesOpinionWomen's healthHeard about the ‘luteal uglies’? Women know more about our hormones than ever – and that’s beautifulRhiannon Lucy CosslettWhen I was younger, female biology was seen as something to be overcome. Now we can talk about the reality of living in our bodiesWed 12 Aug 2026 06.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTShareHave you got the “luteal uglies”? I’m not trying to insult you, merely deploying the latest hormonal buzz phrase on social media, which refers to the phase in a woman’s cycle, two or so weeks between ovulation and menstruation, when she apparently feels at her lowest and most unattractive due to a drop in oestrogen levels.Women’s hormones have become trending topics and, as someone who only found out what a “luteal phase” is when she Googled it, mid-fertility panic, in her late 20s, I am somewhat in awe of the expertise with which younger women discuss their menstrual cycles now. They’re just so incredibly literate.Beyond being taught at school about periods and my mum explaining PMT, the impact of hormones on our emotional lives wasn’t discussed much when I was younger. In the “post-feminist” 1990s and early 2000s, female biology was seen as something to be suppressed and overcome, and the emphasis of most sex education was preventing teenage pregnancy. Being on the pill from 14 didn’t exactly put you in touch with the natural rhythms of your cycle, either, though of course it had other benefits (such as preventing the aforementioned teenage pregnancy).You can understand the rationale, which was that female biology should never hold you back. Yet sometimes that felt like pretending your reproductive system didn’t really exist, or that you should simply push through the more difficult, painful aspects. “My period always comes as a surprise to me,” a friend said recently. She’s not the only one.‘Why do I feel crappy?’: women are learning about their luteal phases - and Maha is weaponizing itRead moreThere were always girls who diligently marked the days in their diaries, but a large proportion of us barely kept track, unless of course your period arrived very late (prompting an urgent trip to the school nurse). By contrast, today’s young women have access to a plethora of period tracker apps and products, not to mention an avalanche of content pertaining to menstruation, ovulation, the luteal phase and how our hormones can impact everything from our psychological states to our body image to our sex lives. This also applies to postpartum and older women, with topics such as matrescence, perimenopause and menopause being discussed far more widely.Despite the proliferation of psychobabble and therapy-speak, there’s also some good science. I can’t help but be impressed. Knowledge is, after all, power. I’m glad I was taught that biology doesn’t have to be destiny, but it shouldn’t have meant needing to play catch-up on educating myself about my own reproductive system. Knowing what’s going on in your body and having the language to describe it can have all sorts of psychological benefits. It’s comforting that the negative body image and the tiredness, bloating and other symptoms that come with the luteal phase can be fleeting. There’s a reason you feel this way, so maybe you don’t need Botox, you just need a rest.And maybe, actually, you don’t want to have an affair, you’re just ovulating, which can increase your libido (or, to quote another friend, cause you to “go a bit feral”) andmake you appear extra attractiveto members of the opposite sex.For me, it has been important to understand that a monthly desire to explode my life is probably a mild form of premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Knowing this not only helps me warn my loved ones in a “here be dragons” sort of way, but also prompts me to try to take better care of myself instead of deciding to get divorced and move to Crete to become a ceramicist. I don’t think my symptoms are serious enough to warrant treatment, but the increase in online discussion about these issues has helped equip many with the language needed to access diagnosis. Misinformation can be an issue, though, which is why the curriculum needs to catch up.The fact is, hormones can shape our lives in profound ways. It’s something I explore in my fiction. That is not to say that we should always let them. We must, too, be vigilant. We have seen, especially in the US, how women’s cycles can be co-opted to forward patriarchal, authoritarian agendas, as in theperiod tracker data scandal, and Maga’s attempts to put women off taking birth control. I’m less worried about women’s willingness to adopt labels than I am about capitalism’s inevitable response to labels: a “fix”, whether that’s a pill that can “cure” the luteal uglies, an app that “tracks” your cycle and sells the data on, or something even more sinister.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUsually, when the mainstream media talks about this subject, it is almost always in a pro-natalist context of women needing better “fertility education” so that they don’t leave it too late to have babies, despite the fact that the biological clock is one of the few things we are very used to being lectured about. That’s why hearing reproductive education discussed in the context of aiding women’s self-understanding, wellbeing and mental health feels so radical.The information itself isn’t new – I could have looked it up in a textbook – but the way of talking about it is. It’s emancipatory, in that it encourages women to know and take control of their bodies, but it’s also realistic about the reality of living in those bodies. Women of previous generations have also navigated that balance – they weren’t all sold on the notion of “burying the body” – but never so many, all at once. It’s basically a movement, and I am here for it.Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist and the author ofFemale, NudeExplore more on these topicsWomen's healthOpinionMenstruationReproductionHealthBiologycommentShareReuse this content

title: Nigel Farage looks trapped and rattled – now the nationalist tide can be turned | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: There are more votes in tolerance and decency than in toxic division. It doesn’t take a great leap of political courage to fight back against Reform, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: There are more votes in tolerance and decency than in toxic division. It doesn’t take a great leap of political courage to fight back against Reform, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Nigel Farage canvassing in Clacton, Essex, on 8 August 2026.Photograph: Jacqueline Lawrie/LNPView image in fullscreenNigel Farage canvassing in Clacton, Essex, on 8 August 2026.Photograph: Jacqueline Lawrie/LNPOpinionNigel FarageNigel Farage looks trapped and rattled – now the nationalist tide can be turnedRafael BehrThere are more votes in tolerance and decency than in toxic division. It doesn’t take a great leap of political courage to fight back against ReformWed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 09.11 EDTShareNigel Farage can be confident of victory against a man posing as an ennobled space traveller with a dustbin on his head. At least, in Clacton he can.The refusal of major parties to contestthis week’s byelectionsets the bar low. But even if the competition were more serious than Count Binface, the Reform UK leader would be the favourite to win on his chosen turf. He picked the constituency as his safest shot for a parliamentary seat in the 2024 general election for a reason. Now he is betting that the stench of scandal around his personal and party finances, pungent in Westminster, won’t sicken his fans on the Essex coast.He’s probably right, which is why Labour and the Conservatives sensibly denied him the spectacle he craved – a “people versus the establishment” prize fight. The plan was to put the question of his failure to declare a£5m donationto the electoral court of Clacton. It would be settled not by adjudication of the parliamentary standards authority but with a knockout blow from the fist of Furious Farage.Unfortunately for the crypto-billionaires’ champion, the investigation hasn’t disappeared and could resume if he wins his pantomime bout witha bin.If a subsequent decision goes against him, a second byelection could follow. That twist could easily be written into Farage’s script as further proof that the system was rigged against him; that the acclamation of his innocence by his loyal Essex jury was not sufficient and they must vindicate him again, louder.The shape of the argument is textbook populism. A candidate’s virtue is measured by the volume of clamour he can summon from a crowd. Institutions of established democracy are valued only as ladders aiding his ascent. If they hold him accountable in any way, they are dismissed as tools of the elite that conspires against the will of the people.It is a sign of vulnerability that Farage’s definition of “the people” has shrunk to whatever portion of Clacton constituents turns out for him on Thursday. When his cause was Brexit, he could wield a national referendum mandate to denigrate dissent. When opinion polls and council ballots showed Reform on course to win a general election, the party leader had a putative prime ministerial swagger in his step. He has slipped.For now, Reform strategists are not too anxious about losing their headline lead to Labour. Second place, after a period of unusually hostile media coverage, while a new Downing Street regime enjoys a (probably brief) honeymoon is not a calamitous position. It could be proof of resilience as much as weakness. More worrying for Farage are histanking personal ratingsand evidence from recent Greater Manchester byelections (two for parliamentary seats; one for the mayoralty vacated by Andy Burnham) that aversion to Reform is coalescing into an effective tactical bloc vote.That sentiment is resolute. Farage has been a prominent British public figure for two decades. People who see his multiple, rebranded parties as one metastatic malignancy in the body politic are not open to persuasion that he can be something more benign. He used to curate his brand with feinted moderation. That is harder now that Reform faces competition fromRupert Lowe’s Restore Britain partyin the far-right zone where hostility to immigrants dispenses with non-racist euphemism.Lowe is more anchor of a social media channel than leader of a party. He harvests clicks in the field of digital paranoia, irrigated by extreme content on Elon Musk’s X platform, where it is axiomatic that “indigenous” Europeans face systematic replacement in their homelands by dark-skinned aliens.Restore took almost 9% of the vote in the first round of the Manchester mayoral byelection, ahead of the Tories and Liberal Democrats. Lowe, elected to parliament in 2024 as a Reform MP,has offered to form an alliancewith his old party, but with conditions attached, including the insistence that Tory defectors be barred from any future role in government.A less-rattled Farage would heap derision on his former comrade. He might even have exploited the schism to confect a new boundary between “mainstream” and “far” right. He could highlight tonal differences between his and Lowe’s politics and apply them as camouflage of respectability.That he doesn’t suggests lack of confidence in the loyalty of Reform’s hardcore vote. More disturbingly, it implies openness to the idea that, where immigration is concerned, British politics is not yet maxed-out at the furthest limits of rightward expansion.The shift is stark enough already. Parliament has passed a new act tightening border control or limiting migrants’ rights every year since 2022. Such assiduous attention to the issue has done nothing to satisfy demands for harsher measures. Nor has it refuted the absurd suggestion that mainstream politics and media, constrained by timorous liberalism, refuse to address a question that has, in reality, dominated the agenda for a generation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe legislative ratchet is also a rhetorical dial, turning public debate more shrill. The language of invasion, once the metaphorical preserve of extremists, has been normalised. Gangs ofmasked marauderswho go on racist rampages through UK towns are cast as protesters manifesting legitimate concerns. The articulation of their grievance in terms that make foreignness synonymous with parasitic consumption of benefits, criminality and sexual predation goes unchallenged.Meanwhile,net migration has fallen dramaticallyfrom its peak earlier this decade. Instead of welcoming the turning tide, the anti-immigrant right has shifted its focus from resisting new arrivals to undermining the status of legally settled communities, denying theirentitlement to public services, blocking paths to naturalisation and building a case formass deportations. This used to be the stuff of skinhead rallies and crank byelection candidates who lost their deposits. Now resistance depends on the guy with the bin on his head. Or at least, in Clacton it does.Elsewhere the picture is less bleak. Farage retreated to his coastal haven for an electoral comfort break, getting relief from scrutiny in a place where he can still enjoy unchallenged status as the man of the people. But his people are fewer than they were and never as many as he claims. If he has hit the ceiling of his national support and feels part of his base wobbling beneath him, he will try to consolidate by further radicalisation. That will then give more urgency to the anti-Reform voter coalition.He is trapped. But only if other parties refuse to follow him a single step further down the road to ethno-nationalism, where immigration policy degenerates into sinister fantasies of demographic engineering, and instead push back.It isn’t a hard choice. There are many more people in Britain who like to live happily alongside their neighbours, regardless of skin colour and country of origin, than want to burn them out of their homes. It doesn’t take a great leap of political courage to draw a line between rigorous migration control and racist demagoguery.There were good reasons for major parties to sit out this Thursday’s byelection. But from Friday onwards, the task of fighting Farage can’t be delegated to a man with a bin on his head. Not even in Clacton.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsNigel FarageOpinionClacton byelection August 2026ByelectionsLabourConservativesReform UKImmigration and asylumcommentShareReuse this content

title: Ceuta showed just how easy it is to divide Europe | Paul Taylor | The Guardian
description: The migrant influx prompted recriminations and a tit-for-tat dispute between Italy and Spain. Putin, Erdoğan and others will have taken note, says the European Policy Centre’s Paul Taylor
Author: Paul Taylor
Headline: The migrant influx prompted recriminations and a tit-for-tat dispute between Italy and Spain. Putin, Erdoğan and others will have taken note, says the European Policy Centre’s Paul Taylor
Content: Spanish police check documents of travellers from Italy at Madrid Barajas airport, 8 August 2026, after a dispute between the two countries.Photograph: Spanish Police/ReutersView image in fullscreenSpanish police check documents of travellers from Italy at Madrid Barajas airport, 8 August 2026, after a dispute between the two countries.Photograph: Spanish Police/ReutersOpinionSpainCeuta showed just how easy it is to divide EuropePaul TaylorThe migrant influx prompted recriminations and a tit-for-tat dispute between Italy and Spain. Putin, Erdoğan and others will have taken noteWed 12 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 03.13 EDTShareWithin hours of the first pictures of tens of thousands of migrants swimming the short distance from Morocco to the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta hitting social media on 30 July,22 European Union leaders, the Trump administration and Israel had piled on to criticise Madrid.The outbreak of hysteria and recrimination was a case study in 21st-century politics, driven by real-time images in a media echo chamber where populists set the agenda on migration, propagating fear, prejudice and demagogic proposals. Above all, the kneejerk reactions undermined trust between European allies and dealt a setback to EU efforts to jointly manage migration, counter people-smuggling and resist the weaponisation of migrants by non-EU countries.That Donald Trump and JD Vance should seize the opportunity to accuse socialist Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez of inviting the mass influx byallowing more than 1 million irregular migrantsalready working in Spain to apply for legal status is hardly surprising, given the US administration’s own relentless drive to detain and expel illegal immigrants.On the other hand, European leaders who signed a letter to the European Commision, criticising Spain and demanding an emergency meeting of interior ministers, should ask themselves how their behaviour helps the EU implement a coherent response to migratory pressures. Many are open to charges of hypocrisy, since Germany andItalyhave, between them, regularised hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrant workers at the request of employers who need their labour as the home workforce dwindles.There was also a monstrous foreign policy double standard in the initial EU response.When Poland and Lithuania faced a sudden influx of irregular migrants from Belarus in 2021, the EU rallied behind its eastern members and imposed sanctions on Minsk’s authoritarian regime, which stood accused of weaponising displaced people from the Middle East. The previous year, the EU sent its Frontex border agency to help Greece repel a surge of migrants from Turkey at the countries’ shared border in Thrace, which had apparently been encouraged by Ankara to put pressure on the EU.View image in fullscreenCrowds gather near Fnideq on the Morocco-Spain border, 31 July 2026.Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty ImagesYet this time, EU governments quickly fell into a divisive blame game, terrified by images that recalled the loss of control over borders in south-eastern Europe in 2015, when more than 1 million mostly Syrian refugees entered the bloc. Amid the internal finger-pointing, neither the EU leaders nor the European Commission dared question the role ofMorocco, whose border guards apparently stood aside as more than 72,000 Moroccans, mostly young men, risked their lives swimming to Ceuta after seeing viral social media claims that “Spain is open”.The incident occurred on Morocco’s annual Throne Day when King Mohammed VI, who does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over the territories of Ceuta and Melilla, just happened to be visiting the nearby northern city of Tétouan, once part of the Spanish protectorate. Some commentators have called the stampede to Ceuta a “Blue March”, in reference to the massGreen Marchthat the king’s father, Hassan II, launched in 1975 in an attempt to claim the vast territory of Western Sahara, then a Spanish colony.“In Morocco, nothing happens by chance,” says Anna Terrón Cusí, a senior fellow at theMigrationPolicy Institute and a former Spanish secretary of state for immigration. Even if the stampede to Ceuta started spontaneously with social media posts, she believes “this was a multi-actor, multi-factor event. It was more a geopolitical than a migration crisis.”Intra-European party politics played a big role. It was not surprising that the Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, should lead the assault on Sánchez. She heads up the hard-right Brothers of Italy movement and faces a domestic challenge in elections next year from a new, evenfurther-right party, led by a retired general.Some Spanish and UK anti-immigration politiciansrushed to Ceutato take selfies, one from Reform UK doing a standup interview on the beach to cash in on the purported alien “invasion”.It was more bizarre that Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen, who heads a centre-left government, should co-initiate with Meloni the letter to Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, and say that the EU should consider suspendingSpainfrom the Schengen area of open-border travel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA facade of European solidarity was restored after EU interior ministers held a hastily arranged videoconference. By that time, almost all the migrants had left Ceuta and returned to Morocco after realising that they had no chance of reaching Europe. The “invasion” had deflated. In fact, irregular migrant arrivals in Spain fell sharply last year, while across the EU they’re down for the second successive year, and far below the 2015 crisis peak. But the damage was done.Italy and Spain are now engaging intit-for-tat passport and nationality controlson each other’s travellers, and Russian president Vladimir Putin, Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and King Mohammed himself will have noted how easily Europe panics and turns on its own members at the first sight of migrants on its beaches.Whether out of misinformation or malice, some EU ministers distorted the nature of the Spanish amnesty for undocumented migrants, labelling it a “pull factor” for mass migration. Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani,claimed they were being grantedSpanish and therefore European citizenship, rather than simply being given a chance to apply for temporary work visas.Europe faces what in game theory is called the “prisoners’ dilemma”, and in social sciences a “collective action problem” . EU countries have a shared interest in preserving the Schengen zone of free movement, with open internal borders vital to the smooth operation of the economy, well-managed external borders to deter irregular migrants and combat people smugglers, and legal migration routes to permit an inflow of workers needed by businesses as the European population ages and shrinks.Yet they keep undermining cooperation due to a seemingly irresistible short-term political interest in anti-migration grandstanding.Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy CentreDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsSpainOpinionMigrationMoroccoEuropeEuropean UnionPedro SánchezItalycommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Nightmare fodder’: Roku’s AI slop channel is even worse than expected | Television | The Guardian
description: Fairground TV is a 24/7 channel devoted to low-quality AI content for viewers sick of watching real people move in ways that won’t haunt you
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Fairground TV is a 24/7 channel devoted to low-quality AI content for viewers sick of watching real people move in ways that won’t haunt you
Content: Roku’s Fairground AI Creator TV is television with vanishingly low production costs. You probably will not tune in, and that’s sort of the point.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoku’s Fairground AI Creator TV is television with vanishingly low production costs. You probably will not tune in, and that’s sort of the point.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersTelevision‘Nightmare fodder’: Roku’s AI slop channel is even worse than expectedFairground TV is a 24/7 channel devoted to low-quality AI content for viewers sick of watching real people move in ways that won’t haunt youStuart HeritageWed 12 Aug 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe appeal ofRokuis that, whatever you happen to want to watch, there will almost certainly be a live channel for it. Just want to watchLittle House on the Prairie? There’s a channel for it. Just want to watch Duck Dynasty? There’s a channel for that too. Purely want to watch nothing but local news from Wisconsin? Guess what: there’s a channel for that too.But despite this wealth, a section of the population was still to see its needs fulfilled. What about people who hate plot and vision and the sight of people speaking convincing dialogue that synchronises perfectly with the movement of their lips? What about the people who just want to watch an unyielding torrent of eerily weightless nightmare fodder? Well, good news. Roku has finally caught up.It was reported last week that Roku launched theFairground AI Creator TV channel, the first free, all-AIstreaming channel that pulls content from roughly 100 AI creators around the world. Early reactions were, to put it mildly, not great. The Vergecomparedit to eating from a trough, while Futurismcalled it“bottom-of-the-barrel slop”.AI ‘actor’ Tilly Norwood has a movie coming out. Spare us this future | Dave SchillingRead moreIn truth, you will not watch Fairground AI Creator TV, and that’s sort of the point. This is television with vanishingly low production costs. Compare an hour of this cheap slop with, say, the tens of millions of dollars it takes to produce an episode ofStranger Things, and you’ll soon understand why executives might find the prospect irresistible. In this landscape you don’t need breakout hits, just enough stoned and curious students at 3am to turn a profit.That said, I have actually just spent a few hours watching Fairground AI Creator TV, more out of self-hatred than anything else, and it would appear that the early reviews are right. On the plus side, the channel is evidence that artificial intelligence has come on in leaps and bounds over the last couple of years. Had this been attempted in 2023, we would have had a 24/7 feed of mutant Will Smithchoking down handfuls of writhing spaghetti, and everyone would have vomited themselves dry. Generally speaking, what Fairground has to offer is much better.However, it is still awful. Categorically, catastrophically awful. The channel doesn’t so much offer shows as a drifting dreamscape of bad ideas rendered as horribly as possible with no thought paid to scheduling. At one point on Wednesday, a shrill high-frequency anime gave way to a long and staid German-language short about Nazi bureaucracy. After that came a sort of Gladiator ripoff that had all the dynamism of an exhibit you’d see at the fourth-best museum on a poorly planned family holiday.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onplatform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueIn fact, as an aside, there seems to be an awful lot of this. Switch on Fairground at any time of day and I’d estimate you are no more than 15 minutes away from seeing a witless, sepia historical drama of some description, full of craggy, burly men glowering at each other, dramatically lit by sunset regardless of which direction they’re facing. There is so much of it that it worries me about the future of the medium. The promise ofAIis that it allows limitless story potential, and yet the bulk of it ends up looking like what would happen if your dad lucked himself a job scheduling Sunday afternoons on ITV3.There are still horrible glitches to navigate – stray mouths that don’t move in time with dialogue, impossible physics, one specific instance of a man trudging through snow while his feet bizarrely made a clip-cloppy hoof noise – but these are becoming less and less frequent as the technology improves. The bad news about this is that you’re forced to concentrate on the storytelling ability of the people who made this. And you simply cannot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChristopher Nolan says people ‘disdain’ AI and the idea it will replace humans is ‘nonsense’Read moreBecause it – all of it, every last stinking second of every godawful film – is completely inert. It is devoid of weight, of life, of vision and wit. The channel just flatly sits there, impressed by itself despite being physically unable to hold anybody’s attention. You may as well be watching a screensaver, a CD-Rom menu screen or a fridge.The hope is obviously that something like Fairground will be the future of entertainment, churning out muck for pennies while an entire stratum of creatives go hungry. And who knows, one day it might achieve this. The technology is moving so quickly that it isn’t impossible to see it eventually developing the capacity to convincingly entertain.But on the basis of what I’ve seen, that day is still a long way off. At one point, the channel cut away to a commercial for Roku’s Dr Phil channel, and the sight of an actual flesh-and-blood human acting in an identifiably human way almost moved me to tears. And surely anything that makes you emotional about Dr Phil of all people doesn’t deserve to exist.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionAI (artificial intelligence)US televisionComputingAIfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Houses with long histories are magical’: David Olusoga on the home history show that’s gripped the UK | Television | The Guardian
description: At first, I worried that only historians would find A House Through Time compelling. But its appeal is so enduring that fans of the show stop me in the street to ask when they can watch more
Author: David Olusoga
Headline: At first, I worried that only historians would find A House Through Time compelling. But its appeal is so enduring that fans of the show stop me in the street to ask when they can watch more
Content: ‘The architecture of Edinburgh is special’ … David Olusoga in the Scottish capital for his new BBC Two series of A House Through Time.Photograph: BBC/Twenty Twenty Productions Ltd/Richard RankenView image in fullscreen‘The architecture of Edinburgh is special’ … David Olusoga in the Scottish capital for his new BBC Two series of A House Through Time.Photograph: BBC/Twenty Twenty Productions Ltd/Richard RankenTelevision‘Houses with long histories are magical’: David Olusoga on the home history show that’s gripped the UKAt first, I worried that only historians would find A House Through Time compelling. But its appeal is so enduring that fans of the show stop me in the street to ask when they can watch moreDavid OlusogaWed 12 Aug 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy is that some TV programmes find an audience, catch people’s imaginations and become not just watched but loved? Most of course do not. Having been making TV since my late 20s and been involved in a number of “first” series that ended up being the only series, I am painfully aware of that. If producers knew in advance which shows would be hits, there would be no flops, as the industry cliche goes.Producers and presenters are lucky if, during our careers, we get to be involved in a single show that makes that rare transition from being part of the schedule to part of people’s lives. Almost a decade ago, while we were filming the first series ofA House Through Timefor BBC Two, I was not at all convinced that this was a show that had the potential to break through.Having studied urban history for my master’s, I always loved the central premise: that we could explore the histories of Britain’s great cities through the people who had lived in a single house, from the very first resident right up to the current owners. Likewise, I was, from the start, enamoured of the astonishing array of human stories which the brilliant teams that worked on the series managed to unearth.I liked the way thehistory of the housein that first series, 62 Falkner Street in Liverpool’s Georgian Quarter, perfectly followed the broader history of Liverpool: the city’s rapid rise to wealth and power as the great port of empire, its devastation in the blitz, then a precipitous postwar decline that saw 62 Falkner Street become a warren of slum apartments seemingly doomed for demolition only to be reprieved by the gentrification of the early 21st century.However, I was concerned that audiences would struggle to understand why we had locked ourselves into the straitjacket of a single house. Why were we viewing the past through such a tiny aperture? What were we missing by being so tightly focused? At times during the scripting and the filming of that first series, I worried that perhaps I was too close to the subject and that only historians of the city would find the show compelling. I was, it turned out, doing what TV producers are infamous for doing. I was underestimating the audience.View image in fullscreen‘One of those shows that only TV could make’ … David Olusoga with Kate Lister in the garden of the Edinburgh House in A House Through Time.Photograph: BBC/Twenty Twenty Productions Ltd/Richard RankenThis month, almost 10 years after the first series was commissioned, series six of A House Through Time goes to air. We have now made 24 hour-long episodes that have explored the hidden histories of houses in Liverpool, Newcastle, Bristol, Leeds, London, Berlin and nowEdinburgh.Like everyone who presents TV shows, I am regularly stopped on the street by people who recognise me from their screen. Most often what they want to talk about is A House Through Time.Amazingly, that remains the case even after I appeared on the great TV juggernaut of our time: The Celebrity Traitors. The first question I am asked by the fans of A House Through Timeis almost always the same: when is the next series coming out? So I am left to wonder why a show about which I had doubts has been such a hit. What had I not appreciated 10 years ago?What I didn’t get back then, above all, is what old houses mean to the people who live in them. Houses with long histories are magical places. Anyone who has ever lived in such a house has, on a sleepless night or perhaps after too many glasses of wine, found themselves wondering who else had lived out their life in those same rooms. Whose hands once gripped the same banisters; who, like you, knew where the creaky floorboard was and which windows would start rattling on a windy night?A House Through Time reveals – in incredible detail – the sorts of human stories that would tumble out of our own home if only we had the time to go looking. It reminds us that houses have longer lives than we do. That no matter how many years or decades we live in them, our time there represents a single chapter in their far longer story.After making 24 hours of A House Through Time,and with the TV industry in a less healthy state than it was a decade ago, I also now appreciate, more than ever, that it is one of those shows that only TV could make.Only TV – and let’s be more specific, only public service TV – would invest the time and money needed to uncover history at this level of granularity. Only TV would believe that the stories of ordinary people – not kings or presidents or movie stars – could grip audiences of millions. And only TV is capable of assembling teams of specialist researchers, assistant producers, producer/directors, series producers and executive producers with the skills needed to track down the thousands of documents that become the jigsaw pieces that make up the bigger historical puzzle.In every series, breakthroughs have arrived at the last minute, often in the last weeks of filming, all because an assistant producer or a researcher, digging in the archives and working far beyond the call of duty, has located a missing link or noticed a tiny detail that answers a nagging question or confirms a long-held suspicion.This new series follows the same pattern but in a new nation. I have long wanted to take A House Through Time to Scotland, and series six is set in an 18th-century house up on Calton Hill in Edinburgh. The Scottish capital was hard to resist. Edinburgh is one of the handful of cities that are not just architecturally but also topographically breathtaking. Built around a castle that sits on top of an extinct volcano, with other volcanic features looming on the horizon, Edinburgh is up there with Cape Town, Hong Kong and Rio de Janeiro when it comes to the sheer drama of its setting.The architecture of Edinburgh is similarly special. Encircled by city walls, Edinburgh had a scarcity of space that meant the only direction in which to build was up. The result was a vertical city of stone tenements, some rising to 10 or more floors. Edinburgh has been described as a medieval Manhattan. When it comes to urban density and vertical living, it has more in common with Prague and Stockholm than it does with most English cities. Our house, up on Calton Hill, is one of Edinburgh’s smaller tenements – a stolid stone structure built over five floors.As with the previous series, the life stories of the people who lived in those rooms are diverse and idiosyncratic. Among the earliest tenants was a man at the centre of one of the strangest trials in Edinburgh’s history, having committed a crime so bizarre and infamous that it was depicted in engravings that were sold on the city streets. Another resident took up arms, joining a volunteer regiment during the fraught and divided years after the French revolution, when the elite and the middle classes saw the spectre of revolution in every darkened corner.One of our Victorian residents was a woman who, more than any of the figures from the past who have appeared in any of the previous series, successfully eluded the efforts of the production team to pin down her story. Why was she so elusive? Perhaps because she converted the house into what Edinburgh police records rather delicately describe as “a house of ill-fame”. Another of our 19th-century residents was a sculptor who created monuments that are still peppered across the Edinburgh cityscape, statues I have been walking past since I was brought to the city as a child in the 1970s.If there is another reason to explain why A House Through Time has caught on it is that the series plays a small part in a bigger story: the expansion of history. History has for decades been getting bigger and more inclusive. History is no longer just about “great men”. The emergence of social history, working-class history, women’s history and imperial history has uncovered the lives of people once deemed of little interest. The genealogy revolution has made millions of people into amateur historians. Today our ancestors – all of them, no matter how humble their lives – are deemed worthy of study and remembrance.A House Through Time is on BBC Two on Thursday 13 August at 9pmExplore more on these topicsTelevisionDavid OlusogaDocumentaryFactual TVSocial historyEdinburghfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for Amy Lee of Evanescence | Music | The Guardian
description: The metal icon is here to answer your questions about the band’s 90s origins, MTV fame and being trailblazer in a male dominated genre
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The metal icon is here to answer your questions about the band’s 90s origins, MTV fame and being trailblazer in a male dominated genre
Content: Amy Lee performs at the Evanescence 2026 World TourPhotograph: Scott Legato/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAmy Lee performs at the Evanescence 2026 World TourPhotograph: Scott Legato/Getty ImagesFilm & Music reader interviewMusicPost your questions for Amy Lee of EvanescenceThe metal icon is here to answer your questions about the band’s 90s origins, MTV fame and being trailblazer in a male dominated genreLaura SnapesWed 12 Aug 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 12.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is 23 years since Evanescence released one of the defining debut singles of the 2000s, Bring Me to Life, frontperson Amy Lee’s account of escaping an abusive relationship. Since then, the Arkansas band – essentially Lee’s project – have become a towering force in rock, selling millions of records, winning Grammy awards and reshaping how the genre can sound thanks to their inclusion of classical music and piano-led balladry.In June, the band released their sixth album, Sanctuary, produced by former Bring Me the Horizon member and now metal super-producer Jordan Fish. The album, Lee has said, confronts the political turmoil of her country, and stands “against tyranny, against human rights violations, against blowing people up”. The record arrives on vinyl for the first time in September (after its digital release in the summer) and heralds an in-demand UK tour.You can ask Lee about that, or anything else, when she sits for the Guardian’s Film & Music reader interview. Perhaps you want to know about the band’s 90s origins – she started the band as a teenager – or what inspired her to fuse classical music with metal; her experience of peak-MTV fame and her distaste at her label forcing a rap on to Bring Me to Life to keep pace with the nu metal of the period; being a trailblazer in what was an extremely male space and her successors – Evanescence took Nova Twins and Poppy on tour last year– or what it takes to keep a band going for three decades.Post your questions in the commentsby 10am BST on 17 Augustand Lee’s answers will appear in a future edition of the reader interview.Explore more on these topicsMusicFilm & Music reader interviewPop and rockIndiecalloutShareReuse this content

title: Death Note: The Musical review – wildly popular manga mystery is a killer night out | Stage | The Guardian
description: The multi-platform phenomenon makes its way to the stage, with all the supernatural hijinks, J-horror tropes and emotional intensity intact
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The multi-platform phenomenon makes its way to the stage, with all the supernatural hijinks, J-horror tropes and emotional intensity intact
Content: Schoolkid killer … Xander Pang as Light, in Death Note: The Musical.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreenSchoolkid killer … Xander Pang as Light, in Death Note: The Musical.Photograph: Manuel HarlanStageReviewDeath Note: The Musical review – wildly popular manga mystery is a killer night outBarbican, LondonThe multi-platform phenomenon makes its way to the stage, with all the supernatural hijinks, J-horror tropes and emotional intensity intactAndrew PulverWed 12 Aug 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe know that people like to dress up for the theatre, but some of the crowd at Death Note: The Musical take it to a whole other level. Coiffured and corseted, bedecked in gauze or festooned with diamanté, it is a sight to behold, with an appreciable element going for full cosplay. This, for the uninitiated, is because the source material has emerged from the fan-cultivating world of Japanese manga, originating in 2003, and which has (in a characteristic manner) sold millions of copies in comic book and novel form, jumped to an animated TV series and feature film iterations, and evencrossed over to a Hollywood treatment in 2017.A live musical seems a bit of a sideways step, though; this kind of material doesn’t often find itself in theatres, but perhaps the success of the Barbican’s staging will see more given the go-ahead. (This is actually a second London appearance for Death Note, after a short run at the Palladium and Lyric in 2023.) You can certainly see the appeal. Shorn of the original’s convoluted digressions, and with a dilution of the original manga’s play for the teen-boy readership, this emerges as a smart, metaphysical whodunnit – or perhaps, more accurately, howdunnit – with a nice line in emotional intensity cranked up by its power-ballad musical score.Despite its elaborate plot superstructure, Death Note (again, for the uninitated) rests on a fairly simple idea, familiar from J-horror of yore. Someone’s name gets written in a spooky notebook and … THEY DIE. All sorts of random, self-imposed rules materialise to make things difficult, as well as a bunch of supernatural presences/deities who face their own set of pulled-from-nowhere consequences for their actions.View image in fullscreenTop-notch cast … Death Note: The Musical.Photograph: Alan West/Hogan Media/ShutterstockThe adapters – Frank Wildhorn (music), Jack Murphy (lyrics) and Ivan Menchell (book) – have slimmed things down to focus on three principals: drunk-with-power schoolkid killer Light (Xander Pang), maverick but brilliant detective L (Colin Ryan) and pop princess turned lovelorn slayer Misa (Stephanie Zaharis). Light and L’s struggle to, respectively, rule like a god and head off the tide of carnage the death note triggers forms the meat of the show, and all three performers attack their roles with grade-A gusto. Telly Leung and Grace Mouat as apple-munching chaos-stirrer Ryuk and goth-bride lookalike Rem, respectively, provide top-notch support as the presiding deities.Fortunately, the whole thing starts strong, with a floodlit opening scene that combines brilliantly athletic dance moves (by a supporting company that is excellent throughout) and a schoolroom debate about the ethics of justice, and just keeps going from there – with neat forced-perspective sets, flashy back projections and amusing sliding stage elements. Death Note purists might not be completely on board with the alterations, but I would challenge anyone not to have a good time with this.AtBarbican, London, until 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageMusicalsMangaTheatreComics and graphic novelsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I turned down Gandhi because I’m terrified of snakes’: the amazing movie memories of Bruce Dern | Movies | The Guardian
description: Famed for playing loners, cranks and wayward angels, the Hollywood star is now a wolfish 90 – but he still jogs daily. As he takes his latest film to Edinburgh, we meet the man Hitchcock called ‘the golden calf’
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: Famed for playing loners, cranks and wayward angels, the Hollywood star is now a wolfish 90 – but he still jogs daily. As he takes his latest film to Edinburgh, we meet the man Hitchcock called ‘the golden calf’
Content: ‘I don’t consider myself old’ … Dern, whose new film Northbound premieres in Edinburgh.Photograph: Christina House/Contour RA by Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I don’t consider myself old’ … Dern, whose new film Northbound premieres in Edinburgh.Photograph: Christina House/Contour RA by Getty ImagesMoviesInterview‘I turned down Gandhi because I’m terrified of snakes’: the amazing movie memories of Bruce DernXan BrooksFamed for playing loners, cranks and wayward angels, the Hollywood star is now a wolfish 90 – but he still jogs daily. As he takes his latest film to Edinburgh, we meet the man Hitchcock called ‘the golden calf’Wed 12 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 05.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Can you take another story?” asks the veteran actor Bruce Dern towards the end of our talk, as though every tale is a drink and the landlord has called last orders. He doesn’t want to keep me and knows we’re running out of time. It’s just that one memory sparks another and these tales won’t tell themselves. He says that the next one is a doozy. “It’s about Marilyn Monroe.”Throw out all the questions and turn the clocks to the wall. One does not interview Dern so much as say hello, hit record and sit back. The man began his career acting alongside Montgomery Clift and Mary Astor and has collaborated with everyone from John Wayne to Tom Hanks, Hitchcock to Tarantino. He’s the lawless survivor of American movies, blown in from the past, and talking 19 to the dozen. “I’m 90 fucking years old,” he tells me. “So I’m not going to be around to see all this AI shit or whatever. But I don’t consider myself old. I still walk and jog every day.”double quotation markI was always second or third banana – but I’d come up from behindHe used to run seriously and was good at it. Running, he says, taught him how to pace himself, stay focused and not lose heart when his rivals streaked ahead. “Every time I ran I used to have to come up from behind. And it was the same in showbusiness, I was always the second or third banana, never the first choice for anything. But when you’re running a marathon you learn that the first 16 miles don’t matter. It’s really only the last 10 miles that count.”I confess that I love Dern in his lagging, dragging early years, too, when he played Jack Nicholson’s shady brother inThe King of Marvin Gardens, Robert Redford’s nemesis in the 1974 version of The Great Gatsby, and the world’s last botanist in theeco-fable Silent Running. But his final straight has been a blast, a downhill dash after all those gruelling hard yards.Dern’s turn as a lost, flailing dreamer in Alexander Payne’s Nebraskawon him the Cannes best actor award at the age of 77. He returned to the festival again this year as the star of a documentary tribute, Dernsie, named after his signature habit of breaking from the script. The scene in Once Upon a Time in Hollywood when Brad Pitt’s hero introduces himself as Cliff Booth, only for Dern’s befuddled old rancher to mutter, “John Wilkes Booth?” That was a Dernsie, cooked up on the spot.View image in fullscreenEarly years … Dern as the world’s last botanist in Silent Running, 1972.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyBoth visits to Cannes were terrific, he says. After the documentary screened, the organisers sat him on stage and the applause rolled on for six minutes. The festival boss, Thierry Frémaux, asked what that meant to him. “And I said, ‘Well, what it means is that Cannes gives a shit.’ I’ve gone through my whole life trying to find people who give a shit about Bruce Dern. And I’ve found it twice – both times in Cannes.”Who is to say that he’s not about to find it in Scotland? Next week he’s booked at theEdinburgh film festivalwhere his latest movie, Northbound, receives its world premiere. Dern plays incorrigible Arthur, who’s on a final lap of his own, fleeing a stuffy US nursing home for his old boyhood shack on a Canadian lake. Northbound is scratchy on the surface and sentimental underneath. It’s like Nebraska’s sweeter and sunnier cousin. “Yeah, they’re related,” Dern says, although further details elude him. “This one was a little movie that we made in Canada for about a million-six American dollars. We made it in 30 days during the Olympics. But it was two years ago now.”I’m surprised to hear that Dern feels overlooked. He’s such a distinctive, arresting presence; the wolfish guide to America’s wonky corners, perfect at playing loners and cranks and wayward angels alike. Nicholson – his onetime rival and close friend – ranked him among the finest performers of the late-60s Easy Rider generation. If actors are cattle, Hitchcock liked to joke, “then Bruce is the golden calf”. He landed juicy roles and made money, but it was always an insecure life. It took an Oscar nomination for his role in 1978’s Coming Home to make him feel he belonged – and even then, only slightly.Arthur in Northbound longs for his childhood home. Dern can’t relate. Where is home anyway? He was born into a wealthy, well-connected Chicago family (Adlai Stevensonwas his godfather; Eleanor Roosevelt babysat) who all but disowned him when he quit college to act. He trained at the celebrated Actors Studio in New York, studying under Elia Kazan and Lee Strasberg, but was rarely given any lines and struggled to make much impression. “I got very impatient,” he says. “The other men at the Actors Studio were starting to make it: Harry Guardino, Ben Gazzara, Tony Franciosa. They were all acting and directing and going off to Hollywood. Not Brucie! I was on stage not speaking. I was still Harpo-fucking-Marx. When I finally made my Broadway debut, it was in a play called The Shadow of a Gunman. I had one scene and six lines and was on stage for 52 seconds. So you tell me, who’s going to give a shit about that?”View image in fullscreen‘A little movie we made in Canada’ … Bruce Dern in the film Northbound.Now he’s on a roll; the old days bubble up. He says: “The Actors Studio had a baseball team. Our best pitcher was George C Scott. Peter Falk with one eye was our third baseman. On Memorial Day weekend we’re playing softball in the park. And Gadge – that’s what we called Kazan, Gadge – turns to me and he says: ‘What are you still doing here? Why aren’t you in California? We never said you couldn’t go.’ Well, that’s what I’d been waiting for. The next day, a Tuesday, I went to California and I never went back. Memorial Day 1960.”Hollywood, he explains, was first his lifeline, then his base. He worked on Hitchcock’s TV show and acted in Roger Corman B-movies, before bagging his first big respectable movie in1969’s They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?“You can’t even find that movie any more,” he tells me. “It came out, won an Oscar and then disappeared. I got a copy for my birthday. It’s probably the only one.”I’m wondering how Kazan kept him quiet all those years. The man’s a glorious loose cannon, garrulous and digressive; two parts Ancient Mariner to one part Grandpa Simpson. His stock of stories is bottomless, although he has his favourites. Dern remembers the time he introduced Hitchcock to the director John Frankenheimer and the day Bette Davis called Joan Crawford a cunt. The Hitchcock-Frankenheimer meeting, he adds, happened the same week a stray boulder blocked the Pacific Coast Highway, which meant that you had to drive to the boulder, squeeze past on foot and then continue your journey in a second car. This in turn made him late for lunch at the Bel-Air Hotel. He says, “I don’t know if you know the Bel-Air Hotel. It’s not very big. It has, like, two storeys.”View image in fullscreenHome straight … with June Squibb in 2013’s Nebraska.Photograph: Photo credit: Merie W Wallace/Paramount Vantage/AllstarI don’t know it, I tell him, but he has already moved on to another lunch date. This one is with Sir Richard Attenborough. The director is practically begging our hero to play the American journalist in Gandhi. Dern re-enacts the exchange; their back-and-forth dialogue. “I said, ‘Where do I have to go?’ and he said, ‘India’. I said, ‘India? The country, India?’ I said, ‘I have a confession to make. I need to run every day and I am terrified of snakes. If I run outside my hotel in the morning, will there be a guy on the steps with a basket and a snake?’ He said, ‘Probably.’” That was enough, Dern was out. “Martin Sheen ended up playing that part.”Can I take another story? Keep them coming; the more the merrier. Dern once met Marilyn Monroe at the Actors Studio. He walked her all the way across town to her home near Sutton Place, in the east of Manhattan. At one point they passed Greta Garbo on the street and Monroe broke down crying because she thought Garbo didn’t know her.Dern has told this story before; it’s part of his regular repertoire. All being well, he’ll be telling it another decade down the line. “I’m done,” says Arthur towards the end of Northbound, gazing out from his deck at the morning mist on the lake. By this point I suspect that the interview might be done, too. We’ve been talking for two hours and Dern’s voice has turned croaky. I thank him for his time, because he has been ridiculously generous. “You’re welcome,” he says. “Thank you for giving a shit.”Northbound screens at the Edinburgh film festival on 17 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmEdinburgh film festivalNebraskaCannes film festivalFestivalsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: In Venice, it’s not politics as usual as film-makers aim to recapture our attention | World news | The Guardian
description: As social media shrinks and distorts the EU’s crises, the Venice film festival is delivering politically forthright epics from directors such as Sergei Loznitsa and Alex Gibney
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: As social media shrinks and distorts the EU’s crises, the Venice film festival is delivering politically forthright epics from directors such as Sergei Loznitsa and Alex Gibney
Content: Russian journalist Ksenia Mironova in the film My Undesirable Friends: Part One. Part Two is at the Venice film festival in September.Photograph: Julia LoktevView image in fullscreenRussian journalist Ksenia Mironova in the film My Undesirable Friends: Part One. Part Two is at the Venice film festival in September.Photograph: Julia LoktevThis Is EuropeWorld newsIn Venice, it’s not politics as usual as film-makers aim to recapture our attentionAs social media shrinks and distorts the EU’s crises, the Venice film festival is delivering politically forthright epics from directors such as Sergei Loznitsa and Alex GibneyDon’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up herePhilip Oltermann, European culture editorWed 12 Aug 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEurope is in an economic crisis that, unlike the eurozone downturn at the beginning of the millennium, cannot be measured in ratings downgrades and borrowing costs. For metrics, try engagement depth and consumer trust instead.The unedifying spectacle of the European Union’s falling out over the Ceuta crisis looks like the latest symptom of Europe’s shrinking attention economy. When more than 70,000 people crossed over from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the start of the month, Rome hastily reintroduced air and sea border checks with Spain for one month; Madrid retaliated with spot-checks on travellers to Italy.Politicians were falling over themselves to match the wildfire speed of social media, for this was a geopolitical flashpoint that appears not just to have been engineered but also politically processed via short video clips online. The crossings were reportedly triggered by viral videos suggesting that Spain’s border with Morocco was opening, while their framing as an “assault” or “invasion” was amplified by accounts with links to the Russian military,as Aisha Down reported. Platforms such as Instagram, Facebook and TikTok are built to reward content that instantly hooks in viewers – three seconds long is the golden rule. How can lawmakers ever keep up?View image in fullscreenImperium, a film about the USSR created from archival footage.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FesitvalYet what if, paradoxically, our attention economy is both shrinking and expanding at the same time? I’ve found it hard to shake that impression after perusing thelineup at the forthcoming Venice film festival, opening on 2 September.This year at the Lido, you can watch a three-hour film about the Italian Communist party sending a camera team to the Soviet Union (Imperium, by Ukrainian auteur Sergei Loznitsa); a four-hour documentary about Elon Musk (Musk, by American director Alex Gibney); or a more than five-hour video diary about Russian dissident journalists in exile (Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II). Too short for you? Then, get tickets for Luca Guadagnino’s Joie de Vivre, a lengthy analysis of the films of compatriot Bernardo Bertolucci. It clocks in at seven hours.For the most part, these are surprisingly politically forthright titles at a film festival that in the recent past has focused on glitz and glamour. Loznitsa’s documentary seeks to shatter the remnants of the left’s illusions about the Soviet Union; Loktev gives a voice to the journalists silenced by Putin; Gibney’s Musk film has already been preemptively dismissed by the far-right tycoon as a “hit job”. But are they trying to stretch out attention spans so much that they risk playing only to a gallery of cinephiles?On the topic of impactful film-making …skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA call to creative action … Dr Lina Qasem-Hassan, a Palestinian doctor in Israel’s healthcare system, in the documentary, The Oath.Photograph: Guardian DocumentariesPerhaps there is a point between both extremes to capture people’s imaginations and attention. That’s what the Guardian is hoping to prove, in collaboration with Franco-German culture channel Arte. We are inviting film-makers to propose short-form documentaries exploringdemocracy in Europe today. The winning submission will be presented at theDOK Leipzig film festivalat the end of October, and subsequently receive funding, editorial support and distribution through Guardian Documentaries and Arte platforms. The deadline for submissions is 14 September.Crucially, they should be no longer than 20 minutes – a length that Jess Gormley, the Guardian’s executive producer of documentaries, argues “encourages participation and debate”. She points to recent Guardian documentaries such as Liane Aviram and Louis Hollis’s 23-minute shortThe Oath, about a Palestinian doctor in Israel’s healthcare system, which led to its protagonist being invited to speak in front of the UK parliament – a film that held, rather than overwhelmed our attention.To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is EuropeEuropeVenice film festivalFestivalsVeniceDocumentary filmsAlex GibneynewslettersShareReuse this content

title: From sensation to spectacular, to silence: the strange history of Coleridge-Taylor’s Song of Hiawatha  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Chances to hear Samuel Coleridge-Taylor’s choral masterpiece in concert are rare. Ahead of its belated Edinburgh festival premiere with the Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal, we look at the epic work - and its epic baggage
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Chances to hear Samuel Coleridge-Taylor’s choral masterpiece in concert are rare. Ahead of its belated Edinburgh festival premiere with the Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal, we look at the epic work - and its epic baggage
Content: Symphony of 1000… a dress rehearsal for the staging of Hiawatha at the Royal Albert Hall in 1937.Photograph: Smith Archive/AlamyView image in fullscreenSymphony of 1000… a dress rehearsal for the staging of Hiawatha at the Royal Albert Hall in 1937.Photograph: Smith Archive/AlamyTom Service on musicClassical musicFrom sensation to spectacular, to silence: the strange history of Coleridge-Taylor’s Song of HiawathaTom ServiceChances to hear Samuel Coleridge-Taylor’s choral masterpiece in concert are rare. Ahead of its belated Edinburgh festival premiere with the Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal, we look at the epic work - and its epic baggageWed 12 Aug 2026 10.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 10.42 EDTShareThe Song of Hiawatha, Samuel Coleridge-Taylor’s setting of Henry Longfellow’s poem, comes to theEdinburgh international festival next week. It’s the first time the work will be performed there, a very belated premiere for the three-part cantata that sealed the composer’s reputation nationally and internationally, inspiring Coleridge-Taylor societies in the US, and making him the world’s best-known Black classical composer of the Edwardian era, before his tragicallyearly death at the age of just 37 in 1912.The performance history of The Song of Hiawatha makes for an astounding story. In the early years of the 20th century the work quickly became a sensation, with hundreds of performances on both sides of the Atlantic.In 1924, and then every year from 1926 to 1939, the Royal Albert Hall housed a spectacular and vast staging that involved around 1,000 performers – 200 dancers and hundreds of singers of the Royal Choral Society – dressed up to play out a series of exoticised and racialised caricatures to be part of the pageant of Hiawatha, Minnehaha and their tribespeople.
