The Mohawk chief also performed in the shows, granting an apparent authenticity to The Song of Hiawatha’s dramaturgy.Post the second world war, performances of the massive work in concert – let alone staged – became rare, and, this century, there’s been barely a handful done professionally.Coleridge-Taylor’s decision to set Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s epic poem was far from novel by the late 1890s. Since the work’s publication in 1855, US composers in their dozens had turned it into cantatas, operas and symphonic works. It inspired the middle movements of Dvořák’s New World Symphony, his tribute to the country that had adopted him and his vision of what might inspire a new American music. But Longfellow’s poem can be read today as a piece of colonialist caricature, mixing Indigenous stories and turning them into a parable of Hiawatha’s noble savagery, as he accommodates the missionaries at the end of the story, before sailing his canoe into the glorious west. It’s a white-empowering fantasy.View image in fullscreenMelodic ideas and directness … Samuel Coleridge-Taylor.Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty ImagesBut such readings concerned few in the first half of the 20th century, and Coleridge-Taylor’s setting was popular with its performers and audiences for less complicated reasons: the immediacy of its melodic ideas, the directness of its choral writing and the emotional clarity of all it sets out to do in its three parts of celebration, lamentation and farewell. The work is exquisitely made for amateur singers to get their teeth into, and, in the context of a British musical culture at the end of the 19th century that was dominated by choral societies and gigantic-scale performances of Handel and Mendelssohn, Coleridge-Taylor’s musical language was sufficiently challenging to reward its singers, but simple and accessible enough to guarantee that choruses all over the world could champion it enthusiastically.Before his death, Coleridge-Taylor apparently sanctioned the idea of the staged performances, produced by TC Fairburn, that took over the whole arena level of the Royal Albert Hall for a fortnight at a time, in annual performances mostly conducted by Malcolm Sargent. The photos of the production and its stars arejaw-dropping in their red-face exoticism. And despite Os-ke-non-ton’s presence, there is nothing that seems authentic about their representation of Native American life, culture or music. Coleridge-Taylor’s score is similarly devoid of ethnographic inspiration of indigenous musical cultures. Beyond a melodic focus on wide-open intervals, fifths and octaves, and piquant modal inflections and orchestrational flourishes, the sound world of The Song of Hiawatha is typical, and marvellous, Victoriana.View image in fullscreenOs-ke-non-ton in Regent’s Park, in a break from being part of the Royal Albert Hall production of The Song of Hiawatha in 1937.Photograph: Fox Photos/Getty ImagesThe significance of The Song of Hiawatha, and especially the success of the first part,Hiawatha’s Wedding Feast, is that it opened Coleridge-Taylor’s horizons to the US. After his first visit there in 1904, he took his place on the world stage as a Black composer, the musician who would take “24 Negro Melodies” as the inspiration for one of the most important collections of British piano music of the early 20th century. He went on to make African music the foundation of orchestral pieces such as his visionarySymphonic Variations on an African Airand his “rhapsodic dance”,The Bamboula, which was premiered by the New York Philharmonic in 1910.There are plenty of other postscripts to The Song of Hiawatha story: the fact that Coleridge-Taylor never saw any royalties from performances of his most successful piece – a sorry state of affairs that led, in part, to the creation of the Performing Rights Society. And there’s Coleridge-Taylor’s catalogue of later cantatas from Kubla Khan toEndymion’s Dream, and his only opera,Thelma, which have been performed even less than the Hiawatha trilogy in the postwar decades.The world has changed: and hopefully theEdinburgh festival performance next weekwill be the start of another life for The Song of Hiawatha, music that’s both uncomplicatedly powerful in its expression, and endlessly rich in its multi-dimensional cultural histories.This week Tom has been listening to:Robin Ticciati’s 2019 recording of Debussy’s Nocturnes and Duruflé’s Requiem with the DSO Berlin. The Nocturnes have a breathtaking combination of sensitivity and viscerality, the Duruflé is a revelation to me. I wish I’d heard this years ago!Explore more on these topicsClassical musicTom Service on musicEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Today’s Brazilians have no idea what it feels like to lose democracy’: Joyce Moreno on her battles to become a Latin musical great | Music | The Guardian
description: After her defiant femininity outraged many in Brazil, she lived through a military dictatorship and was boycotted for years. But after more than 30 albums, she explains how she kept going
Author: Jane Cornwell
Headline: After her defiant femininity outraged many in Brazil, she lived through a military dictatorship and was boycotted for years. But after more than 30 albums, she explains how she kept going
Content: Beach girl … Joyce Moreno performing in 2011.Photograph: Myriam Vilas BoasView image in fullscreenBeach girl … Joyce Moreno performing in 2011.Photograph: Myriam Vilas BoasMusicInterview‘Today’s Brazilians have no idea what it feels like to lose democracy’: Joyce Moreno on her battles to become a Latin musical greatJane CornwellAfter her defiant femininity outraged many in Brazil, she lived through a military dictatorship and was boycotted for years. But after more than 30 albums, she explains how she kept goingWed 12 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 10.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 78, Joyce Moreno is one of Brazil’s musical icons, but for decades that status seemed far from assured: this headstrong singer, guitarist and composer was frequently viewed as a threat by her country’s establishment. Aged 19, the reaction to her song Me Disseram – which began “I was told my man didn’t love me” – almost torpedoed her career before it even started. “I’d often heard the expression ‘my man’ sung by Billie Holiday and Edith Piaf, so for me it was normal,” she says. “But I was a beach girl from Ipanema, writing and singing in the first person. People were shocked.”Then, inspired by trailblazing actor Leila Diniz (“her liberal attitudes lost her jobs”), Moreno refused requests that she “dress like a sexy bimbo”, and endured male critics who thought her music “too good to have been written by a woman”. When, in 1980, she discovered that her label had given another female singer the blueprints for songs she had written, she “looked for a lawyer, of course” and successfully sued; in her memoir she claims she was then boycotted by Brazil’s major record companies for a decade.View image in fullscreenPartnership … Joyce and Tutty Moreno pictured in 2007.Photograph: Courtesy of Far Out RecordingsBut come 2026, Moreno has written more than 400 songs, released more than 30 albums, and become one of the defining voices of Música Popular Brasileira – the genre-blending movement that grew out of bossa nova. Her latest album, Joyce & Tutty Moreno, is just out but she already has another one finished. “It’s always been about my love for the music,” she says from her home in Humaitá, a quiet, leafy Rio neighbourhood, where she lives with jazz drummer Tutty Moreno, her partner of nearly 50 years. Behind her, shelves of CDs tower to the ceiling. Elsewhere in the house are six guitars and a library of books; she is currently re-reading Katherine Mansfield’s short stories.The youngest of three children, Moreno was raised by her single mother, a public servant, in Rio just as bossa nova was being invented in the 1950s. “My brother was 13 when I was born, and mum gave him a guitar as compensation,” she says. “He’d invite friends like [bossa pioneers] Leny Andrade and Roberto Menescal over. I’d watch them closely. By the time my family took notice, I was playing very well on my own. I’d even set my school homework to music to help me memorise it.”Going mononymously as Joyce, Moreno became one of the first Brazilian women to write and perform unapologetically from a female perspective, and has been compared to Joni Mitchell for her blend of intricate musicianship and deeply personal songwriting. Wider recognition came with her 1980 album Feminina, whose title track is a conversation between a mother and daughter about femininity: “It prepares and sets the table,“ she sings. “Then it lights another fire and lets it burn.”“In my youth, my mother always told me I should wear heels and makeup,” she says. “Although I learned from her that a woman could be a head of a family, and be respected for her work, she was born in 1912. I was a 1960s beach girl from the golden age of Rio. We had very different ideas of what femininity was. For me, it was something internal. I had a sense of these things, even though I wasn’t yet an avid reader of feminism. I wouldn’t encounter Simone de Beauvoir until the 90s.”View image in fullscreenThe only girl on the block … Joyce Moreno in the studio, date unknown.Photograph: Raymond Ross Archives/CTSImagesThe cultural freedoms and social transformations of the 1960s were abruptly curtailed in Brazil by the 1964 military coup. The dictatorship suppressed dissent, imposed censorship and persecuted artists and intellectuals. While touring Italy in 1975, Moreno recorded Passarinho Urbano, an album of songs by friends – Chico Buarque, Milton Nascimento, Caetano Veloso – whose music had been silenced. “Today’s young Brazilians have no idea what it feels like to lose democracy in a country, to not be able to vote,” she says of a regime that finally collapsed in 1985. “I didn’t vote until I was 40.”She hails Brazil’s current liberal president Lula as “our only alternative. The far right is pushing into Latin and South America, which is a very dangerous path to follow, and we know very well who is sponsoring all that. We feel the responsibility. It’s kind of scary …” She pauses, and asks if we might stick to music.In 1977, Moreno – then divorced from musician and composer Nelson Angelo – was performing at upmarket Brazilian club Cachaça where she met drummer Tutty Moreno, who was part of a circle that included saxophonist Michael Brecker and percussionist Naná Vasconcelos. “We fell for each other’s music first,” she says. “I thought: wow, he plays so elegantly, like he’s driving a convertible. We were both young, beautiful hippies. We both wanted change.”‘This janitor’s daughter became a state deputy’: Leci Brandão, the Brazilian samba star turned communist lawmakerRead moreShe recorded an album in New York that year with Claus Ogerman, the arranger who worked with Antônio Carlos Jobim and Frank Sinatra, and remembers the disparity between their worlds. “We were counting pennies to get the subway, but Claus would take us to fancy restaurants with dress codes. Tutty would have to wear funny loaner jackets that were always too short in the sleeves.” The album was intended to launch her global career, but was shelved after it failed to find a commercial label. “That was painful,” she says, though it was eventually released in 2022 by UK label Far Out Recordings after her international profile received a major boost in the 1990s, when Gilles Peterson and London’s acid jazz scene embraced her music, and Far Out became her longtime label. “The UK thing was a gamechanger,” she smiles. “Those young DJs gave me the confidence I needed to keep going.”The new album Joyce & Tutty Moreno features songs of love, healing and renewal, performed with guitarist Adrian Younge. It was meant to also include veteran pianist João Donato, Moreno’s longtime friend and collaborator, who died aged 83 in 2023. The record is dedicated to him. “Recording without João was hard and beautiful at the same time,” says Moreno.There’s no trick to her career longevity. “Early on, it didn’t matter that I was the only girl on the block. Self-esteem has never been a problem. Somehow I knew I deserved the attention.” She smiles. “Music lives inside me,” she says.Joyce & Tutty Moreno is out now via Jazz Is Dead. Moreno plays EartH, London, 15 November; and Band on the Wall, Manchester, 16 NovemberExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockBrazilfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: You and Me (and Whoever Comes Next) review – theatre crafted with love and care | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Actor Keron Day draws on his experiences of getting along, or not, with live-in carers to give a pithy account of a complex relationship
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Actor Keron Day draws on his experiences of getting along, or not, with live-in carers to give a pithy account of a complex relationship
Content: In safe hands … (from left) Keron Day, Martha Walker, Merle Powell-Smith and Lauren Koster in You and Me (and Whoever Comes Next).Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIn safe hands … (from left) Keron Day, Martha Walker, Merle Powell-Smith and Lauren Koster in You and Me (and Whoever Comes Next).Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewYou and Me (and Whoever Comes Next) review – theatre crafted with love and careSummerhall, EdinburghActor Keron Day draws on his experiences of getting along, or not, with live-in carers to give a pithy account of a complex relationshipChris WiegandWed 12 Aug 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe stories told byPatch of Bluecan be difficult to hear, but this vital theatre company is well aware of that. In the family drama Cassie and the Lights,at the fringe in 2022, one of the abandoned children kindly lent her froggy hat to an audience member to help them through an upsetting scene. In this new show – which shares that play’s mix of emotional veracity, easy humour and social purpose – the cast once more dip in and out of the story to guide us along.You feel in safe hands – which is one of the play’s essential themes. It is inspired by disabled actor Keron Day, who also stars as himself, and gives his experiences with a line of personal assistants who provide live-in care. We are introduced to Keron, 22, as he meets PA Dani (Lauren Koster) in a sweary meet-cute – but it’s the friendship between the two, rather than any romance, that muddies the water.The play, written by Day, Helen Chong anddirector Alex Howarth(a former care worker), dives into the complexities of defining personal and professional boundaries. Keron relies on Dani, whose duties include cleaning and dressing him; she relies on him, as her employer. Some may see Keron as the one in need; his whistle-stop tour of past PAs (played by Martha Walker) shows they can be the needy ones – or cruelly aloof.View image in fullscreenEmotional veracity … Keron Day in You and Me (and Whoever Comes Next).Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe nature of the work is immediately intimate – his PA, says Keron, is the person he sees at the start and end of each day. Two extremes are posited: the PA as confidant or, after Keron and Dani fall out, as “the robot that takes you to the toilet”. As the title makes clear, the set-up is fragile, the future uncertain, with government cuts hovering over both their lives. The script combines the specificity of this situation – and the pity and ridicule Keron faces not just from strangers but also friends – with a striking universality for other relationships.Joined by Merle Powell-Smith, who plays her own soothing and plangent folk compositions on stage, the overall effect is not so much of an ensemble as a community. The piece ends with Keron’s commitment to protect others in his position – and the hour itself is handled with utmost care.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 29 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreDisabilitySummerhallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Buggers review – phenomenal flesh and blood portrait of Francis Bacon and George Dyer | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The painter and his lover are played with real intensity by Alistair Hall and Peter Clements, in a visceral psychodrama of contained violence and sadness
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: The painter and his lover are played with real intensity by Alistair Hall and Peter Clements, in a visceral psychodrama of contained violence and sadness
Content: Between a wrestling match and an act of passion … Peter Clements as Dyer and Alistair Hall as Bacon in Buggers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianView image in fullscreenBetween a wrestling match and an act of passion … Peter Clements as Dyer and Alistair Hall as Bacon in Buggers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBuggers review – phenomenal flesh and blood portrait of Francis Bacon and George DyerPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghThe painter and his lover are played with real intensity by Alistair Hall and Peter Clements, in a visceral psychodrama of contained violence and sadnessArifa AkbarWed 12 Aug 2026 10.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe famously fraught relationship between the artist Francis Bacon and his lover-muse, George Dyer, has been much documented. So it is remarkable that this play byAlistair Hallmakes the story so utterly fresh and arresting. Hall has drawn on documents and letters from the Francis Bacon estate, but if Buggers is anchored in research, it leads with physicality, charged with eroticism and contained violence.Hall plays Bacon, and Peter Clements portrays Dyer, with absolute conviction. Clements’ performance as an initially swaggering man, who Bacon airily describes as his “delicious piece of rough trade” and who over the years succumbs to alcoholism, is especially astute and vulnerable.View image in fullscreenA gem … Peter Clements as George Dyer and Alistair Hall as Francis Bacon in Buggers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianThe play begins in 1963 with a wordless sequence that shows their first night together, drawn somewhere between a wrestling match and an act of passion. The choreography retains its visceral threat throughout (great work by movement director Ken Nakajima). They could be Pinter’s men as they circle one another barefoot on Rosie Elnile’s set, which is somewhere between a Bohemian apartment and a wet-room, complete with toilet and tub.Beautifully directed by Alice Wordsworth, the two-hander proceeds to capture the full span of their intense, complicated love – a melange of eroticism, sadomasochistic power-play and cruelty – from this first charged night to Dyer’s death in a Paris hotel room in 1971.Sanctuary review – tender, uplifting portrait of love in the Aids crisisRead moreThe relationship is initially filled with testy chemistry – and testosterone – but becomes darker. “I’m so bored,” says Bacon to Dyer. “I feel lonely when I’m with you,” Dyer responds. Scenes switch time frames and the play seems to lose its conventional shape, descending into fragments that capture emotional tumult and grief. At points it becomes a little opaque, veering into hallucination or memory, with flashes of light and shadow-play conveying mood over anything more concrete.But the piece hypnotises even in its more abstract moments. Bacon painted Dyer numerous times over his lifetime, the titles and dates of which works are read out at the end, bringing an almost suffocating sense of sadness: for all Bacon’s cruel words, his canvases spoke his love. Wonderful writing, phenomenal performances. A small but perfect festival gem.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreArtFrancis BaconSexualityFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rod Stewart cancels farewell tour dates after undergoing successful heart procedure | Rod Stewart | The Guardian
description: The singer said that he was ‘already feeling better’ but forthcoming dates on his mammoth farwell tour will not now go ahead
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The singer said that he was ‘already feeling better’ but forthcoming dates on his mammoth farwell tour will not now go ahead
Content: Stewart performing in New York on 31 July.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStewart performing in New York on 31 July.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty ImagesRod StewartRod Stewart cancels farewell tour dates after undergoing successful heart procedureThe singer said that he was ‘already feeling better’ but forthcoming dates on his mammoth farwell tour will not now go aheadLaura SnapesWed 12 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRod Stewart has cancelled all coming dates on his farewell tour after undergoing a routine heart procedure.On 9 August, Stewart, 81, pulled a performance in Ohio at the last minute. After the successful insertion of a coronary stent, he announced that all dates would be cancelled.Representatives for the singer told Rolling Stone that Stewart required four weeks off to recuperate.Stewart told fans that he was “already feeling better and very much on the mend”, and extended his thanks to the medical staff who took care of him.“I’m deeply disappointed to miss these shows and sorry to let my fans down, but I look forward to getting back on stage and having a good time with you all again soon,” he wrote in an Instagram story.In June, Stewart cancelled shows on doctors’ advice. Later that month, he paused a show in Utah to use an oxygen tank after almost fainting mid-performance.Stewart had been due to perform a six-date Las Vegas residency, in addition to other dates across the US and Mexico, as part of the ongoing One Last Time farewell tour, which began in 2024.Sing when you’re winning: the 20 greatest songs about football – ranked!Read moreIn October, Ronnie Woodtold Desert Island Discsthat he and Stewart had been making music together again ahead of a potential reunion of the Faces, the rock band that formed out of the ashes of the Small Faces when singer and guitarist Steve Marriott left.Wood joined Stewart on stage at Glastonbury last year when the latterhelmed the festival’s Sunday afternoon legends slot. Prior to the performance, Stewart revealed that his fitness regime includedunderwater swimming, as recommended to him by Frank Sinatra.Stewart, a father of eight, recently welcomed his sixth grandchild.Explore more on these topicsRod StewartPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: LA Phil/Dudamel; Fantasia Orchestra / Fetherstonhaugh/Glennie reviews – high-contrast programming | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The first of two evening proms began with the Los Angeles Phil’s polished but polite Beethoven and intoxicating Adès. Later, the Fantasia orchestra’s bitty playlist-type programme only occasionally sparked into life.
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: The first of two evening proms began with the Los Angeles Phil’s polished but polite Beethoven and intoxicating Adès. Later, the Fantasia orchestra’s bitty playlist-type programme only occasionally sparked into life.
Content: Good clean fun … Gustavo Dudamel conducts the Los Angeles Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenGood clean fun … Gustavo Dudamel conducts the Los Angeles Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouClassical musicReviewLA Phil/Dudamel; Fantasia Orchestra / Fetherstonhaugh/Glennie reviews – high-contrast programmingRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThe first of two evening proms began with the Los Angeles Philharmonic’s polished but polite Beethoven and intoxicating Adès. Later, the Fantasia orchestra’s bitty playlist-type programme only occasionally sparked into life.Flora WillsonWed 12 Aug 2026 08.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 08.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis evening was, in a sense, a tale of two orchestras. On one hand, the international heavyweight, returning to the Proms for the first time in more than 20 years. On the other, the rapidly ascendant homegrown outfit founded while its members were still at school, already making its fourth Proms appearance.Taking the early evening shift, theLA PhilandGustavo DudamelperformedBeethoven’s Pastoral Symphonyin an ultra-polished hybrid of period-performance style and modern instruments. String textures were a deluxe fine-knit, individual notes lifted but phrase endings subtly elongated so that the music seemed to breathe. The woodwind solos were cool and bright, offering further oxygenation to an already limpid sound, where massed trills spoke as one and countermelodies usually buried under orchestral busyness suddenly became audible.Beethoven’s merry peasants inspired some rougher edges, but nothing exceeding good clean fun, while Dudamel bounced on the spot as if on an invisible pogo stick. Later, there were harsh growls of timpani and threatening rumbles of double bass, before the storm dissipated into sunset-mellow brass. Throughout, Dudamel relished the slow blossoming of tutti passages, easing into them after energetic surges forward.You can have too much of a good thing, of course. So much sheen gradually becomes bland, and all those warm glows left me hankering for quieter, riskier pianissimos. After the interval, Inferno fromThomas Adès’s ballet score Dante – hot on the heels of theNYO’s performance of its second part– ditched the historically informed politeness in favour of vigorous snap, crackle and bop. String scrubbing was thunderous, woodwind voluptuous, and trumpets snarked and rasped. Almost-jazz almost-grooves seemed to bubble beneath the surface. Dudamel leaned into the score’s allusions to Wagner and Liszt, Ravel and Tchaikovsky. Yet not even he and this phenomenally accomplished orchestra could prevent the intoxicating farce of the penultimate movement from feeling like the real ending, with the miasmic layers of the actual last movement an effervescent afterthought.View image in fullscreenSuperstar percussionist: Evelyn Glennie with the Fantasia Orchestra at the late-night Prom.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouThe high-contrast approach to programming continued in the late-night Prom, where theFantasia Orchestraand conductorTom Fetherstonhaughwere joined by superstar percussionistEvelyn Glenniefor what Fetherstonhaugh called a concert on the theme of listening. Inevitably, in music, that theme is too broad to have much force. What resulted was a kind of live playlist experience that took in energetically played show tunes (lights! Stage smoke! Instant pizzazz!), an exquisitely intense extract from Morton Feldman’s Rothko Chapel and a movement of Caroline Shaw’s a cappella Partita, compellingly sung by theBBC Singers, plus solo percussion works and a Radiohead arrangement, a snippet of Dvořák in full folksy-mode and Vaughan Williams’s Serenade to Music.It was a peculiar, bitty menu – and not ideal conditions for the world premiere of Héloïse Werner’s The Wood Pigeon in all its gnomic self-ironising and musical multilingualism. Glennie’s extract from Vincent Ho’s Sandman’s Castle for solo tam-tam was most persuasive: seven minutes of fibrillations and rattling, tapping and stroking, turning a single gong into an unfamiliar, haunted surface and inviting us, finally, to listen in.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsClassical musicProms 2026Gustavo DudamelRoyal Albert HallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: fascinating documentary explores the rise and fall of a Russian spy | Television | The Guardian
description: Nothing was ever quite as it seemed as Anna Chapman charmed her way into the higher echelons of society. Plus: Tinie Tempah channels his inner Kevin McCloud. Here’s what to watch today
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Nothing was ever quite as it seemed as Anna Chapman charmed her way into the higher echelons of society. Plus: Tinie Tempah channels his inner Kevin McCloud. Here’s what to watch today
Content: Shrewd … Anna Chapman in 2011.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShrewd … Anna Chapman in 2011.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: fascinating documentary explores the rise and fall of a Russian spyNothing was ever quite as it seemed as Anna Chapman charmed her way into the higher echelons of society. Plus: Tinie Tempah channels his inner Kevin McCloud. Here’s what to watch todayPhil Harrison,Priya Elan,Hannah J Davies,Jack Seale,Graeme VirtueandSimon WardellWed 12 Aug 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpy Next Door: The Anna Chapman Story9pm, Channel 4The tale of Anna Chapman (AKA Anya Kushchenko) is uncannily emblematic of recent relations between Russia and the west. Chapman was a shrewd spy who charmed her way into the higher echelons of society in London and New York. This fascinating two-part documentary explores her rise and fall, hearing from some of her entirely unwitting companions (who ranged from a Brighton techno DJ to a Mayfair financier) and agents who were involved in surveilling her. As Vladimir Putin briefly played at diplomacy with prime ministers and presidents, Chapman was among his foot soldiers. But, inevitably, in her case and that of Putin, nothing was ever quite as it seemed.Phil HarrisonAthens: Birth of Democracy9.35am, PBS AmericaModern populations sometimes take democracy for granted. But the concept’s inception was troubled and this documentary visits Athens to investigate its origin story. The exploration is very literal – it focuses on an archaeological quest to unearth everything from the bodies of dissidents to ancient voting machines.PHExtraordinary Extensions8pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenTinie Tempah with a couple who are planning a ‘Korwegian’ conversion in Extraordinary Extensions.Photograph: Channel 4Musician Tinie Tempah continues to channel his inner Kevin McCloud in the third series of this show about ambitious renovation projects. This week, he meets a couple planning a “Korwegian” conversion (that’s Korean and Norwegian), and a solo renovator who is starting to feel as though her project is cursed.Hannah J DaviesMurder Trial: Death of a Dog Walker9pm, BBC TwoFeaturing footage from the trial, doorbell camera film and face-to-face interviews, this is a closeup look at the murder of Brian Low, a groundsman who was shot while walking his dog in rural Scotland. The accused is David Campbell, a gamekeeper who was, according to the prosecuting lawyer, good at concealing the evidence.Priya Elan999: Critical Condition9pm, Channel 5When an unconscious young mother is rushed into the Queen Elizabeth hospital in Birmingham after banging her head, doctors don’t have much time to work out what caused her to collapse. Elsewhere in the emergency room, octogenarian Clive has fallen off his ladder and is at risk of pneumonia.Hollie RichardsonGuy Montgomery’s Guy Mont-Spelling Bee10pm, BBC ThreeA double helping of the daft spelling quiz from Australia. Eye-popping retro production design and Montgomery’s heroically smarmy hosting make for a heightened, campy experience. The comedic contestants – including standup Rose Matafeo – rise to the challenge.Graeme VirtueFilm choiceView image in fullscreenRebellious … Paul Mescal in Gladiator II.Photograph: Aidan Monaghan/APGladiator II (Ridley Scott, 2024), NetflixIt has taken 24 years for Ridley Scott to get back to the Colosseum. But there’s still a lot of familiarity in his ancient Roman sequel – from returning characters to elaborate fight scenes and animal antics. Paul Mescal stars as Lucius, the son of Russell Crowe’s Maximus, who is living a quiet life in north Africa until an invading Roman army take him into slavery. From there, it’s a short hop to becoming a rebellious gladiator, under the gimlet gaze of his owner Macrinus (a lip-smacking Denzel Washington).Simon WardellLive sportPre-seasonfootball: Man United v Leeds, 7pm, ITV1A friendly at Croke Park in Dublin.Uefa Super Cupfinal:Paris Saint-Germain v Aston Villa,7pm, TNT Sports 1At Red Bull Arena in Salzburg.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A History of the Novel in Britain by Philip Hensher review – a masterpiece of criticism | Books | The Guardian
description: This joyous book takes readers on a literary adventure across 300 years of fiction, from Defoe to Zadie Smith
Author: Kathryn Hughes
Headline: This joyous book takes readers on a literary adventure across 300 years of fiction, from Defoe to Zadie Smith
Content: ‘That blustery old fogey’ … Evelyn Waugh.Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveView image in fullscreen‘That blustery old fogey’ … Evelyn Waugh.Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveBook of the dayBooksReviewA History of the Novel in Britain by Philip Hensher review – a masterpiece of criticismThis joyous book takes readers on a literary adventure across 300 years of fiction, from Defoe to Zadie SmithKathryn HughesWed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his opening paragraph, Philip Hensher declares that a novel not only “tells a good story” but is a good story in itself. We could extend that neat formula to include this book, which is not only a masterful account of fiction since 1719, when Daniel Defoe set Robinson Crusoe down on his desert island, but is itself a wonderful read. There is nothing dreary here; no sense of being back in the seminar room taking notes. Instead it is 600 pages of deep pleasure, an excuse to revisit old literary loves and be reminded of ones that have slipped from view.Hensher is smart enough to know why his book works so well and vain enough to tell us. The usual methodology for a survey is to assemble a roster of academics and invite them to trot out a chapter on their specialism, whether that be “Thomas Hardy” or “High Modernism”. The result is a series of silos, with little sense of historical connection or intellectual unfolding. Hensher, by contrast, gives us a joined-up account of creative call and response. Equally crucial to this project’s success is Hensher’s own experience as a novelist. He brings a practitioner’s informed eye to such questions as why some chapters in Dickens’s Dombey and Son are in the present tense or how Henry James pulls off free indirect speech in What Maisie Knew.After setting out the novel’s origin story, we are plunged into the inky churn of the middle-18th century. Samuel Richardson writes Pamela in 1740, Henry Fielding shoots back with his snarky parody, Shamela (1741), followed by the more sustained inversion of Joseph Andrews (1742). Richardson, in turn infuriated by the lack of moral purpose in Fielding’s Tom Jones (1749), storms back with The History of Sir Charles Grandison (1754).double quotation markOne of the delights of Hensher’s capacious narrative is being alerted to authors and books that never got their proper dueHensher is brilliant on the warring duo’s finances, giving us a forensic account of the risk and reward of their different publishing models. Richardson was a printer before he was an author and hung on to his own copyrights. This allowed him the autonomy to shape the fledgling genre in ways that he wanted which, in the case of Clarissa (1748), meant 1m words written entirely in epistolary form. Fielding, no less lucky, had a patron and printer who supported him no matter how eccentric his artistic choices.Few authors were so favoured. Jane Austen chose to sell Pride and Prejudice for a flat fee to Thomas Egerton in 1812, having previously lost money on Sense and Sensibility when she insisted on retaining copyright and paying for the printing. Under the new arrangement, Egerton was under no obligation to spend more than the minimum on production. When Pride and Prejudice eventually appeared in 1813 it was in such tiny print and scrappy paper that disgruntled readers decreed it “almost unintelligible”.That sort of thing can kill a career, but Austen went on to rise above it, even if it took until the 1940s before the literary establishment caught up with her glory. One of the delights of Hensher’s capacious narrative is being alerted to authors and books that never got their proper due. Hannah More, usually written off as a Sunday school prig, turns out to be “a beautiful and graceful writer”, while Tobias Smollett, who generally gets dismissed these days as an unfunny hack, is rehabilitated as an inventive craftsman with supreme control over narrative voice. Arnold Bennett, characterised as a dreary bore thanks to Virginia Woolf’s unkind take-down of 1924, is lovingly restored as the author of the incomparable Old Wives Tale (1908), which “ought to be acknowledged among the 20 greatest novels in English”.If Hensher is generous with plaudits, he is equally vigorous in his loathing. Ann Radcliffe, author of the hugely popular and preposterously gothic The Mysteries of Udolpho (1794) “was (and remains) a simply terrible writer”. DM Thomas, Booker nominated in 1981 for The White Hotel, is “patently untalented”. And poor David Lodge, who tried so hard with modish literary pastiche in Changing Places (1975), is simply “not up to the task”.Hensher never falls into crankiness, but he is unafraid to point out home truths. Such as the fact that so much of the pleased-with-itself “experimentalism” of the 1960 to 1980 period was merely a retread of things that had been done better before. Tickled by the clever wheeze of having central characters with no name? Fanny Burney was already doing that in 1814. Keen on using fragmentary collage to signal modernity? That blustery old fogey Evelyn Waugh got there first with Vile Bodies (1930). As for self-reflexivity, that device by which the novelist comments on the process of writing a novel, you should go back to Fielding.Hensher doesn’t bring his account right up to date, preferring to stop in 2000 – at Zadie Smith and her “wonderful ear for speech” – on the grounds that it is impossible to form a proper critical judgment until plenty of time has passed. It is a wise decision and a tactful one, underscoring the moral seriousness of this master­piece, quite aside from its buoyant joy. Reader, I could not put it down.A History of the Novel in Britain by Philip Hensher is published by Pelican (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Something Like Happiness by Tom Newlands review – a tender take on hard times, anger and autism | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A twentysomething Scottish couple care for their autistic son in the bleak follow-up to Only Here, Only Now
Author: Suzi Feay
Headline: A twentysomething Scottish couple care for their autistic son in the bleak follow-up to Only Here, Only Now
Content: Tom Newlands.Photograph: Sophie DavidsonView image in fullscreenTom Newlands.Photograph: Sophie DavidsonFictionReviewSomething Like Happiness by Tom Newlands review – a tender take on hard times, anger and autismA twentysomething Scottish couple care for their autistic son in the bleak follow-up to Only Here, Only NowSuzi FeayWed 12 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrazer and Caitlin have been emotionally entwined since schooldays. Now in their mid-20s, and parents of a five-year-old, they live in a grotty flat in a Scottish new town – the faded posters read “Happiness, Here” – that has crumbled into decay. Jobs are scarce and unrewarding; little Jamie, who has autism, is silent; and the pressure is starting to tell.Frazer’s adored Caitlin is “beautiful and driven”, fit, petite – and a rageaholic. At her mildest she’s irritated and unreasonable, at her worst violent and intimidating. She is incensed at Frazer’s refusal to move from their mould-infested block to the new council house they’ve been assigned. Apex Court is where he was brought up, filled with relics of his dead parents, and it’s the only home his son has ever known. “You’ve become the sad sack guardian of a bunch of shite that belonged to your parents, including their hovel of a flat,” Cait sneers.Caitlin’s shrewish mother Janetta also thinks Frazer is the problem, and is forever scheming to separate him from Jamie. Weighted towards Frazer’s dazed perspective, Nothing Like Happiness would seem a better title for the novel. Why doesn’t he leave?Tom Newlands’s 2024 debutOnly Here, Only Nowcentred on vivacious teenager Cora Mowat, tenderly depicted in the manner of fellow Scot Alan Warner’s brilliantly realised portraits of young women. Cora’s physical “fizziness” turns out to be ADHD. For his follow-up, Newlands, himself billed as a “neurodivergent writer”, focuses on a troubled young man. The plot concerns the aftermath of the punch by Cait that fells Frazer during one particularly vicious row.This novel feels thinner in texture than the exuberant Only Here, Only Now, leaving the reader largely to infer the characters’ motivation. Grief-stricken at the loss of his mother, indecisive Frazer could have PTSD or a variant of the autism experienced by his son, while Cait’s hair-trigger fury could be a result of growing up with a violent father, her gruesome amateur boxing bouts a bid to impress him. At least the pair are united in caring for their small son; the concern they devote to a mostly oblivious child is heartrending. Cait screams abuse at teachers and other parents for what she sees as their violation of Jamie’s norms and boundaries. The question looms: is their protectiveness stopping him integrating with peers?Beyond Jamie’s welfare, the pair’s love of childhood pets – Frazer’s budgie Sequin, Cait’s iguana Natasha – hints at a softer connection, but their significance isn’t fully explained. Frazer does have potential confidants, but stubbornly resists seeking help until he reaches the point of breakdown. Hoping to dissolve his shame, one helpful contact avers that one in six domestic abuse cases involve a female perpetrator and male victim. There are angels in unlikely places, the novel proposes, if you look for them.Frazer can get riled himself, bristling at a description of the Apex as “this grey shithole”. Seeing through his eyes, Newlands conjures a bleak poetry in descriptions of the estate: “The wind had changed, and rain was drifting through the gap in the breezeblocks now. Over on Donaldson Drive someone was dragging a wheelie bin with a broken wheel.” Whether the rowing couple’s relationship will ever amount to “something like happiness” is once more left to the reader to decide.Something Like Happiness by Tom Newlands is published by Phoenix (£20). title: Don’t Say Good Luck review – high-school musical weepie puts Sunny Sandler in the spotlight | Movies | The Guardian
description: A mother’s illness threatens to overshadow a stagestruck teen’s big break in a school production
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: A mother’s illness threatens to overshadow a stagestruck teen’s big break in a school production
Content: Anguish … Sunny Sandler, left, and Melanie Lynskey.Photograph: Netflix Inc/PAView image in fullscreenAnguish … Sunny Sandler, left, and Melanie Lynskey.Photograph: Netflix Inc/PAMoviesReviewDon’t Say Good Luck review – high-school musical weepie puts Sunny Sandler in the spotlightA mother’s illness threatens to overshadow a stagestruck teen’s big break in a school productionPeter BradshawWed 12 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo you, like me, have a soft spot for both high-school angst and Broadway showtunes – and maybe Douglas Goodhart’s amusing Master It! Insta reels on how to make it in musical theatre? Then you might find yourself giving a pass to this sugary but heartfelt teen weepie from director and co-writer Julia Hart, co-produced byAdam Sandlerand starring his daughter Sunny Sandler.She plays Soph, the shy theatre kid who unexpectedly gets the lead in her school production of the musical Waitress. Her devoted mom Elizabeth (Melanie Lynskey) has cancer, and thinks she should maybe wait until after the run to tell Soph the awful truth, so as not to spoil her big moment. But will that be ... too late?There’s a shrewd and entertaining scene at the very beginning when Soph gets a first inkling from her phone that something is terribly wrong with her mother just as she is about to go on stage to audition for a lesser role; she almost backs out but can’t bear for her mean-girl blonde rival to think that this is just a humiliating bout of nerves. So she goes on stage and channels her anguish into her singing, thereby impressing the director Ms Parker (Stephanie Beatriz, from TV’s Brooklyn Nine-Nine) that she gets the lead.Ms Parker has of course seen something in Soph; something real, something above and beyond mere stage histrionics. Yet Soph finds herself having to do some embarrassing onstage kissing with her dreamboat male co-star (Jack Champion) on whom she naturally has an excruciating crush. Fans of the 90s TV classic My So-Called Life might enjoy their Angela Chase/Jordan Catalano energy (although accusations made againstJared Letomean that this comparison has rather lost its innocence).I slightly regretted the absence of the comedy and satire that the movie’s opening act appeared to promise in modest quantities; for that, you’ll have to go toMolly Gordon and Nick Lieberman’s acerbic Theater Camp. The keynote here is serious. There’s nice support from Bebe Neuwirth and Steve Buscemi as Soph’s grandparents and Jon Lovitz as the grumpy serving guy in the deli her dad owns. You’ll need a sweet tooth for this kind of emotional sugar rush.Don’t Say Good Luck is on Netflix from 14 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsAdam SandlerSteve BuscemiMusicalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Sometimes they credit the janitor. But not us’: what’s it like to be a child chaperone on a film set? | Movies | The Guardian
description: Safeguarding young people in films is a vital role, often remembered by their charges later in successful careers, but not always recognised. Some of the best share their tips
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Safeguarding young people in films is a vital role, often remembered by their charges later in successful careers, but not always recognised. Some of the best share their tips
Content: The rules are strict, forged by cautionary tales such as Judy Garland’s.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe rules are strict, forged by cautionary tales such as Judy Garland’s.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyMovies‘Sometimes they credit the janitor. But not us’: what’s it like to be a child chaperone on a film set?Safeguarding young people in films is a vital role, often remembered by their charges later in successful careers, but not always recognised. Some of the best share their tipsJessica PhillipsWed 12 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLinda Matthews has rarely had to stop a production in its tracks. Steve Stone’s 2017 psychological horror In Extremis was an exception. Set on an isolated country estate during an apocalyptic storm, it follows a family that have to confront the oncoming disaster and their own personal demons to survive. For Matthews, however, the real drama unfolded behind the camera. “I don’t mind being the big bad person,” she says. “I was working with a young girl who was playing a cancer patient. She had to wear a bald cap and everything. Just as we were about to film, she burst into tears. She told me it reminded her of her friend’s mum, who was going through cancer treatment. That was the end of that.”You may assume Matthews is a producer or a very hands-on investor, but you would be mistaken. After leaving a career in banking, she founded Premier Chaperones in 2010 and has spent the past 15 years safeguarding children on some of the world’s biggest film and television sets.By law, all children under 16 on UK film and television sets require a chaperone. In practice, the role means shapeshifting between that of a pseudo-social worker – making sure children are fed and watered, rested and protected from harm – surrogate parent, and when necessary stand-in sheriff, reinforcing the boundaries of the law.Unlike fellow crew members, chaperones have a duty to protect the child, not the production. Vetted through enhanced DBS checks and licensed by local authorities – some of which ask for safeguarding training and references, others requiring applicants to pass the first stage of a social worker’s assessment – they enforce child performance regulations, and have the authority to call time on a shoot when a child is distressed, regardless of the wishes of executives or its impact on the production company’s bottom line.The rules are undeniably strict, forged by cautionary tales such as Judy Garland’s, whose childhood was sacrificed at Hollywood’s altar. Aged 13, she signed to Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, the studio which controlled her diet of black coffee, chicken soup and cigarettes, while routinely supplying her with amphetamines. She would later die from an accidental barbiturate overdose aged 47.Garland’s experience was sadly no anomaly. In 2022, more than 50 years after starring in Franco Zeffirelli’s Romeo and Juliet, Olivia Hussey and Leonard Whiting sued Paramount Pictures alleging child abuse and sexual exploitation. Both were minors when they starred in the Oscar-winning movie, and they claimed they had been promised flesh-coloured undergarments for an intimate bedroom scene, only to be persuaded by Zeffirelli to shoot nude in order to ensure the film’s artistic vision and commercial success.Although the courts dismissed the case, it posed the uncomfortable question of how much agency a minor has, when creative licence can hold more weight than a child’s ability to say no. Accounts such as these also help explain the penalties productions can face if they breach modern safeguarding rules. In the UK, fines can reach up to £1,000 per offence, with the most serious violations carrying a custodial sentence of up to six months.Yet despite decades of reform, the entertainment industry’s reckoning with child safety remains a work in progress.In the 2024 documentary Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV, former Nickelodeon star Drake Bell alleged that he was sexually abused at the age of 15 by dialogue coach Brian Peck, who was later convicted of child sexual abuse offences.Such incidents reveal the true value of having someone like Matthews in a child’s corner. Although chaperones are often dismissed as little more than glorified prefects, they are the last line of defence for some of the most vulnerable people on set, ensuring that under-16s don’t share toilets or changing facilities with adults, and that children with medical conditions have immediate access to any medication they may need.On the set of theBBC’s 2015 adaptation of Cider with Rosie, Matthews insisted on a closed set when a child was filming a nude swimming scene. “She wore a waterproof bodysuit and had long hair covering her breasts,” Matthews says. “It was important that it was just me, the cameraman and the director with her. Nobody else needed to be there.”View image in fullscreenA significant role … Stephen Rawnsley was head chaperone on much acclaimed show Adolescence.Photograph: APHer job is to anticipate problems before they arise and quietly make decisions in the child’s best interest. It’s essential work that largely goes unseen and unacknowledged – an irony Matthews knows well. After spending an entire summer working on The Fantastic Four: First Steps, she took her husband to the cinema, expecting to show him her name on the big screen. It never appeared. “Sometimes they’ll credit the janitor,” she says, “but not the chaperones.”Stephen Rawnsley, head chaperone onAdolescence– Netflix’s record-breaking drama about misogyny, social media and unchecked teenage rage – is also part of the invisible collective. He was in charge of more than 350 child actors and coordinated a team of more than 40 licensed chaperones during production. Yet look at the show’s IMDb page, and it’s easy to underestimate the significance of his role. He is credited somewhere near the bottom, sandwiched between the runners and a person whose job is listed as “insurance”.Chatting over video call, a few days before his latest stint on the BBC’s Emmy-winning children’s TV show Odd Squad, Rawnsley is pragmatic about where he sits in the pecking order. Though, the more we talk, the disappointment of being TV’s shadow man becomes increasingly clear. “We do an important job,” he says. “It would be nice to get a bit more recognition from production companies and to be treated like the rest of the crew.”If Matthews is more of a disciplinarian, Rawnsley is the everydad, leaning into the pastoral side of the role. He pays particular attention to children stepping on to a professional set for the first time, making sure they find friends and understand the unwritten rules of the world of make believe. “I talk them through how it all works,” he says. “I let them know they haven’t done anything wrong if a director asks them to film the same scene again.”That reassurance, however, is matched by rapport-building candour. Rawnsley is clear with his charges that, while they have agency, their choices have consequences. “Some of the kids don’t want to do the work,” he says. “I’ll tell them that if they want to go home, they can. But the production may not ask them to come back because they’re being paid to do a job.”For many former child actors, it’s this sweet and sour dish that makes a great chaperone. Montanna Thompson, who played Justine Littlewood in CBBC’s The Story of Tracy Beaker, goes so far as to describe her “cheeky” chaperone Mary as “family”. For the best part of half a decade, the pair travelled and worked together, staying in adjoining hotel rooms while filming on location in Cardiff, Newcastle, Manchester and Bristol.Mary was there for Thompson’s big on-screen moments and girlhood’s quieter milestones. “I actually started my period on set,” Thompson recalls. “I didn’t know what was happening, but Mary talked me through it and went to Boots to get me everything I needed.”Then there was Russell, a chaperone with two daughters who made the apartment that Thompson shared with two other child actors feel like home. Sometimes it was the small things: letting her paint his nails, or cooking dinners that helped with homesickness. “I remember thinking he was really cool. He was a great person to have around when I missed my mum,” she says. “If I saw either of them now, I’d give them a big hug.”Despite being among the lowest-paid people on set – often earning little more than minimum wage – having no dedicated trade union behind them, and regularly facing long delays in payments as sign-offs ping-pong between agencies and production companies, it is stories from insiders such as Thompson that illuminate why chaperones keep doing what they do.Both Matthews and Rawnsley keep in touch with some of the children they chaperoned. Several have requested them for future projects, and gone on to full-time careers in film, television and theatre. “A lot of the girls I worked with on Hetty Feather are in their early 20s. I’d consider them friends now,” says Matthews. “They’ll invite me to come and see them in their shows.” Rawnsley has also attended opening nights and film premieres on account of once being the adult in the room who made a child feel safe.This is the kind of recognition that matters most to chaperones. Still, in a billion-dollar industry that trades in underdog narratives and ribbon-tied endings, it still feels as if they are undervalued. After all, chaperones as a group aren’t asking for the spotlight – rather just a validating moment as they watch the credits roll.Explore more on these topicsFilmAdolescenceChildrenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mutants assemble: what does the future hold for the X-Men? | Superhero movies | The Guardian
description: After the introduction of a key character in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Marvel is bringing back one of its most beloved franchises – but the return comes at a precarious time
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: After the introduction of a key character in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Marvel is bringing back one of its most beloved franchises – but the return comes at a precarious time
Content: The cast of 2003’s X-Men 2.Photograph: Marvel/AllstarView image in fullscreenThe cast of 2003’s X-Men 2.Photograph: Marvel/AllstarSuperhero moviesMutants assemble: what does the future hold for the X-Men?After the introduction of a key character in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Marvel is bringing back one of its most beloved franchises – but the return comes at a precarious timeJesse HassengerWed 12 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLater-period Marvel movies have resorted to more fantastical plot devices such as parallel universes and time travel in an attempt to raise stakes in an increasingly complicated, superhero-populated cinematic universe. AfterSpider-Man: Brand New Day, a Marvel/Sony co-production that’s making a run atbiggest-movie-of-all-time status, it feels as if those devices are making incursions into the real world and messing with the sacred timeline of superhero movies. Brand New Day has spurred speculation about the upcoming MCU reboot of the X-Men, seeded with the introduction of powerful telepath mutant Jean Grey (Sadie Sink). It’s like a reversed version of the early-century superhero boom, when the first X-Men movie became an unexpected smash in the summer of 2000, priming audiences for the record-shattering debut of the first Spider-Man two years later.Web of billions: how Spider-Man became the most heroic franchise in HollywoodRead moreThe only teasing of Spider-Man in the 2000 X-Men movie hid in the DVD’s blooper reel, featuringan outtakewhere someone (not Tobey Maguire) runs into the frame in full Spidey regalia, as a prank. At the time, there was no Marvel Studios making in-house movies; the company’s superheroes were at the mercy of whatever studio happened to license them. Fox had the X-Men, and parlayed them into a 20-year, 13-movie franchise. Meanwhile, Sony had Spider-Man, and made five of those (three with Maguire, two with Andrew Garfield) before striking a deal for the ascendant Marvel Studios to produce further installments within their MCU, while Sony retains the actual movie rights.Now the X-Men are back withMarvelfollowing Disney’s 2019 purchase of Fox. Coinciding as this did with the original series’ biggest flops (Dark Phoenix in 2019; The New Mutants, delayed into a pandemic casualty in 2020), there was little chance of those established movie versions, with their own bizarre continuity hiccups and time-travel paradoxes, being imported wholesale into the MCU. Marvel Studios has instead dabbled with them, reviving an iteration of Hugh Jackman’s Wolverine through the dual magic of alternate timelines and shameless pandering and including some X-Men characters such as Cyclops (James Marsden), Beast (Kelsey Grammer) and Professor X (Patrick Stewart), in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday.Brand New Day, however, makes it more obvious that a clean X-Men reboot is on its way, now apparently scheduled for May 2028, directed by Jake Schreier of the MCU’s Thunderbolts. Sink’s high-profile in-movie casting announcement has been followed by several more traditionally disseminated bits of news: Samara Weavingwill probably playEmma Frost, a mutant who has swapped sides between the X-Men and their enemies multiple times in the comics; Kit Connor has beenreported as the “top choice”for Cyclops, the eye-blasting team leader who has been involved with both Emma and Jean in various comics. Disney hasn’t confirmed any of this beyond Sink; more concrete news is expected at the company’s D23 fan event this weekend.Early casting indicates a more youthful take on the material than the original movies, where most of the leads were already full adults. The Fox series actually already tried a younger direction when they did a series of prequel movies starting with 2011’s X-Men: First Class; teenage versions of Cyclops, Jean, Nightcrawler and Storm were introduced in 2016’s X-Men: Apocalypse and then starred in the ill-fated Dark Phoenix.Those movies were seen as two dysfunctional extremes for the previous series: the 80s-set Apocalypse, nominally directed by the erratic andsince-disgraced Bryan Singer, is packed with period-appropriate excess in characters, costume, color and sometimes-dodgy visual effects. The 90s-set Dark Phoenix attempts to ground the characters in more serious drama and winds up feeling more like a dour postscript to the other prequels. Going by Schreier’s work on Thunderbolts, it would be fair to expect a group of mutants engaging in semi-comic bickering that’s informed by more relatable teen-to-twentysomething neuroses, easing into the soapier elements to this corner of Marvel. Don’t expect time travel, ancient Egypt, cosmic powers or other Advanced X-Men weirdness, at least not right away. Those elements all come into play on the current (and quite popular) X-Men 1997 cartoon, a continuation of a Saturday morning series from 30 years ago; though it may be tempting to draw from that popular series in live action, the MCU house style is more restrained, even when it goes cosmic. More likely, the new X-Men movies will (to some degree) emulate the Spider-Man series that introduces Jean: characters who are younger than the MCU average with interpersonal relationships that are as compelling as the more outsized threats they face.View image in fullscreenA still from The New Mutants.Photograph: FoxThe question is: age aside, how can Marvel keep this team movie distinguishable from, well, every other super-squad they’ve assembled over the years? The Avengers was a major-league novelty in 2012; as good as the first two X-Men movies are – and really, they still stand among the best of their genre – it’s arguable that the first two Avengers movies do an even better job of balancing out an ensemble of a half-dozen powers-boosted personalities, a formula with many subsequent variations, including upping the acrimonious absurdities (the Guardians of the Galaxy trilogy), slimming down to a trio of heroes with wildly varied experience levels (The Marvels), focusing on characters with less heroic origins and backgrounds (Thunderbolts), dragging in characters from other universes (Deadpool & Wolverine), and calling every superhero character available an Avenger (Avengers: Endgame). For storytelling and budgetary reasons, the 2000 film simply titled X-Men feels positively spartan by comparison. It also has a directness and efficiency that make it still refreshing today.A new X-Men movie, consciously or not, would be well-served by tapping into that sense of promise that radiated from the 2000 film, even if it has way more budgetary leeway to fill out its ensemble. That’s really the X-Men’s primary mission: re-ignite excitement in Marvel’s ability to offer (sort of) new characters rather than Doomsday’s seeming all-star leftovers approach. Of course, the old X-Men movies advantageously lacked any pre-existing cinematic-universe rules governing their adventures; it’s telling that the MCU has to engineer this huge Doomsday crossover just to make the introduction of the mutants make any sense.View image in fullscreenSadie Sink in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: YoutubeThe showcase factor might limit the characters further; as much as fans want to believe this will represent them finally done “right”, Fox’s efforts had a sense of blase freedom; hence the soft reboot of X-Men: First Class or the solo movies about Wolverine or Deadpool. Not every entry was great, and plenty of characters never got their due. But with Marvel tending to a whole universe while attempting to re-emphasize quality over quantity, it’s harder than ever to imagine the MCU producing anything as tightly focused as The Wolverine, a terrific stand-alone pulp thriller with Jackman’s title character involved in a Japanese crime story. For that matter, it’s hard to picture even later-period Marvel producing something as stylishly rococo and neon-accented as X-Men: Apocalypse. The original X-Men franchise had the luxury of feeling its way through the superhero boom and its own creative near-busts on its own terms.That separateness sometimes rankled longtime fans, yet it also allowed the series as a whole to keep one foot in something resembling our world. The prequel movies playfully interact with 60s, 70s and 80s historical touchstones, however broadly, while two James Mangold-directed Wolverine movies utilize bits of the second world war past and an uncertain, dystopian future. It’s been almost a decade since the MCU interacted with any history that wasn’t an index of its own continuity. Tinkering with US history isn’t going to be job one for the new X-Men movie, and understandably so. (It wouldn’t be a bad thing for the movies to try dropping the reductive Martin Luther King/Malcolm X references from the Professor X/Magneto rivalry, for one thing.) But the new X-Men shouldn’t just function as Marvel’s age-defying time-warp shortcut to fan excitement. They offer an opportunity for the biggest movie series around to get out of its own head.Explore more on these topicsSuperhero moviesX-MenSpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DayMarvelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for John Hannah | Movies | The Guardian
description: Your mum’s favourite star of Four Weddings and a Funeral, Sliding Doors, Spartacus and a new GoPro-filmed thriller is ready to answer your quetions
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: Your mum’s favourite star of Four Weddings and a Funeral, Sliding Doors, Spartacus and a new GoPro-filmed thriller is ready to answer your quetions
Content: More than a great pair of eyebrows … John Hannah on This Morning last month.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMore than a great pair of eyebrows … John Hannah on This Morning last month.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesPost your questions for John HannahYour mum’s favourite star of Four Weddings and a Funeral, Sliding Doors, Spartacus and a new GoPro-filmed thriller is ready to answer your quetionsRich PelleyWed 12 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 01.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe’s your mum’s favourite, after playing the jolly nice man who is jolly nice to Gwyneth Paltrow in Sliding Doors, and the jolly nice man who delivers the heartbreaking WH Auden eulogy for his partner inFour Weddings and a Funeral. But there is far more to John Hannah than a Scottish accent, magnificent eyebrows and an unrivalled ability to look soulfully concerned. InThe Mummyfilms, he played treasure-hunting comic relief Jonathan Carnahan. In 2002’s Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, he took on both halves of Robert Louis Stevenson’s character. He played a psychopathic killer in Truth or Dare, and appeared opposite Denzel Washington in The Hurricane.On TV, he has been a transhumanist scientist in Marvel’sAgents of SHIELD; a gruff but compassionate emergency medicine chief in Transplant; and a gladiator school owner in the blood-soaked, boobs-and-sandals epicSpartacus– which might have given your mum a shock if she was expecting more Mr Nice Guy. He was also the scientist at the beginning ofThe Last of Uswho warned everyone that a fungi could destroy humanity – so don’t blame him, he did try.View image in fullscreenComic relief … John Hannah, left, with Rachel Weisz and Brendan Fraser in The Mummy.Photograph: Universal Pictures/AllstarNow he stars in Bad Day at the Office, an action thriller in which his character wakes in a hotel room with no memory, a corpse in the bath and the police knocking at the door. It’s filmed in the first-person using GoPro cameras, and so looks like a cross between Call of Duty, Peep Show and the video for the Prodigy’s Smack My Bitch Up. Whether he minds starring in a film that for the most part leaves out his best-known feature – his face – is one obvious question. But there’s plenty else to ask about: weddings, mummies, eyebrows, his favourite Prodigy track, or inappropriate Roman orgies to watch with your mum.Post your questions in the comments by 6pm this Thursday 13 August and we’ll print his answers in the next instalment of our readers’ interview series.Bad Day at the Office is in UK and Irish cinemas from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewTelevisioncalloutShareReuse this content

title: Steal This Story, Please! review – Amy Goodman, stalwart of the American left, shows her teeth | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: This comprehensive documentary about the Democracy Now! radio show host and seasoned investigative reporter takes in a massacre in East Timor, the actions of oil giants and a flustered Bill Clinton as it reflects her vital work
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: This comprehensive documentary about the Democracy Now! radio show host and seasoned investigative reporter takes in a massacre in East Timor, the actions of oil giants and a flustered Bill Clinton as it reflects her vital work
Content: Amy Goodman covering the Standing Rock oil pipeline protest in 2016, from the documentary Steal This Story, Please!Photograph: Courtesy of Reed BrodyView image in fullscreenAmy Goodman covering the Standing Rock oil pipeline protest in 2016, from the documentary Steal This Story, Please!Photograph: Courtesy of Reed BrodyDocumentary filmsReviewSteal This Story, Please! review – Amy Goodman, stalwart of the American left, shows her teethThis comprehensive documentary about the Democracy Now! radio show host and seasoned investigative reporter takes in a massacre in East Timor, the actions of oil giants and a flustered Bill Clinton as it reflects her vital workPeter BradshawWed 12 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 18.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore there was Michael Moore, there was campaigning journalist Amy Goodman … and even if Moore seems to have gone a little quiet, Goodman is still there, doggedly asking questions, an earnest gadfly buzzing around the flinching faces of Trump placemen, challenging and provoking and annoying. With her listener-funded syndicated radio show Democracy Now!, on the air since 1996, Goodman is flying the flag for journalism of the unfashionably homespun progressive left, while America’s corporate news media are sheepishly capitulating to their tech oligarch owners.‘They slammed their M16s against his skull’: inside the film about Amy Goodman’s fearless reportingRead moreThis documentary from Carl Deal and Tia Lessin is a portrait of Goodman and her life and times. The title is her somewhat ironic mantra: please, everybody, by all means steal our stories about corruption and demagoguery. Sadly, the big news media are often uninterested (though sometimes they are forced to follow stories broken by Goodman and her team). In fact, the real demand is addressed to their audience: buy this story, please. Democracy Now! accepts no ads or sponsorship, and it relies on money from viewers, listeners and readers of its website, although this documentary is silent on how much it needs annually and how the cash is solicited.Originally employed on TV’s boisterous Phil Donahue Show, Goodman soon showed she had the chops for investigative journalism on radio; apart from everything else it means persistence. She had a breakthrough with her on-the-spot reports in 1991 on Indonesia’s massacre in East Timor, perpetrated mostly with US-made weapons; she was savagely beaten with M16 rifle-butts, along with the New Yorker’s Allan Nairn – who gallantly threw himself on top of her to spare her the worst of the brutality. Goodman also had a brilliant scoop when she boldly walked into Chevron’s corporate headquarters in Nigeria, flourishing her US passport, demanding an interview, and an unwary press officer for the oil company blandly confirmed that, yes, Chevron was indeed helping the military logistically to crush the protests ofthe Ogoni people and their spokesperson Ken Saro-Wiwa.View image in fullscreenAmy Goodman and the New Yorker’s Allan Nairn in 1991, after a massacre of Timorese civilians by the Indonesian army in East Timor.Photograph: courtesy of Democracy Now!And Democracy Now! had a sensational coup when it persuaded Bill Clinton to call on US election day in November 2000, when he was campaigning for senate hopeful Hillary Clinton and White House candidate Al Gore, and stay on the phone for half an hour. Clinton was nettled at Goodman’s disrespectful questioning, perhaps believing that his charm, to which most of the press had succumbed, would soon cause her to melt. He was clearly intensely irritated that it didn’t. Goodman andChristopher Hitchenswere the most prominent anti-Clinton refuseniks on the left, but even Hitchens never got in the president’s face like that.With 9/11 and the subsequent and discredited “war on terror”, Goodman’s work got even more intense. She fiercely attacked the federal government’s decision to get people quickly back to work at New York’s Ground Zero, despite the health hazards. And of course she denounced the scandalous attack on Iraq for its non-existent weapons of mass destruction. But here, in the spirit of tough questioning, this documentary could have been more critical of Goodman. Not everything is the fault of the US government and its corporate lackeys. The threat of Islamist extremism is one of the biggest stories of the 21st century and Goodman seems less interested. Strange, as the jihadis and their sponsors are utterly opposed to democracy now or at any other time.Trump is another difficult one for Goodman, in a way, perhaps because he is so brazen, and also because he attacks the mainstream media – which echoes Goodman’s own rhetoric. Just for a moment in this documentary, as Trump is encouraging his base to get violent with reporters, you might think that Goodman could have maybe sided with her mainstream comrades more. But she is clear enough about Trump’s reliance on complaisant big media. And Goodman’s work goes on in the era of Ukraine and Gaza, and it looks like harder, lonelier work than ever.Steal This Story, Please! is at Bertha DocHouse, London, from 12 AugustExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsRadio industryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Chum review – daft shark attack movie with wedding guests running gamut of toothy undersea beast | Movies | The Guardian
description: Producer-star Alice Eve seems to be laughing along with the audience in this deeply silly high-concept thriller
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Producer-star Alice Eve seems to be laughing along with the audience in this deeply silly high-concept thriller
Content: Having a giggle … Alice Eve in ChumView image in fullscreenHaving a giggle … Alice Eve in ChumMoviesReviewChum review – daft shark attack movie with wedding guests running gamut of toothy undersea beastProducer-star Alice Eve seems to be laughing along with the audience in this deeply silly high-concept thrillerLeslie FelperinWed 12 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo be as clear as the crystalline waters in which the characters here frolic before their blood turns the ocean the colour of sangria: this is grade A tosh. It’s a deeply stupid high-concept feature wherein a bunch of bourgie wedding guests run afoul of an errant great white shark. The twist is (and it’s really not much of a surprise) that the true enemy is not really the shark, which is only following its sharky instincts. No, the bad guy is a bereaved weirdo called Roy (Jim Klock), who wants revenge on the shark for eating his wife in the opening pre-credits sequence.Alice Eve, who is also one of the film’s producers, at least seems to be having a bit of a giggle playing Tina, the most resourceful of Roy’s victims. Tina is a lawyer who should be enjoying the first days of her marriage to Tom (Eric Michael Cole) after their lavish destination wedding – except it looks like they are heading for a swift annulment, because ecowarrior Tom is disgusted with Tina for considering taking on an oil company as a client. They can’t make peace on the topic, and in the middle of an endless bicker they are press-ganged into what is supposed to be a relaxing three-hour cruise with a bunch of disposable secondary characters.The daft script, credited to Joe Leone and director Jonathan Zuck, practically draws targets on these supporting characters’ backs, daring the audience to guess which annoying idiot will be thrown overboard first to engage with the toothy foe. It looks like the film-makers have mostly relied on practical effects for the attack scenes, and even real sharks for some shots – which would be persuasive if only the severed limbs didn’t all look so absurdly plasticky. But you get the sense that everyone involved is in on the joke, and having a laugh along with the viewers.Chum is on digital platforms from 17 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmThrillersSharksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Why we’re going back to the games of our youth | Games | The Guardian
description: As millenials return to the games of their youth, remakes of Star Fox and Halo suggest there is still plenty to learn from the past
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: As millenials return to the games of their youth, remakes of Star Fox and Halo suggest there is still plenty to learn from the past
Content: Star Fox is among the classic games getting a 2026 makeover, as millennials give old-school games a new lease of life.Photograph: ArcadeImages/AlamyView image in fullscreenStar Fox is among the classic games getting a 2026 makeover, as millennials give old-school games a new lease of life.Photograph: ArcadeImages/AlamyPushing Buttons newsletterGamesWhy we’re going back to the games of our youthAs millennials return to the games of their youth, remakes of Star Fox and Halo suggest there is still plenty to learn from the pastDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 12 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs much as some people more or less cease tolisten to new music in their 30s, I have noticed a retreat to safe, familiar gaming territory among some of my fellow millennial gamers.Retro collections are started, or resumed; jewel-cases of PS1 classics or cardboard boxes with SNES or Mega Drive games have started to colonise the living-room shelves. People are replaying things from their university days, or sticking to comfort games such as Stardew Valley. Many of the friends I used to game with never bothered to pick up a PlayStation 5 at its launch, and now that current-generation consoles are becomingprohibitively expensive, they see no need.
